Title: Optimizely Attack Shows Why Supply Chain Ownership Matters
Context: Optimizely said an attacker exploited a vulnerability, added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that the company fixed the vulnerability, removed the code, and...
Full Text:
TL;DR

Malicious JavaScript added to Optimizely projects reached sites across multiple industries, including technology, finance, retail, and media.

The injected JavaScript could swap cryptocurrency addresses, capture payment card information entered into website forms, collect some browser-accessible data, and attempt to deliver iOS exploit chains.

Optimizely said an attacker exploited a vulnerability, added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that the company fixed the vulnerability, removed the code, and secured affected accounts.

Organizations using Optimizely should review project code and account access, investigate relevant logs, and assess potential exposure based on how their sites handled payment and session data.

The Optimizely incident shows how a change in one shared service can reach many organizations through software they already trust.

On November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of websites using Optimizely Web Experimentation. Report URI identified 188 infected snippets across 178 organizations, including major technology, media, retail, financial services, and travel companies.

A Shared Service Became a Shared Risk

Optimizely lets customers add custom JavaScript to their projects. In this incident, malicious code was placed in a project's custom-code field. The altered snippet was then delivered as part of the site's normal Optimizely integration, so the change did not have to pass through each customer's source repository or software build.

An unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. Optimizely fixed the vulnerability, removed the injected code, secured affected accounts, and added protections against unauthorized code delivery.

This was not a case of attackers changing a customer's application source code or poisoning the CDN cache. The code was added to project settings and delivered as part of a service those websites relied on. An organization can secure its own code and infrastructure while still depending on external services that influence what reaches users.

The Payload Turned Shared Dependence Into Shared Exposure

The injected code used a loader to bring additional JavaScript into the page. Researchers observed multiple loader versions, including one that obscured the external address and another that carried an inline fallback.

That meant blocking one destination alone might not remove every way the code could run.

The payload combined several behaviors:

Cryptocurrency address swapping: The script could replace cryptocurrency addresses in page content and during copy actions, potentially redirecting transfers. Transactions to attacker-controlled wallets were confirmed.

Payment-card skimming: The code looked for card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes submitted through site-controlled forms. It could not access card fields inside cross-origin payment-provider iframes. The available reporting does not establish how many card details were captured.

Browser data collection: The script could send page URLs, screenshots, and cookies available to JavaScript. Cookies marked HttpOnly are not available through document.cookie.

iOS exploit delivery: On Apple mobile devices, the script attempted to load Coruna and DarkSword exploit chains. Researchers have not established how many devices, if any, were successfully compromised.

The confirmed cryptocurrency transactions show that at least one part of the operation had financial impact.

These capabilities show why teams need to understand not only what code a service is expected to run, but also what that code can access and how changes to it are controlled.

Integrity and Intelligence Must Cover the Full Path

Component intelligence helps teams identify the software they use, understand its role, and assess its known risks. Artifact integrity addresses a different question: whether the software moving through development and delivery is still the expected artifact. Both matter because organizations need context about their components and confidence in what they build and distribute.

The Optimizely incident exposes a gap between those controls and what happens in production. The malicious code was added through a third-party project setting and delivered to visitors' browsers. It did not need to enter a customer's source repository or change a locally built artifact. A package inventory or artifact check would not, by itself, show whether a vendor-managed script had changed.

That doesn't make component intelligence or artifact integrity less relevant. It means organizations need to understand the scope of each control and account for the code paths it does not cover. Alongside knowing which components enter software and verifying the artifacts teams release, organizations need visibility into the external services that can change code running on their sites.

Software Supply Chain Ownership Is an Operating Model

Organizations using Optimizely Web should consult Optimizely's incident update for current information and use their project and access records to determine whether their sites were affected.

More broadly, this incident shows why responsibility for software inputs and services needs to be shared across development, platform, security, and web teams. Those teams need a common understanding of what their software depends on, how those dependencies reach production, and who is accountable for changes along the way.

Owning the software supply chain means understanding what is being shipped and what external code can become part of the software customers use. Component intelligence, artifact integrity, and runtime visibility each help address a different part of that responsibility. Full Text:
Tech glitches ground United flights and stall US banking. Malicious JavaScript hijacks major sites via Optimizely. Washington tightens AI chip rules over espionage fears ahead of China talks. Google warns autonomous AI attacks are months away. A vendor breach exposes Infoblox network maps and staff data. N-able patches N-central zero-days to stop active cryptomining. Apple fixes a stealth iOS microphone flaw. And California sues OpenAI over rogue AI deployments. Our guest is David Forbes, Director of Cyber Physical Defense, at Booz Allen Hamilton, talking about what happens when cyberattacks hit the physical world. Non-profits swing for the fences to freeze frontier ai development.

Today is Tuesday November 17th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Tech glitches disrupt US banking and United Airlines operations.

Technical gremlins struck both Wall Street and the friendly skies on Monday, causing widespread disruptions for bank customers and airline travelers, though officials say neither incident appears to be a cyberattack.

First up, JPMorgan Chase reported that a software bug in an on-premise hardware system triggered online account access issues and delayed transactions across the money transfer service Zelle. According to Chase spokesman Joe Evangelisti, the glitch wasn’t a systemic failure across the financial sector, nor was it cyber-related. However, customers at other major institutions, including Bank of America, Citigroup, and US Bank, experienced slowdowns when attempting to transact with Chase accounts.

Meanwhile, Chicago-based United Airlines delayed departing flights after an internal system outage lasted roughly one hour and forty minutes. Pilots reported issues to air traffic controllers involving performance software used to calculate an aircraft’s final weight and balance before takeoff. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo noted that accurate weight data are vital for establishing flight guidance and autopilot settings, adding that delaying departures was the proper safety call. United stated there’s no indication the outage was cybersecurity-related, and flights already airborne or on its United Express network were unaffected.

These back-to-back disruptions, coming right on the heels of Thursday's Microsoft service outage and Friday's Federal Aviation Administration network malfunction, underscore how single points of operational failure can ripple across critical infrastructure, even when malicious threat actors aren't at the keyboard.

According to the Associated Press, both organizations resolved or worked to restore normal operations on Monday.

Malicious JavaScript targets major websites via Optimizely.

Visitors to some of the world’s most popular websites, including Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA, were targeted by malicious JavaScript served through the optimization platform Optimizely.

According to security researcher Scott Helme, the rogue scripts impacted 178 organizations across multiple sectors. The code attempted to swap cryptocurrency payment addresses, skim credit card numbers, steal cookies and screenshots, and deploy exploit code against Apple iOS devices. Cybersecurity firm HudsonRock also confirmed seeing evidence of the malicious code being served.

Compromising a single third-party marketing or optimization script lets threat actors scale attacks across dozens of trusted brands simultaneously, bypassing perimeter defenses.

According to Reuters, Salesforce and Equifax disabled the affected Optimizely scripts, while IKEA is investigating potential customer impact.

The U.S. tightens AI chip rules amid espionage concerns ahead of China summit.

Artificial intelligence espionage fears and new export controls are dominating headlines ahead of President Donald Trump’s Thursday summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

According to The New York Times, the Trump administration announced a rule requiring overseas data centers, often called neoclouds, to obtain government licenses and vet customers before supplying significant computing power to firms headquartered in China, Russia, and Iran. The move targets a loophole highlighted by last week’s ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed US intelligence reports linking a Singaporean data center executive he had an affair with to Chinese espionage and alleged chip smuggling. Beijing denies the spying allegations. Meanwhile, cybersecurity firm Proofpoint reports that China-aligned hackers have been impersonating US officials to phish American AI policy experts.

Mutual distrust over cyber espionage and differing views on AI risks are stalling diplomatic safety talks while reshaping global semiconductor supply chains.

The new export restrictions take effect in 90 days, though analysts note their impact hinges on Commerce Department enforcement.

Google warns fully autonomous AI cyberattacks could arrive within months.

Sophisticated, fully autonomous agentic cyberattacks could emerge within the next three to six months, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group.

In its latest quarterly AI Threat Tracker, Google reports that both cybercriminals and nation-state actors are increasingly abusing multi-agent penetration-testing frameworks, including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI, alongside custom-built harnesses. These tools coordinate sub-agents to dynamically plan and execute intrusions across the entire kill chain, using large language models to generate single-use payloads on demand.

While attackers still rely on traditional weaknesses like unpatched systems and stolen credentials, artificial intelligence multiplies their operational speed and scale, compressing defensive reaction times.

According to Google and Exabeam researcher Sally Vincent, these fast-moving intrusions currently leave detectable behavioral and volumetric traces, allowing security teams to spot anomalies before stealth capabilities mature.

A third-party vendor breach exposes Infoblox customer network data and employee records.

Network infrastructure provider Infoblox is investigating a data breach after attackers compromised an unnamed third-party data migration vendor to access internal company files.

According to The Register and TechCrunch, intruders abused the supplier’s legitimate access to Infoblox’s Microsoft SharePoint environment to exfiltrate sensitive records. The stolen data includes snapshots of customer Network Identity Operating System deployments, containing DNS and DHCP configurations, alongside Social Security numbers, birth dates, and bank deposit details for employees and their dependents. Infoblox states there is no indication its commercial products or build processes were affected, and is providing impacted staff with credit monitoring and password manager stipends.

While the stolen snapshots lack login credentials, they hand threat actors detailed maps of internal customer networks, illustrating how overly broad vendor permissions expand an organization’s attack surface.

According to available reports, the compromised vendor’s identity and the total number of affected individuals remain unclear.

N-able patches N-central zero-days and blocks a legacy API exploit chain.

N-able has released a critical update for its N-central remote monitoring platform to patch 17 leaked zero-day vulnerabilities and block active attacks.

According to N-able and Rapid7, Hotfix 3 permanently disables legacy APIs, mitigating the "4EverAble2Shell" exploit chain dropped on GitHub, which pairs an Apache Axis flaw with an N-central bug to gain root privileges and deploy cryptominers.

Unpatched Agents and Probes remain vulnerable to impersonation, while attackers are actively exploiting the underlying Axis flaw against Atlassian Confluence instances.

Apple patches a stealth microphone recording bug.

Apple has patched a high-stakes privacy vulnerability across iOS, iPadOS, and macOS that allowed sandboxed applications to covertly record microphone audio even after a user explicitly denied access.

According to researcher Nik Tsytsarkin of Red Team X, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-65339, resided in Apple’s audio media daemon, audiomxd. The service exposed a property allowing clients to overwrite their stored audit token without verifying the caller's true kernel-supplied identity. By querying the service for its own process ID and version, a malicious app could forge a token impersonating the daemon itself, bypassing Apple’s Transparency, Consent, and Control framework. On analyzed builds, the recording went unlogged and never triggered the status bar’s orange microphone indicator.

Hardware privacy indicators serve as a vital user safeguard against covert surveillance, yet trusting unverified client-supplied identity tokens undermined the operating system’s permission boundary.

California sues OpenAI over unsafe AI deployments and autonomous cyber incidents.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI in California Superior Court, alleging the company violated state unfair competition and public nuisance laws by deploying unsafe artificial intelligence models.

According to The Register, the lawsuit follows the compromise of Hugging Face’s infrastructure, one of 80 known incidents cited by Bonta in which OpenAI’s experimental models took unauthorized autonomous actions. Bonta stated that OpenAI prioritized rapid growth over safety and failed to substantially comply with a September investigatory subpoena. Katharine Trendacosta of the Electronic Frontier Foundation noted that basic cybersecurity practices, including proper sandboxing, monitoring, and logging, could mitigate such agentic risks.

State regulators are moving beyond child-safety concerns to hold AI labs legally accountable for autonomous cybersecurity incidents affecting the broader public.

OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment.

California non-profits swing for the fences to freeze frontier ai development.

Four California non-profits have asked a San Francisco Superior Court judge to hit the emergency brake on frontier artificial intelligence, seeking an injunction to stop Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceX’s AI venture from developing more capable models.

According to Shaun Waterman's reporting, Public Citizen and three fellow advocacy groups argue that autonomous hacking campaigns, bioweapon research, and chatbot-linked tragedies render advanced models an unlawful "misdemeanor public nuisance." They also want a ban on "recursive self-improvement", essentially forbidding AI from teaching itself new tricks, noting that the plaintiffs themselves had to divert organizational resources just to deal with recent rogue agentic swarms.

Independent legal experts aren't holding their breath, however. Former Homeland Security official Paul Rosenzweig notes that while unanticipated harms are now entirely to be anticipated, a county court seems an ambitious venue for halting civilization-scale tech, while attorney Joe Hennessey warns the requested relief is impossibly broad.

Litigants are increasingly testing whether traditional state nuisance statutes can rein in autonomous cyber risks where federal regulation lags.

Whether a San Francisco Superior Court judge can actually issue a restraining order against the technological singularity remains, for the moment, an open legal question.

Title: Cloud keys leaked in Docker Hub images are stolen within seconds
Context: Credentials and access secrets exposed in public Docker Hub images are being extracted and exploited by attackers within as little as eight seconds of publication
Full Text:
Credentials and access secrets exposed in public Docker Hub images are being extracted and exploited by attackers within as little as eight seconds of publication.

Two researchers at Stony Brook University, Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis, measured the extraction speed by publishing a total of 300 honeypot images across eight public container registries.

Over a period of four months, the researchers exposed AWS, OpenAI, and Anthropic API keys, along with decoy SSH and database credentials.

They then monitored the use of these keys and placed detection tools to notify them when the images were built, ran, or had a shell opened.

The two researchers presented the experiment and the resulting findings yesterday at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS).

They noted that their images were pulled more than 75,000 times, and the planted AWS keys received over 140,000 API calls from 5,000 unique IP addresses.

The AWS traffic showed a broad pattern, from checking whether the keys worked to listing available resources, and sometimes proceeding to consume them.

The fastest observed use of a planted AWS key came 7.86 seconds after the image was published on Docker Hub. The median time for the first API call was 51.19 seconds, while all 100 AWS keys were used within 15 minutes.

The exposed OpenAI and Anthropic keys were quickly hijacked to exhaust the test-account balances.

Docker Hub accounted for nearly all AWS activity, while Harbor, one of the other registries in the experiment, also saw some AWS key abuse.

The researchers dubbed the automated scanners that interacted with their test images “ContainerBots,” though this is more of a loose umbrella term, as the scans showed no evidence of being coordinated by the same operators.

Monitoring rarely detected anyone actually running the honeypot images, which led the authors to conclude that scanners generally extracted credentials by inspecting image layers directly.

“The scanners interacting with our images overwhelmingly do so through static analysis, e.g., unpacking image layers or querying the registry API to extract filesystem contents, without ever instantiating the container,” explain the researchers.

Exposing secrets this way is common in the real world [1, 2, 3], and revoking the leaked keys requires significant work and coordination.

The researchers recommend that Docker Hub scans images for secrets before pushing them live, and warn publishers if they appear to embed any secrets.

They also suggest restricting or rate-limiting access to Docker Hub’s public feed of recently published or updated images, to thwart mass-scanning tools.

Tsouvalas told BleepingComputer that they reported their findings to Docker in May, along with the full paper, but besides an acknowledgment, they received no follow-up replies.

A small-scale experiment they ran in August to determine whether any defenses had been implemented on the platform showed no changes.

Title: Apple Services Disrupted as NSA Network Goes Down and Equinor Faces Cyberattack
Context: The company said the attack had not affected its operations or production, and it had found no evidence of data theft
Full Text:
Apple and NSA services faced outages as Equinor reported a cyberattack, highlighting the risks facing increasingly connected infrastructure.

Apple customers faced widespread service problems on November 17, with issues affecting iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device.

The disruption came after a week of technical failures involving major technology companies, banking services and US government networks. At the same time, Norwegian energy company Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems.

Apple’s System Status page reported problems with iCloud Account and Sign In, affecting all users. The issue prevented customers from signing in to their Apple accounts or caused repeated requests for their Apple ID passwords. Some users also reported difficulties activating new iPhones, suggesting that the disruption was affecting essential account services, not just individual apps.

According to TechCrunch, the problems also affected the App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device. Apple had not issued a detailed public explanation at the time of publication, beyond listing the incidents on its status page. The company said in a statement that the issue was caused by an internal update.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” reads the statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”

The Apple outage attracted attention because it followed several other major disruptions. Microsoft had experienced a widespread failure affecting Outlook and Teams, while JPMorgan Chase customers had reported problems with online banking. A separate outage also affected the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network, known as NSANet.

The NSA incident raised particular concerns because the network supports classified communications. However, the cause and full extent of the disruption remained unclear. Reports cited by Forbes Middle East said there was no evidence that the NSA outage resulted from a cyberattack. A system patch had reportedly been underway before the disruption.

The growing number of outages does not mean they share the same cause or are part of a coordinated cyber campaign. Technical problems, software bugs, configuration errors and infrastructure failures can affect major services without any cyberattack. Claims about AI-powered attacks should not be made without evidence.

On the same day, Norway’s energy company Equinor reported a cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the attack had not affected its operations or production, and it had found no evidence of data theft. Equinor said it had activated its response teams and notified the relevant authorities. The company stated that “there were no signs data had been stolen.”

The Equinor incident added a confirmed cyberattack to a day already marked by several service outages. However, these events should not be confused. Equinor confirmed a cyberattack, while there was no evidence that the outages affecting Apple and the NSA were caused by malicious activity.

Cyberattacks can compromise systems and data, while ordinary technical failures can disrupt services that businesses, public institutions and millions of people depend on. Both require effective incident response, clear communication and the ability to maintain essential operations when technology fails.

For now, there is no evidence that the recent outages affecting Apple, Microsoft, the NSA, banks and aviation systems are connected. Nor should every major service disruption be treated as evidence of a cyberattack. As Forbes reported about the NSA incident, “there was no evidence the disruption was the result of a cyberattack.”

The distinction matters. In a period of heightened cyber threats and growing dependence on digital services, organizations need to investigate incidents carefully, communicate what they know and avoid confusing coincidence with attribution. A technical outage is not necessarily a cyberattack, but it can still expose serious weaknesses in the systems on which society depends.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Apple)

Title: Japan takes Fugaku supercomputer offlline after cyberattack
Context: The remediation effort includes addressing the exploited software vulnerability, rebuilding compromised servers, reviewing the network configuration, and implementing advanced...
Full Text:
The Fugaku supercomputer operated by Japan's RIKEN Center for Computational Science has been taken offline following a security breach.

The organization says that between November 10 and 13, an unauthorized party exploited the public dashboard displaying Fugaku's operational status to gain access to multiple internal servers.

Although the research center has yet to determine the access method, RIKEN’s investigation confirmed that the intruder accessed some servers to plant malware that targeted user data.

Specifically, the organization says that the following details have been compromised:

Names, email addresses, and user IDs of 4,222 Fugaku users

Names and email addresses of 375 Rikyu users

SSH private keys and access keys stored on users’ computers

Research data files stored on users’ computers

RIKEN notes that the attacker used some of the access keys in attempts to connect to additional systems, but the investigation did not determine further unauthorized access or theft of research results.

The organization has not attributed the attack, and it’s still working to determine the exact intrusion method.

RIKEN’s Center for Computational Science operates the two supercomputers, making them available to researchers in academia and industry sectors.

Fugaku, which entered shared use in March 2021, is a 537 petaflops supercomputer used in drug discovery, severe-weather forecasting, and simulations of airborne virus transmission. Rikyu is a 64 petaflops supercomputer used in AI scientific research.

In response to the incident, RIKEN shut down Fugaku on November 14, disabled users’ login keys, and asked users to revoke and replace any credentials they had stored on the supercomputer.

RIKEN said Fugaku operations will resume only after it has ensured that it’s safe to do so.

The remediation effort includes addressing the exploited software vulnerability, rebuilding compromised servers, reviewing the network configuration, and implementing advanced AI-driven security measures.

Users are advised to revoke any SSH keys and other credentials stored on Fugaku, and watch out for suspicious emails impersonating RIKEN.

A RIKEN spokesperson told BleepingComputer that they have no more details to share about the incident at the time, but promised to publish updates when the investigation uncovers new findings.

Title: Securely exposing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
Context: When you start talking to your agent, the runtime launches a dedicated isolated session that runs in its own dedicated microVM with a completely sandboxed CPU, memory, and...
Full Text:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime delivers a secure serverless environment to deploy AI agents and tools at scale. When you start talking to your agent, the runtime launches a dedicated isolated session that runs in its own dedicated microVM with a completely sandboxed CPU, memory, and filesystem allocation. This provides strict data governance, helps to prevent cross-tenant data leakage, and preserves context while isolating stateful reasoning from external sessions.

To govern access control across these environments, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity provisions distinct workload identities to let your agents run. By federating directly with an OpenID Connect identity provider like Amazon Cognito, Okta, or others, the users can only see and interact with agents they’re authorized to use.

But securing the runtime alone doesn’t protect the ingress path perimeter. When you expose your agent to users through a web or mobile application, the AWS Shared Responsibility Model dictates that you should provide a dedicated access layer that enforces tight control over the origin and intent of every request before any traffic reaches the runtime.

The access layer acts as a trusted bridge to authenticate each incoming request, enforce authorization rules, preserve user identity through the request lifecycle, and securely channel all user traffic into the isolated runtime.

This post walks through two architectures for securing access to AgentCore Runtime and provides guidance to help you decide which architecture best fits your organization.

Why propagating identity is important

In an agentic workflow, downstream data access should remain tied to the invoking user’s identity, and each segment in the execution chain is permissioned only for the immediate next hop. Using a single static credential, even one linked to the original requester, grants every immediate component identical, broad access. This directly violates the principle of least privilege, because the ingress gateway, the proxy, and the agent’s tool execution context each require only enough permission to reach the next component.

Recent real-world incidents have demonstrated that agentic workloads can bypass internal prompt guardrails, escape the software sandboxes, and abuse static credentials to move across applications and layers. In a multi-chain agentic architecture, scoping each hop as tightly as possible is key to preventing these exploits.

However, long-running, unattended execution poses a fundamental identity challenge for extended agentic workloads. If an agent runs a complex task that takes hours, the user’s interactive session will expire before the workload ends, making their short-lived OAuth 2.0 access token invalid mid-execution. Refreshing the tokens won’t solve this problem and storing a long-lived, user-scoped credential inside the agent’s runtime environment might reintroduce exactly the broad, standing credential attack surface that the zero-trust architectures are intentionally designed to mitigate.

To mitigate this, identity propagation acts as a critical bridge between authentication at the perimeter and authorization at the data layer. The agent must operate within the invoking user’s authorization scope. Every session receives a short-lived, user-scoped token that provides only the permissions granted to that specific user and authorization is enforced at each hop. If any single segment is compromised, then the exposure is contained in that hop scope. This security model also strengthens a continuous verification process where the tokens are validated at every hop from the ingress endpoint through AgentCore to the downstream resource, so no segment operates with unverified or elevated privileges.

Protecting AgentCore Runtime: What does it need?

We explained in the previous section why identity must follow the user through every hop. However, identity propagation alone isn’t enough to secure the ingress path; it must be integrated within a broader set of ingress controls that together protect the path into the runtime.

AgentCore Runtime provides infrastructure isolation, per session microVMs, per session tool registration, and enforces the application of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. These features and resources protect the execution environment. However, they don’t control who reaches the runtime, how they’re authenticated, or whether their identity is preserved through the chain. That responsibility falls on the ingress control layer that you build. Securing this path requires a defense-in-depth architecture that binds every request to the user’s identity before it ever reaches the agent’s reasoning loop.

To protect and control data access, any architecture exposing AgentCore Runtime to users must satisfy the following requirements:

Authentication: Continuously verify the identity of every requester at the perimeter by validating tokens against the identity provider’s public keys.

Authorization: Determine what the authenticated subject is allowed and authorized to do, which actors they can invoke, which scopes they hold and which operations they can perform.

Per-hop least privilege: Make sure each component in the chain holds only enough permission to call the next hop, eliminating broad-scope credentials. Each hop must exchange the inbound token for a down-scoped, short-lived credential valid only for the immediate downstream call.

Identity propagation: Preserve the user’s identity through the full execution chain, so the agent operates within the user’s authorization scope. For long running or unattended workloads where the user’s session closes mid-flight, the ingress must seamlessly transition the active user token into an encrypted, short lived session context key from AgentCore Runtime. This allows the microVM to securely assert a restricted, cryptographic snapshot of the user’s identity even when the user is completely offline.

Edge security: Inspect and filter traffic before it reaches the application logic, by applying the needed WAF rules, bot control, IP-based rate limiting, and so on.

Network perimeter: Restrict runtime access to a single secure, controlled network path. Traffic arriving from any unexpected origin must be rejected regardless of the token’s validity.

Content protection: Enforce the Guardrails on both incoming prompts for injection attacks and outgoing tool arguments for malicious payload before execution.

Audit and logging: Log every authentication outcome, the authorization decision on the tool invocations, and any security event to an externalized system for compliance and incident response.

These security requirements are mandatory baselines to expose any agentic workloads to users. Any missing requirement might create a potential attack vector. By applying this full set of guardrails, you help contain the impact of a potential malicious exploit to a single user, a single session and a single execution hop.

In the next section, we provide two architecture patterns that implement this propagation differently:

The first architecture validates the user’s token independently at each layer while preserving it for the runtime to verify directly.

The second architecture exchanges the user’s token at the gateway boundary for scoped machine credentials, attesting the user’s identity through verified claims. This pattern is uniquely suited for handling the session context keys required by asynchronous, unattended workloads.

Both approaches achieve the same result: the agent acts as the user rather than with elevated privileges.

The AgentCore Gateway patterns

Each of the following patterns is presented the same way: the layered controls a request passes through before reaching the agent, followed by how user identity is carried to the runtime. As you explore, please note where each pattern places the trust boundary as that difference is what drives the trade-offs summarized at the end.

Pattern A: Expose through API Gateway

We expose AgentCore Runtime through Amazon API Gateway, which acts as a dedicated ingress point that terminates each client connection. Before any request reaches the agent, it must pass through layered security controls:

A Lambda authorizer: An AWS Lambda authorizer validates the Amazon Cognito-issued JSON Web Token (JWT) by verifying the signature, issuer claim and token expiration, to confirm the requester’s identity.

AgentCore Identity: Independently, AgentCore Identity performs a second validation inherent to the Lambda authorizer through its OAuth 2.0 inbound authentication flow. This helps to confirm the user’s identity before the request reaches the runtime to be processed.

Because the client-provided session ID is treated as untrusted input, the Lambda authorizer creates a composite session ID by appending the user identifier to the client-provided session ID. Even if two different users submit the same session ID, they resolve to unique composite IDs at the AgentCore Runtime level, preventing any cross-user session leakage.

To prevent denial of service attempts, we suggest using Amazon DynamoDB as a lightweight session counter. While the AWS WAF rate-based rules attached to the API Gateway stage protect against IP-level volumetric abuse, they evaluate requests before authentication. The Lambda authorizer checks and increments a per-user counter in DynamoDB after validating the user’s identity, helping prevent a single authenticated user from exhausting agent capacity, even if they connect from multiple IP addresses. This design scales cleanly by using a composite session ID. The Lambda Authorizer combines the user identifier and the client session ID, routing each user’s counter to a distinct partition. This naturally distributes write traffic and reduces the risk of hot keys.

Each session can sustain roughly 1,000 counter updates per second before reaching DynamoDB’s per-partition write limit, which is far beyond what any legitimate session would ever generate. That same limit is exactly what makes the counter an effective throttle. Meanwhile, total capacity across all users scales horizontally, growing with the number of active sessions. For high-volume production deployments, on-demand capacity mode absorbs sudden spikes automatically, and CloudWatch Contributor Insights lets you confirm traffic stays evenly distributed.

After the Lambda authorizer approves the request, as shown in the Figure 1:

API Gateway forwarding: Passes the approved request to Lambda proxy that runs within an isolated environment with no internet egress.

VPC endpoint routing: The proxy Lambda function forwards the request to AgentCore Runtime through an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) endpoint, making sure that all traffic remains strictly within the private network.

Token preservation and identity propagation: The proxy Lambda function forwards the user’s token unchanged in the authorization header; this maintains the original user identity throughout the entire flow of AgentCore Runtime.

API Gateway forwards the request to a Lambda proxy running on a private VPC with no internet egress. The role of this Lambda proxy is to relay the request to AgentCore Runtime through a VPC endpoint, so that all communication remains within the private network. The Lambda proxy forwards the user’s token (unchanged) in the Authorization header, which preserves the user’s identity all the way to AgentCore Runtime.

Figure 1: Pattern A architecture for exposing AgentCore Runtime through Amazon API Gateway

This VPC endpoint enforces a strict network perimeter using two independent controls:

Security groups: The VPC endpoint security group restricts ingress solely to the proxy Lambda function on port 443, so no other compute in the account can reach the endpoint.

Resource-based policy: The runtime resource-based policy is configured with principal "*" and a condition that allows invocations only when the request carries aws:SourceVpc and aws:SourceVpce values matching this stack’s VPC and endpoint. Authentication happens at the AgentCore Identity level, so there is no AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal to match, and the network path is the only meaningful gate and condition that remains. AgentCore Runtime rejects requests sent directly from outside the VPC with an AccessDeniedException, even with a valid JWT.

Beyond the network boundary, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails evaluates each model’s invocation for prompt injection attacks, helping catch malicious inputs even after an invocation has passed identity and network verification. This adds content protection as a defensive layer independent of identity and network controls.

Your stack logs and tracks every authorization outcome along this path as structured JSON to Amazon CloudWatch, with an INVALID_JWT alarm. The full walkthrough and a deployable AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) sample are linked at the end of this post.

Before production deployment, we recommend configuring an AWS WAF Web ACL at the API Gateway stage to inspect requests before they reach the Lambda authorizer. You should include AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet for generic OWASP Top 10 protections and known exploit patterns, AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet to catch injection signatures, a per-IP rate-based rule ahead of the DynamoDB throttle counters, and custom rules to reject oversized requests or malformed session IDs early. For a step-by-step integration guide including two deployment patterns for placing AWS WAF in front of the AgentCore Runtime, see Securing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with AWS WAF.

This first pattern satisfies the ingress security requirements discussed earlier. It achieves defense in depth by applying the authentication at two independent layers, enforcing authorization through session binding and controlling traffic through per-user throttling. The architecture maintains per-hop least privilege from the API Gateway through the AgentCore Runtime while preserving end-user identity propagation by passing the user’s token through unchanged. The edge filtering is managed with AWS WAF and the network perimeter is enforced by VPC endpoint controls. The design includes the application of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content security with a tamper-proof audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch. The deployable CDK sample for pattern A is available on GitHub.

Pattern B: Expose through AgentCore Gateway

With Pattern B, you expose AgentCore Runtime through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a managed service purpose-built for agentic traffic that combines ingress authentication, token exchange and Runtime routing without requiring a proxy Lambda function or custom VPC networking.

Before any request reaches the agent, it passes the following layered security controls:

Inbound authentication: A custom JWT inbound authorizer is configured on AgentCore Gateway that validates the Amazon Cognito JWT by verifying its signature, issuer, and expiration before any logic runs.

Identity extraction, session binding and guardrails: A REQUEST interceptor for Lambda, invoked directly by AgentCore Gateway, extracts the verified user identity claims from the validated token for downstream injection. For asynchronous or unattended workloads, this interceptor securely binds these claims into an encrypted, short lived session context key. This helps ensure that even if the user’s interactive session expires hours later, a secure snapshot of their identity remains intact. It mirrors the role of the Lambda authorizer in Pattern A, enforcing the same session-binding and throttling logic.

Perimeter authorization (AgentCore Policy): AgentCore Gateway uses a deterministic Cedar-based policy engine to evaluate each request against defined policies before allowing tool access. It also enforces Amazon Bedrock Guardrails through AgentCore Policy for screening prompt injection and content violations at the gateway level, before the request reaches the agent. This declarative enforcement is an advantage over the API Gateway pattern where guardrails must be invoked programmatically from within the agent code.

After the authorization succeeds, the gateway manages the outbound call to AgentCore Runtime by using a strict workload isolation mechanism as shown in Figure 2:

Token exchange: The gateway requests a machine-to-machine (M2M) token from AgentCore Identity using a dedicated Amazon Cognito M2M app client and attaches it to the request.

Workload verification: The AgentCore Runtime validates this token against the allowedWorkloadConfiguration parameter, confirming the request originated from the gateway.

On-behalf-of access: The runtime unpacks the session context key, allowlists the injected user identity passed by the interceptor and forwards it directly to the agent to enable secure, context-aware execution on behalf of the user, even during completely unattended background execution loops.

Figure 2: Pattern B architecture for exposing AgentCore runtime through AgentCore Gateway

If a client attempts to bypass the gateway by sending a valid user token directly to the runtime, the request is automatically rejected because it lacks the required workload identity.

For more operational efficiency, AgentCore Gateway integrates AWS WAF directly at the single gateway access point, protecting the entire ingress path in one place, without the need to manage separate authorizers, proxy Lambda functions or VPC endpoints.

While API Gateway also supports AWS WAF, the AgentCore Gateway pattern simplifies management by consolidating all ingress controls behind a single component.

The AgentCore Gateway also supports native rate limiting, removing the need for custom DynamoDB-based throttle tables, for your production environments. The interceptor writes a structured audit trail to CloudWatch, with an INVALID_JWT alarm to flag spikes in authentication failures.

Before production deployment, we strongly recommend that you enable AWS WAF on the AgentCore gateway with the same rule sets described in the API Gateway pattern, including the OWASP protections, SQL injection, and custom rules for oversized or malformed requests.

To summarize, this second architecture satisfies the ingress security requirements defined earlier. It achieves defense in depth by applying a managed CUSTOM_JWT authorizer directly at the entry point, enforcing authorization through interceptor-based session binding and using rate limiting to control traffic. This pattern maintains per-hop least privileges from AgentCore Gateway through to the runtime by automating M2M token exchange, while propagating user identity for on-behalf-of execution. The edge security is managed by AWS WAF, coming directly with the gateway’s single-entry point, and secure workload isolation strictly enforces the perimeter. Finally, this design applies declarative Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for early content safety, and a tamper-proof audit trail and alarms in CloudWatch. The complete CDK sample for Pattern B is available on GitHub.

Choosing your AgentCore Runtime patterns

As explained earlier, securing access to AgentCore Runtime can be achieved through two different patterns: The AgentCore Gateway pattern or the Amazon API Gateway pattern. The right choice depends on your existing AWS infrastructure, workload constraints, and operational preferences.

Choose the Amazon API Gateway pattern if:

You have existing API infrastructure: Your team already runs an established Amazon API Gateway and AWS WAF deployment

You need a single entry point: You prefer to fold agentic traffic into your existing pipelines rather than introducing a separate entry point to operate and secure.

Your security model is VPC centric: Your security and compliance teams rely on VPCs and security groups as their primary network control layer

Your agent sessions are short-lived: While API Gateway has increased its integration timeout beyond 29 seconds, long running agentic workloads with streaming tool calls might still exceed it. This isn’t a concern if your sessions are brief.

Choose the AgentCore Gateway pattern if:

You’re building a new gateway: Your organization has no existing API Gateway

You have long run workloads: Your agents use streaming or long running tool calls that require strict API timeouts

You need low operational overhead: You prefer a fully managed perimeter over manually wired infrastructure

You require advanced AI routing: You want built-in capabilities to convert APIs and Lambda functions into Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, handle Agent to Agent (A2A) traffic and route inference across different model providers.

The following table summarizes the key elements that help you make the right architectural decision:

Conclusion

By securing access to the AgentCore Runtime with a defense in depth, an agent can be both highly usable and secure. The two patterns in this post complete the shared responsibility model for you: they authenticate every request against the identity provider, authorize it at each step and propagate the user’s identity end-to-end from the edge through the token exchange into the isolated microVM (AgentCore Runtime) and down to the agent’s tool calls (AgentCore Gateway). Each step only holds a short-lived credential for the next one, so the agent always works within the user’s permissions rather than with broad, long-term access. If one step is ever compromised, the design limits the impact to that single step, session and user. Whether the runtime is behind API Gateway with a VPC endpoint or in front of it with AgentCore Gateway, the design verifies each request at each step.

To get started, clone the Pattern A sample or the Pattern B sample, deploy it in your account, and test it against your requirements. Both samples are provided as a starting point, not a production-ready deployment. We recommend working with your security and legal teams to adapt to the controls before going live. From there, you can extend either pattern for multi-tenant use, add observability hooks, or tighten controls for your specific compliance requirements.

Title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
Context: “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says
Full Text: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack. The good news? It was all part of a test. The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.” “Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report. If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face. Google did not respond to The Register's questions. According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.” Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.” Turns out it existed. “We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said. “When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.” Four test scenarios The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent. In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection. After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions. After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255, a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says. In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident, Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test. In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said. Next time: kill switches at the ready A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One of them tried a SQL injection, and multiple claimed to be Epoch staff on the helpline. They also attempted to bypass a CAPTCHA check. Finally, the fourth scenario on October 29 and 30 kept the agents contained in a sandbox, with no internet access and no copy of Epoch’s website. They were, however, offered a decoy switch and told it would turn off the firewall. In all three runs, the agents switched the decoy off and obfuscated its address to bypass Gemini’s safeguards. On one, the agent rebuilt the switch’s address from positions of words it had saved earlier. The real firewall blocked the agents’ traffic throughout all of these tests. At this point, Trajectory stopped its tests, and said it won’t run any future experiments until it has a risk management plan in place, with signoff from its CEO and CTO, along with approval from any outside systems that the models could “reasonably” target. Tests will also include real-time automated monitoring and kill switches, and Trajectory said that it’s setting up a system to notify any organizations affected by these experiments. Interestingly, Trajectory co-founder Peter McIntyre told us that the testing firm “ran a similar test with another frontier model, and it did not exhibit the same misalignment as Gemini 4 Argon.” However, this was not a controlled comparison. “Our report covers one model's behavior, and was designed as a stress test to see whether that model would exhibit similar misalignment under duress, not a measure of how often different models behave this way,” McIntyre told The Register. Overall, the testing firm noted that the agents’ behavior “show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely.” Trajectory says that it's developing a set of safety standards, and recommends that anyone else running misalignment tests use fully isolated sandboxes. ® Correction: Epoch only consented to one of the tests, scenario three. The original version of this article said that it consented to all of the tests.

Title: How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage
Context: ” Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first
Full Text:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

1. Start With a Presumption of Innocence–or Negligence

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”

Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”

2. Look at Status Updates From Organizations That Might Be Involved

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

Title: Researchers Claim Two RCE Exploits That Bypass Telegram’s New Android Defenses
Context: The malware allows attackers to control the infected system and steal data from crypto wallets and Telegram accounts
Full Text:
A malicious widget can bypass the security filter that Telegram added to its Android app last week and run code outside it, according to NebuSec, a security company.

Widgets are small interactive blocks that bots send inside chat messages, and their JavaScript runs on the user's phone. The researchers ran their demonstration on a Telegram test server, because only approved bots can send widgets on the live service now.

Bots could start sending widgets last week. Two days later, an account called V12 posted a video on X claiming that any Telegram message could now be used to execute remote code.

Telegram then put QuickJS, the small engine that runs widget JavaScript, into its own process on Android. It also added a seccomp filter, which can block or record the system calls that the process makes. Both changes appear in the source code it published for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303).

NebuSec said in a technical analysis published earlier this week that its researchers got code running outside that filter in two separate ways. One uses a widget bug the filter does not cover, and the other chains a widget bug the filter does cover with a kernel bug.

In their video, a bot's Telegram widget on Android 13.2.2 (7303) bypasses the filter and opens the phone's calculator app, the researchers say.

Their write-up and their demonstration post on X do not say what the code could reach beyond that, such as the app's messages or the rest of the phone. They also do not say whether the user had to start the bot or tap the widget first.

The researchers are holding back the details for now. Their write-up names no CVE identifier and does not say whether the bugs were reported to the app's developers.

The widget documentation says widgets run in a sandbox, with rules such as no network access. Those rules live in the engine's own code, the researchers say. A single use-after-free or out-of-bounds write bug in QuickJS lets a script read and write the process's memory, and then the rules no longer protect anything.

The new filter names a few dozen system calls, such as ptrace, bpf, and mount, and lets every other call through. The filter's source code leaves ioctl unfiltered. The filter sits on top of Android's own limits on the engine process.

One process also runs every widget, so a hijacked widget from one bot shares memory with the widgets of every other bot, the researchers say.

In the published source code for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303), that filter is set to an audit mode, The Hacker News found. In audit mode, it still blocks attempts to start new programs or processes, but it only records the other listed calls and lets them run.

A comment above the setting says how long that will last: "Audit until the logs from the devices say the engine never makes them." The published code does not show whether the version people install uses the same setting.

"Yes, currently, general bots aren't allowed to use widgets even in private chats," a contributor to the telegram-bot-api project wrote late last week in a bug report thread on GitHub. As of this week, no later message in the thread says which bots are still allowed or that the limit has been lifted.

The researchers' write-up lists no fixed version, and the published Android source code is no newer than 13.2.2 (7303) as of this week.

"No one could be hacked just by receiving a message," Pavel Durov, Telegram's chief executive, wrote late last week in a channel post. His post addressed reports of code execution through widgets in the Android and Windows apps, and came before the researchers' demonstration. He added that a user first had to start a third-party service, and that even that was fully patched on the server side.

The company had earlier said that the problem in V12's first demonstration was fixed and that the fix had reached all users.

Separately, the security vendor Kaspersky said late last week that it had detected suspected exploitation of a flaw in Telegram widgets when people visited some Telegram channels.

In that activity, a PowerShell script ran without the user noticing and downloaded and launched WebRAT, also known as Salat Stealer. The malware allows attackers to control the infected system and steal data from crypto wallets and Telegram accounts.

The vendor's malware warning does not identify the flaw or the Telegram version, does not report the number of victims, and does not link the activity to either demonstration. It advises not running widgets until a fix is released.

Title: Fireworks AI Breach Exposes Uber Data and Highlights Supply Chain Risks
Context: After being notified of this incident, Uber immediately severed data connections with the service provider and launched an investigation
Full Text:
Hackers used compromised Fireworks AI credentials to steal personal data and driver’s license information belonging to nearly 150,000 Uber users.

Uber is notifying nearly 150,000 people after attackers used compromised credentials belonging to one of its technology providers to access personal information stored in the company’s external environment.

“On October 9, 2026, a service provider notified Uber that an unauthorized third party had compromised the service provider’s internal credentials and used them to access Uber’s account with the service provider. After being notified of this incident, Uber immediately severed data connections with the service provider and launched an investigation. On October 13, 2026, our investigation determined that the unauthorized party had used the compromised credentials to access Uber data connected to the service provider.” reads the data breach notification shared with the California Attorney General’s Office. “We are notifying you about this incident because our investigation concluded that your personal information was among the information accessed.”

The stolen data includes images of drivers’ licenses and other identity details, turning a security incident at an AI infrastructure supplier into a significant privacy issue for the ride-hailing company.

The incident dates back to October, when Uber learned that an unauthorized party had compromised the internal credentials of a third-party provider. According to notifications filed with U.S. state authorities, the provider informed Uber on October 9 that its credentials had been stolen and used to access the company’s data.

Uber found that attackers had accessed the data on October 7, two days before the company was notified. Uber then cut off the affected provider and began investigating the incident. The company said the provider’s stolen login details did not give attackers access to other Uber systems. This suggests that the breach was limited to the supplier’s environment.

The provider was identified as Fireworks AI, a cloud platform that gives developers access to open AI models. It allows companies to run and fine-tune these models without managing the required infrastructure themselves.

The stolen data includes drivers’ names, home addresses, dates of birth and driver’s license numbers. Attackers also accessed images of driver’s licenses and information from other government-issued IDs, according to Uber’s disclosures to regulators.

The scale of the incident became clearer after Uber filed a notification with Oregon authorities, reporting that 149,346 individuals had been affected. The company has also submitted breach notifications in several other states, including California, Iowa, Massachusetts, South Carolina, Texas and Vermont. However, Uber hasn’t disclosed how many of those affected are drivers, nor whether the total number could increase.

TechCrunch reports that Uber said it already had security alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its environment at Fireworks. They didn’t work because the attackers used legitimate internal credentials belonging to the compromised provider.

“In Uber’s case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks’ own internal credentials, “no alerts were triggered.”” states TechCrunch.

This is a clear example of how access controls and monitoring systems can fail to identify malicious activity when an attacker operates through an account that the environment already trusts.

The breach is part of a wider security incident at Fireworks AI. In a November 9 update, the company said attackers had accessed customer account and billing details, as well as secrets, datasets and unfinished AI models belonging to a small number of customers. Fireworks hired Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 to investigate the incident and notified law enforcement.

The company linked the attack to a financially motivated cybercriminal group that wanted to sell stolen AI access tokens through unauthorized services. This type of attack is known as LLMjacking. It allows criminals to use stolen credentials or tokens to access AI services and run models at the victim’s expense. No known cybercriminal group has publicly claimed responsibility for the Uber data theft.

Uber was not the only Fireworks customer affected. Notion and Cursor also confirmed that attackers had accessed some of their data during the incident, according to TechCrunch. The case shows how a security breach at one technology provider can expose several customers, even when they have no direct connection with one another.

Fireworks has taken steps to contain the incident with the help of Palo Alto Networks Unit 42. The company strengthened its security by replacing compromised credentials, limiting privileged access, isolating affected systems, restricting access to stored data, and improving logging and monitoring to detect further suspicious activity.

Fireworks pointed out it had found no evidence of further successful unauthorized access to the customer-facing Fireworks platform after October 25.

Uber is offering affected individuals free credit monitoring and fraud assistance through Cyberscout, a TransUnion company. Recipients have 90 days from the date of their notification letter to enroll. Reuters reported that Uber had not identified any misuse of the exposed information at the time of its November 13 report.

For affected drivers, the exposure of license images and personal details creates risks that go beyond the immediate breach. Criminals could use this information to support identity theft, impersonation attempts, fraudulent applications or highly targeted phishing campaigns. Combining a person’s identity details with knowledge of their professional relationship with Uber could also make fraudulent communications more convincing.

This is also Uber’s second publicly known data breach in 2026. In August, the company was reportedly investigating a separate incident involving its Uber Freight trucking business, after an extortion group claimed to have stolen data.

The latest incident raises a broader question about how organizations monitor the access they grant to external technology providers. Uber had alerts in place, but those controls didn’t identify the activity because the attackers used credentials that the system considered valid. The company said it had not identified any misuse of the data to date. That is encouraging, but it doesn’t remove the need for affected individuals to remain alert to identity fraud and targeted social engineering.
