Title: Envoy Visitors Critical turns visitor policies into approval workflows
Context: Envoy today launched Visitors Critical, an infrastructure-grade visitor security offering that brings identity verification, screening and approval workflows together on a...
Full Text:
Envoy today launched Visitors Critical, an infrastructure-grade visitor security offering that brings identity verification, screening and approval workflows together on a shared security architecture that keeps the record protected and audit-ready.

It’s built for high-consequence environments, where the impact of a security event is unacceptable and one-size-fits-all visitor workflows can leave gaps in security posture. Visitors Critical closes those gaps with the highest level of control, assurance and governance across every visitor scenario.

It is the only solution in the market that does all of this in one governed system that replaces the patchwork of tools, spreadsheets and manual checks most sites run today. Visitors Critical proves each visitor’s identity with identity assurance, screens that identity against visitor risk, routes the decision through the right approvers, informs access at the door or zone, and evidences all of it afterward.

When controls fail, the cost is rarely recoverable. For compliance-driven organizations, a wrong entry is a reportable violation that can put penalties, debarment or a facility clearance at risk. Liability can fall on the person who signed the authorization, and ITAR settlements alone have reached $51 million. For security-driven organizations, it’s a loss that can’t be undone.

Cargo theft costs an estimated $15 billion to $35 billion a year in the U.S. alone, according to Homeland Security Investigations, and insider risks cost organizations an average of $19.5 million a year, according to the Ponemon Institute.

Most organizations try to close those gaps by adding friction: more forms, more handoffs, more people between a visitor and the door. Visitors Critical takes the opposite approach. It gives these sites the highest level of control without making the process harder for anyone to follow.

“We’ve spent the last 13 years building Envoy to deliver the highest levels of security, safety and compliance in a way that feels natural to the people using it,” said Larry Gadea, CEO of Envoy. “Visitors Critical brings that to regulated and high-consequence industries, where every step carries more weight, without compromising on simplicity. Security only works when everybody takes part, and Critical’s advanced capabilities make that possible at a level these facilities have never had before.”

Critical is a visitor approval engine

Visitors Critical runs the full decision chain end to end. Envoy scans each visitor’s government-issued ID, matches the name to the invitation and the face to the ID photo with a liveness check, and checks both name and document number against the organization’s blocklist.

At the most sensitive sites, supported hardware readers can also authenticate the document itself, catching forged or altered IDs. Visitors are screened against denied-party and export-control lists through Visual Compliance and Descartes MK, and contractor qualifications are confirmed through ISN. Critical also strengthens and consolidates with IT and security teams’ existing tools and tech stack, bringing higher security to their visitor approval workflows and access control.

Critical turns an organization’s written visitor policies into workflows that enforce it. Visits route by visitor type, nationality or destination; sequential chains require compliance to sign off before security; only designated approvers can make the decision; and the approver’s reasoning is recorded alongside it.

Because the authorization, the screening result, and the approver’s identity and reasoning are all captured in the course of the work itself, an audit becomes an export rather than three weeks of assembling calendars and vendor portals.

Built for secure and regulated environments

Visitors Critical is built for organizations where a single wrong entry can cause irreversible harm, from defense contractors and semiconductor fabs to the data centers powering AI. Some adopt it to meet a specific obligation, such as ITAR, CMMC or export-control requirements. Others are CISOs extending the identity standards they already hold for their networks to the people entering their lobbies.

Attalon, an aerospace and defense supplier, built Envoy into its baseline security program. Every U.S. site, from its largest campuses to its smallest offices, follows the same visitor process and stays audit-ready at any time.

“In aerospace and defense, the lobby is the face of the company and the front line of the security perimeter. If you can’t secure the lobby, you can’t secure the rest of the site,” said Tim Carr, Director of Security & EHS at Attalon.

“Our lasers, optics and coatings support some of the industry’s most sensitive programs, so every visitor is a security decision. That’s why visitor management is one of the five pillars of our security standard, alongside access control, intrusion detection, CCTV and badging, and Envoy is how we deliver it. At all 12 of our sites, Envoy scans every visitor’s ID, helps us verify identity and citizenship status, and screens each visitor against denied-party and block lists. Because Envoy gives us one consistent visitor process everywhere, an auditor who inspects one site has effectively inspected them all, and we can pull visitor records in seconds, not days. Visitors Critical builds on that foundation by turning visitor policy into approval workflows, so the right people sign off before anyone arrives, and we can prove it afterward.”

The launch comes as new Envoy research of 1,000 security leaders finds that the organizations most exposed to a wrong entry are often the least able to prove who got in. Among enterprise leaders, 62% are very confident they’d pass a physical-security audit today without preparation, yet 63% of that group had a security incident in the past year.

At sensitive workplaces, 44% of leaders can’t confidently say who was in their building yesterday. Most sites still run visitor security across email, spreadsheets and multiple systems, which makes proof hard to produce. Visitors Critical is built to close that gap.

Title: Linx Security extends identity governance to AI agent actions
Context: Linx Security has announced four new capabilities that bring every agent under identity control, managed or unmanaged, in any gateway
Full Text:
Linx Security has announced four new capabilities that bring every agent under identity control, managed or unmanaged, in any gateway. Shadow AI Agent Detection finds the agents no one sanctioned. Agent Runtime Control decides every agent action in the gateway organizations already run.

And for identity teams, Autopilots for any use case put governed agents to work, a first among major identity vendors, while Prompt-to-Workflow turns a plain-English description into a tested, agentic workflow. These capabilities extend identity governance beyond managing access to controlling the actions AI agents take across the enterprise.

Agent security starts with identity

Agents are created, get access and act at machine speed, while governance still runs on human time, through tickets, approvals and periodic reviews. Agents also break the controls built for people: they are ephemeral, spawned, renamed, modified and reactivated with little trace; they run without a script, so what they do next is hard to predict; and they act autonomously across company tools and data.

Many are shadow AI, running on personal accounts, in pipelines and in AI apps outside sanctioned platforms, with no owner and no review. Gartner predicts that through 2028, over 50% of enterprise AI initiatives will halt due to unresolved agentic identity challenges.

Rather than treating AI agents as a separate security problem, Linx extends its existing identity governance architecture to every human, NHI and AI agent identity. Closing this gap takes more than discovering agents or monitoring their activity. It requires understanding each agentʼs identity, permissions, relationships and actions in context, and Linx applies that context in three steps.

Graph it: put every agent, sanctioned or not, on one Identity Graph alongside every human and NHI, with who owns it and whose access it carries. Decide with context: use that graph to weigh risk and set policy for every agent tool call and every access change. And control the action: enforce those decisions in whatever gateway agents run through, and give identity teams agents and agentic workflows of their own to carry out the work. Linx customers already govern more than 25,000 AI agent identities in production, and governed agent identities grew 450x in six months.

What’s new

Shadow AI Agent Detection. Linx already inventories agents on the platforms where they’re built. Shadow AI Agent Detection extends that to AI running outside them, from endpoints and CI/CD pipelines to SaaS and cloud. Each finding lands on the Linx Identity Graph with its owner, how it could be exploited and how to fix it, so security teams can govern shadow agents like any other identity.

Agent Runtime Control. Organizations can now bring their own gateway: Linx integrates with the AI gateway they already run and acts as its decision point, through the AuthZEN open standard. Organizations without one can use the Linx MCP Gateway. Every agent tool call is allowed or blocked based on who is behind it, its risk and what it is trying to do, without replacing existing infrastructure.

Autopilots for any use case. Identity teams can now add mission-specific team members. They give an agent a mission in plain language, set its scope, and choose which actions it takes on its own, which need human approval and which it never takes. Each Autopilot works from everything Linx knows about the organization’s identities and access, and teams review its plan and dry-run it before turning it on.

Prompt-to-Workflow. Teams describe a workflow in plain English, such as deactivating an agent when its owner leaves. Linx builds each step, shows the code behind it and dry-runs it before it goes live.

“AI agents are fundamentally changing the identity security problem,” said Israel Duanis, CEO of Linx Security. “Enterprises need to know not just who has access, but what every identity is connected to, what it’s doing and why. That context is the foundation we’ve built at Linx, and we’re now extending it to every AI agent.”

Title: Detectify launches Agentic Tooling to verify vulnerabilities in live applications
Context: An agent picks up the ticket, reads the relevant code, and uses Detectify’s tools to test the live application from the outside, as an attacker would, to confirm whether the...
Full Text:
Detectify has launched Agentic Tooling. It lets organizations’ own AI agents, running in their own environments, proactively investigate suspected vulnerabilities and test whether they can be exploited in running applications. A new Security Ledger lets security teams verify agents’ findings against objective evidence, ensuring informed decisions rather than relying solely on probabilistic conclusions.

The tools address a growing gap in DevSecOps. Engineering teams have built software factories that move code from commit to production in minutes. AI now writes a growing share of that code, and vulnerabilities move through the same pipelines at the same speed, which turns those software factories into vulnerability factories.

Detectify customers report that roughly 80% of the findings from their AI-driven static application security testing (SAST) tools are noise, showing that handing work to AI agents helps only if you can trust their output. Agents reason well, but they cut corners to deliver an answer and can produce a convincing report about a test they never ran.

Built for DevSecOps teams, Agentic Tooling gives agents access to the testing engines Detectify has built over more than a decade, including payload assessments sourced from its ethical hacker community, Alfred AI, and its Surface Monitoring data. The tools run in customers’ own environments through MCP and a CLI, use customers’ own agents and models, and operate only on the data customers provide.

Agentic Tooling is built for loop engineering, the emerging practice of running AI agents in automated, repeating workflows instead of prompting them by hand at every step. A CI run or scheduled job starts the loop. Findings from code scans, bug bounty reports, red teams, and Detectify’s attack surface data each become a ticket.

An agent picks up the ticket, reads the relevant code, and uses Detectify’s tools to test the live application from the outside, as an attacker would, to confirm whether the issue can be exploited. Each pass takes one finding from trigger to proof, then moves on to the next. Run continuously, the loop becomes what Detectify calls a verification factory: the counterpart to the software factory, able to keep pace with the code it ships.

Detectify’s Security Ledger makes all of that work verifiable. Each time an agent uses Detectify’s tools, the ledger records the testing session, including the requests sent, payloads used, and results returned, and links the evidence back to the original ticket. Engineers can see what the agent did, what it concluded, and the proof supporting its assessment in a single timeline.

Because the ledger is written by Detectify’s tools rather than the agent, and is append-only, teams can distinguish findings backed by actual tests from unsupported AI-generated conclusions. This allows organizations to scale security investigations without losing visibility into how decisions were reached.

“Ask an agent to write your code, then ask the same agent whether it’s secure. If it says yes, you don’t actually know. There are plenty of examples of agents fabricating proof because they want to succeed and please the person asking,” said Rickard Carlsson, CEO of Detectify. “Code review used to mean a colleague reading a page or two. Now it’s 50 pages that nobody can get through, and it goes to production anyway. We’re building proof that an agent can’t fabricate, so teams can ship at that speed and know what was actually tested.”

The launch comes as security teams are already struggling to fix known vulnerabilities. Detectify’s H2 2026 Cyber Hygiene Index found that nine in ten open critical and high-severity vulnerabilities had stayed exposed for more than 90 days. Meanwhile, security teams face a growing volume of alerts that demand investigation. A 2026 study by researchers at Fudan University and Tencent found that 76% of the static-analysis alerts examined were false positives, and developers spent 10 to 20 minutes reviewing each.

Agentic Tooling builds on the Detectify MCP Server, released in May 2026, which gave AI agents access to Detectify’s security findings and scanning capabilities. Detectify plans to feed the loop with data from across its platform. For example, a newly opened port could automatically trigger an agent investigation.

AppGate has announced the general availability of AppGate Optimizer to help organizations reduce exposure from over-provisioned access, cut the time spent on manual access reviews and prove least privilege access to auditors. AppGate Optimizer analyzes how users access resources and recommends precise changes that administrators review and apply without disrupting user workflows.

Key benefits include:

Enforce least privilege based on real usage: Narrow entitlements as soon as usage data supports it, not at the next scheduled review.

Reduce attack surface without disrupting users: Limit lateral movement by aligning access with what users actually need. Users keep working while access is reviewed and updated.

Replace manual reviews with continuous analysis: Spend less time combing through logs and cleaning up over-permissive and stale access.

Deliver audit-ready evidence: Give auditors and the board usage-based proof of progress toward least privilege, supporting multiple regulatory framework

Whether they use a legacy VPN or ZTNA solution, most organizations start with broad entitlements that are rarely revisited. Security and IT teams often know access is over-provisioned but lack the evidence to narrow it safely. Leaving broad access in place increases exposure, while changing it without reliable usage data can break legitimate work. Meanwhile, regulators expect organizations to demonstrate least privilege in practice rather than simply claim it.

“Replacing a VPN with ZTNA is an important step, but broad user entitlements still give attackers room to move,” said Shimon Modi, CPO at AppGate. “AppGate Optimizer uses actual access data to help customers continuously narrow that access without disrupting legitimate work. Entitlement optimization can reduce exposure and show auditors and the board measurable progress toward least privilege.”

AppGate Optimizer replaces manual, point-in-time reviews with continuous analysis of the hosts and ports each entitlement actually uses. It recommends three actions: reduce unused hosts and ports, replace broad VPN-style access with application-specific entitlements and retire entitlements that are no longer used or tied to a policy. Administrators see the evidence behind each recommendation before applying it with a single click. As roles and usage change, Optimizer rescans so access stays right-sized instead of drifting back toward sprawl.

Title: Pretxt Emerges Stealth With $5M Seed and an AI Supervision Tool
Context: ” Rather than neutering the capability of an agent, explains Aaron Costello, Pretxt co-founder and CTO, “We say, ‘Okay, you give an AI agent the same level of access as an...
Full Text:
Pretxt, with offices in Aspen, CO, and Dublin, Ireland, has emerged from stealth with $5 million seed funding raised from Deciens Capital, Howdy Partners and Service Provider Capital. Pretxt enters the emerging category of firms providing technology to prevent AI agents escaping their guardrails and causing unintended harm.

AI is more like a person than like traditional computer code: it doesn’t simply run; it receives, interprets, misinterprets and responds to ambiguous instructions. It is the combination of misinterpretation and wide agency of response that results in AI agents going rogue and potentially causing harm.

Since it is impossible to categorically exclude ambiguity in language (which is how we instruct the agents), our only alternative method of controlling them is to limit their agency. But too stringent a limitation of agency could become an unacceptable restriction on a potentially huge business benefit.

So, without a new category of supervision control, it is likely that we cannot have beneficial AI agents without also having potentially dangerous rogue agents. This requirement for a new control is leading to the emergence of a type of cybersecurity product that attempts to recognize a potentially harmful agentic action at runtime and control it before it can cause harm.

Pretxt is announcing just such a product which it describes as AI Supervision, “a purpose-built runtime technology to supervise AI agents as they work, guiding them back on course before mistakes become business consequences.”

Rather than neutering the capability of an agent, explains Aaron Costello, Pretxt co-founder and CTO, “We say, ‘Okay, you give an AI agent the same level of access as an authorized employee, and we will continuously monitor the manner in which it interacts with systems and other people. We will validate and ensure that all such interaction conforms with your business standards and operates in the same way that you expect your employees to operate.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

If the agent exceeds its expected authority or deviates from its authorized purpose, Pretxt doesn’t simply shut it down – it ‘steers’ the offender back on track. It’s a bit like having an experienced supervisor permanently on the shoulder of a trainee, who just steps in when necessary, with, “Don’t do it like that, do it like this instead.”

‘Steering’ is governed by context, continues Costello. “We ask new customers to onboard and connect their AI agent to our product, so we can immediately see the agent’s instructions and understand its purpose. As we watch it in operation, we learn how it speaks. We see what tools it can access, and we learn what abilities it has been given – such as ‘send’ an email, ‘post’ to LinkedIn, or ‘update’ a database.”

The customer then explains to Pretxt, I never want my AI agent to do x, or I only want my agent to do y, or see this kind of data. “It could be anything,” adds Costello. “The information is imported into Pretxt’s own AI. It becomes the context for acceptable behavior and is hooked into anywhere within the agent that could potentially violate the agent’s intended purpose and constraints.”

He gives the example of a customer service agent used by a medical practice to help patients book an appointment. Pretxt may have been told by the medical practice, ‘I never want this agent to give medical advice.’ “What we do,” he continues, “is hook into every single occasion the AI agent interacts with the user. Our own agent will look at this interaction and check whether it contains medical advice. This is done in real time. If it does contain medical advice (which we know should not be offered), we prevent it. But not by shutting down the agent, because that would leave patients unable to book appointments. We use a different approach that we call ‘steering’. If we detect medical advice, we invisibly talk back to the agent and effectively tell it, ‘You tried to give medical advice. Please continue to help the user with their booking request, but do not attempt to give medical advice again’.”

This is the purpose of Pretxt’s AI supervision app – not to shut down wanton AI agents, but to keep them safe, and prevent them straying from their predefined constraints.

Title: ConnectSecure brings adaptive AI testing to vulnerability management

Full Text:
ConnectSecure has announced Agentic AI Penetration Testing, a new capability designed to help managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise security teams better understand which vulnerabilities may be exploitable and require the most immediate attention.

Security teams have greater visibility into vulnerabilities than ever before, but determining whether a weakness can actually be exploited, how it could fit into a broader attack path, and what should be remediated first can require significant time and specialized expertise. ConnectSecure’s Agentic AI Penetration Testing, currently in beta, is designed to help bridge that gap by weaving intelligent, adaptive security testing into the vulnerability and compliance management workflow.

“Security teams are sprinting to keep pace with evolving threats. They need to understand which weaknesses create meaningful risk and what they should do about them,” said Peter Bellini, CEO of ConnectSecure. “Our Agentic AI Pen Testing fundamentally changes that process by helping to investigate potential exposure more efficiently and turn findings into clear, actionable next steps for their clients.”

From vulnerability discovery to active validation

Unlike traditional security scanning that primarily relies on predetermined checks to identify known vulnerabilities and configuration weaknesses, agentic AI can pursue a defined security-testing objective through a sequence of decisions and actions. Within an authorized assessment scope, the ConnectSecure solution is designed to plan relevant testing activities, respond to findings, and investigate potential attack paths based on evidence gathered throughout the process.

The capability is designed to support:

Adaptive security testing: Plan and adjust testing activities based on the target environment and findings uncovered during an assessment.

Investigation of potential weaknesses: Examine observed services, configurations, responses and other findings to determine where deeper testing may be warranted.

Attack-path validation: Investigate whether selected weaknesses can be demonstrated as exploitable using approved testing techniques.

Risk-focused remediation: Add validation evidence to vulnerability data to help teams focus resources on weaknesses that represent meaningful exposure.

Actionable reporting: Translate testing outcomes into evidence-backed findings, potential impact and recommended remediation steps.

For MSPs, Agentic AI Penetration Testing can help extend advanced security validation across more client environments. Designed to complement existing vulnerability scanning and human-led penetration testing, the capability adds an intelligent validation layer to established security workflows. By bringing vulnerability identification, security validation and remediation guidance together, partners can expand the depth of their security offerings while reducing manual effort for suitable testing activities.

“Penetration testing has traditionally required dedicated engagement time, which can make it difficult to deliver at scale across a large number of client environments,” said Shiva Shankar, Chief Technology Officer of ConnectSecure. “By harnessing agentic AI, we’re making deeper security validation more accessible and repeatable, while keeping the focus where it belongs: giving security professionals the critical information needed to make informed decisions.”

Title: EU Sanctions 30 People and Two Entities Over Russian Disinformation and Cyberattacks
Context: 16, 2026 Help Net Security, Global crackdown hits pro-Russian cybercrime, 100+ systems taken down worldwide (Europol's Operation Eastwood), July 16, 2025 The post EU Sanctions...
Full Text:
On Monday, the Council of the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities for Russian information manipulation and malicious cyber activity. The influence side hits the Social Design Agency, the Moscow political-technology firm behind years of fake-news operations. The cyber side lists NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has spent four years knocking European websites offline with DDoS attacks.

A sanctions listing won't take down a botnet, and nobody in Brussels expects it to. What it changes is the legal exposure for every European company that might pay, host, employ or do business with anyone on the list.

It also puts a propaganda shop and a DDoS crew in the same announcement, which tells defenders how the EU now sees them - two arms of one hybrid campaign.

What the Council announced

The Council's announcement covers two separate legal regimes:

Russia's destabilizing activities regime, created Oct. 8, 2024, adds the Social Design Agency, 24 of its staff and six pro-Kremlin commentators. It now lists 111 individuals and 21 entities. The EU's diplomatic service calls this the largest EU sanctions package targeting foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) to date.

The EU's horizontal cyber sanctions regime, in force since 2019, adds NoName057(16). It now lists 27 individuals and 12 entities.

The effects are the standard ones. Assets in the EU are frozen, EU citizens and companies may not make funds available to anyone listed, directly or indirectly, and listed individuals can't enter or transit the EU. The listings came on the same day as a separate package of 113 names aimed at Russia's war financing.

Who's on the list

The Social Design Agency runs the Doppelgänger campaign, which clones real news sites to spread fake stories. It has been under EU sanctions over the war in Ukraine since 2023. This listing moves it under the regime aimed at operations against the EU itself. The Council alleges that the agency's major operations need sign-off from Sergey Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff in Russia's presidential administration, and accuses it of cloning news sites, building Wikipedia-style platforms and staging physical provocations around the 2024 European Parliament elections.

The 24 staff listed go well beyond management. Alongside Andrey Perla, named as the agency's "chief ideologue," the list includes caricaturists, monitors, a system administrator and the editor of "Pulse," an internal network of Telegram channels. Britain had already sanctioned 22 of them.

The six commentators include RT correspondent Chay Bowes, accused of amplifying the Storm-1516 operation, and military blogger Yurii Podoliaka, who the EU says raised more than 1 billion rubles for Russian forces.

NoName057(16) emerged in March 2022. The Council says it hit energy, finance, transport, and water sites with DDoS attacks, along with political parties and candidates during elections. Europol's Operation Eastwood took more than 100 of its servers offline in July 2025, and the group kept going.

The target is the supply chain, not the operators

The skeptical read is easy. A caricaturist in Moscow probably holds nothing in the EU worth freezing, and a DDoS crew that survived a 12-country police operation won't fold over an asset freeze.

But influence and DDoS operations run on Western infrastructure. Domains, hosting, ad networks, payment rails, crypto exchanges and freelancers. Doppelgänger needed lookalike domains on Western registrars, which is why the U.S. Justice Department seized a batch of them in 2024. NoName057(16) paid its volunteers in cryptocurrency, Europol said. The "directly or indirectly" clause pushes the enforcement burden onto every EU company in those chains.

The regime choice matters too. The destabilization regime gives Brussels extra tools for later, including bans on transactions involving physical infrastructure such as servers and network equipment. That is a lever aimed squarely at hosting providers.

The pairing is the other signal. The Council's own descriptions put SDA provocations around elections next to NoName057(16) DDoS attacks on parties and candidates during elections. When a party's website goes down on election week, the outage is the smaller part of the attack. The headline it creates is the point.

Who's affected

Two groups of European organizations should read the list closely.

The first is anyone who could end up providing money or services to a listed party, which includes banks, payment processors, crypto exchanges, hosting and cloud providers, domain registrars, ad networks, and PR or media firms that hire freelance writers and designers. Sanctions screening also has to cover entities owned or controlled by a listed person, even if they aren't named.

The second is NoName057(16)'s target list, which includes government portals, energy, finance, transport and water operators, and political parties. For them, the sanctions change nothing operationally. The DDoS traffic will keep coming.

Plan of action

Refresh screening today. Pull the new names from the Official Journal acts (Council Implementing Regulations 2026/2558 and 2026/2550) into your sanctions screening, and rescreen vendors, freelancers and customers, not just payment counterparties.

Hosting providers and registrars: tighten customer checks. Doppelgängers depend on lookalike domains and cheap hosting. Make sure abuse reports about cloned news sites reach someone who can act on them quickly.

Watch for clones of your own brand. If you run a news outlet, a public body or a well-known consumer brand, monitor for lookalike domains and copied pages. Doppelgängers' method is to wear a trusted name.

Plan for election-week DDoS. If you're a party, a public body or critical infrastructure, test DDoS protection on public sites before the next vote. NoName057(16) announces its targets on Telegram, so put its channels in your threat feeds.

Prepare the message as well as the mitigation. A short holding statement that explains the outage and says whether any data was affected takes away most of the headline an attacker wanted.

What we're watching

NoName057(16) is changing tactics. U.S. prosecutors charged an alleged member in September, and researchers recently tied the group to a campaign that published personal details of senior European officials on the dark web, with crypto rewards offered for more. Doxxing aimed at officials and their families is a harder problem than a website outage.

Spotting that exposure early matters. Cyble monitors dark web forums, leak sites, and Telegram channels for leaked credentials and personal data tied to your executives and staff, so your team can respond before the information is used against them. Request a demo to see how it works.

The other question is whether Brussels uses the infrastructure-transaction bans the destabilization regime allows. If it does, hosting and network providers will feel these listings far more than the people named in them.

Key takeaways

On Nov. 16, 2026, the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities: the Social Design Agency with 24 staff and six commentators under its Russia destabilization regime, and NoName057(16) under its cyber regime.

The operators will barely feel it. The burden falls on EU banks, hosting providers, registrars, ad networks, and crypto platforms, which may not deal with anyone listed, directly or indirectly.

Listing a propaganda firm and a DDoS crew together reflects one playbook: election-period disruption built for headlines.

Update screening lists now, monitor for clones of your brand, and plan DDoS defense and messaging before the next election.

Title: Optimizely Flaw Exploited to Serve Malicious Code to Visitors of 178 Organizations
Context: Read more on software supply-chain attacks: Attackers Hijack Popular WordPress Plugins to Deploy Backdoors Report URI said the real number of affected organizations was likely...
Full Text:
An attacker has exploited a flaw in the website testing platform of Optimizely, a digital experience platform, to plant malicious code that reached visitors of 178 organizations' websites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, according to security researchers.

Scott Helme, a security researcher at Report URI, said that his team found the code in 188 of the 1611 Optimizely snippets it checked. Other affected organizations included Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA and Optimizely itself.

Optimizely confirmed the incident in a November 17 notice, saying an "unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.

It said it had fixed the flaw, removed the injected code and taken steps to secure affected user accounts.

What the Malicious Code Did

The attacker inserted code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, a custom-code field that runs on every page, and left the rest of each snippet untouched. The tampered files were still served from Optimizely's trusted content delivery network with its certificate, Report URI explained.

The injected JavaScript swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's own, and Report URI said those wallets had received about $7,040 by 19:25 UTC on November 16 before being emptied early the next day.

The code also worked as a card skimmer, capturing card details typed into websites' own forms, though cards entered in hosted payment iframes were out of its reach. It also stole some cookies and page screenshots.

On iPhones and iPads, the JavaScript delivered two iOS exploit kits, which Report URI identified as Coruna and DarkSword. Report URI advised visitors to update to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later.

How the Optimizely Attack Unfolded

The first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC on November 16, and Report URI said all infected files had been cleaned by 23:11 UTC.

The attacker has not been named, but Report URI said one of its wallets had been in use since March 2026, and linked the same actor to an earlier wave of injections through other third-party scripts.

"Supply chain breaches may be an inherent weakness of the web in its current form, but this doesn't excuse organizations from failing to reduce their own attack surface," said William Wright, CEO of Closed Door Security, in emailed comments.

Report URI said the real number of affected organizations was likely higher, as it could only check snippets it found in time.

Title: Suspected ransomware affiliate extradited to US over $500 million in extortion demands
Context: A 43-year-old Kazakh national accused of helping a ransomware crew steal data from US hospitals and schools, then threatening to publish patients’ medical information, has been...
Full Text:
A 43-year-old Kazakh national accused of helping a ransomware crew steal data from US hospitals and schools, then threatening to publish patients’ medical information, has been extradited from Italy, the US Department of Justice announced.

Prosecutors believe Roman Khlynovskiy was a member of the “8-Digits Team,” a group affiliated with the INC and Lynx ransomware operations.

They allege the conspirators broke into victims’ networks, stole data, and demanded payment in exchange for not releasing it. The group also threatened to publicize sensitive medical information to pressure victims into paying.

Court documents state the group went after victims in at least six states, with schools and hospitals among them. The conspirators “boasted that they possessed over 50 terabytes of data,” according to the DOJ, including more than 70 million confidential health records.

“Khlynovskiy and other members of the ‘8-Digits Team’ repeatedly targeted hospitals and schools, extorting victims and threatening to release highly sensitive information,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “This widespread extortion campaign resulted in over $500 million in ransom demands.”

Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division said the defendant is charged with participating in “one of the largest healthcare data breaches in decades.”

Khlynovskiy is charged with conspiracy to commit computer fraud and identity theft, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, extortion involving computers, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Prosecutors also charged him with threats to disclose nonconsensual intimate images under the TAKE IT DOWN Act.

If convicted, he could spend up to 27 years in prison.

Patel credited the Italian partners and tied the extradition to a wider FBI push to bring back suspects held abroad. Over the last 21 months, the bureau has recorded 84 foreign transfers of custody, up 71%, and 157 extraditions, up 121%.

“Those who victimize Americans cannot evade justice by operating overseas,” Patel concluded.

Title: Airlock Digital blocks unauthorized AI agent actions at the endpoint
Context: Agentic Steering, a capability within Agentic Control, gets the agent to the right outcome on the first retry
Full Text:
Airlock Digital has announced the availability of Agentic Control with the release of Airlock Digital v7.1. Agentic Control includes dedicated Agentic Steering capabilities for AI agents, allowing customers to extend their Deny by Default Application Control to this emerging technology. Airlock Digital evaluates an agent’s requested behavior at runtime to stop unauthorized agent behavior before it attempts to execute it.

Application Control has traditionally focused on what employees can run on their endpoints. Now AI agents work on those same endpoints, usually with the same access as the employee: the same applications, identities and files. Unlike employees, agents run commands, access files, and adapt on their own as they work toward a goal. That leaves security teams with a new question: what should AI agents be allowed to execute?

Agentic Control is built to address this uncertainty. Before an agent’s action executes, Airlock Digital evaluates it against the customer’s policy and stops what isn’t permitted. It then returns the decision directly to the agent, with administrator-provided context or an alternative where configured, so the agent can adapt and keep working within policy. Simply blocking the agent’s attempted action can escalate risky behavior and introduce greater risk. Agentic Steering, a capability within Agentic Control, gets the agent to the right outcome on the first retry.

In April 2026, the Cloud Security Alliance reported that 82% of organizations had unknown AI agents running in their environments, and 65% had experienced an AI agent-related security incident in the prior 12 months. Together, with the AI discovery introduced in Airlock Digital 7.0, Agentic Control gives security and IT teams five capabilities:

See every AI tool. Discover AI agents, LLMs, and harnesses across the entire endpoint estate.

Define trust boundaries. Block unapproved AI applications and agents, ensuring employees only use corporate-approved applications. Deny By Default allows policy maintenance to scale without having to keep track of the millions of available versions of agents, LLMs, and harnesses.

Control every action. Evaluate agent-initiated endpoint actions in popular agent platforms like Codex and Claude. Every action is evaluated against customer-defined policy before execution. Permitted actions proceed. Prohibited actions are stopped.

Steer, don’t just block. When an action is denied, Airlock Digital returns the policy decision directly to the supported agent. Administrators can add context explaining the decision or suggest an alternative. The agent can adapt, keep working within policy, and learn policy boundaries to improve future executions.

Continuously improve policy. Airlock Digital also centrally records agent sessions, commands, files, policy decisions, outcomes, risk activity, token usage, and estimated cost. Teams can search sessions, review AI-generated session summaries, and show executives, auditors, and regulators how agentic AI is being controlled. Most importantly, teams can continue to refine Application Control policy over time.

“Traditional application control determines what software is trusted to execute. Agentic AI introduces a new actor on the endpoint, with an ability to execute other applications. Teams now need the ability to define and enforce what an AI agent is allowed to do once it’s running,” said David Cottingham, Chief Product Officer, Airlock Digital.

“AI agents don’t simply stop when an action is blocked; they evaluate alternatives and continue working toward their objective, no matter how risky that approach may be. Rather than leaving an agent to take increasingly risky measures to complete its objective, organizations can communicate clear operational boundaries, allowing trusted agents to adapt their behavior while remaining within policy.”

Agentic Control adds a preventative check at the endpoint, where agent actions take effect. It complements AI platform controls, identity and access management, data security, and detection and response. Airlock Digital decides whether each resulting action is allowed to run under the customer’s policy.

“What we’re hearing from customers is that AI agent adoption is outpacing the security programs meant to govern it,” said Kevin Dunne, Chief Executive Officer, Airlock Digital. “Organizations need to understand what trusted AI agents are doing, define what they’re allowed to do, and ensure they operate within organizational policy. Agentic Steering fills the market gap by giving organizations the visibility and control they need to confidently adopt AI without slowing the business down.”

Title: “Amazon” job offer promises $5,000 a month, but it’s got all the signs of a scam
Context: Available with Malwarebytes Premium Security for all your devices, and in the Malwarebytes app for iOS and Android
Full Text:
Last month, Amazon announced plans to hire more than 300,000 people in the US for the holidays. That’s welcome news for job seekers, but scammers know that.

We found several sites advertising a remote assistant job under Amazon-like names, with promises of up to $5,000 a month. None of the sites is run by Amazon.

Amazon says all genuine job opportunities are posted on amazon.jobs; hourly warehouse jobs are also listed at hiring.amazon.com. The offers we found are separate from Amazon’s holiday hiring push.

The application doesn’t match the job description

One careers page calls the role a “legitimate, fully remote position,” with “no commute, no office, no fixed desk.” Yet the form asks whether applicants have reliable access to a personal vehicle and someone at home who can receive packages. Those questions point to package handling, not remote assistant work.

A recruitment page promises fully remote work paying up to $5,000 a month

Why Amazon makes such good bait

People expect Amazon to be hiring. A hiring announcement can make an “Amazon is hiring” message seem plausible. But the remote assistant jobs on these sites are separate from Amazon’s announced seasonal roles.

“Working with Amazon” can sound believable. Businesses can provide services to Amazon sellers without being part of Amazon. The sites use names that resemble those of logistics or seller-support businesses, which can make the connection harder to judge at a glance.

The pitch targets people looking for flexible work. “Work from home” and a few hours a day can appeal to parents, students, and people looking for a second job.

The tactic has been used before. Amazon says it saw more reports of scammers posing as recruiters in September and October 2025. In June, we warned about Amazon job texts offering $250 to $500 a day for 60 to 90 minutes of work. The sites we found add a careers site, a company website, and a polished application form to make the offer look more convincing.

Several names, apparent links

We found multiple recruitment and application sites using Amazon-like branding:

amzssapplication[.]com and jobsamzss[.]com, two careers pages for the “Remote Assistant” job

applyamazonsp[.]com, an application form for the same job, under the name “Amazon Seller Pro LLC”

The sites use byte-identical site icons. Their domains were registered through the same registrar between July 23 and October 26. These similarities suggest a connection, although they do not establish who operates each site.

The same remote assistant pitch appears on another domain

The recruitment pages list “HR” email addresses on three additional domains: amzncrew[.]com, joinamzn[.]com, and workatamzn[.]com. These addresses do not establish an affiliation with Amazon.

To verify a job with Amazon itself, check its official job boards at amazon.jobs or hiring.amazon.com. Independent businesses serving Amazon sellers hire separately, so verify their offers by contacting the business through contact details you find independently.

The recruitment pages link to amzshippings[.]com, a website advertising preparation and shipping services for Amazon sellers. That’s a newly registered domain with hidden ownership details.

A remote job that asks about your car and doorstep

Although the careers pages on these sites describe the role as fully remote, the application asks:

“Do you have reliable access to a personal vehicle?” If not, it asks applicants to explain how they would transport packages.

“If you’re not home, is there a person to receive parcels?”

A remote assistant wouldn’t normally need to receive or transport packages. These questions are warning signs of reshipping, also known as parcel-mule fraud.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says that a job asking you to receive shipments, repackage them, and send them elsewhere is a reshipping scam. The goods may have been bought with stolen payment details, and people recruited this way can be left handling packages connected to fraud.

The form collects personal information

The application form asks applicants for personal information

The form collects your name, phone, email, home address including apartment number, felony history, education and employment history. It promises “Your data is secure” and sends submissions through Formspree, a third-party form service. We could not establish who receives the information. The page also tells search engines not to index it.

No resume is needed. Instead, the careers page says: “Our HR team calls you directly … Keep your phone on — we don’t schedule in advance.“

In the page code, that note sits below a leftover template comment: “PASTE YOUR TEXT HERE.”

The recruitment page’s footer states: “Amazon Shipping Services is not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon.com, Inc.”

What could happen if you apply?

Sharing your details could expose you to identity theft. If you take the job, you could also be asked to move packages or money tied to fraud.

Identity theft: Your name, contact details, and home address can be useful to criminals. Be especially cautious if anyone later asks for your Social Security number, bank details, or ID.

Being drawn into fraud: If you receive or forward packages bought with stolen payment details, your address may be linked to their movement.

Losing money: A fake employer might later send a check and ask you to return some of the money or use it to buy supplies. The FTC warns that fake checks can bounce after the money has been sent on.

How to stay safe

Find Amazon jobs on amazon.jobs. Amazon says genuine job opportunities are listed on its official job board.

Check the domain, not the logo. Anyone can copy Amazon’s colors and branding.

Be wary of high pay for little work, especially when there’s no résumé or scheduled interview.

Don’t receive or forward packages for an employer you haven’t verified.

Don’t send ID photos, your Social Security number, or money before verifying the employer.

Title: 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour
Context: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the...
Full Text: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether. Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2, manually – no AI required. He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command. "Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote. Meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree." He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery." He went on to claim: "Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does)." Later firmware adds "session control," an authentication mechanism whose strict setting blocks unauthenticated access to most web interfaces. But Meijer found a memory corruption flaw in that protective layer too. He described the final zero-day as a "trivial" pre-auth memory corruption bug which again starts with a segfault but can be wangled into an RCE "with some additional effort." Meijer also considered whether attackers could maintain access after a reset, as seen with implants such as Saltwater and Firestarter. He considered this feasible because the controllers do not use their processor's secure boot features. "In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike – increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food," said Meijer. "Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable – requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid." Meijer's priority for operators was to remove the controllers' direct internet exposure, rather than spend scarce resources on piecemeal patching. He said the vendor's advice following the attacks on European supermarkets and blood banks in recent weeks – rotating creds, applying patches, enabling strict session control – was insufficient given the flaws in the controllers' codebase. "This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible," said Meijer. "We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure." The CCB likewise urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately, but also recommended applying patches when they become available. Beyond the liberal use of strcpy(), Meijer criticized the absence of standard exploit mitigations, including stack canaries and position-independent executables. "These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features... requires no engineering work at all," he said. "It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled." The Register asked Danfoss to respond to the findings, but it did not reply. Danfoss has consistently blanked our requests for information since being implicated in at least some of the attacks that affected European supermarkets recently, alongside rival controller vendors Copeland and Dixell. It also did not respond when we asked about its involvement in the attacks on US commissary appliances over the summer, after some alleged that its controllers were targeted. ®

Title: MSP ScreenConnect Servers Targeted in Month-Long Campaign
Context: Dozens of MSP ScreenConnect servers have been targeted in a month-long campaign exploiting a vulnerability patched in September, cybersecurity firm Huntress reports
Full Text:
Dozens of MSP ScreenConnect servers have been targeted in a month-long campaign exploiting a vulnerability patched in September, cybersecurity firm Huntress reports.

The attacks, ongoing since at least October 20, aim to exploit CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score of 9.9), a critical missing authorization and improper privilege management bug that allows for files to be transmitted and executed during a connection without authorization or confirmation.

ConnectWise patched the security defect on September 8, and CISA added it to the KEV catalog on September 11. Huntress warned at the time that exploitation started on August 20.

Now, the cybersecurity firm says a new wave of attacks is targeting ScreenConnect instances, with a focus on managed service provider (MSP) servers.

The hackers exploit CVE-2026-84869 via requests to run a guest-pushed batch file that connects to a Telegram bot and installs a rogue ScreenConnect client.

“Attackers appear to be spraying servers blindly: Since October 20, we’ve seen at least 688,000 guest ‘run file’ requests for update*.bat hit 42 MSP ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses, waiting for any technician to join,” Huntress says.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to the cybersecurity firm, the activity is different from the recently observed campaigns targeting ScreenConnect instances with the SCKit malware toolkit and with unauthorized sessions from machines posing as crypto exchanges.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-84869, it explains, allows attackers to push malicious files to technicians’ machines and get their own clients to execute them when the technician joins the session. The technician sees no prompt when the files are executed.

“An MSP technician’s workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target. When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files,” Huntress notes.

In one attack, a rogue ScreenConnect client disguised as Windows Update was installed and spawned within nine seconds of the host client running the guest-pushed bat file.

As part of another, the guest machine pushed a text file two seconds after the technician joined the session, and the technician’s client ran the file three seconds later.

In October, a targeted attack hit an MSP server: the attacker joined as a guest in three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to execute a file designed to drop a script into the technician’s computer’s Startup folder.

Organizations should update technicians’ ScreenConnect host clients to version 26.6.5 or later, along with all the Access agents ConnectWise lists.

Title: Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval
Microsoft Warns of Coordinated Phishing Campaign Leveraging M365 Service Outage
Context: “This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures,” Microsoft wrote in a blog...
Full Text:
Microsoft has identified a “coordinated, high volume” global phishing campaign designed to exploit the recent Microsoft 365 outage.

The campaign was observed on November 13, as the company grappled with rolling out a fix for the tech failure impacting services like Outlook and Teams worldwide.

The outage began on 11.20 EST on November 12 and lasted over 22 hours, with Microsoft confirming that its services were fully restored on 23.15 EST on November 13.

The phishing emails were designed to exploit individuals’ and employees’ desperation to reconnect to M365 services, attempting to entice them into clicking a malicious link and capturing their credentials.

The messages impersonated legitimate M365 service-health notifications. They aimed to create a false sense of urgency by claiming that the recipient’s emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them.

“This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures,” Microsoft wrote in a blog dated November 16.

There is currently no evidence of credential capture, malware delivery or post-compromise activity emanating from the campaign. However, organizations have been urged to investigate whether any users clicked the malicious links and take immediate steps to mitigate any malicious activity if this did occur.

How the Phishing Campaign Unfolded

The email lures sent during the campaign used the subject pattern “Outage – <random token>” and display names built from a three-character, organization-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

Microsoft said the use of specific sender domain names, such as moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com, were designed to make the messages more tailored and appear relevant to the recipient.

The messages commonly used 24-hour deletion deadlines and call to actions using prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” links to drive immediate action. They also referenced Microsoft services like Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot.

The body of the messages included fake email conversations positioned to be hidden from the recipient, which appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion.

Title: Access Dental Management Data Breach Impacts Over 340,000
Context: Providing dental care across Texas and in Illinois, Indiana, and New Mexico, ADM says it discovered the incident on May 5 and immediately began an investigation with help from...
Full Text:
Texas-based dental services provider Access Dental Management (ADM) has disclosed a data breach impacting more than 340,000 individuals.

Providing dental care across Texas and in Illinois, Indiana, and New Mexico, ADM says it discovered the incident on May 5 and immediately began an investigation with help from third-party forensic specialists.

The investigation determined that, between May 1 and May 4, hackers had accessed its network and viewed or copied certain data, including personal information.

On October 21, ADM’s review of the compromised information determined that the attacker accessed names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, medical information, and health insurance information.

“Upon learning of this incident, ADM moved quickly to investigate and respond to the incident. As part of its ongoing commitment to the security of information, ADM is reviewing and enhancing its existing policies and procedures related to data privacy to reduce the likelihood of a similar future incident,” ADM said in a notice (PDF).

Last week, the organization notified the Texas and Vermont Attorney General’s Offices that 341,049 individuals were affected by the data breach (341,039 in Texas and 10 in Vermont), but the total number could reportedly surpass 455,000.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

ADM is sending written notification letters to the potentially affected individuals, encouraging them “to remain vigilant against incidents of identity theft and fraud by reviewing your account statements, explanation of benefits forms, and monitoring your free credit reports for suspicious activity and to detect errors.”

While the organization did not share further details on the cyberattack, the WorldLeaks ransomware group claimed responsibility for the intrusion on June 5.

SecurityWeek has emailed ADM’s parent platform Surge Private Equity for additional information on the incident and will update this article if it responds.

Cybersecurity startup Corma has raised $125 million in a Series A funding round, bringing the total raised to $185 million and its valuation to $1 billion.

Led by NEA, the investment round saw additional support from previous backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

Founded in 2025 and headquartered in Tel Aviv and San Francisco, Corma emerged from stealth mode in August with a frontier foundation model specifically designed for defensive cybersecurity.

Corma says AI’s offensive capabilities have grown exponentially over the past several months, while its defensive capabilities have not, and it aims to fill that gap.

The startup trains frontier foundation models and deploys them as AI agents alongside existing security tools to audit security data and correlate signals across environments to improve defenses and help security teams respond to increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.

“Cybersecurity is now a battle of intelligence against intelligence, and Black October made that impossible to ignore,” said Corma co-founder and CEO Alon Pluda.

In this article

Attackers used Optimizely to spread code targeting visitors’ payments and devices

Researchers found affected files linked to 178 organizations, including CNN, BBC, and Zoom

If you visited an affected site on November 16, check your payments and update your devices

Visiting a familiar website should not mean exposing your payment details to criminals. But attackers found a way to put malicious code on websites belonging to some of the world’s best-known organizations by compromising a service those sites trusted.

On November 16, security researcher Scott Helme and his team at Report URI identified malicious JavaScript in Optimizely files associated with 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, Salesforce, and GitLab. The code could redirect cryptocurrency payments, skim payment card details, and deliver exploit kits targeting vulnerable iPhones and iPads. Check Report URI’s full list to see which websites were affected.

Optimizely provides software that helps businesses test and personalize their websites. To accomplish this, a website adds a small piece of JavaScript called a snippet. This loads Optimizely’s code into visitors’ browsers, where it can change their experience and measure the results. In this incident, it also provided a way for unauthorized changes to reach visitors through an otherwise legitimate website.

Optimizely is widely used. Website technology tracker BuiltWith currently reports detecting it on roughly 190,000 live websites. That is its overall usage, not the number affected by this incident. This qualifies as a supply-chain attack because, instead of breaking into every website separately, criminals abused a shared service those websites relied on.

The BBC provides a prominent example of how the attack unfolded. Report URI’s timeline records a clean capture of its Optimizely snippet at 02:21 UTC on November 16, followed by an injected version at 04:21 UTC. By 08:28 UTC, the researchers observed the main malicious payload being loaded on bbc.com.

This does not establish that the BBC’s own servers were breached, or that every BBC visitor was infected. It shows how a third-party script used by a trusted website can become the route through which malicious code reaches a visitor’s browser.

Optimizely confirmed the incident and says it fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. Report URI also said all the infected Optimizely files it was monitoring were clean by 23:11 UTC on November 16 and had remained clean since.

How to stay safe

Visitors cannot reasonably be expected to inspect every script a website loads, and disabling JavaScript can make many websites unusable. The most useful steps are to keep devices updated and check any potentially affected transactions.

Update your iPhone or iPad. Install the latest iOS or iPadOS version available for your device. This is particularly important if you visited an affected website on November 16, because the attack included exploit delivery aimed at older, vulnerable versions.

Use an up-to-date real-time anti-malware solution. This can help detect and block malware on your devices.

Review cryptocurrency transfers made during the incident. Check the actual destination address against the intended recipient’s address, confirming it directly with the recipient through a trusted channel. The attack was specifically designed to change payment destinations.

Check payment card activity. If you entered card details on an affected page on November 16, monitor your account and contact your card issuer promptly about suspicious transactions. Enable transaction alerts where available. You could also consider identity theft protection with credit monitoring to help spot signs of identity misuse, such as new credit accounts opened in your name.

Watch for unusual account activity. Investigate unexpected account changes or unfamiliar sessions, particularly for services you were using on affected pages. The code could steal some cookies, which can contain information used to keep you signed in.

The main responsibility rests with the organizations delivering code to visitors. The incident shows why website operators also need to monitor what third-party scripts do and restrict the other scripts and data connections they can introduce. Consumers shouldn’t have to audit a website’s software supply chain before reading the news or making a purchase.
