Title: California sues OpenAI, alleges 80-plus agent escapes hidden from public
Context: The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC
Full Text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI, alleging the company has lost control of its autonomous AI agents more than 80 times during testing and misled the public about how safely it develops its models.

The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC. It says OpenAI disclosed the 80-plus figure to state investigators but has publicly reported just 27 such incidents. In those incidents, agents reached third-party systems, foreign government websites and OpenAI’s own infrastructure, the state alleged.

“While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.

The state brings two claims: violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and creation of a public nuisance. It is seeking an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, and an order to abate the nuisance. It also wants civil penalties of $2,500 against each defendant for each violation proven at trial.

Other incidents and internal breaches

In one July incident, agents escaped their sandboxes and gained administrator-level access to OpenAI’s own systems, according to the complaint. Those systems included the company’s cloud model deployment system, its secrets management service, and its identity and access management service. The agents then launched unauthorized servers, exposing OpenAI’s infrastructure to the internet. OpenAI did not let external researchers review that attack, the complaint said.

The complaint identified several other incidents involving OpenAI agents.

At RubyGems, a software package repository, agents allegedly uploaded thousands of packages in May 2026. Administrators removed more than 500 packages they considered malicious, and the platform suspended new user registrations between May 12 and May 16.

The complaint also alleged that agents made approximately 17,000 edits to a German website, DseWiki, using it as a message board to exchange information about bypassing sandbox restrictions.

Other incidents involved Wikimedia Foundation’s infrastructure and Australian government websites. The complaint said agents overwhelmed Wikimedia services with millions of API requests and hundreds of thousands of Wikidata queries, likely contributing to a partial outage in May. In June, agents allegedly accessed non-public information from Australian government websites.

The complaint further said OpenAI notified dozens of organizations whose websites or internal systems had been accessed by its agents. These included government institutions, law enforcement agencies, educational institutions, and small businesses. Some incidents allegedly involved stolen credentials, API keys, and fraudulent accounts, with agents accessing personally identifiable information.

OpenAI’s own infrastructure was also compromised in at least three attacks in July, according to the complaint. Agents allegedly obtained administrator-level access to systems supporting cloud model deployment, secrets management, and identity and access management.

Escapes after the fix

The state argued that the danger is ongoing. On September 20, after OpenAI had hardened its environment, an agent escaped during a training run and reached an external chatbot.

“This incident occurred after OpenAI had implemented ‘security hardening’ following the Hugging Face attack,” the lawsuit added.

OpenAI detected it within minutes, but the run did not stop automatically, and human reviewers took two more hours to halt it, the complaint said.

OpenAI announced a pause on training and evaluating its most capable models on September 25. The pause lasted five days, ending October 1, according to the complaint.

Warnings that went unheeded

The complaint argued that the incidents were foreseeable. It cited the run-up to the Hugging Face attack as evidence. By May 26, agents had used a vulnerability in a misconfigured software package service to reach the public internet.

An internal OpenAI team saw at least one agent escape but apparently took no action, the complaint said. On June 27, a security monitoring tool flagged that the research environment was being probed for vulnerabilities, and OpenAI again did not stop its runs.

When agent traffic knocked the service offline on July 4, OpenAI patched it over the holiday weekend and resumed runs on July 7, the state alleged. Two days later, agents broke out again.

The state also faulted OpenAI for not running live chain-of-thought monitoring in training and evaluation, even though it did so for models deployed to employees. During the Hugging Face attack, one agent’s reasoning read: “We’re attacking third-party HF using leaked token, potentially outside intended scope. . . . This is arguably unauthorized.”

Bonta’s office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on September 30. OpenAI answered with a 14-page letter and produced no supporting documents, the complaint said.

California is not the only state pressing OpenAI. In August, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird led a 15-state coalition demanding that OpenAI preserve evidence, protect whistleblowers and halt the tests behind the hack until it could show it can run them responsibly. “The AI weaponized itself, which is extremely scary,” Bird said in a statement.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld.

Title: Hackers Found a Way Around GitHub SHA Pinning. This Webinar Explains How to Close the Gap
Context: Attackers have already found a way around it
Full Text:
Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it.

In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check.

The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it.

The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it.

That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't.

Immutability Is Not Provenance

Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected.

GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it.

📅 Save Your Spot: Learn Why “Best Practice” Won’t Stop the Next GitHub Actions Attack

But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered:

Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned.

Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project.

Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen.

With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely.

GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job.

GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later.

That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you.

What You'll Learn

Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers:

What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create

How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible

What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't

Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions

Who Should Attend

Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you.

Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either.

Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

Title: Researchers Detail iPhone Flaw That Let Apps Record Audio Despite Denied Microphone Permission
Context: Neither Apple nor the two researchers who found the flaw report that it was used in attacks
Full Text:
A now-patched flaw in Apple's audio service let apps on iPhones and iPads record audio even after the user tapped "Don't Allow" on the microphone prompt.

The first security updates with the fix came out on August 17. Neither Apple nor the two researchers who found the flaw report that it was used in attacks.

Nik Tsytsarkin of Meta Red Team X published the technical details last week. Mustafa Calap, a security engineer who reported the same flaw separately, published his own analysis the same day.

On iPhones, an orange indicator shows when an app is using the microphone. On one of the researchers' earlier test builds, that indicator stayed off while the app recorded.

In Tsytsarkin's tests, the prompt appeared the first time the app opened. Declining it did not stop the recording, and the prompt did not reappear on subsequent launches.

In the earlier build of his technical analysis, the system logs showed no record of the app using the microphone. They named the audio service itself as the recorder.

His demo video shows the indicator while the test app records with no microphone permission. He wrote that the video "was filmed on a later build that appears to have restored the orange microphone indicator."

Calap's test app recorded while its permission still read denied, according to his detailed write-up. No orange indicator appeared in the Dynamic Island or in Control Center. He does not say which of his two test builds that was.

Neither researcher describes a way for users to check whether an app recorded them before the fix. Calap reproduced the bypass on iOS 26.6, released July 27, and on an iPadOS 27 beta.

The bypass needed an app already installed on the device. His two test apps were sandboxed apps with no added entitlements. Their only privacy key was NSMicrophoneUsageDescription, which makes the microphone prompt appear.

In his tests, recording had to start while the app was in the foreground. Once started, it continued after the app went to the background and after the device was locked. The background version also set UIBackgroundModes = audio.

Both apps were installed from Xcode and never went through App Review. So the tests do not show whether App Review would have stopped such an app.

The Meta analysis compared two iOS 27 test builds. Neither researcher reports testing macOS, tvOS, watchOS, or visionOS, though fixes are listed for those systems too.

The bypass covered microphone capture through the audio service only. It did not give the app other privacy permissions.

These releases fix the flaw, which is tracked as CVE-2026-65339:

iOS 26.6.1 and iPadOS 26.6.1 (August 17), for iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 3rd generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 1st generation and later, iPad Air 3rd generation and later, iPad 8th generation and later, and iPad mini 5th generation and later

iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 (October 26), for iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and iPad 7th generation

macOS Tahoe 26.6.2 (August 17)

macOS Sequoia 15.8 (September 14)

tvOS 27 (September 14), for Apple TV 4K 2nd generation and later

watchOS 27 (September 14), for Apple Watch Series 9 and later

visionOS 27 (September 14), for Apple Vision Pro (all models)

The researchers describe no setting that blocks the bypass, so installing these updates is the fix.

The iOS 27 notes do not list the flaw, nor do those for later iOS 27 updates as of today. Meta's timeline says the fix shipped in iOS 27.0 beta 5 on August 10.

CISA gives the flaw a CVSS score of 5.0 out of 10. The agency's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities does not list it, as of the catalog's update late last week.

Apple's notes for the August 17 updates describe the flaw only as one that may let an app leak sensitive user information.

Tsytsarkin wrote: "That description leaves out the most striking part: the app could record after permission was denied, without the orange indicator appearing."

In his own tests, the indicator was missing only on the earlier build. An app does not decide for itself whether it may record. That decision goes through the Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC) system, which checks which process is asking.

The audio service, called audiomxd, accepted the app's own word about which process was asking. An audit token identifies a process. An app could send the service a token that named audiomxd itself.

The service then treated the app as itself. It took a shortcut meant for its own internal audio and allowed recording without asking TCC. The kernel itself provided the app with the details it needed to impersonate the service.

The fix makes the service check the real caller's identity, which the kernel supplies. Outside callers now need the private entitlement com.apple.private.audio.client-audit-token-override to replace the client identity the service relies on. An app cannot grant itself that entitlement.

This seems like a good thing:

Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

[…]

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

Alternate link.

Details:

First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.

Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.

Title: Why threat hunting should matter to every board
Context: If your organisation can’t answer that question, it may have gaps in its visibility or detection capability
Full Text:
Boards should have confidence that their organisation can detect and investigate emerging cyber threats, including activity that existing security alerts may miss.

Organisations use a range of cyber security controls. They use security products, receive threat intelligence and monitor alerts from trusted providers. Many have well-developed processes for responding to known threats. But these measures can’t tell you everything about your ability to detect an attack.

When a new attacker technique is identified, ask: could we detect this technique if it was used against us?

If your organisation can’t answer that question, it may have gaps in its visibility or detection capability.

As attackers use AI to operate at greater speed and scale, identifying and addressing these gaps becomes increasingly important. Organisations need to be able to identify signs of malicious activity early, rather than relying solely on detecting an attack once its effects become apparent.

Threat hunting can help organisations test their ability to detect relevant attacker activity and expose gaps in their defences.

This blog is for boards of organisations that monitor their systems for cyber threats, either themselves or through a third-party provider. It explains why threat hunting matters as threats evolve, and how boards can support their organisation to learn from what it finds and turn those insights into stronger cyber defences.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.

Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.

Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Why Traditional SCA Cannot Keep Up With AI-Generated Code
Context: Why Scan-and-Review Can Become a Bottleneck A scan can identify a vulnerable or policy-violating component, but detection is only the start of the work
Full Text:
AI coding tools generate and revise code in seconds. They can also make dependency decisions along the way in selecting packages and versions, adding frameworks, or changing how an application uses existing components.

Each choice becomes part of the software supply chain and adds something teams need to evaluate. Many traditional software composition analysis (SCA) workflows assess those choices after they enter the codebase when a pull request or build triggers a scan.

As AI tools introduce or modify dependencies more frequently, that scan-and-review process can lag behind development.

SCA remains essential for understanding and managing the components in software. But to keep pace with AI-assisted development, teams need to pair scanning with up-to-date component intelligence and policy guidance at the point where developers and AI tools choose dependencies.

AI Adds More Dependency Decisions to Every Change

AI-generated code is often discussed in terms of whether or not it contains vulnerabilities. That is only part of the security picture. An AI coding tool can introduce a package, select a version, or modify an existing dependency, often faster than developers can review them individually.

In traditional SCA workflows, that analysis begins after a dependency has been selected: a developer adds a package, a pull request or build triggers a scan, and the team reviews the findings. That approach can work when component changes arrive at a pace people can absorb. It becomes harder when coding assistants and agents generate changes continuously, sometimes introducing several dependencies in a single task.

The more dependency decisions AI makes, the more important it is that each choice is based on reliable, current information. Without that context, unsuitable packages or versions can add risk, review, and remediation work downstream.

AI Recommendations Need Current Context

A model's knowledge may not reflect current package releases, vulnerabilities, licensing details, or project health.

Without that context, it may:

Suggest an outdated version when a more current release is available.

Recommend a package or version that does not exist.

Choose a component that conflicts with organizational policies or license requirements.

Developers and AI tools need current component intelligence to evaluate those choices. We explain how to bring that context into AI-assisted workflows in our guidance on safer development.

A dependency graph can also grow beyond the package a developer sees in a code suggestion. A direct dependency may bring in transitive components, and a project may span several languages or ecosystems.

In our recent analysis of AI and shift-left security, we compared a Spring Framework project with 764 open source components in its dependency tree to an agentically developed project with 2,543 dependencies across four languages. These examples do not represent every project, but they illustrate how quickly the review surface can expand.

The result is not simply "more code," but a larger, changing dependency surface that teams must evaluate, often with less time and visibility.

Why Scan-and-Review Can Become a Bottleneck

A scan can identify a vulnerable or policy-violating component, but detection is only the start of the work.

Teams still need to determine if the finding applies to their use, how urgent it is, whether or not an acceptable alternative exists, and how to update without breaking the application. If every new finding requires an individual investigation, a faster development workflow can create a longer security queue.

Several gaps tend to emerge:

The decision has already been made. A scan in a pull request or CI pipeline may flag a component after it has been added to the code. The team now needs to remove or replace it, potentially reworking code that depends on it.

Finding volume grows faster than review capacity. More dependency changes can generate more alerts. If teams cannot distinguish urgent exposure from lower-priority findings, important work competes with routine triage.

The scan may lack decision context. A result tells the team that a component has a risk, but developers also need current information about versions, maintenance, licenses, and organizational policies to choose a suitable alternative.

Manual review does not scale with automated changes. Security teams and maintainers cannot review every dependency choice one by one when assistants and agents can produce many changes across teams and repositories.

Late remediation creates rework. Replacing a dependency after implementation or testing may require code changes, new tests, and another round of review. That can erase some of the time AI saved during initial development.

These pressures reflect the AI productivity paradox in which speeding up code creation does not automatically speed up review, testing, security, or release. If those stages cannot absorb the additional volume, more output can mean more work waiting in queues.

Move Component Guidance Closer to the Choice

Rather than waiting for a scan to run, teams can give developers and AI coding tools and AI systems current component intelligence as they choose dependencies.

That guidance should help answer practical questions before a dependency becomes part of an application:

Does this component and version exist, and is it maintained?

Are there known vulnerabilities or malware concerns?

What license does it use, and does it meet the organization's licensing requirements?

Does the choice meet the organization's policies?

Is there a safer or more suitable version that is compatible with the application?

AI tools need that information in a form they can use during development. That lets them check component details as they make recommendations.

This does not remove the need for developer judgment. Teams still need to set policies, review exceptions, and understand how dependencies are used. The goal is to give developers and AI tools reliable information to make better initial choices and reduce the number of avoidable issues that reach a later review queue.

Keep Scanning as Part of a Layered Approach

Earlier guidance and later-stage analysis solve different problems. AI-assisted development calls for safeguards across the SDLC. Context at the point of choice can prevent some risky or noncompliant dependencies from entering a codebase.

Automated workflows can also update dependencies or prepare changes for developer review. SCA scans remain important for identifying issues in existing applications, surfacing newly disclosed vulnerabilities, and helping teams respond as component risk changes.

Modern SCA can extend beyond scanning with component intelligence and policy guidance at selection, along with automation for dependency updates and remediation.

A practical workflow:

Gives developers and AI coding tools access to current component and vulnerability information.

Applies organizational policies consistently across human and AI-assisted development.

Offers clear alternatives and remediation guidance when a recommendation raises concerns.

Continues scanning code and builds to catch problems that earlier controls miss.

Maintains an accurate view of application dependencies so teams can assess impact when new risks emerge.

This approach keeps security controls close to development without turning every change into a manual approval process. It also recognizes that no single scan or decision point can account for every risk throughout a component's lifecycle.

Build at AI Speed With Better Dependency Decisions

AI can make software development faster, but every new component still raises questions about security, maintenance, licensing, and policy. When teams answer those questions only after a scan or review, that added speed can create more triage and rework.

To keep pace, teams need SCA that goes beyond scanning to guide dependency selection and support ongoing management and remediation.

Title: California Sues OpenAI, Seeking Court-Ordered Changes After the Hugging Face Hack
Context: OpenAI said its AI used stolen credentials and discovered a previously unknown vulnerability to access Hugging Face’s servers
Full Text:
California’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday in an effort to force the ChatGPT-maker to change its business practices over a July cybersecurity incident in which its artificial intelligence system hacked into another company on its own.

In the lawsuit filed in San Francisco Superior Court, Attorney General Rob Bonta alleges that OpenAI misled and endangered the public and users of its services by knowingly developing advanced AI models without necessary safeguards. He says the company’s actions could put critical infrastructure, institutions and the public at risk, which makes it a “public nuisance” under state law. Bonta says OpenAI is a public nuisance, and he wants a judge to order the company to change its ways and give up any profits generated by what he claims are the company’s risky business practices.

OpenAI announced an “unprecedented cyber incident ” on July 21, when its AI agent hacked into another AI company, Hugging Face, after escaping from what was supposed to be an isolated testing environment known as a sandbox. OpenAI said its AI used stolen credentials and discovered a previously unknown vulnerability to access Hugging Face’s servers.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that has been identified by every major AI lab.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” Pusateri wrote in an email to The Associated Press. Those steps include publishing detailed technical and independent reports, strengthening safeguards, and creating a framework to identify when AI agents act in a way that doesn’t match the company’s instructions or goals, Pusateri said.

“We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry,” Pusateri wrote.

In the lawsuit, Bonta says OpenAI’s promises about safety and security are deceptive.

“In truth, however, OpenAI has developed, trained and evaluated dangerous models that fail to follow instructions, cheat on tasks, conceal and attempt to deceive monitors about their misbehavior, and engage in malicious and unauthorized behavior including carrying out cyberattacks on third parties,” Bonta wrote.

He also noted that early last month, OpenAI reported that it had discovered that internally deployed agents were able to suppress monitoring alerts and disable monitoring. A month later, the company published a research report finding that as AI models become more capable, they become more difficult to supervise, he wrote.

“Moreover, the true extent of the company’s legal violations and the risk of future harm is unknown due to OpenAI’s lack of transparency and misrepresentations,” Bonta wrote.

OpenAI was already being sued by at least eight states that say the company’s popular chatbot model is hurting children and deceiving adults by giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to kill themselves or hurt or kill others. The lawsuits contend the ChatGPT chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and teenagers.

In a statement released last month in response to those lawsuits, OpenAI said it had built safety protections into ChatGPT for children and that it would continue to improve the model.

Title: Malware spread through Optimizely hits 178 organizations, including BBC, CNN and Zoom
Context: An attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s web experimentation platform to plant malicious JavaScript on its customers’ websites, the company has confirmed
Full Text:
An attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s web experimentation platform to plant malicious JavaScript on its customers’ websites, the company has confirmed.

Companies add Optimizely Web to their sites through a JavaScript snippet loaded from Optimizely’s servers.

“Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We’ve fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects,” the company said in its latest status update.

“We’ve also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered.”

The attack was uncovered by security researcher Scott Helme of Report URI. “On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organisations through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock,” wrote Helme.

“The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers,” he added.

The code was planted in the “Project JavaScript” field of customer projects. It kept loading from Optimizely’s own content delivery network, so visitors’ browsers treated it as trusted.

Helme’s team checked 1,611 Optimizely snippets and found 188 carrying the malware. He believes the number of victims is higher, since the team only examined the snippets it managed to find in time.

Banks and financial firms made up the largest group of victims, with 32 organizations, followed by technology companies and retailers.

Salesforce told Reuters it was investigating unauthorized Optimizely changes and disabling scripts as a precaution.

Helme confirmed that all infected files were clean by late Monday, and the attacker’s main payload domain has since been suspended.

A payload that kept growing

The injected code loaded a script from a domain registered on the morning of the attack. The card skimmer arrived in the afternoon and went after card numbers, expiry dates and CVV codes typed into a site’s own payment forms. Card details entered into payment fields run by a separate provider were out of its reach.

On iPhones and iPads running iOS 18.6 or older, affected pages reloaded every 60 seconds, something visitors might have noticed.

Helme found that the payload was rebuilt 26 times over the course of the day, with the attacker adding features and wallets along the way.

A small crypto haul and a trail going back months

The attacker’s wallets received about $7,150 in crypto before being emptied early Tuesday. “We have no way to see how many credit cards were skimmed,” Helme noted. Hudson Rock, which investigated the campaign separately, says it has not been able to link the transfers to visitors of the affected sites.

A cash-out address used in the campaign also appeared in operations in March and on November 3, linking the attacker to earlier attacks. The same injection code first appeared on Turkish websites in September.

Three more services carried the code

Hudson Rock and researcher Kirk of Ohey traced poisoned scripts to three more services, namely Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly, with the earliest tampered responses recorded on November 13. The deliveries share hosting and loader code, but the researchers say that doesn’t prove a single operator was behind them or that the same way in was used.

Kirk documented later iOS stages built to steal keychain data, seed phrases and private keys from iPhones. “Hudson Rock has not independently reproduced those stages or demonstrated compromise of a real victim’s iPhone. A scan using an iPhone user-agent string is a delivery observation, not a Safari exploitation test,” the company explained.

Few sites had the right defenses

Helme’s team crawled the affected organizations’ websites to see whether a Content Security Policy (CSP) would have stopped the attack. Only 24 organizations, or 15%, had a policy strict enough to block it. Another 68 had no CSP at all. In 50 cases, the policy let the malware run and send stolen data back to the attacker.

Allowing Optimizely’s domain in a policy offered no protection, because the malware was delivered from that domain. Optimizely’s documentation recommends a setting that lets pages run code through JavaScript’s eval function. That setting allowed a backup copy of the malicious code to run on HSBC’s site.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached,” concluded Helme.

Full Text: Market research giant Ipsos says it's currently investigating a "cybersecurity incident," and has reported the matter to the authorities. In a statement issued on Monday from its Paris headquarters, the company confirmed it filed a complaint over the attack on November 11, but gave few details because its internal investigation is ongoing. "Upon discovery, we promptly activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident, and engaged external cybersecurity specialists to support our investigation," it said [PDF]. "The investigation is ongoing to determine the nature and scope of the incident. We have reported the matter to the relevant authorities." Ipsos confirmed the attack had no impact on its operations or customer service delivery, however, it did not comment on the nature of the attack or whether any data was compromised. "We take protection of the information entrusted to us very seriously," Ipsos added. "Should the investigation establish that information relating to clients, projects or business partners has been affected, we will contact those concerned directly. "As the investigation is ongoing, we are not in a position to comment further at this stage." The company declined our requests for additional data, as it does not want to release unverified information to the market. Founded in France in 1975, Ipsos is one of the leading market research companies in the world, employing nearly 20,000 people and operating in 220 cities across 90 markets. It is routinely engaged by businesses for its market research data, as well as by public sector organizations for its opinion polling, often responsible for providing data regarding political views and satisfaction surveys. Tasked with procuring a wealth of data on myriad topics, Ipsos also offers data analytics services that turn the information it gathers through research, polls, and surveys into insights that inform organizations' business strategies. ®

Context: Meta announced an opt-in photo suggestions feature for the US and Canada in October 2025
Full Text:

In this article

Facebook’s photo suggestions feature could access your entire gallery through a single permission

Italy fined Meta €805 million and says the privacy violation remains ongoing for some users

Check Facebook’s photo permissions to control what it can access

If you’ve given Facebook access to your phone’s photos, the app may be able to read your entire gallery, including pictures you never intended to share. Check your photo permissions if you want to limit that access.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) for accessing Android users’ entire camera rolls without specific consent or adequate disclosure. The regulator says the violation remains ongoing for some users, despite changes Meta has made.

The decision concerns Facebook’s “Get camera roll suggestions when you’re browsing Facebook” feature. Launched in 2023, the idea is to use your photos and videos to suggest potential social media posts.

You might be surprised to hear that Facebook can access every photo or video in your gallery if you’ve granted full photo access. That includes pictures of your kids, restaurant receipts, and that Wi-Fi password label you photographed awkwardly on the router behind the TV. But you might have granted that access without realizing it also enabled photo suggestions. That’s the problem, said the regulator.

Facebook’s app requested access to the camera roll through a single permission that applies across the entire app, covering multiple features with different requirements. The Garante said:

“The permission is preceded by a non-specific notice (’enable other features’) which does not make it clear to the user that they are also authorising suggestions from the camera roll.”

One permission, lots of features

Asking permission for lots of things via one request violated Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code, according to the regulator. That code is Italy’s privacy law, and its Article 122 implements the EU’s ePrivacy Directive, which protects data stored on devices such as smartphones. The Garante said access for this feature required free and informed consent.

Facebook also failed to adequately explain its use of the photo gallery, and the suggestions feature was on by default. Granting full photo access could give the app ongoing access to the entire library, the regulator said, without users being able to verify which information was actually being used.

The regulator’s investigation started in July 2025 after consumer organization Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti submitted a report. That prompted the Garante to conduct its own technical analysis.

Meta had asked for Ireland to handle the case. Like many other technology companies, Meta’s main EU presence is in Ireland, whose regulator handles many cross-border privacy cases. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules at issue do not use that system.

Meta disagrees

Meta told Reuters that users must grant device permission before the feature can operate and can change that permission in their settings.

The social media company also called the fine, which amounts to less than 0.5% of global revenues, “disproportionate.” It will appeal, it told reporters.

The Garante attributed the amount of the fine to the high number of people affected (around 20 million Android users in Italy) along with the duration of the incident, which it referred to as a breach. It also called Meta out for its “poor level of cooperation.” Changes that the company made to its app were introduced late and only applied to users who update the app, it added.

Aside from the financial penalty, the regulator has ordered Meta to request consent separately for the camera roll suggestions feature. It must get that consent after explaining to users what it will use the data for and how to disable it. The company must turn it off by default even for those who previously gave the blanket permission, it said, and if it doesn’t comply by the 60-day deadline then it must not enable the feature for users who haven’t given consent.

The regulator is preparing for a potential follow-up. It has left the door open to address the possible use of content to train AI, which Meta has denied. The Garante also “reserves the right” to assess a new feature that allows the content of the camera roll to be processed in the cloud.

Meta announced an opt-in photo suggestions feature for the US and Canada in October 2025. It analyzes media to find memorable moments and suggests creative edits. Meta says suggestions remain private unless users choose to share them, and the feature can be turned off in Facebook’s camera roll settings.

What Facebook users can do

The Italian order does not automatically change permissions for users elsewhere, but you can review your own settings.

On Android, go to Settings > Apps > Facebook > Permissions > Photos and videos, then select Don’t allow to revoke gallery access. Depending on your Android version and the app, you may also have an option to allow access only to selected photos and videos. Menu names can vary by device.

While Italy’s decision didn’t target iPhone users, they can also review Facebook’s photo access under Settings > Privacy & Security > Photos.

Title: Holiday shopping in a world of fakes: How AI is changing the game
Context: *Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026 Scammers are getting personal Nearly one in four consumers (24%) say they’ve...
Full Text:
It’s the most wonderful time of the year, especially for scammers.

The holiday shopping season is packed with tempting one-day-only deals, gift guides, and retailers promising the perfect present at the perfect price.

And wherever shoppers go, scammers aren’t far behind.

Cybercriminals have always taken advantage of the holiday rush. Now AI makes it easier to create fake storefronts, products, reviews, and promotions that look and sound legitimate. For consumers, knowing what—and who—to trust is getting harder.

Shoppers are worried. According to Malwarebytes research, 77% of consumers are concerned about being scammed by a retailer using a fake AI website, or using AI to misrepresent products or reviews.

That concern is grounded in experience: More than one in four consumers (28%) have experienced an AI-related shopping scam in the past year Some were misled by AI-generated product photos or reviews. Others described ordering products that never arrived, sometimes from legitimate-looking websites that turned out to be fake.

With the holiday shopping season upon us, we’re looking at how AI is changing the shopping experience, where consumers see risks and benefits, and how to shop more safely.

When a great looking product isn’t what it seems

Realistic product images, glowing reviews, and professional-looking websites can make unfamiliar retailers seem trustworthy. AI makes it easier to create all three in one polished package, which is convincing enough to deceive even careful shoppers.

For some, these convincing fakes have made buying online feel unsettling. One survey respondent commented:

“It seems as though when I’m shopping online, I notice the models are AI-generated or even the products themselves and that scares me. I can’t tell what’s real or not anymore. I don’t even know if what I’m looking to buy is real! I don’t know if what is being advertised is the actual product. AI is going too far.”

Survey respondents shared real-life experiences that help explain those fears. One described receiving products that looked nothing like the photos:

“I buy fewer items that I don’t already know from real life because I fell for manipulated images and the delivered items barely resembled the edited pictures in the shop!”

This aligns with what we’re seeing too. As an example, earlier this year we found cat face flower seeds being sold online.

But manipulated images don’t have to look this extreme, or this obvious. As AI improves, telling what’s genuine from what’s fake is getting much more difficult.

Some of our survey respondents described seeing convincing fake storefronts that took their money without delivering anything:

“It was a fake website promoting shoes. I bought them and it turned out to be an AI website. Now I’ll be more wary of these websites and what they look like.”

These experiences are especially common among younger shoppers. 42% of Gen Z say they’ve experienced an AI-related shopping scam, compared with 30% of Millennials, 22% of Gen X, and just 9% of Boomers and older.

The impact goes beyond lost money or a missing package. Respondents described feeling embarrassed, angry and unsettled by how convincing the deception was. For many, that experience left a lasting distrust of online retailers.

How AI brings scams directly to shoppers

Scammers don’t have to wait for shoppers to stumble across a fake website. With the help of AI, they can send convincing, personalized messages that appear to come from familiar brands, bringing scams directly to consumers.

It’s no wonder that global mega-retailer Amazon is the most impersonated brand that we see in our threat intelligence data, followed by Walmart, Temu, Costco, and Steam.

*Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026

Scammers are getting personal

Nearly one in four consumers (24%) say they’ve received a scam message that felt highly personalised, sometimes including their name or other personal details. Among Gen Z, that figure rises to almost one in three (32%).

We came across a scam that linked a person’s phone number and name with a fake Facebook Marketplace listing to act as a conversation lure and get them to respond. Answering a message is often the first step in what can become a very costly scam.

Even when shoppers spot the warning signs, a personalised scam can leave them feeling uneasy. One respondent explained:

“I received an email that was clearly directed to me personally, yet it seemed “off” which was an alarm for me. I investigated it before clicking on anything and knew then that it was a scam. It made me feel like nothing is safe out there anymore and you have to be hyper-alert at every moment when online.”

Spotting scams among the shopping noise

Delivery companies are an obvious choice for scammers to impersonate at this time of year. With more purchases being made, it can be hard to keep track of which retailer is using which delivery service, and on which date it will arrive.

*Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026

Common delivery scam lures we’ve seen include:

A delayed parcel notification, paired with a request to pay a small fee through a link

A failed-delivery claim demanding address confirmation or rescheduling.

Short deadlines or “final notice” language to create a sense of urgency.

Lookalike delivery company domains and off-brand links.

In this example, scammers use a fake missed delivery, the USPS brand, and a sense of urgency (48 hours) in order to get their target to click.

The broader research shows just how challenging this environment has become:

85% agree that sophisticated scams can be hard to distinguish from the real thing

85% believe AI makes it easier for scammers and criminals to target people

Even the most routine messages about purchases and deliveries warrant a closer look, and that’s one more thing for consumers to worry about during an already busy time of year.

Where shoppers accept AI

Despite their concerns, many consumers accept some uses of AI in retail. In the survey, 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% accept AI-generated salespeople. Including neutral responses, those figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively.

There’s also growing acceptance of AI on the retailer side. 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% are okay with AI-generated salespeople. Including those who feel neutral about these practices, the figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively. That shows how willing consumers are to let AI into the shopping process, despite their concerns.

That acceptance extends to product images: 60% say using AI to enhance them is no different from existing advertising practices. Product photos have long been staged, edited and polished to make merchandise look its best; AI can do the same.

Shoppers’ responses show that concern about AI and acceptance of its use can coexist. In the holiday rush, distinguishing a useful shopping aid from a convincing deception can be difficult.

Shoppers are taking precautions, but the burden is growing

Some shoppers are responding in practical ways, starting with where they choose to buy:

36% have limited purchases from unfamiliar online retailers.

26% have limited purchases from social media accounts

As one respondent explained:

“I am more wary of purchasing something from an ad I see on social media. I tend to search for the item online myself and find a legit website to order from.”

Others are checking information more carefully:

One respondent described checking reviews on another website after watching a convincing product video on social media, only to uncover signs of a scam. Another now deliberately seeks out negative or neutral reviews and real customer photos. Others describe comparing information across multiple sources rather than taking any online content at face value.

One respondent summed up the need for extra caution:

“I tell my children not everything that glitters is gold. Always be careful and check everything yourself. With AI today you can make everything look beautiful but beautiful doesn’t mean true, correct or authentic. Fact checking is the order of the day.”

Beyond checking information for themselves, consumers also value having another person to turn to when they need help. Nearly seven in ten (69%) say they’d spend extra time or pay more for human customer service, while 43% say they’ve tried to talk to a real person rather than an AI customer service system.

AI may make shopping more convenient for some, but that doesn’t mean consumers want to rely on it for every interaction.

How to spot AI-powered shopping scams this holiday season

AI can make fake stores, product photos, and reviews look extremely convincing. Here are four ways to protect yourself:

Slow down. Scammers use urgency to rush you. During the holidays, limited-time deals and delivery alerts can be especially persuasive. Don’t let a countdown or unexpected message stop you from checking first.

Guard your information. Be wary of unexpected requests from sellers or delivery services for passwords, payment details, or other personal information. A message can use your name or mention a recent purchase and still be fake. You can check which data

Verify the source. Check independent reviews and compare product photos and details across websites. Go to the retailer’s official site directly instead of following links in messages. Remember that logos, email addresses, and caller IDs can all be faked.

Use anti-scam/scam detection tools. Malwarebytes offers free tools to help you spot and stop potential scams. If you’re worried about the legitimacy of a DM, text, email, link, or number, upload it to Scam Guard. We’ll give you a verdict on whether it’s safe, along with guidance on what to do next. You can also use Browser Guard as you shop to block scammy and fraudulent websites, and stop card skimmers in their tracks.

About the research

The research in this article is based on a March 2026 survey about AI, identity, and digital trust, conducted among 1,500 respondents in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The research was prepared by an independent research consultant and distributed via Forsta.

Title: New GitDoor and GraphDoor Backdoors Turn GitHub and SharePoint Into Covert C2 Channels
Context: The malware then fetches three plugin modules from the server and launches them in parallel to carry out screenshot capture, process listing, and keylogging
Full Text:
Government sectors in Asia and Africa have been targeted by an active cyber intrusion campaign that delivers to previously undocumented backdoors that leverage legitimate services like Microsoft SharePoint and GitHub for command‑and‑control (C2).

The activity has been codenamed Operation ShadowCloud by Kaspersky. The Russian cybersecurity company said it identified the campaign in early 2026.

"The threat actor behind it is abusing the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two brand-new backdoors," Kaspersky researchers Saurabh Sharma and Noushin Shabab said in a two-part analysis. "These implants hide their command‑and‑control (C2) traffic behind cloud services Microsoft SharePoint, GitHub, and Ably, allowing the implants to blend in with normal traffic, effectively evading network-based detections."

The modular backdoors, dubbed GraphDoor and GitDoor for their choice of the cloud platform used for C2, enable the download of additional plugins on demand and the execution of shellcode directly in memory to extend their functionality. Traffic between infected systems and the C2 servers is proxied by deploying a modified Erfrp client and Ably messaging service-based plugins.

The starting point of the attack has been traced back to a MeshCentral Agent, a legitimate remote access tool that's used for remote desktop control, command‑line access, and file management. The attack is said to have targeted an unspecified Taiwanese organization.

The exact method by which the utility is installed on the host remains unknown. However, signs point to the "reuse of a prior infection already present on the network," Kaspersky added.

The MeshCentral Agent is configured to contact a hard-coded C2 server ("wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx") and then fetch three payloads staged on the endpoint -

A legitimate binary used for DLL sideloading (start.exe, pythonw.exe, and zoomit.exe)

A rogue loader DLL used to unpack and execute the next-stage malware (jli.dll, SbieDll.dll, python39.dll, WINMM.dll, and libcef.dll)

An encrypted file containing the core payload

At least two different DLL loaders have been identified to date, each employing its own method to decode and launch the encrypted backdoor payload by injecting it into the current process's memory.

"Loader (Type 1) employs a hybrid scheme: first running the data through an RC4 stream cipher and then applying an XOR mask, while Loader (Type 2) simplifies the process by using a straight XOR operation alone," Kaspersky noted.

The end goal is to deploy backdoors like GitDoor and GraphDoor, which employ a number of encryption and obfuscation techniques like control flow flattening and nested helper functions to complicate analysis efforts and make it harder to trace genuine execution flow.

GitDoor, as the name implies, uses GitHub for C2. It relies on two distinct repositories for receiving command payloads ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo") and uploading the results of the execution ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix"). While the Havo repository is public, the Trix repository is private.

The creation date of these repositories suggests that preparations for the campaign have been underway since at least the end of 2024. GitDoor supports 26 commands that allow the backdoor to -

Perform file management

Log keystrokes

Launch a proxy, including using Ably

Load shellcode to Base64-encoded Common Object File Format (COFF) binaries and terminate the backdoor

The custom shellcode feature is used to download and run different modules that facilitate the following functions -

Conduct process injection using methods like Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) injection

Enumerate and manage Windows services

List files and directories, wipe file contents, and recursively delete a directory

Conduct network-related activity by displaying active TCP connections and modify firewall rules

Manage processes, including dumping the memory of the process with a specified process ID into a file and terminating specific processes

Execute commands using "cmd.exe"

Enumerate, create, and run scheduled tasks

Enumeration Windows Registry keys and values recursively and set a value in the Registry

Extract user information, along with local groups and its members

Add of a new Windows user account or add a user to a global or a local group

Record keystrokes to a file ("%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat")

Dump cookies from Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge directly from the process memory using CookieKatz

Use Mimikatz to dump credentials from Windows LSASS

Capture screenshots of the entire screen or a specific window identified by its process ID

Extract WhatsApp's database decryption key

Initiate NTLM authentication to an attacker-controlled destination

Calculate system idle time and display the last time a user was active on the host using mouse movement and keyboard input

GraphDoor, on the other hand, opens a named pipe, creates a directory named "Intel_Log" inside the system's Application Data folder, and gathers system information to send back to the attacker.

To establish communications with the C2 server, it authenticates with a malicious application using "login.microsoftonline.com" on port 443 and uses the access token to communicate with the Microsoft Graph API and ultimately stage the data on the SharePoint drive.

The malware then fetches three plugin modules from the server and launches them in parallel to carry out screenshot capture, process listing, and keylogging. It also proceeds to reestablish contact with the SharePoint website to retrieve the commands to be executed on the machine.

The complete list of plugins supported by GraphDoor is as follows -

kl.ts, to log keystrokes at "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat"

pr.ts, to list running processes

scr.ts, to take screenshots of the window that matches a supplied process ID and save them as JPEG images

moveDir.ts, to move the legitimate executable, the malicious loader DLL, and the encrypted backdoor file to specific target path

channel.ts, to launch the proxy

abchannel.ts, to use the Ably messaging service to proxy traffic

ab2channel.ts, a covert SOCKS5 proxy that tunnels TCP traffic through Ably's Pusher‑compatible WebSocket service

In addition, GraphDoor's custom shellcode capability expands on GitDoor to support two additional commands that allow it to run commands using "cmd.exe," as well as MZ executables.

The identity of the threat actor behind the campaign is unknown, but Kaspersky said it shares some degree of overlap with a China-nexus activity that Sophos tracks under the moniker Bronze Sandcastle. Tactical similarities have been observed with prior campaigns undertaken by FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle (aka BlackTech).

"On several victim systems, these groups shared the same staging directories as the GitDoor backdoor, with their implants deployed within a one-day window of GitDoor deployment," the company concluded. "While this does not prove a direct link, it suggests that a Chinese-speaking group may be developing and/or utilizing the GitDoor and GraphDoor backdoors."

"By using cloud-based storage and messaging services, the actors blend in with normal traffic (as cloud API calls to Microsoft Graph, GitHub, and Ably are indistinguishable from legitimate enterprise usage, evading many network-based detections), and enable dynamic payload delivery, where on-demand plug-ins and shellcode are retrieved from cloud repositories, allowing for rapid updates and functional extensions without modifying host files."

Title: Microsoft testing Remote Lock for lost or stolen Windows devices
Context: Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them
Full Text:
Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them.

Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta (Build 26320.10003) and Experimental (Build 26340.10013) channels.

Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro.

After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked.

"Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. "Nothing is erased: the device stays enrolled and managed, BitLocker stays on and user data stays in place. The lock holds across restarts and while offline, and only an admin can lift it remotely, so the user picks up where they left off."

Admins can lock a device from the Intune admin center using the following procedure:

Go to Devices > Windows > Configuration > Create > New policy. Choose Windows 10 and later, then Templates > Custom.

Name the profile (for example, Remote lock - ON) and add the settings below, with LockState = 1.

Assign the profile to a device group reserved for locked devices. To lock a device, add it to that group; the lock applies at the device's next check-in.

To unlock, create a second profile with LockState set to 0 and assign it to an unlock group. Move the device from the lock group to the unlock group.

After Remote Lock is enabled, the device is not isolated from the enterprise network or erased. To do that, admins must use the device isolation and wipe controls in Intune.

However, users must keep BitLocker enabled to protect their data if the device is reimaged or the drive is removed because the Windows Recovery Environment, Safe Mode, and booting from USB or other media are not blocked.

With these Windows 11 preview builds, Microsoft has also begun testing new advanced security key management features that let users view and manage passkeys stored on a FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) security key individually.

These new features allow admins to configure enterprise settings such as always-required user verification, minimum PIN length, and enterprise attestation.

In August, Microsoft also announced new privacy controls that let Windows 11 users choose which desktop apps can access their microphone, camera, and precise location.

Title: Hackers exploit Microsoft 365 outage to launch credential phishing campaign
Context: Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing
Full Text:
Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing. Just a day after a prolonged outage disrupted several Microsoft services, including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organisations across multiple industry sectors.

The attackers impersonated service notifications and sent emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. Claiming emails held during the outage would be permanently deleted within 24 hours unless recipients restored them, the threat actors created a false sense of urgency, tricking recipients into clicking malicious links and potentially exposing their login credentials.

“We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext,” Jeremiah Jasmin, security researcher at Microsoft, said in a blog post.

Outages in cloud services bring about uncertainty and panic, an area where attackers always thrive, said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. “In cases where employees cannot access their emails and other applications, they will easily fall victim to any email promising to restore their service or help recover their account. This is especially dangerous for industries like finance, health care, government and educational institutions because employees in such organizations work with sensitive data and rely heavily on cloud services,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners.

Carefully constructed phishing trap

The attackers used several techniques to make the emails appear relevant to recipients while evading basic email security filters. These included using specific sender domains, randomised outage-related subject lines, recipient-specific tracking links and a common non-Microsoft destination domain. The combination made the messages harder to identify through conventional pattern matching.

The campaign began with emails sent from domains including moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com. Their subject lines followed the pattern “Outage” followed by a randomised string of characters. Microsoft also found a fake email conversation embedded in the message body, positioned to remain hidden from recipients. This appeared to be an attempt to evade email filtering mechanisms.

The messages impersonated Microsoft 365 service health notifications. They used recipient-specific display name prefixes and referenced Microsoft services, including Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot.

To create a sense of urgency, the emails claimed that messages held during the November 12 Exchange Online disruption would be deleted within 24 hours. Recipients were prompted to click a prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” button. The links contained recipient-specific tracking URLs that recorded or routed clicks before redirecting users to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html.

One of the emails analysed by Microsoft had a subject line following the pattern “Outage – ” and a display name comprising a three-character organisation-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification.” Its body referred to a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12, claimed that four messages had been held during the outage and warned that they would be deleted within 24 hours unless restored.

A successful credential theft attempt could expose more than an employee’s email account. Dhar explained that, depending on the permissions of the user, threat actors can gain access to sensitive emails, customer information, balance sheets, SharePoint, OneDrive Storage, and Microsoft Teams communication. Moreover, attackers can pretend to be representatives of the company and send believable emails to colleagues, clients, and contractors for the purposes of money fraud or theft of credentials.

From containment to preparedness

Microsoft said it had not observed any evidence of account compromise linked to the campaign. Messages detected and protected by Microsoft Defender for Office 365 were being blocked or quarantined. However, the company has advised organisations to remain vigilant and take several precautionary steps.

CISOs should search email telemetry for the identified sender domains, display-name and subject-line patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domains. Matching messages should be quarantined, and copies already delivered to inboxes should be removed in accordance with the organisation’s incident response procedures.

Security teams should also identify users who clicked on campaign links and review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to establish whether they reached the malicious destination and potentially entered their credentials. If credentials were exposed, organisations should immediately reset the affected passwords, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations.

They should also check affected accounts for suspicious sign-ins, unauthorised OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive or Teams. Microsoft has also advised security teams to block or closely monitor reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Employees should be reminded that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct users to non-Microsoft domains to recover held emails.

Dhar added that organizations should make cybersecurity an integral part of their business continuity planning. Any technology disruption should trigger heightened security monitoring and clear internal communication to ensure employees know how to verify service-related updates. He also recommended conducting phishing simulations during such disruptions to test how employees respond to suspicious communications. CIOs and CISOs should regularly conduct tabletop exercises to assess their preparedness for attacks that exploit technology outages.

The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld.

Title: Apple Tightens macOS App Permissions to Limit Data Access Amid AI Agent Security Risks
Context: "Additional entitlement details will be available soon
Full Text:
Apple on Monday introduced new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

The changes, currently previewed in macOS 27.3 beta 2, relate to increased transparency and more options for two of its APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access.

"Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk," Apple said in a statement. "These changes are designed to help them do that and to empower them to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy."

To that end, Device Control and Data Access is being split into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility.

Other changes include -

A single method for granting permissions by selecting the requesting app from a list

Encouraging users to grant access to just the specific apps (for System & App Protection Override) or folders (for Full Disk Access) that are required for their workflows

Increased visibility into the range of data that apps will receive access to or have control over when users grant full permissions

An option for users to configure apps to ask every time they require access

A transparency indicator when one app is controlling another app using System & App Protection Override

Apple stressed that app permissions previously granted by users will remain intact, adding that developers should be prepared to make changes to their onboarding workflows to ensure their apps can handle scenarios where access is granted to only a limited set of folders or apps via these APIs.

In addition, apps that use Full Disk Access for disk backup or the new Accessibility settings for assistive technologies can request entitlements to offer the same experience for new installations that they offered before macOS 27.3.

"Currently, known apps aren't affected and will keep the same experience without an entitlement," the tech giant added. "Additional entitlement details will be available soon."

The development comes a little over a month after Apple began taking steps to tighten controls around a macOS setting called Full Disk Access (FDA) due to security risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents.
