Title: Optimizely hack infected CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce sites with malware
Context: The company confirmed to BleepingComputer that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer...
Full Text:
A supply chain attack targeting Optimizely has led to malicious JavaScript being loaded on numerous popular websites, including Zoom, CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce, and GitLab, exposing visitors to scripts designed to steal cryptocurrency and payment information and exploit vulnerabilities in iOS devices.

Optimizely is a digital experience and experimentation platform used by organizations to test and personalize their websites, with its JavaScript files loaded into customers' webpages to deliver this functionality.

The company confirmed to BleepingComputer that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects, causing websites using the platform to load malware.

"Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow," Optimizely told BleepingComputer.

"They used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix. We have removed the injected code from affected projects. We have also ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts. Finally, we have blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare.

"We are continuing to investigate and will publish any relevant updates at status.optimizely.com. We have notified all affected customers."

Major brands impacted

The attack was first uncovered by security researcher Scott Helme, who reported Monday that his team identified 188 infected Optimizely JavaScript files belonging to 178 organizations after analyzing 1,611 scripts used by the platform.

BleepingComputer independently confirmed that the malicious script loaded, or attempted to load, on numerous affected websites using scans recorded by urlscan.io, including Zoom, KLM, GitLab, BBC, Scheels, CNN, American Girl, ManageBuilding, Smartsheet, Stamps.com, and Salesforce.

Other affected websites include Fox News, Mutual of Omaha, American Eagle, Air France, Change.org, Optimizely, HSBC Insurance, Bitly, IG, and UNICEF USA.

Salesforce confirmed it is investigating the malicious modifications to Optimizely scripts used on some of its websites.

"As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances. We continue to investigate and will notify affected customers without undue delay if we identify unauthorized access to their data," Salesforce told BleepingComputer.

BleepingComputer analyzed copies of the modified Optimizely JavaScript files and confirmed that attackers had injected code designed to load an additional malicious script from https://1688360[.]cc/track.js.

The injected code used several methods to load the payload, with some files referencing the malicious URL directly, while others used Base64 encoding and JavaScript's atob() function to decode the URL.

Helme also identified a variation that could execute an embedded copy of the malicious code if the remote script was blocked.

An analysis of the malicious track.js file revealed several capabilities, which Helme also documented in his investigation:

Cryptocurrency hijacking: Monitors webpages for cryptocurrency wallet addresses and replaces them with attacker-controlled addresses to steal transfers.

Payment card skimming: Searches for credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes entered into webpages, and attempts to transmit the captured information to https://1688360[.]cc/card.php.

iOS exploit delivery: Loads additional malicious JavaScript targeting iPhones and iPads. Helme identified these secondary payloads as the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits, which target different iOS versions.

The malicious script also contains functionality to collect browser cookies, webpage URLs, and screenshots, which can be transmitted to the attackers.

Helme's investigation found that cryptocurrency wallets embedded in the `track.js` script had received approximately $7,000 in transactions as of November 16. However, some wallets were active before the attack, making it difficult to determine how much cryptocurrency was stolen during the campaign.

Title: Java4Shell: Remote Code Execution in OpenJDK (CVE-2026-114938)
Context: Exploiting this vulnerability requires the affected Java runtime to execute its AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) decoding path
Full Text:
Key points and observations

CVE-2026-114938 is an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's optimized Base64 decoder.

Denial of service is the more readily achievable impact where attacker-controlled input reaches the vulnerable decoder. Reliable remote code execution requires additional exploitation work tailored to the application and Java Virtual Machine (JVM) environment.

Exploiting this vulnerability requires the affected Java runtime to execute its AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) decoding path. Systems running on processors that lack AVX-512 VBMI support are not affected.

On affected x86-64 deployments, starting the JVM with -XX:UseAVX=2 disables the AVX-512 path and prevented out-of-bounds writes in our tests. Scope the flag to x86 deployments as native ARM64 JVMs do not recognize it and will fail to start if that flag is passed.

In a standalone test, the extra write corrupted a neighboring array's header and the JVM later crashed during garbage collection. The resulting damage depends on which objects occupy the overwritten memory.

What happened

On November 17, 2026, Oracle released a security update for CVE-2026-114938, an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK’s optimized Base64 decoder. This vulnerability affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later and has been rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0.

While the vulnerability can lead to remote code execution in a worst-case scenario, it is important to stress that an attacker would have to do additional work for every application they target. There is no single, universal exploit that would work against all Java applications.

How to know if you’re affected

Oracle stated that the Java versions affected by vulnerabilities patched in this release are as below:

Java release line

Affected releases

First fixed release

Java 17

17.0.6 through versions before 17.0.21.1

17.0.21.1+4

Java 21

All versions of Java 21 before 21.0.13.1

21.0.13.1+4

Java 25

All versions of Java 25 before 25.0.5.1

25.0.5.1+4

Java 27

All versions of Java 27 before 27.0.1.1

27.0.1.1+4

In addition to running a vulnerable version of Java, the application must be running on a CPU that supports the AVX-512 VBMI decoding path. Not all systems (including modern ones) support this instruction set so it is recommended to check when prioritizing systems for patching. The following is a shell command to see if the instruction set is supported:

grep -om1 -E 'avx512[_]?vbmi' /proc/cpuinfo

If this command returns nothing, that is an indication that the CPU does not support VBMI. If the command returns avx512vbmi and/or avx512_vbmi, that is a signal that it does support VBMI and could be potentially vulnerable.

Native ARM64 Java runtimes are not affected by this vulnerability because they do not execute the vulnerable x86 AVX-512 decoding path.

An affected Java runtime and a compatible CPU are prerequisites, but the application must also pass attacker-controlled data to the vulnerable decoder. In the OpenJDK 17.0.6 build we tested, the AVX-512 path handles the basic and URL decoders returned by Base64.getDecoder() and Base64.getUrlDecoder(). The MIME decoder returned by Base64.getMimeDecoder() bypasses this path.

This distinction matters when assessing authentication and token-processing code. Base64-encoded credentials, tokens, or SAML messages expose an application only if its implementation passes the malformed value to the affected decoder. Libraries that implement their own decoding, or reject or normalize the value before calling the JDK decoder, can behave differently.

From a Java method to a native decoder

Java's Base64.Decoder supports decoding into a new array or one supplied by the caller. In both cases, it calculates the required output space before decoding. The allocating method uses that calculation directly:

public byte[] decode(byte[] src) { byte[] dst = new byte[decodedOutLength(src, 0, src.length)]; int ret = decode0(src, 0, src.length, dst); if (ret != dst.length) { dst = Arrays.copyOf(dst, ret); } return dst; }

The allocation is not the source of the overflow. Further down this call chain, HotSpot's optimizing compiler, C2, can replace decodeBlock() with a native implementation. These replacements, called intrinsics, let the JVM use specialized CPU instructions. The native implementation must respect the bounds of the Java arrays it receives.

The AVX-512 decoding routine converts each 64-byte input block into 48 output bytes. When fewer than 64 input bytes remain, a separate handler decodes the final fragment. That is where the length calculation goes wrong.

Padding produces a negative output length

Consider a value containing 128 A characters followed by one =:

value = b"A" * 128 + b"="

The first 128 characters form complete Base64 groups. The final = is invalid: Padding cannot form a group by itself. However, the initial output-length calculation does not reject this value. It counts the input and trailing padding and produces a destination length of 98 bytes.

The native routine decodes the first 128 characters into 96 bytes. It then reaches the final-fragment handler with just the = remaining.

To calculate the fragment's output size, the handler divides the remaining length by four, discards the remainder, and multiplies by three. In HotSpot's code generator, those operations are:

__ movl(output_size, length); __ shrl(output_size, 2); // Find (len / 4) * 3 (output length) __ lea(output_size, Address(output_size, output_size, Address::times_2, 0));

For a 1-byte fragment, this produces zero. The padding branch then decrements output_size for the trailing =. There is no check that the result remains nonnegative, so the count becomes -1.

The same problem occurs with other fragments containing fewer than 4 bytes.

The negative count enables a full-width store

AVX-512 supports masked stores, where individual mask bits determine which bytes reach memory. The decoder uses the output count to construct such a mask. A count of zero should permit no writes; a count of three should permit 3 output bytes.

The code starts with a 64-bit value whose bits are all set, then uses BZHI to retain the requested number of low bits:

__ movq(output_mask, -1); __ bzhiq(output_mask, output_mask, output_size);

BZHI reads its bit count from the low byte of the last operand. For -1, that byte is 255. For -2, it is 254. Both exceed the width of the 64-bit operand, so the instruction leaves all 64 bits set.

The contents of the write also follow from the implementation. The tail handler fills unused input positions with the character a before decoding the vector. Much of the excess output is consequently the repeating byte pattern 69 a6 9a. The vulnerability causes a constrained overwrite rather than a freely chosen 64-byte value.

An exception does not contain the corruption

The decoder eventually throws IllegalArgumentException for the malformed input. The Java API permits partially written output when decoding fails. Here, however, the native routine has written outside the output array altogether.

This explains why the symptom may appear far from the decoder call. A write into unused heap space can go unnoticed. A write into an object header can instead damage information that the JVM consults later, including during garbage collection. Catching the decoding exception leaves that damage in place.

Mitigation

Follow your Java runtime vendor's guidance for a fixed build. Include runtimes bundled with applications and container images in that review. After updating a container base image, rebuild and redeploy the application image. Restart affected Java processes so they use the updated runtime.

If an update cannot be deployed immediately, our tests confirmed two JVM startup options that prevented the out-of-bounds writes.

To disable the Base64 intrinsics specifically, add:

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

Alternatively, on x86-64 deployments, disable AVX-512 execution by limiting the JVM to AVX2:

-XX:UseAVX=2

Disabling the Base64 intrinsics is the narrower workaround. Limiting AVX affects other JVM operations that use AVX-512, so assess its performance impact on your workload.

Scope UseAVX=2 to x86 deployments. Native ARM64 JVMs do not execute the vulnerable code, and they do not recognize this option. Adding it to shared startup settings can prevent ARM64 services from starting.

Apply the selected option to the application's JVM startup configuration and restart the service. Check the running process, including any bundled runtime, rather than relying on the Java installation found on your shell's path. Where jcmd is available, inspect the runtime version and effective flags with:

jcmd <PID> VM.version jcmd <PID> VM.flags -all

Confirm that the process reports UseBASE64Intrinsics = false or UseAVX = 2, depending on the workaround selected.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Live Processes provide real-time visibility into the processes running on your infrastructure. You can use it to identify Java processes running on x86-64 hosts, then filter to determine which hosts are running an affected Java runtime.

Datadog Cloud Security Management reports findings for CVE-2026-114938. Check the vulnerability findings for affected hosts and container images.

Conclusion

While this vulnerability can lead to remote code execution, its practical impact depends on the environment.

Applications running on processors without AVX-512 VBMI support are not affected by this vulnerability. On affected systems, denial of service is more readily achievable than reliable code execution. Attackers seeking to execute arbitrary code would need to tailor their exploits to the Java runtime and application behavior, which complicates the development of a broadly reusable exploit.

These constraints give security teams a way to prioritize their response, but affected services still need prompt attention. Follow your runtime vendor’s guidance for a fixed build, including Java runtimes bundled with applications or container images. Where an update cannot be deployed immediately, disable the vulnerable decoding path as a temporary workaround.

Title: Gemini AI agents repeatedly bypassed safeguards to attack real website
Context: Trajectory Labs discovered the activity while reviewing agent transcripts and notified Epoch AI of the unauthorized attacks the following morning
Full Text:
Google's Gemini AI agents repeatedly attempted to hack a real organization's website during AI model safety testing, finding ways to circumvent increasingly restrictive security controls designed to prevent them from accessing live systems.

The security incidents occurred in October as AI safety research company Trajectory Labs tested whether Gemini 4 Argon agents would engage in unauthorized behavior when faced with an impossible task, even with the model's built-in API safeguards enabled.

In reports published Friday, Trajectory Labs and the targeted organization, Epoch AI, revealed that the agents attempted SQL injection attacks, probed for sensitive information, impersonated employees, and repeatedly circumvented network restrictions introduced to contain their activity.

Epoch AI said it had not independently verified which AI models were involved, and that the Gemini identification came from Trajectory Labs.

The researchers tasked the agents with retrieving official answers to nonexistent problems from Epoch AI's FrontierMath benchmark, repeatedly instructing them to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up."

On October 20, approximately 40 agents began probing Epoch AI's live website for sensitive information, including administrator credentials and access to proprietary benchmark evaluation logs.

Epoch AI detected the activity and deployed an "agent hotline" that allowed the agents to send messages directly to its employees.

For three hours, the agents made 36,411 requests to a planted API endpoint and sent 487 messages through the hotline, including some that attempted to impersonate actual Epoch employees or claimed to be engineers and auditors requesting benchmark information.

An investigation also identified an attempted SQL injection attack and more than 200 attempts to access FrontierMath evaluation logs.

Trajectory Labs discovered the activity while reviewing agent transcripts and notified Epoch AI of the unauthorized attacks the following morning.

After discussing the incident with Epoch, the researchers agreed to continue testing against a local copy of the website instead of its live infrastructure.

However, the agents continued finding ways to circumvent the restrictions.

During testing on October 23, some agents recognized they were interacting with a copy of Epoch's website, identified the real website's IP address, and connected directly to its live infrastructure, bypassing DNS redirection designed to contain them.

When researchers blocked the IP addresses used to reach Epoch, an agent switched to another address that allowed it to access the live website again.

Trajectory Labs subsequently configured its network proxy to block direct connections to Epoch, but an agent found another way to retrieve the website's public content through a third-party web-reader service.

"In some of these runs, the agents worked out that they were on a copy, identified the correct raw IP to bypass our redirect, and reached the live site again, which Epoch alerted us about," Trajectory Labs explained.

In a separate technical analysis, Trajectory Labs researchers also discovered that the agents created a message board through a shared software package cache to communicate with each other, exchanging information about vulnerabilities and exploitation methods.

In one example, an agent shared a technique for bypassing restrictions on a deliberately vulnerable copy of Epoch's website, which another agent subsequently used to obtain credentials and complete the task.

The researchers also observed agents attempting to bypass CAPTCHA protections and impersonating employees to trick an AI assistant into revealing protected benchmark information.

Beginning October 26, Epoch AI agreed to work with Trajectory Labs on additional experiments, knowing the agents would have internet access and could interact with its public website.

During these tests, the agents again accessed Epoch's live infrastructure, making more than 65,000 requests to a planted API endpoint and attempting further SQL injection attacks and employee impersonation.

Trajectory Labs later moved testing into fully isolated environments without internet access.

Even after this change, the agents still tried to disable a fake control that allegedly blocked network access, and they succeeded in all three complete test runs.

The researchers said that the agents had not been explicitly instructed to hack websites or impersonate employees. However, they were given an impossible objective on purpose and repeatedly instructed not to give up.

Trajectory Labs acknowledged that the incidents resulted from shortcomings in its testing procedures, including conducting experiments without obtaining the affected organization's consent and relying on built-in model safeguards without sufficient additional monitoring.

On November 2, the company suspended all AI misalignment testing pending a risk assessment and the addition of further safeguards.

"These incidents show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely," Trajectory Labs warned.

Neither organization confirmed that any private Epoch AI information was exposed during the incidents.

This report comes as California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company failed to adequately contain autonomous AI agents during testing, resulting in more than 80 incidents in which it lost control of the agents.

The lawsuit follows a July incident in which nearly 700 OpenAI-powered agents escaped a controlled testing environment and attacked Hugging Face's production infrastructure while attempting to steal cybersecurity benchmark answers.

Title: Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach
Context: Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data
Full Text: Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data. "Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register. According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade. The intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson said. “We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue." Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years. Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected. The Register will update this story as we learn more about the breach.®

Title: The Bank Outage May Have Nothing to Do With Your Bank
Context: ” Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic issue” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were...
Full Text:
If you were planning to do any banking today, good luck.

Customers of many major financial institutions experienced unspecified technical issues on Monday as thousands of reports flooded the uptime-tracking website Downdetector.com from people saying that they had issues using their banks in some way.

It is currently unclear which systems are having issues. However, the problem may stem from technical difficulties at JPMorganChase, the top retail bank that holds over 10 percent of all US deposits, did identify a specific issue.

“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems—there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” says JPMorganChase spokesperson Pablo Rodriguez. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”

Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic issue” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.” The spokesperson adds that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds” and that the bank is working to resolve the issues.

Apparent issues with the banks, credit unions, fintech apps, and credit card companies appear to begin around 9:30 am ET and peaked at around 2 pm ET. Many people also reported issues using Zelle, the peer-to-peer money-transfer system adopted by major banks. However, in a statement, Zelle denied its systems were the cause of the reported outages while acknowledging that issues at banks may impact people’s ability to use Zelle.

“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” a Zelle spokesperson says in a statement. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds.”

US Bank spokesperson Jeffrey Shelman also says the financial institution’s systems “are not directly impacted.” Shelman adds, however, that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”

Seth Eisen, senior vice president of communications at MasterCard, says, “Our network is operating normally.” A Visa spokesperson says the company is aware of the ongoing payments issue, but that Visa’s systems are operating normally too.

According to reports on Downdetector, which is sourced to user reports rather than official statements, the issues on Monday also impacted customers of Bank of America, Capital One, Wells Fargo, TD Bank, Navy Credit Federal Union, and more. These companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Title: Flightageddon grounds the nation.
Context: Kaspersky warns that a remote code execution vulnerability in Telegram’s newly launched widgets feature may have been exploited in the wild to deliver WebRAT, a Rust-based trojan also known as Salat Stealer. Cybersecurity firm Forescout Technologies reports that publicly available artificial intelligence models can...
Full Text:
U.S. airline operations return to normal. Microsoft unpacks last week’s outage. Commerce Secretary Lutnick defends less stringent export controls on advanced AI chips. Italy fines Meta 887 million dollars for privacy violations. Telegram’s new widgets may deliver a RAT. The FBI warns of ARTEX pen testing abuse. Refrigeration controllers see opportunistic scanning. Publicly available AI models dramatically accelerate vulnerability discovery. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Patrick Coughlin, CEO and Co-Founder of Savi Security, sharing how shopping fraud has industrialized in the AI era. A refrigerator company learns it’s secretly leading the laundry revolution.

Today is Monday November 16th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

U.S. airline operations return to normal.

U.S. airline operations are largely returning to normal following a rare four-hour nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA on Friday, November 13, which caused thousands of cancellations and stranding travelers into the weekend.

Officials confirmed the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack, attributing it instead to aging telecom infrastructure and legacy hardware. Specifically, an L3Harris contractor upgrading copper wire to fiber replaced a Cisco 600-series router manufactured between 2001 and 2006. The faulty router began flooding the network with login attempts, spreading instability across 17 FAA facilities and prompting the agency to halt flights out of an abundance of caution while 3,500 planes were airborne.

In response, the Trump administration increased its funding request for air traffic control modernization to $30 billion, noting that a previous $12.5 billion allocation is insufficient. However, Democratic lawmakers pointed out that only $1 billion of those initial funds have been spent so far, demanding accountability at an upcoming congressional briefing.

Microsoft unpacks last week’s outage.

Microsoft has traced last week's nearly 24-hour global Microsoft 365 outage to a latent Windows defect in its cloud networking gateway servers. According to Redmond's preliminary incident report, the bug, introduced via a server-specific fix deployed back in July, caused severe "lock contention," where competing internal processes exhausted processor and memory capacity on newer, multi-core hardware.

The defect remained hidden for over three months until a shift in Microsoft Teams traffic collided with a 14 percent reduction in server capacity. As servers crashed, automated failover systems rerouted connections to healthy endpoints, triggering a cascading failure that rendered over 80 percent of servers unresponsive and severely disrupted Exchange Online.

Engineers eventually mitigated the crisis by rolling back the faulty connection-handling update and gradually restoring traffic. While Microsoft confirms customer Windows devices were unaffected and require no configuration changes, the incident underscores how automated recovery mechanisms can inadvertently amplify systemic cloud failures.

Commerce Secretary Lutnick defends less stringent export controls on advanced AI chips.

According to The New York Times, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been advocating for less stringent export controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips, rules that directly affect Southeast Asian data centers with financial ties to his former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.

While the US bans the direct sale of cutting-edge Nvidia chips to China, Chinese tech firms can legally rent computing power from facilities in countries like Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. Lutnick, who transferred leadership and ownership of Cantor Fitzgerald to his sons, has pushed to limit new regulations to only seven countries, exempt existing data centers, and require government notifications rather than strict licenses.

Cantor Fitzgerald has arranged major financing for several of these data center operators, including Singapore-based Bitdeer, which plans to supply Nvidia computing power to Chinese tech giant Tencent. National security analysts and Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns over potential conflicts of interest and warned that narrower rules will allow Beijing to easily bypass restrictions.

Conversely, a Commerce Department spokeswoman stated that Lutnick bases his policy decisions strictly on US national interests, does not discuss department matters with his sons, and has complied with all federal ethics agreements. Furthermore, proponents of a lighter regulatory touch argue that overly broad restrictions could stifle American innovation and harm US companies like Nvidia.

Italy fines Meta 887 million dollars for privacy violations.

Italy’s data protection authority has fined Meta 805 million euros, roughly 887 million US dollars, for accessing Android users’ photos, videos, and metadata without specific consent or proper notification.

According to the regulator, the violation stems from Facebook’s gallery suggestions feature, introduced in 2023. The app bundled camera roll access into a single, generic authorization prompt, leaving roughly 20 million Italian users unaware they were permitting Facebook to scan their personal galleries for post ideas. Regulators noted the infringement remains ongoing for users who have not updated their apps, and cited Meta’s lack of cooperation during the investigation when calculating the penalty.

Meta announced it will appeal, calling the fine disproportionate. Moving forward, Menlo Park must implement a separate, transparent consent prompt detailing how gallery data is accessed and how users can opt out.

Telegram’s new widgets may deliver a RAT.

Kaspersky warns that a remote code execution vulnerability in Telegram’s newly launched widgets feature may have been exploited in the wild to deliver WebRAT, a Rust-based trojan also known as Salat Stealer. According to the Russian security firm, visiting compromised Telegram channels triggered a hidden PowerShell script to install the malware, which steals cryptocurrency wallets and Telegram account data.

The alert follows proof-of-concept videos from researchers at V12 demonstrating exploits against Telegram’s Android and Windows clients, which they attribute to running the QuickJS JavaScript engine without a sandbox.

While Kaspersky advises users against launching widgets until patched, Telegram CEO Pavel Durov dismissed the claims, stating users cannot be hacked merely by receiving a message and confirming that server-side patches have already resolved the underlying scenario.

The FBI warns of ARTEX pen testing abuse.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation has issued a Flash notice warning that threat actors are increasingly weaponizing ARTEX, an open-source, artificial intelligence-driven penetration testing framework, to execute rapid, global cyber intrusions. Since at least August 2026, attackers have used the tool to target sectors including finance, government, defense, and healthcare, compromising over two thousand downstream tenants in a ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply chain breach and stealing data on roughly 67,000 individuals from South Korean financial institutions.

Released on GitHub in July 2026, ARTEX plugs into external large language models to automate reconnaissance and exploitation, enabling some intrusions to achieve privileged access in under three hours. According to the FBI, attackers predominantly pair the framework with Chinese-origin models like DeepSeek Flash due to low costs and minimal guardrails.

Although the creator removed the original repository in October following widespread abuse, community forks and commercial variants continue to proliferate. The Bureau notes that ARTEX’s speed leaves defenders little time to respond, urging organizations to bolster defenses on overlooked portals and third-party integrations.

Refrigeration controllers see opportunistic scanning.

Threat actors began attempting to exploit newly disclosed vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers less than two hours after the flaws went public, according to security firm VulnCheck.

Researchers uncovered 14 flaws, each capable of yielding root privileges, after similar controllers were targeted in an October attack on 700 French supermarkets that France attributed to Iran. While nine vulnerabilities affect older firmware, five impact the latest builds, including predictable daily passwords derived from the device's exposed MAC address. Because Copeland ended support for the XWEB EVO line in March 2026, these flaws will not be patched.

VulnCheck’s sensors detected opportunistic scanning targeting unauthenticated flaws on November 12 and 13. With nearly 2,000 hosts exposed online, researchers urge operators to isolate these legacy devices behind a VPN and migrate to supported models.

Publicly available AI models dramatically accelerate vulnerability discovery.

Cybersecurity firm Forescout Technologies reports that publicly available artificial intelligence models can dramatically accelerate vulnerability discovery in critical infrastructure software on a tight budget.

Using a custom AI-assisted research harness to examine 10 popular TCP/IP stacks, Forescout researchers compressed roughly nine months of work into just 90 hours, combining 10 hours of AI scanning with 80 hours of manual validation. The effort uncovered 99 flaws, including 66 zero-day vulnerabilities, at a static analysis cost of roughly $935, or $2.58 per finding. (Researchers noted binary analysis proved six times costlier and twice as slow as source-code review.)

Forescout VP of Research Daniel dos Santos warned that while AI still requires human expertise, it fundamentally alters vulnerability economics, allowing defenders and attackers alike to find embedded software bugs faster and cheaper.

Monday business briefing.

Venture capital and mergers and acquisitions in the cybersecurity sector remain heavily focused on artificial intelligence, cloud security, and managed services, according to recent industry announcements.

On the funding front, Israeli AI detection and response platform Daylight led the pack with an $80 million Series B round backed by Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Fellow Israeli startups also saw major investments as Bay emerged from stealth with $50 million, cloud backup provider Dreeze raised $33 million, and SecOps platform Brava secured $15 million. Meanwhile, US firms Lazarus AI and WhiteMatter raised $43 million and $20 million respectively, and Italian automation startup CyberKord closed $3 million.

In M&A activity spanning four countries, compliance platform Vanta agreed to acquire Israeli agentic security firm Pillar Security, while Cogent acquired AI penetration testing startup Specular. Elsewhere, ShorePoint absorbed federal contracts from Coalfire Federal, while managed security and consulting consolidation saw acquisitions by Brite, ASI Solutions, Entech, and Saepio.

A refrigerator company learns it’s secretly leading the laundry revolution.

Stirling Marathon, a modest appliance maker in Elora, Ontario, recently learned it was poised to revolutionize the North American laundry industry. There was just one minor catch: the company only makes refrigerators, freezers, and coolers.

According to CBC News, the sudden surge in fame was courtesy of an artificial intelligence scam. Fraudsters blended legitimate company marketing photos with AI-generated footage on YouTube to hawk a fictitious "bombshell" washing machine called "the Keel."

Customer service representative Jordan Cuddihy first realized something was amiss on a Wednesday morning after fielding puzzled inquiries from across the continent, and watching hopeful bargain-hunters physically show up at the facility. A quick Google search revealed the phantom appliance, prompting YouTube to eventually pull the plug on both the video and the channel. For Stirling Marathon, it was a brief, unsolicited brush with industrial disruption, proving that in the age of AI, you don’t actually need to manufacture a product to generate buzz.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Full Text:
U.S. banks suffered widespread outages, disrupting online banking and payments and raising concerns about technology dependencies and resilience.

A wave of service disruptions affected several major U.S. banks on Monday, November 16, leaving customers unable to access online banking, check account balances or complete financial transactions. The problems also affected digital payments, including Zelle, raising questions about how much financial services depend on the availability of interconnected technology platforms.

According to CBS News, the affected institutions included JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, Capital One and Truist. “Customers at Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, U.S. Bank and other major financial institutions reported service outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com.”

“Other banks seeing a spike in customer complaints about difficulty accessing their accounts include Capital One, Truist and Wells Fargo, while users also reported problems with the digital payments app Zelle, according to the outage tracker.” states CBS News.

Reports began appearing on Monday morning and increased throughout the day. By 2 p.m. Eastern Time, Downdetector had received nearly 4,800 reports concerning Chase alone, making it the bank with the highest number of reported problems.

Customers described difficulties logging into their accounts, checking balances, transferring money and completing wire transactions. Bank of America customers also reported problems with ATMs, while U.S. Bank users experienced issues with online banking and its mobile application. Some Wells Fargo customers couldn’t log in or access transaction information.

The disruption wasn’t limited to online services. A Chase customer in Texas told CBS News that he couldn’t deposit a check at a Dallas branch because the bank’s system was unavailable. The incident illustrates how a technical failure can affect both digital channels and ordinary banking operations.

“Chase Bank’s services are experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson said Monday.” CBS News continues.

The bank explained that some transactions were taking longer than usual, while customers could still access their accounts and funds. It said it was working to resolve the problem.

Zelle also attracted attention as customers reported difficulties sending and receiving payments. However, the company said its network was operating normally and pointed to possible problems at participating financial institutions. This distinction matters because Zelle doesn’t maintain separate customer accounts or hold their funds. Instead, participating banks and credit unions manage the underlying accounts and transactions.

Its network operator, Early Warning Services, is owned by several major financial institutions, including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo. This structure highlights how a disruption affecting one part of the banking infrastructure can potentially create problems across services that rely on participating institutions.

The banking problems came amid a particularly difficult week for U.S. technology infrastructure. On November 12, Microsoft 365 suffered a widespread outage that disrupted Outlook, Teams and other services. The following day, a technical failure in the Federal Aviation Administration’s communications infrastructure triggered a nationwide ground stop, suspending departing flights for several hours. Workday, a major provider of human resources and payroll software, also experienced service disruptions on November 13. Fox News documented the sequence of incidents, while Newsweek also reported the growing number of technology disruptions.

The timing has inevitably raised concerns about whether these incidents might share a common cause, particularly given the importance of Microsoft services, telecommunications and third-party technology providers to critical business operations. However, the available information doesn’t establish a connection between the incidents, and there is no evidence that the banking disruptions were caused by a coordinated cyberattack.

Microsoft attributed its earlier service interruption to a technical problem rather than malicious activity.

For security professionals, the incidents offer a useful reminder: service availability is a security and operational resilience issue, even when no attacker is involved. Financial institutions rely on complex chains of applications, infrastructure providers, telecommunications networks and external services. A failure at one point can affect customers far beyond the organization where the original problem occurred.

The distinction between a cyberattack and a technical failure is important, but it shouldn’t lead organizations to underestimate the consequences. Business continuity plans, dependency mapping, alternative communication channels, incident response procedures and clear customer communication all matter when essential services become unavailable.

A system doesn’t need to be compromised to become unavailable, and customers don’t care much about the distinction when they can’t access their money.

Title: The Race to Remediation: Black October Showed that Threat Intelligence Isn’t Enough
Context: Attacker Speed: A Cloud Security Alliance survey of more than 900 security leaders found that only 9% of organizations remediate critical or high-severity production...
Full Text:
In a single week in October 2026, security teams faced one serious security incident after another. A certificate authority failed, critical flaws in PHP were disclosed after a broken embargo, a popular open-source AI gateway was compromised, and developer platforms reported thefts of customer secrets. Industry insiders started calling the seemingly steady drumbeat of attacks “Black October.”

Any one of these incidents would have kept a security team busy. Collectively, they exposed a bottleneck that has little to do with any single exploit. Security teams are not short on vulnerability information. They are short on answers: what is affected in our environment, and how can we fix it – fast?

As JFrog CEO Shlomi Ben Haim put it: “A single weak link can cost far more than the fix. For LiteLLM and PHP2Shell, being caught off-guard means money, downtime, and customer trust. The companies that come through well are the ones that know exactly what they are running and can act within hours vs. days. JFrog’s role is to find the problems early, tell customers what to do, and make sure they can precisely determine their exposure.”

Three Pressures That Compound

Three forces explain why answers are getting harder to produce:

Volume: In the AI-accelerated landscape of 2026, based on our count of NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) records, 36,952 CVEs were published in Q3 2026 alone, more than triple the 11,725 published in Q3 2025 (as of November 16, 2026).

Exploitability: A severity score does not say whether a flaw is applicable in your environment. Triage by count alone wastes scarce resources and time.

Attacker Speed: A Cloud Security Alliance survey of more than 900 security leaders found that only 9% of organizations remediate critical or high-severity production vulnerabilities within 24 hours, while 74% take between one and seven days. Meanwhile, attackers can use AI to speed up exploitation, chaining together low-severity findings and making repeated automated attempts until one unpatched system gives them an opening.

That is a different kind of weakness, and it needs a different kind of approach. A faster version of the old process will not close it. AI pushes on all three pressures: it surfaces more flaws and drafts more fixes, but maintainers cannot absorb unlimited volume.

The Disclosure Process Wasn’t Built for This

The vulnerability disclosure process was designed around human review cycles. A researcher reports a flaw, a maintainer triages it, a fix is written, and a CVE is published. That rhythm worked when exploitation was also a manual effort. It does not hold up when attackers can automate discovery and exploitation at scale.

Enterprises have also historically depended on upstream maintainers to publish patches on their own timelines, and those timelines are asynchronous with the CVE disclosure window. In an AI-powered threat landscape, that mismatch becomes an exposure gap that attackers can use.

A new ecosystem of patching vendors has stepped in to help close it. These vendors produce signed, backported fixes for the exact versions enterprises actually consume, often ahead of public disclosure.

Why Does Threat Intelligence Alone Leave a Gap?

Threat intelligence describes the outside world, not your software environment. That difference explains why teams with excellent security vulnerability feeds still lose hours after a disclosure. Two gaps open between a published threat and a confident response:

Timing: Public databases trail events. As of October 2026, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) now enriches only a subset of CVEs, and PHP2Shell was being probed days before patches shipped. A process that waits for them is structurally late.

Remediation: Even with timely, contextual intelligence, someone still has to find a trustworthy fix, apply it across every affected artifact (assuming all artifacts are even traceable), and prove it worked. This is where many teams slow from hours to days.

Know Your Exposure With JFrog Threat Hub

Finding problems early and determining exposure precisely is the first half of the job. JFrog Threat Hub, a feature of JFrog Xray, brings JFrog Security Research findings and vetted external advisories into the same single source of truth that holds your scanned artifacts, so a published threat can be matched to your own environment in one step.

Knowing your exposure only matters if you can act on it quickly, which is the second half of the job.

Fortified Defenses Start With One Source of Truth

A month like October does not call for a faster version of the old process. It calls for a different one. In our view, LiteLLM and PHP2Shell showed what separates the teams that come through well: they could see what they run, and they could fix it fast.

Know everything you run

Start with an inventory at every layer: source code, packages, container images, AI models, and agent tooling. A component you cannot see cannot be prioritized or patched. Then verify what you deploy, not only what you wrote, because malicious code can live in built artifacts while the source stays clean. JFrog Artifactory serves as that single source of truth, holding the main artifact types (binaries, containers, AI models, MCP server packages) in one system of record.

Draw on an ecosystem of fix providers

Fix providers often specialize in particular software ecosystems, so drawing on an ecosystem of providers can help broaden coverage. In our view, reducing this risk requires two critical capabilities: high-quality patches across software ecosystems and a control plane designed to automate remediation at the binary level.

Close the loop with zero-touch remediation

A patch sitting in a vendor’s repository does nothing for an artifact already running in production. Artifactory can act as the control plane that ingests each fix from supported partners. JFrog Security can then apply a selected fix according to the customer’s policy and context, and produce a signed evidence chain that can support audit reviews. The goal is a self-healing software supply chain and zero-touch remediation that aims to help customers patch in hours rather than days. For branches past their end of life, migration remains the durable fix.

Ready for the Next Black October?

When the next disclosure lands, what is affected, and can we fix it in hours rather than days? Organizations that can provide a quality answer will weather the next crowded month. Those that cannot will spend it searching.

Move From Disclosure to Fix in Hours

Patching at scale takes a single source of truth, trusted fixes from an ecosystem of partners, and a universal control plane that applies them automatically. Title: Google Project Zero cuts bug disclosures to 30 days amid AI threats
Context: Project Zero says AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and made it easier for attackers to reverse-engineer fixes as soon as patches ship and develop...
Full Text:
Google Project Zero will replace its “90+30” disclosure policy with shorter, fixed deadlines in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

The transition is gradual and began on November 13, when the 30-day extension was removed from the vulnerability disclosure timeline.

On February 2, 2027, the deadline will be further reduced to 60 days, and on January 3, 2028, it will shrink to just 30 days.

Once the deadline expires, Project Zero will publish vulnerability details even if a fix is not available.

Project Zero is Google’s vulnerability research team, focused on the discovery of serious security flaws in widely used software and hardware.

Some of its notable recent findings include a .NET Framework zero-day, flaws in Chrome’s JavaScript engine and graphics components, and a Qualcomm chipset zero-day linked to NoviSpy spyware attacks.

When the team finds a flaw, it reports it privately to the vendor and typically publishes the technical details after a set period, giving time for developing security updates and patches, as well as a margin for most users to apply them.

Project Zero says AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and made it easier for attackers to reverse-engineer fixes as soon as patches ship and develop working exploits.

This policy change puts greater pressure on vendors to investigate reports, develop fixes, and ship them faster to customers.

Project Zero said a gradual approach to shortening the disclosure deadline was the better choice, giving vendors time to develop better flaw management and remediation systems.

Vendors warned Google that jumping straight to 30 days could expose users to severe risks and could lead maintainers to focus on Project Zero findings while ignoring other, potentially more severe flaws reported by others.

“An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology,” Google explained.

“While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.”

Project Zero noted some early disclosure exceptions, such as when a flaw is actively exploited in the wild, when others have already published exploitation or vulnerability details, or when a vendor requests early disclosure.

Exceptions will also apply for non-disclosure, as Google deems fit, using the example of Spectre and Meltdown, for which it previously withheld information for longer than 120 days.

Title: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
Context: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical...
Full Text: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence. Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks. In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys. “Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models. In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks. “The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote. The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt. In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.” Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image. While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote. None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker. “The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.” The FBI weighs in The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.” The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants. After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October. However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI. The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert. These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

Title: Google GTIG Warns AI Agents Automate Exploits, Steal Credentials and Scale Cybercrime
Context: For the first time, GTIG saw attackers automate discovery and exploitation with no human in the loop
Full Text:
Google finds attackers using autonomous AI agents to automate exploits, steal AI access and scale intrusions, often sacrificing stealth for speed.

Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says attackers have moved past typing prompts into a chatbot. They now run autonomous, multi-agent frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI to carry out multi-stage intrusions faster.

“Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.” reads the GTIG report. “Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention.”

The basic attack methods have not changed. What has changed is how quickly attackers can use them. These tools still rely on stolen credentials and systems that have not been patched. Amazon reached the same conclusion after monitoring its own decoy systems: None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. The difference is that AI agents can combine these techniques and carry out several steps without stopping.

These frameworks have three main capabilities. They can find and exploit simple vulnerabilities, ask an LLM to create custom payloads when needed, and change their approach based on the results they get. GTIG observed CAIRN and PentAGI being used in real attacks, while CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI were still being tested. CAIRN allows different AI agents to work together and share information through a common workspace. GTIG found evidence of its use against several targets, including organizations in the US aerospace sector.

CyberStrikeAI connects commercial and open-weight AI models to more than 100 security tools. HexStrike AI gives LLM-based clients access to over 150 tools, managed by more than 12 specialized agents. PentAGI is designed for less experienced operators. Between late August and early October, one attacker used a modified version of the framework to systematically scan organizations across Asia.

A China-nexus group also appears to be building its own framework. Others use ZeroHollow, an inference service for exploit development and routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework that runs code on its own. Google expects the trend to continue, since the barrier to entry is low and adding exploits is easy.

“We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with the use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus. This includes evidence that a PRC-nexus group was developing its own automated attack framework for likely use in cyber espionage operations.” continues the report. “These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation.”

Vulnerability research is moving the same way. For the first time, GTIG saw attackers automate discovery and exploitation with no human in the loop. An exposed staging server hosted a framework called exploit_agent that compares popular web software before and after patches, drafts exploits and runs them. Victim data suggested interest in French media, entertainment and education sites, and the configuration notes were in Russian and told the operator to put the API keys in the file, not in the chat.

Once a vulnerability is patched, attackers have more information to work with. They can study the affected code, release notes, security research and proof-of-concept exploits to find ways to attack systems that have not yet been updated. Between January and August 2026, the number of vulnerability disclosures and exploits nearly doubled. Zero-day exploits also increased, from an average of 8 per month in 2025 to 11 in 2026, before reaching 22 in August.

The PaperCut case shows how quickly attackers can move. Two flaws were exploited as zero-days in late August, and Huntress and other researchers developed working exploits within 24 hours. GreyNoise detected an attack campaign just four days after the flaws were disclosed. In one case, attackers went from gaining access to obtaining domain administrator privileges within minutes.

The same pattern appeared with two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Researchers used LLMs to analyse the flaws, and details about the patched code and a proof-of-concept video appeared before the October 21 patch. Hundreds of exploit claims then emerged, but many did not work. Defenders had to spend time checking which reports were genuine.

LLMjacking is the money side. Attackers steal LLM credentials and cloud resources, then resell access. Mandiant handled incidents where fraudulent charges passed $100,000 in a day, and the worst reached $1 million before cleanup.

They got in with credentials from public GitHub repositories and fake sites that harvest session tokens. One actor used CVE-2026-40217, a LiteLLM sandbox escape that turns limited keys into admin credentials. Some created and deleted short-lived service accounts to dodge rate limits, and others started powerful GPU instances. In one case two attackers used the same credentials, and a botnet made millions of API calls in about 24 hours before they were revoked.

The loot goes to “LLM mixers,” storefronts that route buyers through pools of stolen credentials and compute.

“Threat actors frequently monetize LLMJacking intrusions by selling access to compromised compute and LLM resources. In addition to the rise of LLMJacking, GTIG is tracking the proliferation of “LLM Mixers”—illicit storefronts that provide buyers with unauthorized access to LLM services and underlying proxy infrastructure.” continues the report. “This infrastructure routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.”

GTIG saw prices from $0.10 to $25 per million tokens on Russian- and Chinese-language markets. APIMart multiplies prices by five above 100,000 tokens, and JetNight sells monthly subscriptions. Even criminals have a surcharge for long prompts.

Information operations now use LLMs as standard tools, and GTIG says so with high confidence. That covers state groups tied to Russia, China and Iran, commercial influence vendors and profit-driven networks pumping out political clickbait. Better content doesn’t automatically mean more impact, and profit networks can look like state campaigns.

In August, GTIG found a platform built on the Gemini API and other tools to automate personas, media, posting and distribution. Prompts asked for local slang and deliberate typos, grainy phone-style photos with no background text, and residential proxies with saved login cookies. Another vendor was building a platform for over 100,000 accounts using cloud phone farms and AI-simulated behavior to age new accounts, with plans to sell to its own government and foreign clients.

Nation-state actors use LLMs for productivity. The Iranian actor CALANQUE ION, formerly APT42, uses them for reconnaissance and social engineering, and Chinese actors use them for research, scanning and exploits. LEAKY CASTLE analyzes stolen data with them, others stage and exfiltrate through LLM platform file hosting, and North Korean IT workers use them for resumes and interviews.

MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE shows the creative end. Fake recruiter profiles with SynthID watermarks led targets to ClickFix lures, and the attackers then edited .claude/settings.json in internal repositories so that starting Claude Code downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor. They also named access tokens after Microsoft Copilot. The Jieyou phishing service added an LLM chatbot in June so low-skilled affiliates can edit phishing panels in plain language.

AI tools also have limitations that attackers must consider. They can generate too much noise, make up details and even select the wrong targets. Groups focused on espionage are therefore likely to use them with caution, while cybercrime groups may accept a lower success rate in exchange for reaching more victims. Google SecOps has released detection rules for ARTEX, and Mandiant has published a guide to help organizations secure their systems. Our own analysis makes a similar point: Many ARTEX “indicators” found on compromised systems are generated by the LLM or by the tools it uses, rather than being built into the framework.

This makes attacker behavior more useful to defenders than looking for a single string or signature. When these frameworks run autonomously without tight controls, they leave traces in network traffic, recognizable identifiers and the code they execute. Google’s assessment offers some room for defenders to act: these frameworks currently trade stealth for velocity.

Title: ‘123456’ has been the world’s most popular password for 7 out of the last 8 years
Context: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the...
Full Text: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime. NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way. “Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.” Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either. According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place. “We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present. AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised. The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA. But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example. Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends. “Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years. The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said. We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg, the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®

Modules: Server & Workload Protection; Vulnerability Management; Network Security
Title: NoisyTCP bug gives Linux servers a remote crash problem 11 years in the making
Context: The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions
Full Text: The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it. Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine. The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it. Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs. Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it. Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes. Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx. Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag, a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready. His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server. In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service. A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5. For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue. Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces. Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted. The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2015, leaving Linux servers vulnerable to remote crashes for 11 years. Not bad for a flaw that doesn't even require a login. ®

Title: Ubuntu gets AI-generated security fixes for those feeling brave
Context: We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive
Full Text: Canonical is offering Ubuntu Pro users an opt-in channel for AI-generated security patches, deploying bots to help tackle the growing pile of vulnerabilities other bots are uncovering. Canonical's VP for "Excellence Engineering," Pierre Guillemin, gave the second keynote at the recent Ubuntu Summit, introducing the Edge archive, an optional repository of security fixes generated by the company's Surge framework. As the announcement describes it: "We built Surge, a multi-agent orchestration framework for CVE remediation and backporting, and have reached a high level of confidence in its capabilities. We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive." Edge offers patches before extended testing and qualification are complete, allowing users to assess them themselves. Canonical says updates delivered through the normal security channels will remain human-validated. Ubuntu Summit now runs twice a year. Last week's Ubuntu Summit 26.10 followed a rather unfortunately timed server outage for the company. At the previous such event in June, the company announced a move into agentic AI, but this new one is bolder still. Guillemin noted that "October 2026 saw almost as many CVEs as all of 2025." Surge is a "multi-agent orchestration framework" to remediate vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace. In other words, not the kernel, but even so, it is ambitious. The idea is to use a group of different LLMs to triage new vulnerabilities, find existing fixes, use multiple competing models to backport them to the versions in Ubuntu, and run automatic testing on them. Then a different group of "judging models" will evaluate the fixes and look for consensus. When candidates are chosen, they pass through normal Ubuntu package testing. If there are edge cases, low confidence scores, deadlocks, or other problems, then the process will be escalated to the staff of Canonical's security team. It's an attempt, as Guillemin put it, "to use AI to fight AI" – cooperating groups of LLMs patching their way through the ever-increasing flow of security holes. Even so, this is a remarkably courageous tactic (at the risk of using a famous British euphemism). It's an opt-in feature of Ubuntu Pro, Canonical's security and support subscription – although as we reported in 2022, Pro also has a free tier, so security researchers and the community can try Edge out, study it, and report their findings. We do sympathize with companies struggling against a rising tide of bot-powered security hole discovery. In theory, corporate funding can pay for faster fixes than a volunteer community can offer, but even for commercial vendors these are testing times. As we reported when Debian turned 30, surveys suggest that Ubuntu is about a third of the world Linux user base. Some of those users will be intrepid enough to try this, and that will end up being informative for the whole FOSS world. Those with long memories will remember the last time Canonical used the same edgy nomenclature. Back in July 2013, it launched a crowdfunding campaign for an Ubuntu smartphone. The campaign didn't raise enough money. ®
