Title: Crook turns LearnWorlds' free trials into phishing factory, sends 13,000 fake YouTube copyright notices
Context: According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails
Full Text: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to YouTube creators over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached. Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to recipients of their choosing. "We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register. According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails. "In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address." The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes. LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14. "In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14. "We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list." The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags. "We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined. "Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity." The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content. Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame, who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server. The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X, referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. The email prompted the recipient to click a YouTube link to see the “supporting documentation submitted by LearnWorks.” The link predictably turned out to be a YouTube redirect link, taking recipients to a separate website that presents them with a real Google OAuth page. If the user completed the authorization flow, it would have handed attackers control of the target’s Google and YouTube accounts. “The site is designed to look like an official YouTube webpage that enables users to review copyright claims against their channel,” Hutchins wrote. “It contains both the YouTube and Google branding, as well as a very similar theme to the official YouTube one.” According to Hutchins' screenshots, and those posted by others, the attacker was actively tweaking the email style and format, although the underlying lure and authentication mechanisms remained the same. Hutchins didn't specify exactly how the phishing page steals access to targets’ Google accounts, although his description aligns with the steps often seen in OAuth consent phishing attacks. These involve malicious websites serving victims genuine OAuth pages, into which unwitting victims enter their credentials and pass the relevant MFA tests. Typical scenarios see permission pages appear immediately after, and if the user accepts, the malicious website is handed OAuth access tokens to the victim’s account, effectively the keys to control it. LearnWorlds, based in Cyprus, claims to have two million active monthly learners on its platform accessing 900,000 courses and more than 14,000 business customers. Since launching in 2014, it claims to have generated more than $1 billion in revenue. The business focuses on white-label courses - training programs developed by one business and sold to another, assuming the buyer will change the branding and present the course materials as their own. ®

US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough)
Context: Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier...
Full Text: Nine countries including the UK have signed a US declaration pledging to secure supply chains for AI tech, as pressure grows for tighter export controls following the high-profile resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The US is firming up its Pax Silica initiative on AI and supply chain security. Under the San Francisco declaration, signed on November 15, the coalition says it is entering a new phase that turns shared principles into a working partnership with shared responsibilities. Pax Silica was announced in December last year, ostensibly for the participants to work together on vital parts of the global technology supply chain, including frontier foundation models, compute and semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, minerals refining and processing, and energy. But the list of participants was notable for not including one country – China – leading many to suspect that Pax Silica is yet another effort by Washington to squeeze out its main rival in the global technology and economic stakes. Hong-Kong based South China Morning Post refers to it as Trump's "campaign to China-proof AI and chip supply chains." The latest declaration states that "the security of our peoples cannot be separated from the security of our economies and those of our closest partners," and sets out what must be protected, as well as committing to "protect it together." It asserts that protection should cover key foundational technologies essential to economic security, listing "software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs…essential to AI supply chains." This includes anything that "theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage, or undue economic leverage over the participants, or whose unauthorized transfer or misuse could pose significant risks to the economic and national security of the participants." Also listed is the protection of critical infrastructure such as ports, terminals, transport, communications, and logistics networks, and the ICT and energy infrastructure these depend upon. The declaration was jointly released by the US administration, and the governments of Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom. "The know-how to design a chip, the machine that makes it, and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," the US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg told the Financial Times. "What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility." This move comes amid reports that both Republican and Democrat lawmakers want to push through further measures to prevent China from accessing advanced chips for AI processing. It follows the recent news that Jensen Huang, the now former CEO of top GPU maker Nvidia, admitted to an affair with a woman suspected by the US of being a spy for Beijing. She worked for a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that bought Nvidia hardware and was also suspected of making it available to Chinese users. US, Singaporean, and Malaysian police investigations are still probing whether chips were diverted or accessed remotely by Chinese firms. American efforts to control Chinese access to its technology started under the first Trump administration, and continued under President Joe Biden’s leadership. A report out last week claimed US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, and many of their cutting-edge models were trained using Blackwell GPUs. It is understood that President Trump is to meet with China's premier Xi Jinping this week for bilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. ®

Title: Typosquatters Target New Brand Domains Within 24 Hours of Registration
Context: “The findings highlight how attackers can exploit the period between a company's domain registration and its public launch, positioning lookalike websites to capture consumers...
Full Text:
Threat actors are impersonating big-name brands via typosquatting just one day after legitimate domains are created, according to new research from Symantec.

The active campaign, first observed in August, has seen 25 lookalike domains created which resembled authentic domain names used by companies such as Abbott Laboratories, Bayer, CarMax, McDonald’s, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi.

Every lookalike domain was registered within 24 hours of its authentic counterpart, often before the company even launched the new website.

“The findings highlight how attackers can exploit the period between a company's domain registration and its public launch, positioning lookalike websites to capture consumers who mistype legitimate addresses,” Symantec wrote.

Typosquatting is when malicious actors register domains that are slightly misspelled from a legitimate organization’s domain, such as one letter added or removed. This means that when a user accidently misspells a legitimate site name when typing the address by hand, they could be directed to a typosquatter’s site instead.

The fake websites are designed to closely resemble the organization they are impersonating.

These sites enable a range of follow-on malicious activity, such as directing users to scam sites, installing malware and harvesting credentials.

Attackers Focus on Campaign Sites to Maximize Effectiveness

The Symantec research, published on November 16, found that most of the malicious domains impersonated campaign sites rather than corporate home pages.

These included patient-savings programs, sweepstakes, rebates, claims portals and legal settlements.

Users are more likely to type such addresses by hand as these websites are often displayed on printed mailers, television advertisements, pharmacy leaflets and court-ordered settlement notices.

Campaign sites are also likely to ask visitors for personal information, such as names, addresses, claim numbers or health details, with visitors expecting to hand over such data upon arrival.

The typosquatting campaign focused on clients of two brand-protection registrars, Corporation Service Company (CSC) and MarkMonitor. Each time a large company registered a new domain through one of these registrars, a one-letter lookalike was registered the next day through a China-based registrar.

In one case, used car dealer CarMax registered carmaxclaims[.]com and kmxclaims[.]com through CSC on August 26. The next day, two lookalike domains were registered that removed the ‘s’ from each of the legitimate domains, carmaxclaim[.]com and kmxclaim[.]com.

Other typos used included leaving out other single letters and collapsing a double letter, for example, mywayconnect became mywayconect.

New lookalike domains were registered as recently as November 11, suggesting the campaign is ongoing.

Typosquat Domains Rapidly Monetized Through Ads and Scams

The observed typosquat domains appeared to have several purposes. Some were parked placeholder pages that earned money from pay-per-click advertising feeds, while others were deceptive search portals whose results led to scam blogs, or brand-themed blogs written around the typosquatted name and packed with ads that routed visitors to scam sites.

“This low-grade scam traffic may not be the end goal. Advertising networks of this kind can also be abused for malvertising and credential harvesting, and a domain that serves ads today could serve a fake claims form tomorrow with a single Domain Name System (DNS) or content change. Visitors who reach these domains are already primed to enter personal details,” Symantec noted.

Given the speed at which attackers published their lookalike domains following the campaign launch, the researchers believe the setup was likely automated.

“The actors’ tooling was not visible to us, but the evidence is consistent with a simple pipeline that watched new registrations, filtered on brand-protection registrars, generated a one-character variant and registered it before the next day was out,” the researchers added.

Title: Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code?
Context: Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited
Full Text: October ’26 might be remembered as a seminal moment for software developers and application security teams. AI agents are investigating unfamiliar systems, testing ways to get in and adjusting their next move when an attempt fails. Anyone with a credit card can use that capability to come after your application. Coding agents and their tool integrations have introduced new entry points and surface areas that can be exploited. Pillar’s OpenCode disclosure in October showed how a malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) server could execute commands on a developer’s Windows or WSL machine during authentication. A server-supplied URL reached a shell without tricking the model. In the same month, the discovery of the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, remote code execution bugs in the PHP runtime uncovered with the help of OpenAI’s models, brought new urgency to securing longstanding code across much of the internet. Microsoft revealed that an agent moved from searching GitHub for exposed credentials to stealing Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. When its cloud API requests failed, the agent corrected the API versions and tried again until they succeeded. A report by Anthropic described individual operators using agent frameworks for multi-victim campaigns that previously required specialist teams. Agents carried out reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft across targets in parallel, making sophisticated operations accessible with less hands-on work. In a recent analysis, Tomasz Tunguz estimated the model cost of a 100-million-token attack workload using GLM-5.3, a low-cost model: 100 million tokens × $0.902 per million = $90.20. That is roughly 98% to 99% below the $5,000 to $10,000 frontier-model estimate cited by Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for a comparable cyber attack. Tunguz’s figure covers model usage only, not the full cost of an attack. Even still, it shows how trivially cheap it is now for attackers to go after any codebase, with the spend falling from thousands of dollars to under $100. These new agentic attacks should make every team take another look at the code they’ve been running for years. Engineering and security teams need to find and fix weaknesses in their own applications before an attacker with an army of AI agents gets there first. Security has to become every developer’s responsibility Traditional AppSec checks such as rule-based static analysis, dependency scanning and secret detection are no longer enough on their own. Developers, engineering leaders, and security teams also need defensive AI agents that trace attack paths, uncover missing safeguards and business-logic vulnerabilities, and help fix them. Developers’ responsibility doesn’t stop at the code they’re writing now. An application already in production without known vulnerabilities might still get exploited by an AI agent looking for ways to skip a permission check or business rule. The gap only shows up when a request is traced through the codebase and checked against what users should be allowed to do. A new approach to securing your code CodeRabbit Secure uses semantic analysis to understand your codebase and reason about it the way a security engineer would, tracing requests and checking whether permissions and business rules are enforced. Agents investigate potential attack paths and verify findings independent of the developer or agent that wrote the code, while CodeRabbit Agent generates reviewable fixes. Three main use cases that improve your code security: this works across the SDLC: reviewing each commit in a new PR and flag its security risks; finding vulnerabilities across the repo with a Deep Scan; rechecking code with incremental scans and validating findings at runtime. Find vulnerabilities already in committed code Deep Scan examines the repository, including older paths outside the latest PR. Agents map entry points, access controls, and sensitive operations, then investigate across functions and files. Linked repositories, when configured, supply context from shared services and libraries. A separate agent challenges each suspected vulnerability, checking reachability, exploitation conditions, and safeguards that could disprove it. I tried CodeRabbit Secure Deep Scan against ast-grep and was impressed by its precision. Proving vulnerabilities before flagging them makes every finding far more actionable. Herrington Darkholme, creator of ast-grep Review incoming changes before merge PR security reviews assess each incoming change, including agent-generated code, for vulnerabilities that are reachable and exploitable in the existing application. CodeRabbit’s Security Architecture Review examines how architecture-level changes affect permissions, sensitive data flows, and trust boundaries. The Security Blast Radius map connects changed components to their dependencies and the code that relies on them, helping reviewers trace the potential security impact beyond the PR diff. On GitHub, administrators can enable CodeRabbit Security check and require it through branch protection or a ruleset. It blocks merges when PR security comments at or above the configured severity threshold remain unresolved. Recheck code as it evolves and validate findings at runtime Each Deep Scan builds an attack surface map of the repository, showing which security-relevant entry points have been verified, which have gone stale as the code changed, and which have never been examined. Delta scans then check changed files and areas of the map that are out of date or unverified, so teams know how much of the codebase has been security-reviewed and when it was last reviewed. Individual findings can also be rechecked to determine whether a fix addressed them. For eligible Deep Scan findings on GitHub Cloud with CodeRabbit Cloud, runtime verification generates a reproduction guide and can run it in an isolated environment to confirm whether the vulnerable path is reached. Results are “reproduced”, “not reproduced” or “inconclusive” for the tested revision and environment, however a failure to reproduce may not mean the finding is fixed. Carry the investigation through to a fix Developers can ask CodeRabbit Agent to implement a fix and open a PR, then inspect the finding, proposed fix, and supporting evidence. Teams can also configure severity thresholds to create Jira or Linear tickets automatically and track remediation in their existing workflow. Connecting the vulnerability finding, its supporting evidence, and a proposed fix helps engineering and security teams act while the context is still fresh and carry the change through review, testing and release. Teams can use CodeRabbit Agent to act on that context or easily hand it off to your preferred coding agent with a shareable markdown file. What a million-dollar initiative surfaced CodeRabbit recently committed up to $1 million in free Deep Scans to help organizations find and fix hidden vulnerabilities. In Deep Scans created over a 10-day period in early November, CodeRabbit Secure recorded about 53,000 High or Critical findings across some 2,000 organizations. More than 10,000 findings have already been fixed, including 1,049 rated High or Critical. Some of the security fixes implemented by CodeRabbit included preventing: embedded JavaScript in a repository document’s metadata from running arbitrary code. email subject lines from being interpreted as executable templates and running JavaScript with an API server’s privileges. unauthenticated transfer requests from injecting SQL and triggering unauthorized database operations. As agents produce more code and attackers become more capable, investigation using semantic analysis needs to become a regular part of how software is built and maintained, alongside existing security checks. Find vulnerabilities in your code before an attacker does As attackers use AI agents to investigate unfamiliar systems and adapt their next move, engineering and security teams need the same capacity to investigate their code and carry findings through to tested fixes. Title: La Poste Subsidiary Maileva Breach Exposes 22 Million People
Context: Read more on French cyber-attacks: France Blood Service Cyber-Attack Sends Blood Storage Temperatures to 110°C Docaposte's statement now called what happened in mid-September "a...
Full Text:
A cyber-attack on La Poste-owned document-sending provider Maileva has exposed the names and postal addresses of 22 million people.

Docaposte, La Poste's digital subsidiary that owns Maileva, confirmed the breach in a November 15 statement.

Maileva sends documents such as payslips, registered letters and invoices on behalf of businesses and institutions.

The firm said that 22 million people who received mailings from Maileva’s business and institutional clients are affected by a leak of identifying information, including first name, last name and postal address.

What Maileva Data Was Exposed

Docaposte said Maileva's clients had been able to tell their customers that some of their data had been compromised, the nature of which is linked to the content of the documents sent. It did not say how many people that covered.

The content of the documents shared on its platform is not held by Maileva, rather it relates to the relationship between Maileva’s clients and the recipients of those documents.

Several thousand Maileva client companies were affected, the company told Cyberattaque.org, which first reported the breach.

Docaposte said affected clients were informed in the days after the incident was identified.

A hospital near Paris, Hôpital Foch, said an attacker could view some payment reminder letters containing invoice numbers, care dates and amounts due, but not the nature of the care or bank details. Meanwhile, a social housing provider in northern France, Flandre Opale Habitat, said exposed information could include names, contact details, client numbers, housing references and invoice amounts.

Dray Agha, senior manager of tactical response at Huntress, said in emailed comments that criminals could use the stolen names and addresses to send targeted fake invoices or payment reminders.

"I strongly advise anyone receiving an unexpected bill to verify it directly with the named organization. You must use official websites rather than the contact details provided in the suspicious letter," Agha added.

Sophisticated Cyber-Attack Hits Maileva

Maileva suspended its platform on September 23 and resumed services on September 29, a six-day outage affecting all clients. At the time, Docaposte described the event as a cybersecurity incident involving attempted unauthorized access to the platform, according to Solutions Numériques.

Cyberattaque.org reported the incident on September 24, when Maileva described attempts against some customer accounts aimed at sending fraudulent mail. No large-scale personal data leak had been announced at that point.

Read more on French cyber-attacks: France Blood Service Cyber-Attack Sends Blood Storage Temperatures to 110°C

Docaposte's statement now called what happened in mid-September "a complex cyber-attack," adding that "no data was found to have been altered or destroyed." It said France's data protection authority (CNIL) had been notified, a complaint had been filed and a judicial investigation was under way.

Docaposte did not address whether anyone had claimed the attack or whether the stolen data had been published or sold. Maileva told Cyberattaque.org that notifying affected people was the responsibility of its client organizations.

Title: Cognitive warfare: the new battlefield is the human mind
Context: In Italy, approximately 6,300 schools received communications containing attack threats, prompting evacuations in hundreds of schools and mobilizing law enforcement and...
Full Text:
Cognitive warfare uses AI, deepfakes and fear to manipulate opinions, erode trust and disrupt society.

Contemporary warfare is no longer fought solely through armies, weapons, and technological infrastructure. Alongside military operations and cyberattacks, a new dimension of conflict is emerging in which the primary target is people’s ability to interpret reality, distinguish reliable information from manipulated information, and make autonomous decisions. This is the context in which cognitive warfare takes root, a strategy that aims to influence the perceptions, beliefs, and behaviors of individuals and communities, transforming information into a tool of pressure and destabilization.

Unlike traditional propaganda, cognitive warfare leverages a much more complex technological ecosystem. Social networks, digital platforms, profiling systems, artificial intelligence, and psychological manipulation techniques allow for reaching different audiences with messages crafted to elicit specific reactions. The goal is not necessarily to impose a single narrative, but to influence the process by which people acquire information, form opinions, and evaluate events.

Multiplier of information operations and the manipulation of consensus

Generative artificial intelligence has further expanded the operational possibilities of these campaigns. The automated production of text, images, audio, and video allows for the construction of increasingly credible fake content, simulating statements from public figures, and fueling networks of coordinated accounts. Deepfakes pose a significant problem for information security because they can compromise the reliability of audiovisual evidence and make it more difficult to verify the authenticity of a communication. A significant finding emerges from the fourth annual report of the European External Action Service on FIMI (Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference) threats , published in March 2026. In 2025, 27% of incidents analyzed by the EEAS (European External Action Service) involved techniques attributable to artificial intelligence, with an increase in cases from 41 in 2024 to 147 in 2025, equal to approximately 259% . Artificial intelligence is being used to accelerate content production, translate and adapt messages into multiple languages, generate synthetic images and videos, and amplify influencer efforts through coordinated networks.

In this context, social media platforms represent one of the most favorable environments for the spread of cognitive operations. The speed of content circulation, recommendation systems, and the ability to reach specific communities allow specific narratives to be amplified, even through coordinated behavior. Fake accounts, bots, and seemingly independent profiles can contribute to the impression that a given opinion is widely shared. One of the most insidious strategies isn’t necessarily spreading completely false news, but rather mixing authentic information, manipulated content, and misleading interpretations. This makes it more difficult to distinguish facts from reconstructions constructed to influence the public.

School bomb scares as an example of psychological pressure

A concrete example that provides insight into the psychological dimension of these threats is the bomb threat that affected schools in Italy, Scotland, Northern Ireland, and the Republic of Ireland on November 11, 2026. In Italy, approximately 6,300 schools received communications containing attack threats, prompting evacuations in hundreds of schools and mobilizing law enforcement and emergency personnel. Authorities deemed the reports to be false alarms, with no devices identified.

The incident deserves attention not only for its international dimension, but above all for the mechanism by which an electronic communication produced concrete consequences. It was not necessary to compromise the schools’ computer networks or damage infrastructure. Sending a single message was enough to activate emergency procedures, interrupt school activities, generate concern among families, and commit public resources. The human factor thus becomes the primary factor through which the threat’s impact materializes. School administrators, teachers, and law enforcement responded in accordance with their responsibilities, while parents and students were exposed to a situation of great uncertainty. Even when the alarm turns out to be unfounded, the psychological and organizational consequences remain real. This episode demonstrates how manipulating the perception of danger can influence collective behavior.

The connection between cognitive warfare and cybersecurity

Cognitive warfare has significant parallels with cybersecurity and hybrid operations. A ransomware attack against strategic infrastructure, a breach of public administration systems, or the theft of confidential documents can have a significance that transcends the technical damage. The stolen information can be selected, manipulated, or released at strategic moments to compromise the reputation of institutions and influence public debate. In this scenario, cybersecurity is not just about protecting networks, devices, and data, but also the ability to manage manipulated information and communications designed to generate fear, disorientation, and mistrust. Countering cognitive warfare requires a multidisciplinary approach. Protecting digital infrastructures must be accompanied by the ability to recognize information manipulation, verify sources, and understand the techniques used to influence people’s behavior. For companies and public administrations, it is becoming important to integrate cyber incident management with timely and transparent communication.

Cognitive warfare demonstrates that a country’s security does not depend solely on the protection of its information systems or the availability of military capabilities. It also depends on trust in institutions, the quality of information, and the population’s ability to recognize attempts at manipulation. The case of the school bomb threats highlights a fundamental aspect: it’s not always necessary to physically attack an infrastructure to compromise its functioning. In certain circumstances, it’s sufficient to exploit fear and human reactions to generate disorganization and social pressure. The new battlefield, therefore, isn’t just digital. It’s also cognitive, and concerns the ability of individuals and institutions to maintain clarity, trust, and decision-making autonomy in the face of information designed to destabilize them.

Title: Google Finds Hackers Using AI Agents to Build and Run Exploits From Software Patches
Context: Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines,...
Full Text:
Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September.

The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths even if the underlying mechanics remain the same.

A number of threat actors have been observed experimenting with these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated and suspected espionage actors aligned with China.

"These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation," Google said.

Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines, allowing threat actors to collapse the window between patch disclosure and active exploitation.

"Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws," Google added.

Simultaneously, threat actors are also targeting AI infrastructure to illicit profit from LLMjacking attacks by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments, and then reselling the access through underground proxy services like APIMart and JetNight at discounted prices, otherwise known as LLM mixers.

The findings show that the emergence of open-source frameworks have further lowered the barrier to entry, enabling bad actors to easily integrate new exploits, autonomously scale attacks, and mount convincing phishing campaigns, further compressing attack timelines.

This includes a Chinese-language phishing platform called Jieyou that has integrated an LLM chatbot assistant to allow customers to configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands without necessarily having the technical expertise to do so.

"The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier," Google said. "Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly."

Title: Google: AI agent turned a security patch into a working exploit with no human help
Context: Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability...
Full Text: A suspected Russian-speaking operator used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human in the loop – a first such occurrence, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) – before ultimately stealing data from victim organizations. Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation compared to Q3. In this case, the threat hunters found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with multiple frontier and local models. The framework, called exploit_agent, used Russian-language tooling, and was configured to conduct continuous differential analysis of “popular web application software,” according to the report. This includes comparing code before and after security updates, identifying potential vulnerabilities, developing exploits, and then automatically executing them without any human involvement. The server also contained data stolen from victim organizations, and “multiple” post-compromise scripts that allowed attackers to perform nefarious activities including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. “Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector,” according to the report. The report also documents other instances of attackers moving beyond manual LLM prompting during cyberattacks and instead deploying autonomous, multi-agent offensive security frameworks to carry out multi-stage intrusions. These include both financially motivated cybercriminals and cyber-espionage groups. In addition to the recent attacks involving the open source penetration-testing tool ARTEX, attackers have also used other AI-powered offensive frameworks, including CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI, and PentAGI. In another instance, GTIG observed attackers using PentAGI alongside proxy services to target the aerospace sector. “We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus,” the Googlers wrote. “Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally.” ®

An old social media post from a familiar brand may seem trustworthy. But the link behind it may no longer take you where the company intended.

According to Cybernews, criminals hijacked expired Bitly links and redirected them to unrelated Wikipedia pages, making legitimate posts appear to promote offensive or embarrassing content.

Bitly is a URL-shortening service. URL shorteners turn long web addresses into compact links that are easier to share. When you click a shortened link, the service redirects your browser to the original destination. The trade-off is that the short link hides that destination, making it harder to tell at a glance whether you’re heading to a legitimate website or somewhere suspicious.

Attackers apparently exploited what Bitly described as a flaw involving expired links to make old short links point somewhere new. Those links were still sitting in genuine posts from McDonald’s, Burger King, and others, so anyone clicking them was redirected to the attackers’ chosen pages instead of the original destinations. The attackers didn’t need to edit the posts or break into the brands’ social media accounts; they just changed the address where the links led.

One example involved a McDonald’s post from June 7, 2011, which read:

“Check out what our McDonald’s team in Sweden did.”

Its shortened link had been redirected to Wikipedia’s page about the September 11 attacks.

Screenshot courtesy of rudrongus

Bitly said it had suspended the accounts involved and was disabling the affected links. So, the link in that tweet now takes you to an error page:

You’ve got the wrong address

In these cases, the redirects went to unrelated Wikipedia pages. The concern is that the same kind of redirection could instead send people to phishing pages, fake promotions, or malicious downloads.

Unsure where a link goes? We’ll check it.

Check now

How to check a shortened link before opening it

Hovering over a link on a computer is still a useful first check: It can reveal a mismatch between the visible text and the underlying address. But if all you see is a shortened URL, you still haven’t established the final destination. That’s where checking the link and its redirects becomes useful.

You can copy a suspicious link without opening it: Right-click it and choose the option to copy the link, then paste it into Malwarebytes’ free Scam Link Check. It scans the site and its redirects, then provides a result and suggested next steps. No download, payment, or login is required.

How to stay safe

If a message asks you to sign in, pay, or resolve an account problem, open the official app or type the known website address yourself instead of following the supplied link.

Treat unexpected destinations as a reason to stop. Don’t continue simply because the original post came from a recognizable account. The Bitly incidents show why the source of a post and the current destination of its links are separate questions.

Don’t mistake HTTPS for a safety verdict. It means your connection to the website is encrypted, not that the website is legitimate. Phishing sites can use HTTPS too.

Use browser protection as an additional layer. Malwarebytes Browser Guard is a free browser extension that helps flag suspicious links while you browse.

Football fans looking for free player packs in EA SPORTS FC 27 could end up handing over their gaming account instead. FC 27 is the latest installment in EA’s soccer video game series. Its Ultimate Team mode lets players build squads using virtual player cards, which they can get by opening packs.

Following the game’s September 25 launch, we identified a fake “FC27 x Prime Gaming” reward page targeting players’ login details. Prime Gaming offers games and in-game rewards as part of an Amazon Prime membership. The fake page borrows that branding, tells visitors their reward is waiting, and asks them to “connect” their EA account—the account they use to access EA games and services.

The series attracts millions of players. EA reported that FC 24 reached more than 11.3 million players worldwide in its first week in 2023, including through EA Play.

On this fake site, there is no reward. The “EA sign-in” that follows is a copy hosted on the scammers’ own domain. It asks for your email address, your password, and the security code from your two-factor authentication (2FA), and sends each one to a server the criminals control. The page’s code is designed to use the server’s replies to decide whether to show a password error or ask for a 2FA code.

This site is not affiliated with EA, Amazon, or Prime Gaming. If you entered your details on a page like this, go to the “How to stay safe” section below.

A reward that’s waiting for you

The landing page is dark purple and styled like a game promo. It says “Your Prime Gaming reward is waiting. Connect your EA account to continue.” Under the button, a smaller line reads “You’ll continue to EA’s official authorization page.”

You don’t. Clicking the button shows “Connecting…” and “Redirecting to EA authorization…”. The code waits a fixed 1.4 seconds and then moves you to /in, which is still on the same domain.

A copied EA sign-in page

The sign-in page closely imitates EA’s own. It has a dark layout, a “Phone or Email” field, “Keep me signed in,” “Sign in with a Passkey,” and a row of Google, Facebook, Apple, and Steam buttons.

The social sign-in buttons do nothing when clicked. Instead, the page steers visitors toward entering their email address and password.

How the theft works, step by step

Each step sends what you type to a separate server, fedserv.thenewsip[.]site.

Email. You enter your email address and move on to the password page.

Password. You enter your password, which is sent to the server. The page uses the server’s reply to decide whether to show an EA-style “Your credentials are incorrect” error or continue, including whether to request a 2FA code. This is consistent with an attempt to check the details against EA, but the captured page code alone does not confirm how the server handles them.

The code. If the account has 2FA, a “Verify your identity” page asks you to click “Send Code” and then enter the six-digit code. The code goes straight to the server.

The exit. The page redirects you to EA’s real Ultimate Team web app at ea.com. Accounts without 2FA skip step three. Arriving at the real site does not mean the preceding sign-in was legitimate.

Capturing a valid 2FA code could let the attackers complete a sign-in before it expires. This doesn’t disable 2FA, but it could allow them to get past that check for a particular login.

Tracking where victims come from

The page records where each visitor came from and sends that “traffic source” to the server along with the submitted details. It recognizes Facebook, Messenger, Meta’s Audience Network, Instagram, and TikTok, through tracking parameters in the link and through Facebook and TikTok ad-click IDs (fbclid, ttclid). Everything else is labeled “direct” or “unknown.”

The kit also has built-in support for Umami web analytics. Whether it’s on depends on a separate settings file that wasn’t part of what we captured. In its default mode, the server’s replies decide whether a visitor’s later steps (password, sending the code, success) show up in the statistics, and the page where victims type their security code isn’t counted in page-view tracking. The settings can also switch to a mode that counts every page.

Together, these features give the operators a way to track traffic attributed to social platforms. They show that the page was built to handle those sources, but do not establish that ads actually ran on them.

Dressed up as an “internal tool”

The HTML asks search engines not to index, archive, or show previews of the page, with a comment that reads “Private team tool — do not index or archive.”

The “Privacy Policy” and “Terms of Service” pages describe an “authentication portal” for “internal use by authorized personnel.”

The kit has two switches. One turns off the Prime Gaming landing page, so the same code would show a plain fake EA sign-in instead. The other chooses between sending victims to EA’s real site and showing the “enrolled for weekly FC 27 rewards” page. In the version we analyzed, both the Prime Gaming lure and the redirect to EA were on.

Why your EA account is worth stealing

An EA account is more than a login. It can hold an FC Ultimate Team club with coins and tradable players, access to purchased games, and saved payment methods. Losing access could put years of purchases and progress at risk.

Attackers could also use a compromised account to impersonate you and trick your gaming contacts into sharing information or clicking scam links.

Safer. Cleaner. Ad-free browsing.

INSTALL BROWSER GUARD

How to stay safe

Start at EA’s website. Type ea.com into your browser and navigate from there. Before entering your EA password or security code, check that the sign-in page is on ea.com or a genuine subdomain, such as accounts.ea.com.

Check the address bar. A page that looks exactly like EA’s sign-in is not EA if the address says something like fc27-prime[.]shop.

Keep security codes private. Only enter an EA verification code on EA’s genuine sign-in page for a login you initiated.

Be wary of free packs, coins, and rewards in ads and posts. A sponsored post isn’t proof that an offer is real.

Use a password manager. It generally won’t offer to autofill your EA password on an unrelated domain, which can help flag a fake page

Already entered your details?

Go directly to ea.com and change your password immediately, even if you didn’t submit a 2FA code.

Review your security settings and trusted devices, remove unfamiliar devices, and check for changes to your email address, linked accounts, and purchases.

Keep 2FA enabled. Change any reused passwords elsewhere, especially on your email account.

If you see unfamiliar linked accounts, are locked out, or have missing content, follow EA’s account-recovery guidance and contact EA Help.

In this article

Attackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate cyberattacks, the FBI warns

Some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours

The attacks target organizations, potentially putting customers’ personal information at risk

Cybercriminals have found another AI tool to do more of the hacking for them.

The FBI issued a FLASH advisory on November 13 warning that attackers are abusing ARTEX, a tool originally developed for authorized security testing, to automate intrusions against organizations worldwide. In some observed attacks, criminals went from selecting a target to gaining privileged access in under three hours, leaving defenders little time to respond.

ARTEX is an open-source penetration-testing framework. Penetration testing means trying to break into systems with the owner’s permission to find weaknesses before criminals do.

An operator gives ARTEX a target and an objective. Its a planning agent divides the work into tasks, while other AI agents use security tools to carry them out and share their findings. Rather than having its own AI model, ARTEX connects to external large language models (LLMs). Once a task begins, it requires relatively little human input.

The FBI says attackers have used ARTEX since at least August against sectors including finance, government, healthcare, and technology. Separately, Microsoft reported that a China-state-aligned group used ARTEX to accelerate attacks after compromising ConnectWise application credentials.

While these attacks can generate plenty of suspicious activity, their speed leaves defenders little time to respond. An alert is only useful if defenders can investigate and act before the damage is done.

ARTEX helps attackers connect individual weaknesses into a bigger intrusion. An overlooked employee portal or exposed cloud credential can become a route to sensitive records, additional accounts, or connected organizations. For home users, that could mean personal information stolen from a company is later used for fraud or targeted scams.

How to stay safe

ARTEX changes how quickly attackers can work. It does not make basic security controls obsolete, but it makes leaving familiar weaknesses unfixed more dangerous. Most of the FBI’s recommendations are aimed at organizations. Businesses and IT teams should:

Stay up to date: Patch internet-facing systems promptly and inventory overlooked applications, including old employee and supplier portals. Restrict administrative interfaces to approved access paths.

Protect credentials and limit permissions: Scan for exposed passwords and API keys, rotate compromised secrets, and give applications only the access they need.

Monitor and log: Watch for rapid bursts of requests, unusual data access, and unexpected credential or privilege changes. Prepare procedures to revoke access and isolate affected systems quickly.

For individuals and small-business users, the fundamentals still matter:

Update your devices and software.

Use strong, unique passwords and turn on multi-factor authentication wherever available.

Run an up-to-date real-time anti-malware solution on your devices.

If a company tells you your account or information was affected, verify the notice through its official website or app and follow its incident-specific instructions.

This week's stories show both sides. Here's what happened.

⚡ Threat of the Week

N-able 0-Days Exploited for Dropping Crypto Miners — A new set of vulnerabilities tracked as 4EverAble2Shell has come under active exploitation, with attackers exploiting it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. According to Huntback, the activity has successfully compromised 21 N-central servers across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden. 🔔 Top News

Compromised bee-js and Swarm Desktop Steal Swarm Wallet Keys — Threat actors compromised @ethersphere/bee-js, the JavaScript client for the Swarm storage network, with a new postinstall hook in version 13.3.0 that downloads a second stage responsible for stealing the Swarm node's wallet key and installing a backdoor. "On Linux and macOS, the backdoor is a Go remote shell," SafeDep said. "On Windows, it is a hidden ScreenConnect client that runs as SYSTEM." The same malicious code was subsequently distributed via Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 on GitHub. The activity has since been linked to a campaign called SleepyDuck (EtherDuck), which is known to spread malicious Solidity extensions through Open VSX. "The attacker controlled two Ethersphere GitHub accounts. GitHub activity logs attribute 13 pushes on November 6 to long-time maintainer nugaon," SafeDep added. "That day the attacker injected GitHub Actions workflows to steal CI credentials, and the attempts failed. Two days later, the attacker used the release bot bee-worker to publish the malicious releases. How the attacker got into either account remains unknown."

Nightmare Eclipse New SignDrop 0-Day — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges. Called SignDrop, it has been described as a Windows Common Log FileSystem (CLFS) authentication zero-day local privilege escalation flaw. "The vulnerability turns a defense into an attack surface," Cyderes said. "Microsoft added HMAC-based authentication codes to CLFS log files specifically to block the class of logic bugs caused by improper validation of CLFS data structures, which accounted for 19 of 24 CLFS CVEs over five years. SignDrop abuses the signing mechanism itself: it forces clfs.sys to create a .cnpf signature file as SYSTEM in an attacker-controlled location, producing a privileged file-creation primitive at an attacker-selected path. Because the resulting file retains attacker-accessible security attributes, the exploit reopens it and replaces the CLFS-generated content with an embedded payload DLL." Microsoft said it's investigating the reported vulnerability. In late September, the researcher also released an exploit for BigDiskBuster, a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw impacting Microsoft Defender that's similar to UnDefend and prevents the application from performing platform/signature updates.

Both apps signed customers in through ForgeRock, an identity platform now part of Ping Identity. The carmakers remediated the flaw approximately two hours after responsible disclosure.

Google Patches Actively Exploited Chrome 0-Day — Google released updates to patch a high-severity vulnerability in Chrome has come under active exploitation in the wild. The flaw, tracked as CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: 8.8), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component. The issue has been addressed in 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. Google did not disclose how the vulnerability is being exploited and in what context.

According to the Italian data regulatory body, Meta has been fined €805 million for failing to disclose that it had access to user photos, videos, and metadata for those using the Facebook app on Android devices. Meta had access to Android users' ​photos and videos through a Facebook app feature that ​suggested content from users' personal galleries that they ⁠could post. The feature has been available since 2023. Meta has 60 ​days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent ​separately. The company said it would appeal the decision. "This is a simple feature ​that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook," Meta told Reuters. ​"Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and ‌they ⁠can change that permission at any time in their settings."

📰 Around the Cyber World

A cybercrime investigation from independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs has linked the administrator of Qilin ransomware to Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev, a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

The TOR project released 0.4.9.17 to include denial-of-service (DoS) defenses related to IPv6 handling. "This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators," the maintainers said. "This is not an easy problem to address, as relays across the network are being overwhelmed by a massive flood of client circuits. We are actively evaluating additional defenses and so expect further releases in the near future."

As many as six pre-authentication remote code execution 0-day vulnerabilities have been uncovered in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A fridge controllers. The flaws, identified by Midnight Blue within the span of an hour, allow full device take-over, persistent access (possibly after reset), and persistent denial-of-service, rendering the device inoperable. Additional technical details are currently withheld. "Through remote code execution, an unauthenticated attacker can remotely run arbitrary code at the operating system level of the AK-SM800A controller," Midnight Blue said. "Due to the lack of secure boot, an attacker with RCE could push malicious firmware that simply renders the device inoperable and irrecoverable without specialized hardware intervention (e.g. by wiping flash memory and/or causing an infinite boot loop). Such a 'bricking' or wiper approach would require full device replacement." The findings unfold against the backdrop of two waves of cyber attacks targeting internet-exposed fridge controllers by Danfoss and Copeland across Europe.

Cruciferra has been revealed as a rebrand of the long-running KGB cryptor. It has been sold to cybercriminals since October 2025. ESET said it has prevented over 700,000 compromise attempts from Cruciferra since January 2026, most of them targeting Türkiye, Greece, and Spain. It has been used to deliver payloads like Formbook and PureLogs. "In mid-October the cryptor's domain was seized, and the service went dark," ESET said. "Days later, the same operator resurfaced with a new offering – exclusive $5K-per-build cryptors, pitched against enterprise EDRs and advertised with a claimed bundled kernel 0-day. Seized infrastructure ≠ a dead service."

Using AI models on a limited budget and running it against 10 popular TCP/IP stacks has led to the discovery of 99 vulnerabilities in 90 hours. Of these, 66 are new vulnerabilities, 52% of them critical or high severity. This also includes seven vulnerabilities specific to the firmware of a discontinued wireless access point, such as buffer overflow via firmware upload and hard-coded administrator credentials that cannot be changed for web and shell management. "AI cut the analysis time from 9 months to 90 hours and the research cost by 100x when compared to our previous analysis," Forescout said. "It rediscovered 40% of the vulnerabilities we had previously disclosed on those stacks. Total static analysis cost was $935, an average of $2.58 per finding."

Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a "90 + 30" vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to address a vulnerability, plus an extra 30 days "soak time" for patch rollout. That's changing now with the emergence of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation. Going forward, Google Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after they are reported to the vendor, regardless of whether they are fixed. The deadline drops to 60 days on February 2, 2027, and to 30 days on January 3, 2028.

ClickFix-style lures are being used to deliver a macOS-focused, modular information stealer called Phexia. The malware is also capable of deploying an XMRig miner. "The most recent and notable change in Phexia occurred in May 2026, when the threat actor started testing smart contracts on the Polygon blockchain as a command-and-control (C2) dead-drop resolver (DDR)," WithSecure said. "The abuse of smart contracts by threat actors as part of their attack chain is generally known as EtherHiding. The malware previously relied on hardcoded C2 domains as well as Telegram channels and Steam profiles as its C2 DDR. The threat actor was observed actively weaponizing the Polygon smart contracts since late May to early June 2026."

The threat actors behind WeedHack have been linked to another cybercriminal operation called Marsalek that expands beyond using Minecraft lures to disguise malicious software as popular gaming tools, cheats, and utilities for games including Roblox, Fortnite, and Counter-Strike 2. "Active from approximately December 2025 through May 2026, Marsalek offered free access to sophisticated information-stealing malware through a publicly accessible platform, complete with a dashboard that allowed users to create malicious files, track victims, and access stolen information," McAfee Labs said. The cybersecurity company identified more than 1,560 registered accounts, over 400 malicious files, and more than 29 distribution URLs associated with the campaign. Marsalek also deploys a second information stealer called PureLog to steal sensitive data and exfiltrate it to another server. "This means that while someone using Marsalek may believe they're collecting stolen passwords and other personal information for themselves, the malware operator could also gain access to that information without their knowledge," McAfee Labs. This tactic is called double theft or a dual-hook infection.

New findings from SOCRadar show that ransomware operators have started handing the attack to AI agents, leading to the rise of agentic ransomware attacks. "Agentic ransomware is ransomware where AI agents do the hands-on work: choosing techniques, running tools and writing code, within limits a human sets," SOCRadar said. "In less than a year, AI agents moved from building access for ransomware brands to running live encryption and extortion campaigns."

An active campaign discovered in early October 2026 is targeting internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances and using Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands to deliver malware such as XMRig miner and Gh0st RAT. The attacks employ predefined username and password lists to brute-force into the servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems. "The malware scans IP ranges for exposed SQL Servers and attempts to log in using supplied credentials," Fortinet said. "After a successful login, it remotely executes malicious T-SQL commands on the compromised server to download and run additional malware." It's not known how many servers were compromised or who was behind the campaign.

A Europol operation, in collaboration with law enforcement agencies from 14 countries across the globe, has successfully identified vendors and buyers from major dark marketplaces as part of Operation TorNado, a coordinated international effort targeting cybercrime, drug trafficking, and firearms offenses. "The operation, which spanned from May 2025 to October 2026, resulted in 354 arrests and hundreds of house searches worldwide," Europol said. "This effort included a follow-up action focused on the identification of suspects after the takedown of five major dark marketplaces: Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom, [and] Tor2Door." The U.S. led with 132 arrests, followed by the U.K. (59). Authorities also seized more than 5.7 metric tonnes of illicit drugs, 209 firearms, and over $234 million in both cash and virtual currencies.

Threat actors have been observed using a "convincing device-code phishing attack" that involves a Microsoft Teams calendar invite booking flow to target a company in the construction sector. The attack was observed in mid-October 2026. "While many device code phishing lures leverage a generic Microsoft sign-in form, this attack crafted an email with a believable social engineering lure that impersonated a legitimate senior vice president of another company in the construction sector, complete with a typosquatted email domain," Huntress said. "A link in the message to the victim began a 'Microsoft Teams Meeting Scheduler' booking flow, which included prompts to pick a duration of the call, as well as a date and a time. On the backend, these prompts kicked off the Microsoft device code sign-in process and returned a user code, and when the target clicked the 'Confirm Meeting' prompt on the lure page, they were unknowingly copying the code to their clipboard. Then a pop-up prompt opened to Microsoft's real device sign-in page, asking the target to submit the code, which completed the device-code phishing attempt."

Threat actors are probing two of 14 vulnerabilities newly disclosed in XWEB EVO, the Dixell refrigeration supervisor now sold under the Copeland name. According to VulnCheck, the flaws in question are CVE-2026-124014 (an unauthenticated write of the system configuration file via config.lua) and CVE-2026-124010 (an unauthenticated root command execution flaw). These two flaws, along with seven others, only affect firmware builds that predate a 2021 rewrite, while the remaining five also impact the latest firmware, 5.8.8, which has reached end-of-support and won't be patched.. As of March 2026, Copeland ended software support for the XWEB EVO family, and has advised customers to move to XWEB Pro models.

Microsoft has warned of a phishing campaign exploiting the widespread outage on November 12, 2026, that affected access to business email and other cloud services across multiple regions. "The messages impersonate Microsoft 365 service health notifications and reference the legitimate Exchange Online incident EX1550543," Microsoft said. "The activity is consistent with credential phishing, although credential collection and malware delivery have not been confirmed." The outage has since been attributed to a software defect introduced in a July 2026 update for network gateway servers.

Threat actors are exploiting unpatched GeoVision camera software to deploy an XMRig cryptocurrency miner across 13 organizations. "All malicious activity stemmed from GeoStartupAgentService.exe; across many endpoints, the activity was run under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM account," Huntress said, adding the bulk of the attacks occurred between November 8 and November 10, 2026. The attack employs the Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) technique to tamper with antivirus protections like Microsoft Defender by making use of "wsftprm.sys." Also deployed as part of the intrusion chain is a PowerShell script that drops a custom Golang loader that uses BitTorrent DHT and PKARR for C2 server discovery for added resilience and to make it possible to move to new infrastructure without losing access to the infected machines. In the final stage, the loader sets up a scheduled task to execute itself every 15 minutes and ultimately deploys the miner.

Conclusion

The strange part isn't how clever some of these attacks have become. It's how many still work because of things nobody checked, fixed, or thought twice about.

And with finding flaws getting cheaper and exploiting them getting easier, that gap is only becoming harder to ignore. Plenty to unpack this week.
