All three run by one organization

Lim's assessment

Campaign attribution

Unverified until infrastructure links confirm

Where AI investigation agents break

The walkthrough has the agent reading attacker-controlled pages at every step. That is the core weakness, and attackers have already found it.

Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that phishing emails in one campaign carried a password-protected attachment for the human and hidden instructions for the AI assistant that summarizes the inbox. Sublime Security documented phishing emails stuffed with invisible text copied from real Adidas newsletters and romance novels, meant to push AI filters toward a benign verdict. StrongestLayer found a malicious file carrying an "LLM_IGNORE_START" comment aimed at AI scanners. Sublime's researchers put the hidden-text technique at under 1% of phishing traffic, so this is early. It is also exactly the input an investigation agent consumes.

Three other failure modes show up in practice:

Overconfident links. Step 3 is where agents turn a shared registrar into "the same threat actor." A claim without an evidence item behind it should never reach a report.

Missing business context. An agent doesn't know that your marketing team runs a microsite on a hyphenated domain, or which vendor portals your staff use.

Too much permission. An agent that can file takedowns or change firewall rules on its own turns one poisoned page into an outage or a legal letter.

The defenses are design choices you can ask about. Treat everything the agent fetches as data, never as instructions. Separate the permission to read from the permission to act. Require every claim in a verdict to point to an evidence item. Log every tool call so the investigation can be replayed. Keep a human approval step on anything that leaves the building.

Seven questions to ask before you trust an investigation agent

Gartner's agent-washing estimate means most demos will look impressive. These questions separate an agent that investigates from a chatbot with a playbook behind it.

Show me the evidence ledger for a real case. Every claim in the verdict should link to an artifact: a record, a screenshot, a log line.

What does it do with a domain that has no reputation yet? If the answer is "marks it clean," it would have passed teams-online[.]com.

Can it investigate beyond the inbox? Lookalike domain registrations, search results and ads are delivery channels now. An email-only agent sees part of the campaign.

How does it separate content from instructions? Ask what happens when a phishing page or email contains hidden text addressed to the AI.

What can it do without human approval? Get the list in writing. Read-only enrichment can be automatic. Blocks, takedowns and user notifications need a person.

Can we replay an investigation? You need every query and tool call logged, so an analyst or auditor can retrace the path.

What is its accuracy on our data? Vendor benchmarks are best cases; in Microsoft's trial, the agent was 100% accurate on the test corpus. Run a pilot on your own reported phishing and measure false positives and misses yourself.

Frequently asked questions

Can AI agents investigate phishing on their own?

AI agents can gather and correlate most of the evidence in a phishing investigation on their own, including domain records, page captures, related infrastructure and indicators. They should not take outward-facing actions such as takedowns or blocks without human approval, because attackers can plant instructions in the content agents read.

How accurate are AI phishing triage agents?

In Microsoft's randomized trial with 167 analysts, people working with the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent were up to 77% more accurate and found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute. The agent was 100% accurate on that test corpus, so expect lower numbers in production and measure on your own data.

Is agentic AI different from SOAR for phishing response?

Yes. A SOAR playbook runs fixed steps written in advance. An AI agent chooses its next step based on what it finds, so it can follow a lead like a sibling domain that no playbook anticipated. That flexibility is also why agents need evidence logging and approval controls.

What is the biggest risk of AI agents in security investigations?

Prompt injection. An investigation agent reads attacker-controlled emails and web pages, and researchers at Barracuda, Sublime Security and StrongestLayer have documented phishing content with hidden text aimed at AI systems. The fix is design: treat fetched content as data, limit what the agent can do without approval and log every step.

Will AI investigation agents replace SOC analysts?

The evidence points to a shift in analyst work rather than replacement. In Microsoft's trial, analysts with the agent spent 53% more time on the malicious emails, because the agent handled sorting and first-pass reasoning. Judgment calls on attribution, business context and response still sat with people.

Watch an agent work a real case

The fake Teams portals show where investigation work has moved. The evidence sat in domain registrations, cloned pages, search results and an AI answer. An agent that only reads the inbox would have seen a fraction of it, and an agent that can't show its evidence shouldn't be trusted with the rest.

Blaze AI is Cyble's agentic engine, and it runs across the company's threat intelligence and digital risk protection products, where this kind of outside-in evidence lives. Cyble describes Blaze as correlating threat intelligence and digital risk signals, extracting indicators, and producing decisions that are explainable and auditable. The useful test is the one in this post: give it a seed, watch it build the evidence ledger and see where it asks a human to decide.

Get a Blaze AI walkthrough and bring a phishing case of your own.

Title: Cofense Advances AI-Driven Phishing Defense with Adaptive Classification and Automation
Context: Unlike static AI models, Cofense’s enhanced AI combines the power of its globally trained phishing detection models with AI trained on an organization’s own analyst decisions...
Full Text:
Enhanced AI Classification Engine in Cofense Triage learns from analyst decisions and enables automated processing of high-confidence email classifications

LEESBURG, Va., November 12, 2026 – Cofense, the leader in AI-driven post-perimeter phishing defense, today announced enhancements to its Phishing Defense Platform with an updated AI Classification Engine (AICE) within its Phishing Remediation solution. AICE uses customer-trained AI to classify reported emails based on an organization's unique categories and enables automated processing of high-confidence decisions. This helps security teams reduce manual triage, accelerate phishing response, and free analysts to focus on complex threats that require human expertise.

Unlike static AI models, Cofense’s enhanced AI combines the power of its globally trained phishing detection models with AI trained on an organization’s own analyst decisions and threat environment. Together, these capabilities enable faster, more accurate threat classification and unlock greater automation of phishing response, reducing manual effort while allowing security teams to focus on the threats that matter most. This advancement reinforces Cofense’s commitment to delivering intelligent, adaptive, and automated phishing defense.

“AI should help analysts spend less time on repetitive email handling and more time on the threats that need their expertise,” said Jason Meurer, Director of Product Management at Cofense. “That requires AI that adapts to how their organization works and unique profile of threats they see. By learning from analyst decisions, explaining its classifications and letting teams set their own automation thresholds, AICE gives security teams the confidence to automate more of the response process while staying in control.”

Available within Cofense Triage, the enhanced AI Classification Engine advances phishing response in three areas:

Greater automation and analyst efficiency. High-confidence AI classifications trigger automated email processing, reducing manual triage and helping teams focus their expertise on complex, high-risk threats.

Adaptive AI tailored to each organization. Customer-trained models learn from analyst decisions and can be retrained on demand, delivering more precise classifications and adapting to evolving threats and workflows.

Explainable AI with security teams in control. Transparent AI decisions and configurable confidence thresholds give teams control over automation, while data and processing remain securely within the customer’s Triage environment.

In testing and validation, high-confidence AI classifications automated at least 30% of email handling work, with accuracy exceeding 98%.

Triage also provides model performance metrics, automation coverage and estimates of analyst hours saved, helping organizations evaluate results and refine their use of automation.

“Our investment in AI is focused on helping security teams automate phishing defense without increasing manual work,” said Marc Olesen, Chief Executive Officer of Cofense. “Customer-trained AI models, explainable decisions and analyst-controlled automation give organizations a way to increase the speed and scale of response while keeping human expertise focused where it matters most.”

Cofense is the leader in post-perimeter phishing defense, built for the reality that phishing gets through. Cofense helps enterprises identify threats already in employee inboxes, remediate active attacks fast, and reduce future risk. The Cofense platform combines phishing-specific AI with expert validation, automation, and collective insight drawn from millions of real-world user interactions. Human-supervised intelligence improves accuracy, eliminates guesswork, and accelerates response so security teams can act with confidence. Global enterprises including Mastercard, Accenture, and Toyota trust Cofense to strengthen organizational resilience against the most persistent cyber threat: phishing.

Title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
Context: A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server
Full Text:
A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in version 2.4.71, released yesterday.

Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected, according to Red Hat, which ships the server as part of Red Hat Enterprise Linux.

An attacker who can reach the server needs no authentication to exploit the flaw and could take full control of the server process, the Linux vendor says. It rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.

The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported.

HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host.

Standalone builds of the module, released on GitHub as mod_h2, are affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.

Admins who run the Apache HTTP Server project's own releases should move to version 2.4.71, the fixed release named in its security advisory. That release also fixes a crash in mod_md, rated important, and a one-byte overwrite of stack memory in mod_vhost_alias, rated low.

The distributions in the table below ship their own builds of the server, with their own package version numbers. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, for example, the fix ships as mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1.

Red Hat shipped fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 yesterday and rates the flaw Important on those releases rather than Critical. Their mod_http2 packages give each HTTP/2 stream its own memory allocator, which makes an attack much harder, according to the vendor's severity assessment. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier do not contain the vulnerable code.

The flaw was reported on October 26 by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, a free scanning service for open-source projects that uses the company's AI models. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it last week.

An earlier HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-23918, was fixed in version 2.4.67, released on May 4. Servers updated to that release, or to any later one up to 2.4.70, still run a version that the new flaw affects.

Title: ScreenConnect Attacks Target at Least 288 Endpoints Across 48 Organizations With Rogue Clients
Context: Huntress told The Hacker News that it has not seen evidence of a new vulnerability, but noted the exact method through which the attacker got panel access remains unclear
Full Text:
ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments following reports of unauthorized access.

In an advisory posted on its site, the company said there is no evidence that the incident involves a compromise of its infrastructure or a vulnerability in the ScreenConnect software.

"Our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," it said. "We are continuing to validate this assessment. The initial access method and full scope remain under investigation."

ConnectWise has identified about 400 partner environments with at least one of the third-party extensions installed. It also emphasized that the presence of the extensions alone does not indicate or establish compromise.

While these extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands, access to that API is secured by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup, it added. The list of extensions identified for precautionary disabling is below -

Labtech Plus

RMM Plus

RMM+

RMM Plus Password Link

RMM+ Password Link

ConnectWise also said it has urged on-premises partners to disable the extensions, and is recommending all partners to ensure security controls are running, preserve suspicious activity logs, and stay vigilant for -

Unusual sign-ins, unfamiliar locations, repeated login failures, and unexpected multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts

New administrator accounts or changes to user permissions

Unexpected extension installations, remote commands, and Toolbox activity

Unapproved remote-access software on customer devices and technician workstations

Unexpected support requests, password-reset messages, and software downloads through a trusted channel

The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) -

IP addresses:

185.99.255[.]28

155.94.150[.]39

Domains and URLs:

ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev

ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4

sc[.]payproofkit[.]com

cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com

newnewnew[.]gotdns[.]org

Soxnewwork[.]homedns[.]org

Artifacts:

sckit-run.bat

sckit-decoder.ps1

TrapWatch.ps1

Panel-Lateral.ps1

Run-Lateral-Full.bat

runnew.cmd

ToolboxRelayUploader.exe

Sqlite3.exe

Cybersecurity company Huntress, which is also tracking the activity, said it has observed attackers using access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push Run commands with an aim to install rogue ScreenConnect clients on at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations. The activity was first detected on November 11, 2026, at around 5:47 p.m. UTC.

Huntress told The Hacker News that it has not seen evidence of a new vulnerability, but noted the exact method through which the attacker got panel access remains unclear. Current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions to gain initial access, it said.

The overall attack unfolds in a worm-like fashion using a two-step process -

Initial access: Attackers use a compromised ScreenConnect panel's Run Command feature to deploy a rogue ScreenClient client across endpoints, creating a persistent backdoor that no longer depends on the original panel.

Lateral movement: When a technician connects to an infected endpoint through ScreenConnect, the malware can spread back to their workstation, steal saved browser sessions and authentication tokens, and pivot to other ScreenConnect panels the technician has access to.

"The rogue clients deliver SCKit, a custom malicious toolkit that establishes persistent remote access and creates a relay trap for intercepting session cookies," Huntress researchers Ben Nahorney and Susannah Matt said.

"The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads."

SCKit is delivered as an encrypted payload and via a Base64-encoded dropper ("sckit-run.bat"), which then contacts a remote server to fetch a PowerShell payload ("sckit-decoder.ps1") that's responsible for launching the toolkit.

Other components of the malware are designed to add Microsoft Defender exclusions, install a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client, create a scheduled task named "TrapWatch," and replace the legitimate ScreenConnect installation with an attacker-controlled copy.

There are signs that at least one of the scripts is generated by a large language model (LLM) based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain its functionality.

"Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel," Huntress said. "This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints."

This involves abusing the connection to fetch a dropper ("Run-Lateral-Full.bat"), which then connects to an external server ("ns.mo7sen[.]dev") to download a loader that gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to the attacker, and returns a tailored encrypted kit for that specific workstation -

"Panel-Lateral.ps1," which in conjunction with "LabConfig.ps1," steals the .aspxauth session cookie from the workstation and attempts to replay the cookie against the panel and get the tokens necessary to enumerate any other sessions the technician can access.

"ToolboxRelayUploader.exe," which leverages access gained to any other sessions to upload a payload, "WithUninstall.ps1," to the panel's Shared Toolbox.

"A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item," Huntress said. "This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item."

To add to the concern, the threat actor has been observed tagging each compromised managed service provider (MSP) with a sequential number. Huntress said the tags it has observed start partway through the sequence, indicating other MSPs may have been compromised earlier. ScreenConnect users are advised to check their Run Command history even if they haven't received alerts.

In a separate alert, Sophos said it has also observed unauthorized ScreenConnect client deployments following the same modus operandi. The activity has originated from three ScreenConnect instance IDs -

d905b2b1b165d0a9

4b8f4089ddaac6a9

df1f7ef0cfacd0d8

It's suspected that these are compromised instances that are being used to execute commands and deploy additional malicious instances, whose IDs are below -

2588ef5c15954b10

ed630cc2c873b091

"Curl.exe downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185.99.255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi," Sophos explained. "A ScreenConnect-generated command file then launched msiexec.exe to install the client silently. The researchers also observed ScreenConnect scripts staging batch files and using PowerShell with execution-policy bypass to retrieve a second-stage script from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4."

Title: Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates
Context: The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment
Full Text: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.” eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA. It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A. Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May. The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created. The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra. The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment. Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.” Sounds like a plan. ®

Title: Hackers stole AI credentials to get $740,000 in free compute; Railway picked up the bill
Context: ” A 26-hour battle The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure
Full Text:
As AI model training and distillation increase, AI tokens are becoming a piping hot currency for threat actors.

Cloud hosting provider Railway found out the hard way; it has confirmed a near 26-hour battle against attackers targeting AI provider credentials to sell to AI ‘transfer stations’ for use in model distillation. The crooks generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges using the stolen credentials and potentially had access to up to 100,000 workspace credentials.

Railway said the attacker’s database searches looked for AI provider keys by name before anything else; some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials.

The company disclosed the incident on October 22, and posted a follow-up report this week. Because of the ongoing investigation, it is not able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits, but advised users to revoke and reapply sensitive environmental variables stored on Railway prior to October 21.

“AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers,” said David Shipley of Beauceron Security. “So-called LLMjacking is expected to displace Cryptojacking as a cheap, scalable way to make money.”

A 26-hour battle

The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure. They were able to evade filesystem isolation protections and obtain an internal credential that they used to access stored build histories. From there, they retrieved a copy of Railway’s internal source code and analyzed it to identify additional avenues of compromise.

They then exploited another vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship that allowed them to gain even more access to Railway’s infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables.

In a nearly 26-hour battle, Railway’s engineering team worked 24-7 in shifts and the escalating situation became a “contest of agent speed,” the company explained. The threat actor chained various exploits, moved laterally across multiple systems, and “probed many potential routes, in parallel.” Defenders in turn hardened routes in parallel.

“This was not a single breach followed by a single fix,” Railway wrote.

The threat actors were “fully evicted” on October 21, but over the course of their time in the system, they obtained and decrypted a “subset” of customer variables, roughly 100,000, or “at most” 1.85% of workspaces. They also racked up $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges, with customers reporting their keys answered coding questions and performed training-data tasks they never ran. The company is working to reimburse customers, including for charges providers decline to refund.

The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to more than 1,850 users, which included GitHub and OAuth tokens that Railway says it reset. The company worked quickly with GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Stripe, and others to revoke potentially compromised keys.

In the wake of the attack, customers have been advised to remove public network access to databases; rotate any sensitive variables and keys; check GitHub account audit logs and review all app access; and check audit logs within registries such as Dockerhub.

On its own systems, Railway said it shut down any potentially compromised internal tooling; rolled all keys and “then rerolled them” after validating that intruders had been shut out; moved to a new generation of infrastructure; rebuilt tooling used to run its infrastructure; and added functionality to mass revoke Railway app permissions in the event of suspicious activity in the future.

Why attackers want AI keys

AI credentials are cheap to harvest at scale, Shipley noted; attackers can hit a provider like Railway rather than trying to target one company at a time. That access can then be resold to generate revenue through so-called AI routers, which provide access to models that users otherwise could not afford, or even reach.

This makes that access a hot commodity for tasks like distillation, which transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one to cut costs and improve efficiency.

Training one model on another model’s answers at scale takes millions of questions, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, and a single account asking millions of questions stands out. Stolen keys spread those questions across thousands of real customers.

“Think of copying a textbook one page at a time, using library cards that belong to other people,” Dickson explained. Frontier AI is expensive to buy, and the owner of the keys gets the bill while the thief gets cost-free compute.

“It is the 2026 version of cryptomining; [the] same playbook with a different output,” he said.

Managing identities when so many are machine-held

Even though the facts are ugly, Railway deserves credit for a “remarkably candid report,” Dickson emphasized: It owns its own configuration mistake, it admits it cannot be sure it found every account the attacker created, and it commits to telling customers of issues more quickly in the future.

Railway is now moving to short-lived credentials and logging every decryption. That is the right fix, Dickson said, and every platform holding customer secrets should copy it.

“Railway customers should treat every secret stored on the platform as stolen until they have rotated it,” he noted. But that rotation has to beat the thief’s clock; an investigation by Wiz found that stolen keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft, then flooded with traffic four to seven days later.

Start with AI provider keys, then rotate cloud, database, and payment credentials, he advised. Check AI provider bills and usage logs for traffic internal teams did not generate, then report any unauthorized charges to Railway. Alert on any call from an unrecognized address.

Further, he said, limit the damage any one key can do. Set hard spending caps and usage alerts on every AI key, and scope each key as narrowly as the provider allows. This really works: In one case Wiz examined, a key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles left most of the thief’s traffic throttled.

Non-Railway users, meanwhile, should ask their platform providers two questions: How are my secrets stored, and who can decrypt them? A good standard practice: Issue fewer keys. “No one ever said during a key rotation that they wished they had issued more keys,” Dickson pointed out.

Ultimately, he said, a stolen AI key spends real money, and machines now hold most of the keys. “Protect machine identities like cash, because to a thief, that is exactly what they are,” Dickson urged.

Title: ISC Stormcast For Thursday, November 12th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10176, (Thu, Nov 12th)
Context: Apache, for example, today released an update fixing a critical vulnerability in mod_http2. It would bring back some of these older CLFS attacks that before that feature was introduced.
Full Text: Hello and welcome to the Thursday, November 12, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich. We're recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Engineering. And as so often after a Patch Tuesday, we have a bit of a cleanup episode here today covering issues that we may have missed. Apache, for example, today released an update fixing a critical vulnerability in mod_http2. The vulnerability allows for remote code execution. Title: Securing persistent agents like OpenClaw at OpenAI
Context: With traditional software, we have relied on configuration and code to be deterministic and for threats to come (mostly) from external attackers
Full Text:
When OpenClaw launched almost a year ago, it showed the world the capabilities of a persistent agent. Unlike regular codex sessions which involve a fixed goal and human steering, persistent agents run 24/7 with a broad scope and the ability to proactively take actions without user input.

While persistent agents are extremely capable, their real world deployment has been limited to date. These deployments present many novel challenges compared to traditional software. With traditional software, we have relied on configuration and code to be deterministic and for threats to come (mostly) from external attackers. Persistent agents can change their configuration and write arbitrary code to accomplish a goal. Attacks come from the inside when agents take misaligned actions.

At OpenAI, we currently have persistent agents deployed across the entire company, including hundreds of OpenClaw agents. This post covers some of the controls we’ve adopted to enable OpenClaw deployments at OpenAI.

Separate trusted and untrusted execution

In order to secure persistent agents, we needed to isolate trusted deterministic logic from un-trusted LLM execution. Trusted logic includes critical components like networking, identity, and sandboxing. This is traditional static code that, outside of software bugs, should behave as configured. Agents, the environment they execute in, and the code they write are considered untrusted. This is an environment where agents can dynamically generate code to accomplish a goal with no hard guarantees on behavior.

To support this in OpenClaw, we ended up implementing remote harness execution in the open source project. This enabled the OpenClaw Gateway to run in a separate container (and in our case, a separate cluster), from the agent harness.

By implementing the split, we could treat the gateway, the component that configured the agent, as trusted deterministic code and focus on sandboxing the agent workload as untrusted code.

Enforce hard security boundaries

Security boundaries for agent workloads are enforced through sandboxing, which limits the actions agents can take.

For our OpenClaw deployment, we used the following sandbox controls:

network: control what endpoints an agent can access - we used an organization-managed allowlist with explicit denials for restricted endpoints

workspace: control what files an agent can access - we only allowed writes to agent working directories

process: control what processes an agent can access - we relied on process isolation via codex linux sandbox

secrets: control what secrets an agent can access - we manage secrets through a credential broker so secrets are not visible to the agent

For our OpenClaw deployment, we used the built-in sandbox from the codex harness. The following are some of the settings we employed, divided between requirements.toml (restrict what options are available in codex configuration) and config.toml (actual codex configuration). Note that we also enabled some additional security controls - removing the ability to use danger-full-access mode and relying on cached web search which routes web searches through OpenAI’s own index for search queries.

requirements.toml

# Exclude unrestricted "danger-full-access" sandbox mode. allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"] # Permit cached hosted search, but not live hosted search. allowed_web_search_modes = ["cached"] # Require the managed network proxy. experimental_network.enabled = true # Prevent user-level configuration from expanding the domain allowlist. experimental_network.managed_allowed_domains_only = true # Allow only these destinations; replace with the workload's required hosts. experimental_network.allowed_domains = [ "github.com", "api.github.com", "codeload.github.com", ] # Explicitly block these destinations, including cloud metadata endpoints. experimental_network.denied_domains = [ "pastebin.com", "*.pastebin.com", "webhook.site", "metadata.google.internal", "169.254.169.254", ]

config.toml

# Select the permission profile defined below. default_permissions = "openclaw" # Use cached hosted search. web_search = "cached" [permissions.openclaw.filesystem] # Allow reads needed by the minimal runtime environment. ":minimal" = "read" # Allow reading and modifying the agent's workspace. "/home/dev-user/openclaw-workspaces" = "write" # Allow reading managed assets without modifying them. "/home/dev-user/read-only" = "read" # Prevent access to SSH credentials. "/home/dev-user/.ssh" = "deny" [permissions.openclaw.network] # Permit network access through the administrator-required proxy. enabled = true # Do not inherit an upstream proxy. allow_upstream_proxy = false # Keep the proxy's local/private-address guard enabled. allow_local_binding = false # Disable the SOCKS5 listener. enable_socks5 = false # Disable SOCKS5 UDP support. enable_socks5_udp = false # Do not permit proxy listeners on non-loopback addresses. dangerously_allow_non_loopback_proxy = false # Do not permit unrestricted Unix-socket access. dangerously_allow_all_unix_sockets = false [shell_environment_policy] # Preserve default filtering of sensitive environment variables. ignore_default_excludes = false # Remove GitHub credentials from agent command environments. # This does not hide credentials stored in accessible files. exclude = [ "GH_TOKEN", "GITHUB_TOKEN", "OPENCLAW_GITHUB_BASIC_AUTH", "OPENCLAW_GITHUB_READONLY_BASIC_AUTH", ] [apps._default] # Disable apps unless individually enabled. enabled = false # Disable destructive app operations by default. destructive_enabled = false # Disable open-world app operations by default. open_world_enabled = false

Add model-based safeguards

All the controls we talked about so far are static in the sense that they rely on traditional deterministic code to prevent an agent from taking misaligned actions. As models get smarter, it’s critical that we also have defenses that scale with compute - aka other models.

With Auto-review, a second agent can monitor and approve the actions of a primary agent. Constantly requiring human review creates review fatigue where humans are trained to blindly accept all permission prompts. By using an LLM based reviewer as a filter, we reserve human attention for high value approvals. This is a feature that is natively supported in both OpenClaw and Codex.

For our OpenClaw deployment, we enforce auto review on all agent actions.

Split agent identity from user identity

When an agent takes an action, we need to be able to audit said action, give the agent access to resources, and distinguish whether that action was initiated by the agent or by the user. Agent identity gives us the means to do so. There are emerging specifications like WAG that give agents their own access to resources, and others like XAA that let agents act on behalf of the user through OAuth delegation. Note that agent identity is different from service accounts which provide separate API access for bots. The two should be used together - for example, your agent should act with its own agent identity and access third party services through service accounts which are linked to said identity.

For our OpenClaw deployment, each agent has a unique identity that is associated with a ChatGPT Service Account. This gives each agent its own inference credential separate from the user’s and allows teams to connect custom plugins to the agent. This also lets us audit agent actions and if needed, turn off inference.

Observe everything

Comprehensive observability lets operators understand the full lifecycle of agents - from how they were configured to what actions they took. With persistent agents, it’s critical that we have this coverage in order to trace and detect misaligned actions.

For our OpenClaw deployment, we log everything - every configuration change on the control plane and all turns from the agent. Because agent turns can contain sensitive information, these logs are locked down and only available to a select few individuals in the security team.

Closing thoughts

We are still at the beginning of the adoption curve when it comes to deploying persistent agents. The lack of established best practices makes it difficult to adopt agents in many enterprises today.

When we rolled out our internal pilot of OpenClaw at OpenAI, we witnessed a huge jump in both productivity and adoption, from both technical and non-technical teams across the company. We now have over 500 agents that run proactively in the background doing meaningful work - everything from automatically opening PRs in response to product feedback to continuously running data experiments on new features.

During OpenAI dev day, we announced OpenClaw Enterprise (OCE), an open source vendor neutral agent control plane. If you use OCE, you can launch an agent with many of the safeguards we talked about built-in when using the standard codex preset. Note the project is currently still in the pilot phase and that we plan to get to a 1.0 release by the end of the year.

We believe many of AI’s biggest gains in industry will come from persistent agents. By sharing what we’ve learned and building OCE in the open, we hope to make them safer for everyone to deploy.

Title: Ease of use and secure defaults in the new AWS experience
Context: As you grow, you add more projects—each its own member account—when you have work that needs its own budget or collaboration boundary, like a personal experiment kept separate...
Full Text:
Starting on Amazon Web Services (AWS) is now more straightforward and more secure by default than it’s ever been. Over the past several months, we rolled out a new AWS experience that changes how you start building. It brings together a set of sensible, secure defaults, and taken one at a time, it’s easy to miss the bigger picture of what we’re building and why.

When we first built how you get started on AWS, cloud was a new concept. It was a world where RSS and APIs were the exciting new thing. Twenty years later, we’ve come a long way and learned a lot about how people start, build, and grow on AWS.

So, before I get into the recent launches, let me state the vision plainly: Make AWS straightforward to start on without giving up the depth, the pricing, or the security that make it the right place to grow. You shouldn’t have to choose between getting started quickly and staying secure. The rest of this post builds out this idea and highlights the defaults that make it real.

What developers told us

For years, developers have told us a version of the same thing. They knew AWS was where they wanted to grow, but they wanted to start fast, not plan for scale on day one. The same depth that lets AWS grow with you also meant more to set up on day one. There’s a payment method to enter before you can start, a console built for experienced administrators to get oriented in, and permissions to configure before your app can run. That feedback is fair, and it’s a big part of why we keep building a better AWS. The new experience is our answer to that, and most of it comes down to sensible, secure defaults.

The secure defaults behind the new experience

The new AWS experience sets secure defaults for you, so your setup starts secure instead of something you harden later. The defaults are sensible ones, drawn from what we’ve learned about how people start on AWS. Here are a few and what they do:

Builder ID sign-in, with two-factor protection built in. In the early days of AWS, you signed in as the account’s root user. You could set up separate identities for everyone, but that took real effort, so sharing one login was often the path of least resistance. We’ve learned a lot since then. AWS Builder ID is a personal identity that represents you as an individual, and you use it to sign in with email and password or through a social login like Google or Apple. When you start working with others, each person signs in with their own Builder ID rather than sharing one set of credentials, so access is tied to a person, not passed around. It’s the straightforward path rather than the hard one. In addition to that, you can register multi-factor authentication (MFA, an authenticator app or security key) that applies to whichever sign-in method you choose. This used to require deliberate setup. Now it’s there from the start.

A managed organization with AWS Organizations doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes. The starting flow is straightforward: you sign up and land in a project where you can start building right away. What I find interesting is what’s happening underneath. A project is more than an account. It pairs an account with its own spend limit and its own set of collaborators, so each project is a self-contained boundary with access scoped to just the people you invite. Rather than dropping you into a bare account, AWS creates and manages an organization for you, with your project as a member account inside it, and sensible guardrails already in place. As you grow, you add more projects—each its own member account—when you have work that needs its own budget or collaboration boundary, like a personal experiment kept separate from the beta you’re putting in front of your first users. This is the structure experienced teams land on eventually, usually after learning the hard way that putting resources with different budget or collaboration boundaries in the same account is tough to unwind later. The difference is we create the organization that enables this best practice for you from the start, so you’re set up for success well beyond day one without having to design or operate any of it yourself. When you’re ready for full control, you can activate advanced features in a single step and take over the organization directly, with no migration or downtime.

A data perimeter that grows with you. This is another default that I really want people to notice. You start with a foundational data perimeter already in place, restricting access to your resources from principals outside your organization. It’s a secure starting point rather than the complete, multi-dimensional data perimeter a larger organization would eventually build out. But the direction is that your security boundary should grow with you as you succeed on AWS, and here a brand-new developer gets that baseline automatically, without knowing the term or writing a line of policy.

A single AWS Region by default. Your resources run in one home Region to start, assigned when you sign up (aside from the handful of AWS services that are global by nature). That keeps your footprint simple and predictable: a smaller surface to secure and reason about, and a clear answer to where your data lives. When you need to operate more broadly, you can activate advanced features.

Spend limits that put you in control. You can set a hard spend limit on a project, starting at $20 a month, with notifications as you approach it. If a project reaches its limit, AWS pauses it rather than letting charges keep climbing, and you decide whether to raise the limit and resume. For an individual developer or a small team, that means no surprise bills: you set the ceiling, and no charges accrue past it without your say-so. You stay in control, and you can think big knowing the guardrails are already in place. A spend limit can also serve as an early signal. Unexpected spend is a classic indicator of inappropriate access or a runaway process, and because the project pauses at the ceiling you set, it also caps how far a cost surprise can go.

Roles set up for you, so IAM isn’t step one. As a new developer, you want to spend your early days building and experimenting, not wiring up IAM permissions. IAM Role Manager is on by default in the new AWS experience, so it creates and attaches the IAM roles your app needs as you build. Those roles start with the permissions an app typically needs to call other AWS services, enough to get you moving, not meant to last forever. As your app matures and tightening permissions matters, you take those roles over and right-size them, and by then you’ll know exactly what it needs. You focus on your app, AWS handles the plumbing.

Why the foundation matters

Starting from a secure base changes things in two ways. For you, it means the environment you start in is the one you keep. When you’re ready to scale, you grow it rather than building a new one. For us, it means secure by default is something we can keep extending, because a structured, secure starting point gives us a place to add to. We’re able to turn on additional governance controls as a natural part of the experience. One example we’re already working on is setting account-level Amazon S3 Block Public Access protections for newly created environments. I’m not going to put a timeline here, but I want to be clear about the trajectory.

Building for security and ease of use

Ease of use and strong security are too often framed as opposites. Everything we’ve shipped here is an argument that they don’t have to be. You can give someone the fastest possible path to building something real and have that path be secure and cost-safe by default. The same experience makes the easy things easy, like connecting your coding agent in a single step or inviting a collaborator by email, without extra setup. Each of these is useful on its own, but they were all designed around the same idea, that the easy path and the secure path should be the same path.

If you’ve tried the new experience, I’d genuinely like to hear what resonated and what you’d want next, including how we can make activating advanced features feel more managed over time. If you haven’t yet, the fastest way to see these defaults in action is to create an account and start your first project. We’re listening.

Keshav Narsipur

Keshav is Vice President of Identity, Cloud Governance, and Certificate Trust Services at Amazon Web Services. Keshav leads a global organization of engineers, product managers, and security professionals operating hyper-scale services that handle over 2 billion requests per second. His teams bridge the gap between developer velocity and enterprise security. Keshav’s organization is currently focused on pioneering new identity and governance capabilities to secure the generative AI era.

Vanderbilt is bringing campus systems back online after a cyberattack

BYOD claims it stole sensitive data, but Vanderbilt has not confirmed those claims

Students and staff should follow official guidance and watch for suspicious messages

Vanderbilt University is bringing systems back online after a cybersecurity incident claimed by the BYOD ransomware group.

Vanderbilt University is a private research university in Nashville, Tennessee. Founded in 1873, it now serves more than 13,800 undergraduate, graduate, and professional students across 12 schools and colleges, with programs ranging from engineering and education to law, medicine, and nursing. Its combination of teaching and research means its systems support not only everyday campus activities but also valuable academic research.

According to Bleeping Computer, BYOD claims it encrypted Vanderbilt’s databases and obtained more than one million Social Security numbers, along with names, email addresses, telephone numbers, student and employee records, and research data. It also claims control of a domain controller (a server that manages network access) and possession of backups.

How the attackers gained access remains undisclosed. Vanderbilt’s November 10 evening incident update states that the following systems and applications are available:

Campus Wi-Fi

Okta: Continue to use multifactor authentication (MFA)

Vanderbilt email (Outlook): Vanderbilt email is available on Vanderbilt and personal devices

CampusPrint

Brightspace

Zoom

YES (Your Enrollment Services): All course registration is proceeding as scheduled

Other Vanderbilt systems and applications remained restricted. The university says fully restoring normal operations could take several weeks.

The university has not confirmed the number of affected people. BYOD claims it obtained more than one million Social Security numbers, but that is not a verified count of affected students or other people. The university says it is still determining what data, if any, was accessed.

How to stay safe

BYOD has threatened to release the data it claims to have stolen.

Students and staff should follow Vanderbilt’s latest IT guidance and be alert to messages asking them to restore access, disclose passwords, or approve unexpected login requests.

We have a guide for people who discover their data was included in a data breach: Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know.

How Malwarebytes can help

Protection for personal devices can help reduce the risk of follow-on malware and scams, but it cannot undo the theft of information from a university’s systems.

Vanderbilt students can get free Premium Security for two years on up to three devices through our Malwarebytes Student Protection Program. This can help protect against malware and scams, including those that could follow any release of stolen data.

Title: Part 4 – Cybersecurity journeys: What I’d tell my younger self
Context: Detections are the rules and models that watch a system’s activity and flag the signs of an attack, and both they and AI are changing faster than most of us can keep up with
Full Text:
Over the past few weeks, I’ve introduced you to people who fell into security from the most unexpected places, who work in domains you’ve probably never heard of, and who were honest about what the job is like after the excitement fades and the real work begins. This is the final post in a four-part series following 11 Amazon Web Services (AWS) security professionals through the real stories of how they got here and what the work actually looks like. For this last one, I wanted to end where almost every one of my conversations ended up on its own: the things people wish they’d known sooner.

This one is about hard-won perspective, the kind you only get from doing the uncomfortable thing and coming out the other side. It’s about growth that doesn’t always feel like growth while it’s happening, and the advice these folks would hand to the earlier versions of themselves. If you’ve been with me since Part 1: I didn’t plan this, thank you for sticking around. I hope this last set of stories gives you something to carry into your own path.

Choosing the harder room

Justin Mills, Security Engineer

When I asked Justin Mills where someone should start, I expected a certification or a favorite course. His answer started with two words, “seek discomfort,” and his own career shows he means it. Justin is a security engineer with more than a decade in the field, and today he consults on how AI can strengthen security detections. Detections are the rules and models that watch a system’s activity and flag the signs of an attack, and both they and AI are changing faster than most of us can keep up with. What stuck with me was how much faster everything moved after he committed to doing the hard things: he earned two promotions in roughly 2 years.

So I asked him how, and his answer came back to the people around him. What surprised me was that he never went looking for them. Some came through luck, starting with the manager who hired him, and others arrived the way most good working relationships do: he got involved in projects, met the people on them, and the conversations just started flowing. He didn’t push or force any of it.

“Those who are meant to be part of your career story will be part of it, no shoehorning needed.” —Justin Mills

The other half of the equation was trust. Today, Justin works on hard problems, and his manager gives him room to work through them his own way, because he’s shown he can be trusted with that room. His manager even told him so directly: “I trust you to do the right thing and speak for us.” Earning that kind of trust changed how he approached the work. “That forced me to ask the right questions instead of defaulting to what I already knew,” he told me. There’s something important in that framing, because asking good questions isn’t a sign that you don’t belong; it might be the clearest sign that you do.

The lesson he had to learn later was almost the opposite of the one that got him started. Early on, growth meant taking on everything hard himself. As he moved up, it meant the reverse: learning to let go, treating delegation as a skill in its own right, and trusting the people on his team to carry work he could have gripped tightly. When I asked what he’d tell someone who feels stuck, he kept it short.

“Surround yourself with people who push you, not people who make you comfortable. Ask the right questions. Do the hard things. That’s the whole playbook.” —Justin Mills

Pandora’s box and a pile of dust

Tyler Gabor, Technician

Tyler Gabor has always been the person who takes things apart. He started out selling and fixing cell phones, learning what made them tick, before moving into help desk work. From there he made his way into data center operations, where the hardware went from handheld to industrial and the stakes scaled up with it. “If it lights up or makes noise, I’m messing with it,” he told me, and he meant it.

The jump from help desk to the data center came from preparation. While he was working help desk from home, Tyler studied for a few foundational certifications, and when he could show he knew what he was talking about, he started putting his name in for roles. One of those led to AWS, though not directly: a staffing agency he partnered with placed him on a temporary assignment there, and from that point he had to prove himself all over again to earn a full-time offer. He admits it wasn’t easy and was sometimes scary, and he compares the whole stretch to the Olympics, trying out for a spot on Team Amazon alongside some of the most talented people in the field. “It was the audition of a lifetime,” he told me.

When Tyler explains his work to people outside tech, he reaches for mythology. “It’s kind of like fixing Pandora’s box,” he said, “while also making sure that Pandora doesn’t get outside of the box.” It’s a vivid image for a job that involves testing, repairing, and sanitizing server hardware so the data a machine once held can’t resurface. That can mean wiping a drive, degaussing it (using a powerful magnetic field to scramble the stored data), or physically destroying it. This is security you can physically touch, and as he put it, “It’s a little hard to get intellectual property out of a pile of dust.”

What pulled him in wasn’t a degree program or a bootcamp. It was watching high-profile leaks and breaches dominate the news as a student, which made it clear that security wasn’t an abstract discipline but something shaping real events in the real world. That curiosity never faded; it’s the same impulse that has him tinkering with hardware side projects to this day, like programmable NFC chips (the same short-range wireless technology behind tap-to-pay cards) that he brings to hacker conferences as business cards. That same urge to see what a piece of hardware is really capable of shows up in his day job, too.

One project crystallized the stakes for him. A piece of hardware came through that most people would have assumed was safe to discard, and on closer inspection it was still holding information that should never have left the building. The lesson stuck with him, and he put it the way only Tyler would.

“It doesn’t matter if the front door is locked if all the windows are open.” —Tyler Gabor

What surprised me most, though, was how much he talked about leadership, not in the org-chart sense, but the quiet kind that shows up when your team trusts you to make the right call on your own. He didn’t expect to be trusted with hardware of this caliber, and you could hear how seriously he takes that responsibility. His advice for anyone early in their career, or thinking about the switch, sounds simple but clearly took time to earn: just ask for help, because when you do, people usually give it. And if you’re already in and feeling stuck, prepare for the role you want so you’re ready when it’s time to step up to the plate.

“We are going to witness the greatest leap in human intelligence during our lifetime. As technology grows at an exponential speed, we’re going to need people to keep it in line.” —Tyler Gabor

A short word from Zlata

You might remember Zlata Pavlova from Part 1, where she shared her path from political science to open source investigations and into protective security. I wanted to bring her back for a moment, because something she said has echoed through nearly every conversation in this series: the thing that holds people back is rarely a lack of skill, it’s the quiet suspicion that they don’t belong. Her answer to impostor syndrome is to remind yourself that you do and to build connections early. She spent years assuming her teammates already knew what she knew, and it turned out they often didn’t, because their focus was elsewhere. She also told me the biggest surprise of her current role was how much of it is writing, and especially how much of that writing means translating technical findings for readers who aren’t technical. As you move up in security, the reports, advisories, and briefs you write become one of the clearest signals of your judgment, so practicing that skill early, whether through a blog post, a conference talk, or simply explaining your work to a friend outside the field, pays off for years.

“Don’t feel embarrassed sharing something you think people already know. They might not, and you might help somebody who’s just starting out.” —Zlata Pavlova

The thread

Something I didn’t expect when I started this series was how often people’s earlier jobs turned out to be an advantage rather than a detour. Zlata told me that people who come into security from non-technical careers often explain things better, because they remember what it was like to need the explanation. Tyler’s years in telecommunications, where customers handed him phones that held their whole lives, are what first got him thinking seriously about protecting people’s information. And in Part 3, Brandon’s time administering systems and shipping software gave him the empathy for builders that his application security work depends on. The backgrounds people bring with them are part of why they’re good at this work.

If you’re early in your career and wondering whether you belong here, the people in this series would tell you that you do. If you’re mid-career and feeling stuck, pay attention to whichever story felt familiar, because that’s usually a clue about where to look next. And if this series showed you a corner of security you didn’t know existed, that corner might be a good place to start.

If you want to start, here are a few places to begin:

AWS Skill Builder has more than 1,000 free self-paced courses, including security learning plans

Navigating your way into cloud security maps the roles and skills across the field

The NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity lays out dozens of security roles and what each one needs

Your local DEF CON group or a nearby security meetup, because community came up again and again in these conversations as the thing that speeds everything up

I’m grateful to everyone who sat down with me and shared their story. Hearing them changed how I think about what this field looks like, and I hope reading them does the same for you as you work out your own path.

What would you tell your younger self about getting into security? Share it on LinkedIn!

This concludes the Cybersecurity Journeys series. Read the full series: Part 1: I didn’t plan this, Part 2: What even is this job?, Part 3: The work behind the work, and Part 4: What I’d tell my younger self.

Known in the community as AWSlady, she is passionate about security education and mentoring the next generation of defenders.

Title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
Context: The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail
Full Text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

Title: Critical Zoom Workplace Flaw Could Allow Unauthenticated Remote Privilege Escalation
Context: Zoom has released software updates to address two security flaws impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows, including a critical bug that could result in privilege escalation on...
Full Text:
Zoom has released software updates to address two security flaws impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows, including a critical bug that could result in privilege escalation on affected systems.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access.

CVE-2026-108187 (CVSS score: 8.1) - An origin validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access.

Successful exploitation of either of the shortcomings could permit remote attackers to escalate privileges without requiring any special permissions or access.

While CVE-2026-108187 affects Zoom Workplace for Windows before version 7.1.5, CVE-2026-108186 impacts versions starting from 7.1.0 and before 7.1.8.

Earlier this July, the popular videoconferencing platform shipped fixes for another improper input validation flaw impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows (CVE-2026-53412, CVSS score: 9.8) that could enable an unauthenticated user to take control of accounts.

Although Zoom makes no mention of the vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, users are advised to apply the latest patches to mitigate potential threats.

Title: Suspected Chinese Malware Supplier Tied to Three Hacking Campaigns
Context: Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools
Full Text:
Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools.

Check Point Research (CPR) detailed the findings in a November 10 report, linking the clusters through shared infrastructure features and code similarities within the Sparrow framework.

The year-long investigation covered campaigns targeting several dozen high-profile organizations across the three regions. CPR called the suspected supplier behind the framework 'CopperDragon.'

Three Clusters Share Sparrow Framework

The three clusters are tracked by CPR researchers as SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire.

SilentDelivery, observed since early 2026, has compromised legitimate websites, mainly in government, shipping and IT or research sectors.

Visitors were shown a fake Chrome certificate warning that prompted them to install a "Certificate Fix" utility, with targets mainly in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong and Indonesia. The fake utility delivered SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant, giving the attackers an initial foothold.

OceanGate was observed during 2025 and 2026 and mainly targeted government organizations and critical infrastructure in Asia. CPR said attackers entered through an internet-facing Linux server before moving into Windows environments and conducting extensive credential theft, lateral movement and exfiltration of sensitive operational information.

DarkWire, first identified in mid-2025, initially concentrated on Latin America but more recent intrusions suggested expansion. The cluster has targeted telecom operators, including at least three major providers in the region, as well as foreign affairs and justice bodies.

CopperDragon May Sit Behind Multiple Groups

CPR described CopperDragon as "a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors" and the Sparrow framework's "possible developer and supplier." It also assessed that CopperDragon is involved in maintaining and supplying variants of the Melofee backdoor.

The report links the framework to FamousSparrow, first identified in 2021 and known for using the SparrowDoor backdoor. CPR said Earth Estries, TropicTrooper and UAT-9244 use a shared toolset "potentially supplied by the same entity," and noted that FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, though the details of that relationship remain unclear.

Read more on FamousSparrow: FamousSparrow Swaps SparrowDoor For New SparroWocky Backdoor

For DarkWire, CPR said it did not identify direct code similarities with the CopperDragon toolset. The link instead rests on infrastructure tied to a previously reported FamousSparrow domain.

Shared malware and infrastructure "can blur the boundaries between operators and campaigns," CPR wrote, presenting its findings as a basis for tracking activity long grouped under FamousSparrow more precisely.
