Title: What will it take to make VulnOps a reality?
Context: ” Autonomous patching may only be transitional Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove...
Full Text:
Just over a year ago, before advanced AI models began discovering software vulnerabilities at a nearly unmanageable scale in the so-called vulnpocalypse, three industry experts pioneered the concept of “VulnOps.”

VulnOps, as envisioned by Heather Adkins, Gadi Evron, and Bruce Schneier, is a significant phase in the evolution of AI-assisted cyber defense in which vulnerability research and remediation would become scalable, repeatable, automated, and integrated into enterprise operations. They contemplated that this new era of organizational vulnerability management would progress from AI-augmented vulnerability management to self-healing networks.

Since then, the Cloud Security Alliance has developed an operating VulnOps model, SANS has published VulnOps implementation guidance and will be introducing VulnOps training, and practitioners are beginning to experiment with the constituent technologies surrounding the idea.

The real question, however, is whether VulnOps development is happening fast enough to keep pace with the onslaught of vulnerability discoveries.

As Evron, CEO and founder of AI security and data access governance platform Knostic, tells CSO, “I’m looking at the world right now, and I’m seeing that a lot of people are spending a ton of money finding vulnerabilities. But the challenge is: What do we do once we find them? And that’s where it gets really complex.”

Not your father’s vulnerability management program

The most obvious precursor to how VulnOps can create a mindset shift in vulnerability management is the widespread shift in software development created by DevOps. According to IBM, DevOps is “a software development methodology that accelerates the delivery of high-performance applications and services by combining and automating the work of software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) teams.”

Experts stress that VulnOps, however, doesn’t mean doing existing vulnerability management faster by adding AI components. It is an entirely new way of approaching vulnerability management that relies on AI agents to automate and speed up how organizations deal with vulnerabilities.

They say it is nothing short of an entire overhaul of existing vulnerability discovery, prioritization, and remediation practices.

“The core philosophy is moving to more continuous automated processes and faster feedback loops, as we did with DevOps, where we’ve learned to produce more code faster,” Rich Mogull, chief analyst at the Cloud Security Alliance, tells CSO. “We’re now taking that into vulnerability management. If you think about what was different about DevOps, it was the philosophy about going from an iterative cycle to a continuous cycle with fast failure and feedback loops.”

Ed Skoudis, president of the SANS Technology Institute, argues that AI must become central to how vulnerability management operates. “What we’re talking about here is an AI-centric workflow where the AI is doing most of the analysis, and humans are just overseeing the operation,” Skoudis tells CSO.

Not everyone, however, is convinced that VulnOps represents such a fundamental departure from established practices.

“It feels like a rebranding to me,” Chris Elgee, SANS principal instructor and senior security analyst at Counter Hack Challenges, tells CSO.

“Organizations have always had to deal with vulnerability management,” says Elgee, who agrees that the accelerating pace of vulnerability discovery is putting new pressure on organizations, but questions whether VulnOps constitutes a fundamentally different discipline.

Is human-in-the-loop dead?

Experts disagree on one fundamental aspect of VulnOps as they currently understand the concept. The disagreement centers on how much human control can survive when vulnerability remediation has to operate at AI speed.

“The biggest struggle people have with patching vulnerabilities in general is that it’s disruptive to the workflows,” Ali Khan, CISO of AI-powered device security company Iru, tells CSO. “Generally, when there’s a security vulnerability and you need to patch it, you have to upgrade your source code or the third-party supply packages,” Khan explains.

“And generally, that leads to breaking changes, especially in legacy systems that have been long-lived and are in maintenance mode,” Khan says. “You don’t want to bring a company down or destroy their revenue stream by pushing a patch that essentially stops the business process.”

That risk is why most security professionals aren’t eager to take humans out of the loop.

CSA’s Mogull cautions, “We’re nowhere near fully automating [the remediation] part of the process. Eventually, we will need more, but we’re not there yet, even with today’s tools,” he says.

Nor does he envision VulnOps operating without human oversight. “Remember, humans are the ones that are accountable,” Mogull says. He points out that under the CSA operating model he helped develop, AI can make decisions within predefined policies, but potentially disruptive changes still require human intervention.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis argues for what he calls a governance-in-the-loop process where “you have governance that decides that, ‘Hey, if a given action that I take could fall below this governance-in-the-loop level, just do it. Automate it. Don’t even think about it.’”

“Each organization is going to have its own separate line for where governance in the loop will apply, but you could say, for example, regarding important patches for Windows workstations, deploy them if they’re critical, on a rolling basis. So, in other words, do 25% per hour or two, over the space of half a day.”

Knostic’s Evron, however, believes that even these arrangements may prove unsustainable as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“One of the main understandings of the last couple of months is that human in the loop is dead,” he says. “We simply can’t move fast enough for the vast majority of operations to have a human in the loop.”

On top of that, Evron questions whether autonomous patching itself will remain an adequate solution. “We must understand that patching is just not going to be fast enough,” Evron says. “We must start considering how we build security programs in a world where patching is not viable.”

Autonomous patching may only be transitional

Evron thinks automated patching is a necessary interim step, but that even fully automated remediation may eventually prove inadequate as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

“Start your program for autonomous patching today, but understand that we need to prepare for a world without patching,” he warns. “If we have a human in the loop, it’s just a performer. The human would have all the responsibility with no authority and no ability to understand and comprehend what they’re doing.”

Evron argues that the industry should stop thinking exclusively about finding flaws and fixing them after the fact and should opt instead for software and defensive systems that prevent vulnerabilities from being introduced, detect and neutralize exploitation in the first place, or make individual vulnerabilities less consequential.

He sees three approaches to making these preventative systems a reality. The first is to embed them directly into AI coding agents, rather than relying primarily on vulnerability scanning after code has been written. “Control your coding agents and you control your code, so the code itself gets generated more secure,” Evron says. He also advocates scanning code for vulnerabilities upon generation, rather than waiting for it to enter traditional continuous integration pipelines.

The second approach is to detect and neutralize attacks at runtime. Evron describes what he calls “patch in place during runtime.” At this year’s [un]prompted conference, Evron went on stage to show ways of conducting patch in place during runtime. “As an attack is going on, it is detected in the logs and patched,” Evron says.

The third approach to creating a system that obviates the current patching cycle is to make patching less urgent through defense in depth, according to Evron. He suggests moving toward approaches in which critical vulnerabilities become a matter of defense in depth, “so you don’t necessarily need to patch immediately.”

Steps CISOs should be taking now

According to Evron, the most critical step CISOs should take in embracing VulnOps is to stop relying solely on established practices that may prevent them from recognizing how AI is fundamentally changing the threat environment.

For example, basic security hygiene remains important but cannot be treated as a sufficient response to AI-driven vulnerability discovery, he says. “Stop being afraid to imagine, go bigger, and understand that, well, of course our basics always matter; they will not save us,” he adds.

And yet other experts question how organizations can embrace the challenging new world of VulnOps without first nailing down their security basics. Counter Hack’s Elgee says, “A lot of organizations, maybe most organizations, don’t even have a full concept of what their entire asset inventory is.”

Iru’s Khan says that CISOs should start to think about how security and engineering need to renegotiate their relationships, given that security teams cannot simply hand developers remediation tickets and expect faster results. “This wall has to come down, and there has to be comfort letting other teams contribute in a technical way to systems,” Khan says.

SANS Technology Institute’s Skoudis advises CISOs to begin implementing VulnOps without attempting to transform the entire enterprise over to a new paradigm. He argues that organizations should start to establish governance boundaries within which AI agents can operate.

“If it’s above the threshold, if it’s higher business risk, then you have to have a human review it,” Skoudis says. “But if it’s below the governance-in-the-loop threshold, push it.”

Evron is confident that CISOs can expect their existing teams to handle the transition to VulnOps, particularly if they reduce their dependence on the vulnerability scanning tools that kick out so many vulnerability reports. “The existing teams can handle this, but not with the current technologies they use,” he says. “We must stop paying mindlessly to the big scanning services because the bottleneck has always been fixing and patching.”

He adds, “Therefore, building a system where we trust autonomous patching is what we must do right now, in the immediate term, and longer term in our plans we must understand we will not be able to rely on patching.”

Context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem
Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of checkpoint files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Dave Bittner: Hello, good to be back.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, thanks for joining me yet again. And we are as we have been all year talking about the ten-year anniversary of the "CyberWire Daily." Again, congratulations, Dave. That is a wonderful milestone.

Dave Bittner: Thank you.

Maria Varmazis: And we've been in these conversations eventually getting to a topic and ringing the bell of oh, we have to talk about AI. It just feels inevitable when we talk about cybersecurity nowadays.

Dave Bittner: Right.

Maria Varmazis: We're getting that out of the way real early in this conversation today because we're going to be talking about AI and cybersecurity as our topic for today. So --

Dave Bittner: Right, right.

Maria Varmazis: -- ding a ding a ding. Here we are. We're talking about it the entire time today.

Dave Bittner: Yes, it's a funny thing because I feel like in my interviews, you know, as a interviewer you always have go-to questions, right? I refer to it as a bag of tricks. Maria Varmazis: You're giving away our secrets to people.

Maria Varmazis: No, no, we're brilliant. We always think on our feet.

Dave Bittner: That's right.

Maria Varmazis: We don't have shortcuts. Yes, it's great.

Dave Bittner: Exactly. Spontaneous. Yes, but these days you can always say, "Well, how does AI affect this?" And off you go, right?

Maria Varmazis: Off you go. Yes, there's always a great answer to that one because inevitably it's doing something. So, when I was preparing for this chat, I think I'm having the same whiplash every human being is having with how much AI as a concept, as a broad umbrella of technology, has quickly progressed in just the past months, if not years. So, trying to go back ten years thinking about this, I'm not sure how much of my own recollection I can honestly trust. Just putting that out there.

Dave Bittner: Yes.

Maria Varmazis: But if -- I'm trusting you a lot more than I'm trusting myself, Dave, if you can go back ten years and remembering, we were talking about AI back then, but it to me seems like it was one day far off or very vague. We're not there yet tech. Maybe your recollection is different. What do you remember?

Dave Bittner: I think you're right. I was -- I think back then it was more the promise of AI versus the reality and much of the AI that was happening was happening under the hood and it wasn't anything that a regular user could really get their hands on. It was just this thing that the folks with technical expertise had included in whatever platform or package you had purchased and it was somehow going to help you do your work more quickly, more efficiently, more securely, all those good things. I want to say it was 2016 or so was the year at the RSA conference was the first year that everything was AI.

Maria Varmazis: Oh.

Dave Bittner: And it was that kind of AI. It wasn't large language models. It wasn't chatbots. It was just everybody. If you were selling a product, you had to say somewhere under the hood, there was AI. And --

Maria Varmazis: That hasn't changed in ten years. Yes.

Dave Bittner: It has -- no, it hasn't changed. But there was a lot of eye rolling back then because I think the notion of what it is and what it could do and like there are still people who get bent out of shape when you say AI versus machine learning and is it this, is it really that or you know, and you have those debates and conversations till the cows come home. But I guess the challenge back then was how much of this is real and how much of it is marketing, particularly when it's all under the hood and you really can't see it yourself?

Maria Varmazis: Were you seeing it in specific contexts at that time? I mean, I know it was sort of being spammed everywhere as the you know, marketing team has been given their directive. You have to include it. But were there certain defense or attack areas that were seeing you know more successful deployment? And if you remember any of this, what was the (inaudible)?

Dave Bittner: Yes, I mean I guess the promise was that these AI systems could recognize attacks that had never been seen before. Right? So, we were coming from the days of indicators of compromise and malware signatures. So, it was really built off of the fact that somebody saw something, documented it, reported it, and your antivirus software would then start scanning for that. And the idea was that these AI systems didn't need that, that they could just look for anomalies or they could even look at behavioral things and that -- what black magic was that? And so, raise alerts that your normal virus searching software would miss.

Maria Varmazis: Yes, I want to say there's also a confluence of you know, we were coming off of sims being a big thing that -- not that new at that time, but there was just -- we were well into that world of sims and the flood of alerts and that just became a huge problem also that I think AI was being promised as a potential solution for, but again, I don't remember as well as I'd like.

Dave Bittner: I think also, like just a fun thing to remember is like it was back in 2011, I believe, that IBM's Watson competed on Jeopardy and won.

Maria Varmazis: What? What?

Alex Trebek: And now the newcomer, developed and programmed especially for this moment, making its first appearance on our national television program, ladies and gentlemen, this is Watson.

Dave Bittner: Pretty sure that was 2011, and Watson you know, kicked Ken Jennings' butt on Jeopardy. Ken Jennings now the host of Jeopardy.

Maria Varmazis: I was going to say I think somebody might -- well, I mean who really won? Yes.

Dave Bittner: Yes, right, exactly. In the end, Ken got the last laugh. But what was so interesting about that, and I think what captured people's imagination was like we've been used to computers being able to play chess.

Maria Varmazis: Yes.

Dave Bittner: Which is very deterministic. You know, you could -- most people who know how to play chess can understand how computing power could be thrown at the problem of chess, because of the limited amount of things that chess pieces can do and all those kinds of things.

Maria Varmazis: It's basically an extremely complicated algorithm that the more you study it, you understand certain outcomes. I don't play chess, but this is also my understanding. Yes.

Dave Bittner: Right. And so, you could see that how you could throw computing problem at that and get good results. And so, computers had been competing for chess championships for long periods of time up to this point. You know, there -- you could go to your local radio shack, which still existed, and buy a computer chess set that would play against you. And depending on how good you were, well, if you were at my level, it would beat you every time. Right.

Maria Varmazis: Same. Yes, same.

Dave Bittner: By the way, I should add in preparing for today's episode, I went -- I found a clip of me at the 2016 RSA conference. I was being interviewed by Matt Stephenson, who was working at Cylance at the time. And so, we caught up at the Cylance booth, and we actually discussed this very topic about AI and playing chess. So, here's a clip from that interview.

Matt Stephenson: Any other kind of fringe technologies, maybe you personally, that are grabbing your attention? Obviously, AI and machine learning, big deals as that is maturing in the security market. But is there any kind of outlier that's worth keeping your eye on for the next year or two?

Dave Bittner: Oh boy, that's a good question. I mean, I think a lot of it is -- I think we have this huge problem with workforce issues. So, I will tell you, I heard an interesting interview last week with Garry Kasparov, the famous chess player, and he said that we are at the point where any computer, the best chess playing computers can beat any human. However, if he teams up with a chess playing computer, they can beat any machine. So, I'm really intrigued by that notion of not just the AI, but if you team up AI with a really smart human, how does that change the game? I think that's going to be something looking forward to really pay attention to. Do I sound ten years younger, Maria?

Maria Varmazis: Honestly, I didn't want to say it, but you --

Dave Bittner: Butter me up, flatter me. Tell me what I want to hear.

Maria Varmazis: The optimism and brightness in your voice and kind of how like "Isn't this going to be cool?" you know?

Dave Bittner: Right, right. No, the weight of the world had not yet crushed my spirit.

Maria Varmazis: I know.

Dave Bittner: So.

Maria Varmazis: But also, the tenor of which you speak about AI as a great potential thing as opposed to I think the existential dread most of us can't help --

Dave Bittner: Sure. Yes.

Maria Varmazis: -- but inject now.

Dave Bittner: Yes, the cynicism had not completely set in yet.

Maria Varmazis: No. It's a little wild, but it was also kind of sweet. I --

Dave Bittner: Yes. No --

Maria Varmazis: -- no but, how much things have changed in a decade though? I mean, truly.

Dave Bittner: Yes, and you know, of course, Matt was a great host and Matt passed away recently, so we miss him very much. At the time, that took the big compute that IBM's, was it Big Blue or whatever their Watson engine had that was able to do that to be able to just understand spoken word, interpret it and come back with a meaningful answer, that seemed magical at the time. Title: OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models
Context: The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a...
Full Text: In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior. “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post. The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.” OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one. The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development. “Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.” OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.” That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

Title: New malware doesn’t call home, it turns your Exchange server into its home
Context: The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania
Full Text:
There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders.

A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage.

The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks.

While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies, enterprises should still be concerned.

“Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.”

Sophisticated tradecraft

ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk.

The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part.

Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. An automated email collection module is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, allowing threat actors to access and manipulate the email transport pipeline, the researchers explained.

“This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique,” they wrote.

They described a typical attack chain this way: An official in a national government office sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, just as it should; nothing looks suspicious. But before the email departs, a piece of code quietly examines it, identifies whether it is interesting, and if it is, sets aside a copy to be forwarded to “prying eyes.” The original email continues on its way as usual.

The toolset demonstrated that Exchange servers are not just mail servers, they are “durable collection points,” internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft, the researchers noted. The transport pipeline reflects a level of investment in this type of technique that is “uncommon even among sophisticated APT [advanced persistent threat] actors,” they said.

The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania. ESET attributes the toolkit to Russia-aligned APT group Turla.

Attackers made a significant effort to remain undetected

Experts agreed that some of the most notable aspects of Cereal are the lack of a C2 channel and the effort the attackers made to stay in stealth mode.

“ESET found no attacker-controlled server. None,” Dickson noted. The victim’s own Exchange server is the command center, and the backdoor waits for encrypted requests on web paths that look like ordinary Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic.

“Cereal never calls home. It is home,” he said.

This is dangerous because most network defenses watch for traffic leaving for a suspicious destination. But here, there is no destination to block and no server to take down. “The attackers walk in through the front door, dressed as Outlook,” he noted.

Then there is the mail hook: Legitimate transport agents in Exchange allow software to inspect mail as it flows. But Cereal injects itself into Exchange’s mail process and wraps the agents already running in memory.

Mail keeps flowing, but nothing new appears. “It is the postal carrier who steams open the envelope, copies the letter, and reseals it before delivery,” Dickson said.

A component dubbed CerealBox selects messages with .doc, .docx, and .pdf attachments from chosen senders, recipients, and subjects. In Romania, ESET discovered that it collected mail involving The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and EU addresses. This should concern enterprises, Dickson said; swap in your preferred targets: outside counsel, your acquisition target, or your regulator, to retrieve a contract, a deal memo, or a legal strategy.

Further, the commands ESET documented include pulling entire mailboxes, extracting credentials stored on the server, and querying Active Directory for users, groups, and computers. An Exchange server sits deep inside the identity fabric. It is an Achilles’ heel because it is internet-facing, highly privileged, and complex. “Own it, and you hold the keys to the kingdom if you will,” Dickson said.

His advice: Migrate or retire on premises Exchange where possible. Treat whatever remains as a tier-zero asset, “guarded like a domain controller.” Limit internet exposure of Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync to what the business truly needs. Hunt with the indicators described by ESET. Watch for unexpected code loading into Exchange’s transport process.

But while the researchers’ work is excellent because it maps what Turla did once inside an organization in “remarkable detail,” it does not say how Turla got onto those servers, Dickson pointed out. No vulnerability is named, and no stolen credential or phishing email is described.

“A burglar who leaves no fingerprints is impressive,” said Dickson. “A burglar whose way in remains unknown is a problem for every house on the street.”

‘A level above’

And, said David Shipley, CEO of Beauceron Security, we’ve seen the gap between nation state hackers and criminals collapse over the past few years in terms of sophistication, in particular thanks to AI, but “then you see something like this, which is still a level above.”

Running on premises Exchange has been increasingly risky for years, he noted. For government, AI firms, finance, and other high-value targets, the risk of hosting on prem instead of using cloud-based versions continues to grow.

However, it’s worth noting that just having Microsoft host Exchange doesn’t mean you’re safe from nation-states, Shipley said. “It just raises the bar.” Another key challenge with Exchange servers is Microsoft’s own advice not to have anti-virus scanners looking in certain places like ExchangeTransport.exe, because doing so could create instability.

“They basically told criminals where to hide and why it’s good to hide there,” he noted. “Not that they can do much about it, but it points to a huge Catch-22.”

Another Catch-22: With the publication of this report and new ideas that will undoubtedly come from it, “we’ll likely see criminal groups consider the value of this kind of technique in the future,” Shipley noted.

Title: CVE-2026-118383: Use-after-free vulnerability in MongoDB
Context: Remote unauthenticated exploitation is possible, but only during a specific window that the attacker does not have visibility into
Full Text:
Key points and observations

CVE-2026-118383 is a critical use-after-free in MongoDB Server's primary catch-up process, with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5. It affects replica set members, including those used by shards and config servers. Standalone mongod instances are unaffected.

Remote unauthenticated exploitation is possible, but only during a specific window that the attacker does not have visibility into.

We reproduced a crash (segmentation fault) on MongoDB Server 8.0.34.

An unauthenticated client can set up the crash with two ping requests, because vulnerable servers accept ping before login. Turning on authentication does not prevent this.

Upgrade every affected replica set member to a fixed release. Restricting network access can reduce exposure while you upgrade.

What happened

MongoDB announced a security update on November 10. The company said it found the vulnerability internally and was not aware of exploitation attempts at the time of its announcement. The advisory describes a use-after-free when a newly elected replica set primary completes catch-up. During catch-up, the member applies operations it missed before accepting writes as primary.

The vulnerability affects ordinary replica set members. It also affects the replica set members used by shards and config servers in sharded clusters. A standalone mongod does not perform replica set primary catch-up and is not affected by this vulnerability. The advisory rates the issue Critical and says the server may terminate unexpectedly or, under certain conditions, execute arbitrary code in the server process.

How to know if you are affected

The issue affects replica set members, including shard and config server replica set members in sharded clusters. Standalone mongod instances are not affected.

4.4.32

Upgrade to the fixed release for your branch, or use a distributor package that includes the fix. Verify the version running on every member after the upgrade, including members in containers and any members that were offline during maintenance. MongoDB says Atlas clusters are upgraded automatically during maintenance. It urges customers who defer maintenance to apply the upgrade promptly.

Until you can upgrade, restrict network access to MongoDB to the specific systems that need access to it. This limits who can send the unauthenticated requests, but it does not fix the use-after-free.

Exploitation window and likelihood

When a replica set member wins an election, it first catches up on writes it missed, then starts accepting new ones. The bug is in the cleanup at the end of that catch-up step. Before any election happens, an attacker can leave two stale “waiters” on a member. A waiter is a pending notification MongoDB creates when a request asks to wait until replication reaches a certain point. Planting them does not crash the server by itself. The diagram below traces an election timeline and marks where the crash fires.

Plant during steady state: The attacker sends two unauthenticated ping requests that include a readConcern.afterOpTime value to a reachable, vulnerable replica set member. The waiters don't expire. They stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back, or steps down from primary.

Reach catch-up: Later, the same member has to win an election while it is behind another member. The attacker can't cause the lag or the election. Both have to happen on their own, for example during maintenance or an outage.

Crash when catch-up ends: When catch-up finishes, the new primary runs its cleanup twice, uses memory it has already freed, and crashes before it accepts any writes. Once the first two steps are in place, the crash does not depend on winning a timing race.

We created the lag and the failover ourselves, so the roughly 40 seconds our lab run took is not an estimate of how quickly a real attack would work. After the crash, our test cluster had no primary. Another deployment might elect a new primary and keep running.

What we reproduced

We built a four-member replica set from MongoDB's official Linux x86_64 binaries and created the two conditions an attacker can't control: one member falling behind on replication, and a failover that makes that member the new primary. Setting this up took admin access to the lab, to pause and stop mongod processes and to write data with an authenticated client. The attacker's part, the two ping requests, used no credentials, and we confirmed that the same unauthenticated client could not write to the database.

We ran the same failover three times, changing only the MongoDB version and whether we sent the two requests:

Run

Server

Unauthenticated waiter requests

Observed result

A

8.0.34

Both timed out after about 1.5 seconds with MaxTimeMSExpired

The target member exited catch-up twice, logged SIGSEGV, and the mongod process crashed

B

8.0.34

None sent

The target member exited catch-up once, became writable, and remained running through the observation window

C

8.0.37

Both rejected immediately with Unauthorized

The target member exited catch-up once, became writable, and remained running through the observation window

The video below shows run A from start to finish: the two unauthenticated requests, the failover we triggered, and the new primary crashing.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

In run A, MongoDB's log shows the new primary leaving catch-up mode twice within the same millisecond, followed by “Invalid access at address: 0” and “Got signal: 11 (Segmentation fault).” The backtrace points to CatchupState::abort_inlock(). Runs B and C went through the same failover, logged a single catch-up exit, and kept running.

Run C shows that the patched server refuses the requests. It does not test the other half of MongoDB's fix, which stops the double cleanup even when waiters are already in place; MongoDB's own regression tests cover that case. Our results show that the crash can be set up without credentials in this lab setup. They don't tell us how often it would succeed in other topologies, and we did not achieve code execution.

How to detect exploitation attempts

Start with MongoDB's structured server logs. In our vulnerable run, each planted request appeared as a COMMAND “Slow query” event (ID 51803). The useful fields were:

attr.command.ping

attr.command.readConcern.afterOpTime

attr.command.maxTimeMS

attr.errName (MaxTimeMSExpired)

attr.durationMillis

attr.remote

Look for an unauthenticated command with unusual operation-time values and an expired wait.

Also check the logs for the sequence that preceded a crash: a member enters primary catch-up (ID 21359), exits catch-up twice (ID 21363) in one transition, and then logs a fatal signal or backtrace involving CatchupState::abort_inlock(). A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not identify this CVE. The requests may arrive before the failover. Review earlier logs from the same member, not just events around the crash.

Whether these request fields appear in the logs depends on your logging settings. MongoDB documents that client operations enter the diagnostic log when they exceed the slow-operation threshold or when command verbosity is at least one. Check whether your logs retain the command object. Slow-operation sampling or a log pipeline may drop it. The attr.remote field may contain a loopback address rather than the original client IP.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Cloud Security Management reports findings for CVE-2026-118383. Check the vulnerability findings for affected hosts and container images.

Datadog Cloud Security Management also flags security groups that allow inbound MongoDB access from the internet, through the rule Inbound MongoDB access should be restricted. Use it to find exposed replica set members to patch first. Datadog Cloud SIEM detections for CVE-2026-118383 are currently being evaluated, and we will update this post when they are available.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-118383 affects MongoDB replica set members when a newly elected primary finishes catch-up. We reproduced a crash after two unauthenticated requests left abandoned waiters. The patched release rejected those requests. The vendor also identifies arbitrary code execution as a possible impact under certain conditions; our tests did not demonstrate it. Upgrade every affected member to a fixed release, verify the running versions, and investigate unusual readConcern.afterOpTime requests alongside catch-up and crash events.

Title: Reduce alert fatigue by customizing threat detection features in Amazon GuardDuty
Context: Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules
Full Text:
The teams responsible for security today don’t have a problem with the number of alerts they receive; they have a problem turning those alerts into something truly actionable. When an analyst concludes an investigation with “this was caused by our vulnerability scanner” or “this account is configured to share Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) publicly on purpose,” the detection worked as designed, it just wasn’t applicable to the environment. When this happens continuously at scale, alert fatigue sets in. As teams sort through these events, incident response slows down or, worse, teams stop paying attention to the alerts at all.

Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors, analyzes, and processes Amazon Web Services (AWS) data sources and logs in your AWS environment for suspicious or potentially malicious activity. GuardDuty then delivers detailed security findings to you for visibility and remediation. GuardDuty accomplishes this by analyzing independent streams of available sources. This includes logging of management events in AWS CloudTrail, information about IP traffic through Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 DNS query logs to name a few. These sources don’t need to be enabled or configured within your accounts for GuardDuty to use them. When GuardDuty observes activity that looks suspicious or anomalous, it produces a finding that’s a detailed security alert naming the behavior, the resources involved, and any supporting evidence. A finding is a signal to investigate, not a final verdict.

While the managed detections in GuardDuty work consistently across every AWS customer, personalizing detections for your specific architectures and environments is equally important. Over the past year, AWS has released a set of capabilities within GuardDuty that you can use to supply that missing context, most recently with the launch of Custom Detection Rules.

In this post, we walk through those capabilities in three distinct stages. These stages explore how to customize what GuardDuty detects, triage the findings that remain, and accelerate investigations. Throughout this blog post you’ll learn how to:

Efficiently detect anomalous behavior that shouldn’t occur in a specific account, without building detection logic yourself

Measure if a detection will be noisy before it generates a single finding, flooding security teams

Feed your own custom threat intelligence, including file hashes, into GuardDuty

Scope a suppression rule narrowly enough to archive expected activity while surfacing the same behavior elsewhere

Get an automated analysis of a finding, with a risk level and recommended actions, before the finding is opened manually

Prerequisites

For the walkthrough in this post, you must have the following prerequisites in place.

GuardDuty must be enabled in at least one AWS account and AWS Region. Note that these customization features aren’t currently available in all Regions, for more information, see Region-specific feature availability.

Your user or role must have AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to configure these features in GuardDuty. The AmazonGuardDutyFullAccess_v2 managed policy covers the required actions.

If you manage multiple accounts through AWS Organizations, AWS recommends administering GuardDuty using the delegated administrator account. By using this method, you can manage lists, suppression rules, and conduct investigations from a centralized location.

GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring must be enabled to conduct file hash matching and to use Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring. This protection plan isn’t enabled automatically in GuardDuty.

An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket that you control for storage of custom threat entity lists.

The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed.

Stage 1: How to customize what GuardDuty detects

An AMI is a pre-configured template that contains the software configurations needed to launch an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance on AWS. Sharing an AMI publicly can be a routine operation in an account whose purpose is distributing images, and a potential security event in any other account. The same might be said for disabling VPC Flow Logs, or signing in without multi-factor authentication for a legacy service account. Until the release of Custom Detection Rules, there was no way to account for these differences in GuardDuty.

Custom Detection Rules

Custom Detection Rules is a library of prebuilt, opt-in rules that AWS builds and maintains. At launch, it holds 90 rules across AWS CloudTrail management events and GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring events, producing 38 finding types mapped to 13 MITRE ATT&CK® tactics, described using vocabulary from ATT&CK and the Threat Technique Catalog for AWS. The catalog is maintained by the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) and is based on the MITRE ATT&CK Cloud Matrix, documenting threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures specific to AWS as observed by the AWS CIRT during customer engagements. Each entry includes detection guidance and mitigations specific to AWS environments, so a technique ID on a finding points to a public entry that your team can read.

Previously, detecting environment-specific behavior meant ingesting your own CloudTrail logs or host telemetry, normalizing them, building the logic, and maintaining that logic as APIs changed. Custom Detection Rules remove that work. You select the rules for GuardDuty to evaluate against the CloudTrail management events it already analyzes and, where Runtime Monitoring is enabled, the runtime events from the GuardDuty security agent, without the undifferentiated heavy lifting of log ingestion, normalization, and storage. Coverage is extended without adding unnecessary alerts that don’t add value to your teams.

Each rule runs in one of two modes. In dry run mode, GuardDuty evaluates the rule and publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics showing how often an event matched the rule, but generates no findings. Dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days. In live mode, events that match generate findings, and live mode has no expiration.

Custom Detection Rules are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring are available in every region where GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is available.

Walkthrough: Measure a rule, then turn it on

Start in dry run so you can measure the noise level before receiving a finding. This walkthrough uses the AMIExternalAccess rule, which detects when an AMI is shared with an external AWS account or made public, and applies it from the GuardDuty delegated administrator account. In an organization, the delegated administrator manages Custom Detection Rules for all member accounts through an organization configuration, and accounts that join the organization later inherit it.

Using the GuardDuty console

Open the AWS Management Console for GuardDuty and choose Custom Detection Rules.

Figure 1. The Custom Detection Rules catalog with the detection logic for the AMIExternalAccess rule

Select a rule name to see its detection logic on the Details tab. Rules are SQL conditions over CloudTrail fields, so you can review exactly what a rule matches before enabling it.

Choose the rule’s Accounts tab, then under Organization configuration, choose Configure.

Figure 2. Configuring the AMIExternalAccess rule in dry run mode

Under Configuration strategy, select Whole organization. Under Status, select Dry run. Under Accounts, select Apply rule status to all accounts, then choose Save.

Watch the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric in CloudWatch. GuardDuty publishes the metric only when the rule matches an event, so a rule with no matching activity shows no data. Because dry run mode expires automatically after 14 days, a full dry-run period is the longest continuous sample GuardDuty collects without you re-enabling the rule. The metric data persists in CloudWatch under its standard retention after the dry run ends, so you can review it shortly before or after expiry and still base your decision on the most complete data available. Volume alone doesn’t tell you whether the activity is benign, so account for what you see before deciding. If a rule matches constantly and someone can point to the process that causes it, that account is a poor candidate for live mode. If nobody can explain the matches, investigate them as they stand, because a dry run measuring real attacker activity looks the same as one measuring routine operations.

Figure 3. Dry-run match volume for a rule over one week, shown as hourly totals

When you’re satisfied the rule is worth acting on, return to the rule’s organization configuration and change Status to Live to start generating findings. To keep the rule off in accounts where the activity is expected, such as an image-build account, choose Exclude accounts manually under Accounts and select those accounts.

Using the AWS CLI

From the delegated administrator account, apply the rule in dry run to the whole organization. Omitting account lists targets every member account, including accounts that join later.

aws guardduty create-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode DRY_RUN

Review the CustomRuleDryRunSignalsMatched metric over the dry-run period, applying the same judgment described in the preceding console procedure.

Move the rule to live mode by updating the existing configuration. Creating a second whole-organization configuration for the same rule fails with a conflict error. To exclude accounts where the activity is expected, add --exclude-account-ids.

aws guardduty update-custom-detection-rule-org-configuration \ --rule-id ami-external-access \ --mode LIVE \ --exclude-account-ids <image-build-account-id>

Note: In a standalone account that isn’t part of an organization, you enable a rule for that account alone. With the AWS CLI, use create-custom-detection-rule-association with the same --rule-id and --mode parameters. To change the mode later, use update-custom-detection-rule-association with the association ID. Member accounts in an organization can’t enable or change a rule themselves; the delegated administrator manages rules on their behalf. For details, see Managing Custom Detection Rules in multiple-account environments.

Threat entity lists

If your threat intelligence team already tracks known-bad infrastructure and files, you can pass those indicators to GuardDuty and generate findings when they appear in your AWS account.

GuardDuty has two list formats. An IP address list holds IP addresses only. An entity list, the newer format, can hold IP addresses, CIDR ranges, and domain names together in a single file. The difference that matters is coverage: entity list entries apply to CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS query log findings, while IP address lists cover CloudTrail and VPC Flow Log findings only. If you still use IP address lists, the additional DNS coverage is a reason to move.

In addition, entity lists now also accept SHA-256 file hashes. Hashes sit alongside network indicators in the same file, and GuardDuty checks them against Runtime Monitoring. When the runtime agent sees an executable whose hash matches an active list, it generates a high severity Execution:Runtime/MaliciousFileExecuted.Custom finding and names the matching list, so your responder knows which intelligence source was used.

Note: If the entity list is changed, the list must be reactivated to include the updates. Uploading a new version of the file isn’t sufficient on its own. If this step is automated, build that reactivation step into the same process that refreshes the file.

Entity lists are currently available in all AWS commercial Regions, but not in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Stage 2: How to triage the findings that remain

Customizing detection reduces findings at the source, but the work is rarely finished there. New workloads appear, teams change how they operate, and some findings still describe activity that’s expected in your environment. You also need a precise way to route those events away from the queue your analysts work from.

A filter selects findings. A suppression rule is a filter that automatically archives a GuardDuty finding it matches. Archiving isn’t deletion: the finding is retained for 90 days and stays viewable, but the finding isn’t forwarded to AWS Security Hub, Amazon S3, Amazon Detective, or Amazon EventBridge, so it stays out of your security information and event management (SIEM) system and ticket queue.

Two changes have made that routing more customizable.

Wildcards

Filter criteria now support the Matches and NotMatches operators, where * matches any number of characters and ? matches one. Criteria used to be exact-match only, so suppressing findings from every AWS Lambda function in a service meant listing each name and updating it on every deployment. One pattern now covers the naming convention, including functions that don’t exist yet, so the rule stops going stale.

Additional property filter fields

You can now use over 1,000 supported fields from a finding as suppression criteria, including runtime process details, Kubernetes workload metadata, network connection information, and attack sequence signals. Take a vulnerability scanner in one Kubernetes namespace generating expected findings. With no namespace criterion available, you previously either suppressed the finding type more broadly than you wanted or wrote downstream logic to strip them. Now you scope the rule to that specific namespace and leave detection intact everywhere else in the cluster. This expanded field set is available in the aws partition; other partitions continue to use the console-supported fields only. See Filtering findings in GuardDuty for the full list of supported fields.

The recommended method is to assemble your criteria on the Findings page first, confirm the filtered list contains only findings you’re willing to archive, then choose Create suppression rule. The console and CLI procedures are detailed in the user guide.

Figure 4. Findings filtered by finding type and Kubernetes namespace, before creating a suppression rule

Before you write wildcard criteria, know that they can’t be validated with ListFindings or GetFindingsStatistics, the testing workflow AWS recommends for ordinary filters. Instead, start from a filter that takes no action and watch the suppression rule metrics to see how much it would match before you rely on it. Nothing is lost if the pattern is too broad, matched findings are archived rather than deleted, so you can lift the suppression rule and return them to your queue.

Stage 3: How to accelerate investigations

What remains consumes analyst hours. To decide whether a finding is a real event, an analyst pivots into CloudTrail for the operations that identity performed, lines up timestamps, checks IPs and domains against intelligence, and looks for a change ticket that explains the work. That can take hours, and most such investigations end in expected. When one doesn’t, all that time was spent before any actual containment could begin.

GuardDuty Investigation, also called AI-powered investigations performs that correlation automatically. GuardDuty Investigation analyzes the finding alongside related activity from the past 90 days, affected resources, threat intelligence, and threat indicators, and returns a structured summary in minutes: a risk level, a confidence rating, a written summary, supporting detail, MITRE ATT&CK classification, and recommended actions including the CLI commands to carry them out.

Note: Read the confidence rating as carefully as the risk level. High risk with low confidence is a very different indicator to an analyst than high risk with high confidence.

You can investigate a single finding, an account, or a whole organization, from the console, the AWS CLI, the API, or an AWS MCP Server. To turn on AI-powered investigations, go to Settings, find AI powered investigations – Preview, and choose Enable.

Figure 5. A completed account investigation with risk level, confidence, analysis summary, and recommended actions

The preview runs in 10 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). It allows 10 investigations per account per day and 100 per account in total, and can only be started from an administrator account, member accounts can’t create investigations from their own accounts. The feature uses Amazon Bedrock models with Cross-Region Inference (CRIS), which automatically selects a Region within your geography to process the analysis and generate the report. Your data remains stored only in the Region where the investigation request originates, but investigation data and summary results might be processed outside that Region. Review that routing if you have data residency commitments. For GuardDuty Region-specific differences more broadly, see Region-specific feature availability in the user guide.

Putting it all together

Consider a team running containerized workloads on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) across a handful of accounts in one organization.

The threat intelligence team uploads SHA-256 hashes from a recent brief as a threat entity list. Security engineering enables Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode and finds after 2 weeks that AMI sharing fires constantly in the image-build account and nowhere else, so they promote the rule to live across the organization and exclude the build account.

The team’s vulnerability scanner runs in a dedicated Kubernetes namespace, so they suppress that namespace and finding type while leaving the same behavior detected elsewhere. A second rule uses a wildcard on their Lambda naming convention, replacing a hand-maintained list.

Suppressed findings are archived instead of being sent to Security Hub, Amazon S3, EventBridge, or the SIEM, so they never reach the analyst queue. When a finding does warrant attention, an analyst starts an investigation and gets a disposition before manual work begins.

Each stage reduces the work of the next. Customizing detection means less to triage, effective triage means less to investigate, and automated investigation means the findings that reach a human get a decision faster.

Next steps

If you haven’t enabled GuardDuty, start with the 30-day free trial. Most protection plans enable automatically and are included, so you can evaluate them. Turn on Runtime Monitoring separately if you want to test hash matching or Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring..

If you’re already using GuardDuty:

Enable two or three Custom Detection Rules in dry run mode. Choose behavior that shouldn’t occur in specific accounts, measure across the dry-run period, then promote selectively.

Revisit existing suppression rules. Any rule written before the April 2026 field expansion might be broader than you intended, because the field you wanted wasn’t available then; narrow it to that field now.

Audit filters for wildcard opportunities. Any filter with a growing list of exact-match names is maintenance a single pattern can replace.

Migrate IP address lists to entity lists for the DNS query log coverage.

Conclusion

GuardDuty’s managed detections keep expanding, driven by AWS threat intelligence, security research, and customer feedback. These capabilities enable you to decide which activity is worth alerting on in which accounts, and which findings never need to be delivered to a human at all.

Title: November Patch Tuesday boasts over 1,000 bugs, one already under attack
Context: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch
Full Text: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register: “Maybe we should just go home.” “Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one. “It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review. “An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.” Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon. Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files. Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.” “Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register. “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.” For defenders, this means two things, Childs added. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said. Zero-click threats There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958. Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit. CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.” CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers. Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well. And…Xbox remote code execution And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967, that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit. So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

Title: November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs
Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
Context: This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers,...
Full Text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

Title: Ring robots ready to patrol paranoids’ pads
Context: The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a...
Full Text: If you didn't have any privacy concerns about slapping a Ring doorbell on your front door or putting Ring cameras inside, you'll love Amazon's newest offerings, which move around homes and businesses to capture views stationary cameras might miss. The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a telescoping camera mast for automated after-hours business patrols. Both are designed to proactively patrol spaces as well as respond to alerts from connected alarm systems and Ring-connected devices. According to Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, this is something customers actually want, as those stationary cameras just can’t quite see everywhere. “It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have,” Siminoff said. The consumer-focused Ring Drone Cam launches from its own charging dock that Amazon says keeps the thing “out of sight” when not in use, and when in flight is able to patrol a home by flying around pre-programmed routes to take in the sights with its 148-degree FOV, 2K camera that includes LED illumination for night patrols. Amazon says it can also respond to alerts from cameras, sensors, and alarm systems. The Ring Rover Cam, designed with businesses in mind, is sort of like a security Roomba that sports a camera on a telescoping mast that Amazon says can be programmed to certain heights to let it see over counters, shelves, and other workplace obstacles. The Rover can also perform 360-degree scans and includes a siren, lights, and two-way audio so you can yell at intruders who aren't dissuaded by its presence. The Rover streams and records video in up to 4K while moving or patrolling and is designed to make regular patrols of businesses during off hours. It can also detect people and respond to alerts from connected Ring devices. Of course, given that this is Ring we're talking about, these flying and free-wheeling cameras use Amazon's cloud for some processing, likely inviting privacy concerns about what footage and mapping data the company can access and retain. The Amazon-owned security tech firm has faced a number of privacy complaints over the years, some of which have resulted in multimillion-dollar settlements. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million in a 2023 settlement with the FTC over allegations that employees and contractors improperly accessed customers' private videos and that the company failed to adequately protect accounts against unauthorized access – just imagine the privacy concerns raised by flying robots. More recently, the company took heat for partnering with surveillance outfit Flock Safety, a relationship which it has since canceled. Amazon/Ring also invited criticism for a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting a new feature called Search Party, which would remotely activate Ring cameras to search for lost pets, suggesting that Amazon had the ability, in theory, to use Ring cameras like a dystopian neighborhood surveillance network. Another Ring feature, Familiar Faces, which uses AI-powered facial recognition to identify people captured by compatible cameras, prompted a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in June. The complaint alleges that the feature collected biometric information from visitors and passersby without their consent. If we can’t have iRobot, we’ll do it with Ring Amazon abandoned its efforts to buy Roomba robot-vacuum maker iRobot in 2024, blaming regulatory scrutiny for the move. The FTC, under then-chair Lina Khan, examined the deal's potential effects on competition and consumer privacy, including concerns about the information Roombas collect while mapping customers' homes. European regulators, meanwhile, raised concerns that Amazon could use its marketplace to disadvantage rival robot vacuum makers. With this Ring move, Amazon is once again putting robots capable of mapping interior spaces into customers' hands, reviving some of the privacy questions raised during its failed iRobot acquisition. As Amazon explains in Tuesday’s press release, both new Ring robots are powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” To help the Ring robots understand where they're operating, the devices generate floor plans of interior spaces, according to Amazon. “Carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan,” the company explains of the setup process. AI Pilot takes the reins in identifying the types of rooms it sees and suggests key patrol areas it should focus on, which users can add to in the Ring app. Amazon claims that videos captured by these new flying and free-wheeling cameras will be protected by an encryption scheme it calls Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The system temporarily allows Ring's cloud services to access recordings for enabled features before the relevant encryption keys are deleted. Ring announced the scheme in August, presenting it as a way to limit access to customer recordings without sacrificing cloud-powered features. “With TAKE, your Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys,” Amazon explained. “A copy of the keys is temporarily held inside a secure enclave within the cloud; think of it as a sealed vault that can only provide Ring access to the key under strict, limited conditions.” The keys, Amazon claims, are later deleted so that only users and those they allow access to can see videos, with Ring only retaining them “to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.” “We take privacy concerns seriously, and we believe privacy and customer control are fundamental to building products people trust,” a Ring spokesperson told The Register when asked about prior privacy concerns. “That is why customers decide where these devices go and when.” We asked about floor plan security, but didn’t get an answer about that. As for when those devices will be available, the Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16 at a price of about $1,000, but the Drone Cam might not ever actually make it to homes. Amazon’s announcement mentions a release date of January 27, 2027, but that’s subject to the FCC giving its blessing. “Ring Drone Cam has not been authorized as required by the rules of the FCC,” Amazon’s release states. “This device is not, and may not be, offered for sale or lease, or sold or leased, until authorization is obtained.” Amazon told us that the Drone Cam would still start shipping in January, luckily giving everyone a few months to figure out how to deal with this new, more mobile, invasion of privacy. ®

Title: AWS refreshes ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment to enhance customer’s third-party due diligence
Context: This assessment approach replaces static spreadsheets with a dynamic system that combines advanced analytics, threat intelligence, and risk models with vendor input
Full Text:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce renewal of the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment. This validated assessment report helps customers perform effective cloud supplier due diligence on AWS and enhances their third-party risk management process.

What is the AWS ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment

Many customers use third-party cyber risk management (TPCRM) services such as ProcessUnity to better manage risks from their evolving third-party environments and to drive operational efficiencies. To help with such efforts, AWS has completed the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange assessment of its security posture. ProcessUnity’s assessors perform the review of Global Risk Exchange assessment and validate the results annually.

This assessment approach replaces static spreadsheets with a dynamic system that combines advanced analytics, threat intelligence, and risk models with vendor input. Vendor profiles continuously update as cloud provider risk levels and AWS security posture evolve, keeping risk matrices current in near real time. Additionally, customers can also use Framework View which maps AWS assessment controls to threat profiles, MITRE ATT&CK scenarios, and global compliance standards and frameworks including National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 27001, Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), significantly reducing customers’ third-party due diligence burden.

How can you access the assessment?

Customers can request access to the report by completing an access request form, available on the ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange page. If you are an existing ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange member, you can request access from within ProcessUnity Global Risk Exchange portal.

To learn more about our compliance and security programs, see AWS Compliance Programs. As always, we value your feedback and questions; reach out to the AWS Compliance team through the Contact Us page.
