Full Text:
Sega has revealed that around 2.2 million customer email addresses have been exposed as result of a third-party incident.

The video gaming giant revealed on November 9 that an unauthorized third party leaked the email addresses after gaining access to Arara Inc., a Japanese email delivery provider used by Sega to distribute its email newsletter.

“We deeply apologize for the great inconvenience and concern caused to our customers and all parties involved,” Sega wrote.

“Currently, Arara is working to identify the causes of unauthorized access and prevent further damage, and we are working with Arara and related companies to confirm the details of the leaked information.”

The Japanese firm said the breach is limited to 2.196 million email addresses for various email newsletters, and 92,273 items related to distribution.

The leaked information does not include customer names, dates of birth, genders, addresses, phone numbers, credit card information or login passwords.

No misuse of the leaked data has been currently confirmed. However, Sega has warned customers to be vigilant for suspicious emails purporting to be from Sega or Sega Fave Corporation, or using product or service names operated by both companies.

Sega Fave is a subsidiary of the broader Sega group, which focuses on the production of toys and arcade machines.

“Please do not open or reply to URLs or attachments provided in emails you do not recognize. Accessing URLs or opening attached files may lead to entering personal information or affecting your device. Neither our company nor Sega Fave will ask you for your password or credit card information by email. If you receive such an email, do not access the reply or the provided link; delete it,” the company said.

Sega Breach Part of Large-Scale Third-Party Incident

Arara revealed it had been compromised in a statement issued on October 29, which said that unauthorized access was gained to certain server systems of its email distribution service a day earlier, on October 28 after a hacker exploited vulnerabilities in web servers.

The distribution service ‘Arara Message’ was suspended on October 31 and remains offline at the time of writing, according to a dedicated incident page set up by the firm to provide updates.

According to a report by The Japan Times, Arara’s parent company Paycloud Holdings confirmed on November 2 that hackers gained unauthorized access to servers operated by the subsidiary, which exposed information held by around 380 corporate clients using the service. This included 77 million email addresses.

Paycloud also noted that depending on the company, the breached data also included names, telephone numbers and addresses. However, it said that no credit card details have been exposed.

Title: Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways
Context: In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day
Full Text: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails. The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures. Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information. The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails. The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required. Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed. Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more. SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both). The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response. To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place. A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation." "Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue." Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected. Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well. It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

Context: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7
Full Text: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders. The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29, a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation. Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access. Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns. The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers. Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity. There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised. It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ, Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion. Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed. Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected. Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer. The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

Title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Targeted in Reported $133m Heist
Context: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out
Full Text:
A leading French banking group has moved to reassure customers that their funds are safe after reports emerged of a $133m heist.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out.”

The hackers reached the bank’s network via the platform of a service provider, it added in an FAQ on the incident.

“The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms,” it said.

“They did not, therefore, use customer accounts belonging to its federations or subsidiaries. We have communicated that this incident has no financial consequences for our customers. As soon as this attack was identified, our teams immediately activated the necessary security measures to contain the incident and prevent any further fraudulent activity against us.”

Read more on big-money heists: Brazilian Fintech Giant Sinqia Reveals $130m Heist Attempt

Suspicious Withdrawals Traced Across Multiple Exchanges

The incident first came to light on November 2 when blockchain investigator, “ZachXBT,” claimed in a Telegram post that an unnamed “EU entity” had lost $106m from “multiple centralized exchange accounts.”

ZachXBT ruled out the involvement of notorious North Korean hackers the Lazarus Group.

“Over the past 24 hours the illicit actor has been aggressively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring to instant exchanges (WellWallet, Kyrrex, etc), converting to XMR via Wagyu, and bridging across multiple chains,” they explained.

The investigator posted an updated the day after claiming to have spotted an additional $27m of fraudulent centralized exchange account (CEX) withdrawals.

“My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it’s currently being covered up,” they said. “No proper incident disclosure has resulted in $30m+ being laundered away which could have been frozen by EU law enforcement.”

However, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa noted in its FAQ that it was “still too early” to say for sure how much was taken.

“Our teams are continuing their work to precisely assess the financial consequences of this attack: some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them,” it said.

“We can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.”

The bank urged customers to be on the lookout for potential phishing attempts in the aftermath of the incident and resulting publicity.

The news comes just days after North Korean hackers stole an estimated $6.3bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what has been described as the biggest theft of its kind ever seen.

Title: DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185,000 Times Since Trump Took Office
Context: To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only...
Full Text:
Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that normally takes on transnational crime, estimates it has sent out at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration, according to a recent court filing. The figure shows how HSI has increasingly relied on this warrantless authority to conduct investigations.

To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only sent out around 170,000 of a type of administrative subpoena called a 1509 customs summons.

The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed as part of a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security filed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the nonprofit, says the EFF hopes to get more details about the 185,000 estimate. The EFF originally asked for information about how many administrative subpoenas were sent to technology companies, internet platforms, and service providers by ICE or DHS since January 20, 2025. It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.

Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool. Unlike with a grand jury subpoena or a court order, the government doesn’t have to explain to the courts why it needs the documents or what data it’s requesting from a company.

Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government has used DHS’s administrative subpoena power to try to unmask anonymous online critics and pursue broad customer records about protesters. This includes, for example, a list of people in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific green beanie from REI.

Congress originally granted the use of 1509 customs summons to the then stand-alone US Customs Service nearly a century ago, with the idea that it would let customs officers inspect business records related to importing merchandise and figure out whether they owed customs duties. In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.

In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes. The DHS inspector general admonished Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Professional Responsibility in 2017 for trying to use a customs summons to unmask an anonymous Twitter poster, pointing out that its own procedures manual said that customs summons could only be used to obtain information related to customs or immigrations laws.

Title: Anti-Money Laundering Watchdog FATF Targets Scam Compounds
Context: Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment...
Full Text:
A leading anti-money laundering (AML) organization has called for global action to disrupt the scam compounds responsible for a considerable volume of transnational fraud.

AML watchdog the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) warned in a new report that large physical scam compounds are a major driver of a global fraud economy estimated to be worth $500bn annually.

Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment platforms, money mules, social media, messaging services and AI-enabled content, FATF said.

The trend is increasingly one of smaller and more mobile operations, with compounds created out of repurposed casinos, rented rooms, apartments, coffee shops and even moving vehicles, the report warned.

Read more on scam compounds: Scam Centers Expand Global Footprint with Trafficked Victims

The FATF report noted that countries are generally better at tackling scam compounds through downstream action such as asset tracing and targeting victim payments.

But it called on FATF member nations to combine these efforts with upstream disruption targeting things like fraudulent advertising, recruitment activity, malicious domains and suspicious phone numbers and telecom indicators,

“With criminals weaponizing AI and other technologies to intensify their scam operations, we need to urgently modernize and accelerate our response,” argued FATF president, Giles Thomson. “This means focusing on dismantling the criminal networks behind scam compounds, working proactively with technology, social media and communications sectors to prevent and disrupt more scams before they happen, and quicker intervention to freeze and seize the proceeds of scams once they’ve happened.”

Six Principles to Combat Illicit Money Flows

With this in mind, the FATF report promoted six pillars to its approach:

Shift the focus from physical compounds to criminal leaders, recruiters and traffickers, and other supporting players

Disrupt the infrastructure and services, including stopping, tracing, freezing and recovering victim payments

Share information between financial institutions, technology companies, telcos and authorities

Act at speed across borders, as the first 24-72 hours after a scam are critical for freezing funds and recovering assets

Ensure investigations put the protection of trafficked and scam victims front and center

Continuously update approaches as scam operations decentralize and adapt

Jonathan Frost, director of global advisory at BioCatch, welcomed the focus on compounds and the need for action by platform providers.

“Those platforms need to act on what they can already see. But when push comes to shove, banks are often the last and sometimes the only line of defense,” he added. “Funds can leave an account in minutes, and customers are often groomed into trusting the scammer over their bank. Banks must detect the manipulation itself, not just the transaction, and intervene before the money moves.”

A CybSafe report published last month found that over a fifth (22%) of Brits have received a scam call impersonating a familiar person’s voice or appearance. Over a third (36%) of these reports have led to their employer losing money or data.

Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked
Context: That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI
Full Text: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds. Writing in his weekly kernel update post, the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons. One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel. The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.” Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. “This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote. That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel. “I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.” If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®

Title: On the hunt for ARTEX: understanding agentic attacks in AWS environments
Context: In early November 2026, Datadog tied ARTEX activity to IP addresses that resolved to a hosted console, and found hundreds of additional internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, often in...
Full Text:
Key points

In October 2026, Datadog observed in-the-wild activity from ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework, against several AWS environments, with a focus on accessing financial data.

Using compromised long-term IAM access keys, ARTEX searched through CloudWatch using FilterLogEvents, hunting for financial information, file paths and secrets such as long-lived AKIA access keys and passwords.

We also observed unauthenticated abuse of public Amazon Cognito user pools, including anonymous sign-ups, token collection, and follow-up AWS account enumeration attempts.

In early November 2026, Datadog tied ARTEX activity to IP addresses that resolved to a hosted console, and found hundreds of additional internet-exposed ARTEX consoles, often in Mandarin and hosted with providers in locations including Singapore and Hong Kong.

Background on ARTEX

ARTEX is an AI-native penetration framework in which an operator supplies a target and an objective, and a team of LLM agents plans and runs the attack. A Chinese developer published it on GitHub in July 2026 and made it closed-source on October 8, after it had passed 12,000 forks.

Microsoft tied it to Storm-0940, a China-aligned actor behind a recent supply-chain compromise. In recent months, ARTEX has been documented attacking Okta, Entra ID and Cognito across IT and software vendors.

Those reports center on identity providers and web application logs. In this post, we provide more details on the cloud control-plane view, in particular how ARTEX behaves once it has compromised an initial set of AWS credentials, through leaked long-lived access keys or following a successful anonymous sign-up on a public Cognito pool.

First, we will dive into ARTEX as a platform. Then, we'll describe specific behaviors and indicators we identified in the wild.

Inside the ARTEX console

ARTEX started as a repository and has grown into a platform running on live infrastructure. Operators run it as a hosted web console, and many of those consoles face the internet. We found hundreds of hosts serving the same Chinese-language login page, titled ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台 (ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console). We've also seen the same platform appearing under other names:

Page title

English translation

ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台

ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console

ScopeWeaver — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console

(original in English)

LUCK — 自主资产控制台

LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console

观澜SEC渗透测试平台

Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform

A similar console is rendered across many of these hosts.

The platform user supplies API keys to chosen AI inference providers and points ARTEX at almost any provider through three request formats:

openai: OpenAI Chat Completions and any compatible gateway, which covers OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax, OpenRouter-style resellers and self-hosted models.

openai-responses: OpenAI's newer Responses API.

anthropic: Anthropic's Messages API, plus vendors that expose an Anthropic-compatible endpoint, such as DeepSeek.

When one provider bans or cuts off a key, ARTEX moves to the next to continue activity. Therefore, a single campaign can be spread across several providers and keys.

An agent planner directs a small team of workers. The planner sends "intents" to workers, which run three at a time by default. A main agent handles chat with the operator, with a /btw command for side questions.

Everything is recorded on a "blackboard" graph of tasks, goals, intents, facts, findings, hints and compression digests. Each task carries operator-defined allow and deny constraints, a timeout with a wrap-up step, and a planner heartbeat of at least 10 minutes. A fixed task timeout would explain bursts that end at a consistent length, though we have not confirmed the value operators set.

Command interception rules, written as regex or plain strings, can allow, deny or ask a human for a judgment. In some versions, a global asset blocklist excludes .gov, .gov.cn, .edu and .edu.cn by default.

API paths expose core routes, such as:

/tasks /exploration/findings /exploration/graph /exploration/intents /traffic /companies /llm/profiles /llm/pool /intercept /mcp /skills /agents /notify

One version we observed shipped with a sample demo engagement. It walks through a full external-to-internal compromise, from a public web app to a DMZ foothold, internal lateral movement, and finally the Active Directory domain controller.

We often found the agent reading the front end of web apps hosted in S3, looking for build manifests and runtime configurations.

Wiz noted that before each fuzzing run, ARTEX requested a path that should not exist (/zzz-nonexistent-xyz123) to learn what "not found" looks like. We saw the same habit against S3, with keys such as zzz_nonexistent_abc.txt and Notexist-xyz. A request for an object named like a placeholder, right before a burst of guesses, is a useful signal to hunt on.

This behavior is one example from agentic pentesting tools, which continue to evolve whether they're used directly as a tool or hosted as an interactive platform.

ARTEX sightings in AWS environments in the wild

In this section, we share some activity we've identified in real-world AWS accounts, and that we have attributed to ARTEX usage.

The two initial access vectors we've witnessed ARTEX start from are:

Compromised long-term AWS access keys

Public Cognito user pools

Before either, every session we reviewed opened with unauthenticated S3 requests. In CloudTrail, these show a userIdentity.type of AWSAccount and an accountId of anonymous, calling GetObject, ListObjects and similar read APIs.

Activity cluster 1: Post-exploitation following compromised access keys

In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents. The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like Fund, Invoice, Billing and LLC.

Every FilterLogEvents call was set with a limit of 1000, below the API's 10,000-event maximum. That constant shows up across sessions.

On October 20, the same long-term key was used again from 103.54.154[.]40, an address associated with zeofast[.]cn. This session widened the search, looking for file and storage links, internal secrets, internal IP addresses, and database information.

Files and storage links

Databases, internal IPs and secrets

Errors

"s3://" || "presigned" || ".pdf" || ".xlsx" || ".csv" || "rawData_" || "transformedData_"

?mongo ?172. ?10. ?password ?AKIA

?Error ?❌ ?⚠

Activity cluster 2: Self-registration through public Cognito user pools

In an instance where no long-term access keys were obtained, ARTEX went after public Cognito user pools. Wiz reported account-recovery abuse through InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword and ResendConfirmationCode. We saw the agent go further, registering an account, collecting tokens, trading them for AWS credentials, then enumerating resources.

One example came as a spike on October 26 and 27 from 154.64.252[.]77. The observed SignUp calls sometimes named the tool in the user agent such as Mozilla/5.0 ARTeX, while other user agents included curl or typical browser user agents.

Getting through sign-up was noisy. The pool had a PreSignUp Lambda trigger that checked a tenant domain, and the agent iterated against it and continued probing. For example, below are errors generated as the agent continued attempting to sign up:

PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenant domain: api[.]github[.]com. PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenant domain: example[.]com PreSignUp failed with error tenantId does not match tenant domain. PreSignUp failed with error Invalid tenantDomain format: hxxps[://]artex-hqheizfk[.]invalid/x. Attributes did not conform to the schema: Type for attribute {custom:isAdmin} could not be determined

Once registered, it walked the standard user pool flow: SignUp, InitiateAuth, RespondToAuthChallenge, GetUser and GetTokensFromRefreshToken, followed by Get* requests and attempts to call ListUserPools.

In CloudTrail, that session appears under the CognitoIdentityCredentials role session name with short-term AWS credentials. The agent used it to try nearly every read-only discovery call it could, such as:

ListBuckets

GetBucket*

ListSecrets

DescribeParameters

ListTopics

DescribeLogGroups

GetRestApis

DescribeRepositories

ListFunctions20150331

In this case, all of them failed because the identity pool's authenticated role did not grant the required permissions.

Hunting for ARTEX activity

In this post, we've shared some in-the-wild sightings of ARTEX-attributed activity in cloud environments. It's important to remember that while ARTEX is an offensive AI-native orchestration framework, distributions we analyzed don't appear to have an opinionated methodology for targeting or performing post-exploitation in cloud environments: the playbook is therefore left to downstream AI inference, and can vary greatly depending on the model in use.

In this context, research such as "I Gave 14 LLMs AWS Keys. Here’s What They Wanted to Do Next" by Adan Alvarez is valuable for gaining a broader understanding of how LLMs tend to behave when faced with compromised credentials.

When hunting for ARTEX activity in your environment, we recommend following the methodology below.

Start with quick wins, namely ARTEX user agents (see IOCs), to identify noisy ARTEX probing or exploitation requests. Note that user agents can easily be changed, but they aren't always updated to a stealthier value.

Review your environment for activity originating from IP addresses known to be associated with ARTEX activity (see IOCs).

We've seen ARTEX behave noisily in a number of cases: identify large volumes of permission denied errors, enumeration of objects in S3 logs, unusual access patterns (for instance, credentials vended from an EC2 instance role being used by a non-AWS IP), and CloudTrail events that relate to known cloud attack techniques (Stratus Red Team, Datadog's Cloud Security Atlas and TrailDiscover are useful resources for these).

How Datadog can help

Cloud SIEM

Datadog Cloud SIEM contains several out-of-the-box (OOTB) rules that can detect ARTEX-related post-exploitation and initial access in your AWS environment:

A user received an anomalous number of AccessDenied errors

Anomalous number of S3 buckets accessed

Anomalous S3 bucket activity from user ARN

AWS ListResources by long term access key

AWS ListResources executed by new principal identity

AWS Cloudtrail possible secret enumeration in multiple regions and secret retrieval

Cloud Security Misconfigurations

Datadog Cloud Security Misconfigurations ships with out-of-the-box (OOTB) rules to help you identify risky long-lived AWS credentials proactively:

Access keys should be rotated every 90 days or less

IAM access keys that are inactive and older than 1 year should be removed

Unused credentials should be deactivated or removed

Title: Building a retro handheld game with Codex and ModRetro Chromatic
Context: You can build and play your first game on your computer
Full Text:
With all due respect to the iPhone, the Game Boy might be the most iconic handheld device of all time. A generation of kids stomped Koopas on the bus and battled their friends in Pokémon over a link cable, all on a device that fit in your pocket. Or at least a pocket of your backpack.

With today’s powerful coding models and tools like Codex, building your own games has never been easier (or, in my opinion, more fun). But there’s something special about a game running on purpose-built hardware, like the Game Boy Color, that’s hard to replace. That’s why I am sooo excited to share that the ModRetro plugin for Codex lets you build Game Boy Color games and play them on a Chromatic.

Order the special edition ModRetro Chromatic.

Let’s jump right in and explain how it works.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

Install the plugin

In the ChatGPT desktop app, select Codex from the ChatGPT dropdown.

Open Plugins and search for ModRetro Chromatic. Select ModRetro Chromatic Plugin by ModRetro, then click Install.

Open a local project folder and start a chat. Type @ and choose the plugin so Codex knows which tools to use.

Ask Codex to set up the plugin and check for any missing build tools. You can build and play your first game on your computer.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

Prompt your first game

With the plugin selected in your Codex chat, describe the game you want to build. To follow along with the video, use this example prompt.

Build a top-down adventure game called Lodge Podge where a pixel beaver must chew down small trees to gather sticks to build a lodge in the center of the level.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

Next, ask Codex to build the game and open the preview. You can also ask it to point you to these files in your GB Studio project folder.

Open the .gbsproj file in GB Studio to edit scenes, actors, and events.

Look in assets/ for the sprite sheets, backgrounds, and audio used by the project.

Run the compiled .gbc file in an emulator or install it on a cartridge.

From there, play a few rounds and tell Codex what would make the game more fun. In Lodge Podge, I asked Codex to make the beaver chonkier (for maximum cuteness) and to require mud and leaves as well as sticks to build the lodge.

What’s in the plugin

The ModRetro Chromatic plugin contains developer tools the model can use on your behalf.

Animate a character

Ask Codex to create a sprite sheet and show you the frames side by side. To revise the animation, identify the pose or direction you want to change, then ask Codex to rebuild the preview.

Build a map the player can walk through

Ask Codex to show you a scene’s background and collision map side by side. The collision map marks which tiles block movement. Use the background to identify the area you mean, then tell Codex which tiles to mark as blocked or walkable.

Play the ROM in Codex

Ask Codex to open the game preview in its built-in browser. Use the arrow keys for the Game Boy’s D-pad, Z for A, X for B, and Enter for Start. Use the toolbar above the emulator to pause or resume.

Point to the part you want to change

Choose Annotate game in the preview toolbar, then click the game display to freeze a frame. Select the sprite, tile, or area you want to change and describe the edit. Choose Resume game to return to the emulator. After Codex makes the change, ask it to rebuild the ROM and reopen the preview.

Have Codex test a sequence of moves

You can also control the emulator from chat. Ask Codex to run the ROM, send a sequence of button presses, and capture a frame after each step. Ask for the frames side by side so you can inspect them together.

Edit in GB Studio

GB Studio is a visual editor for building Game Boy games. Open your project’s .gbsproj file and choose Game World. Select a scene in the navigator to see its properties in the sidebar. You can drag an actor to a new tile or edit collisions directly on the scene. Save the project, then return to your Codex chat and ask it to rebuild and open the preview. The GB Studio guide to scenes explains how backgrounds, actors, and triggers fit together.

Other development options

Extend a GB Studio game. If the built-in events don’t cover a mechanic, you can add a custom event in GBVM, GB Studio’s virtual-machine language, or extend the engine in C. See the GB Studio plugin guide.

Write the game in C with GBDK-2020. The ModRetro plugin can compile standalone C with GBDK’s lcc compiler. GBDK’s Game Boy APIs give you access to buttons, sprites, tiles, and palettes. Ask Codex to start with a game loop that reads the D-pad and moves a single sprite.

Write your own engine. You can have Codex implement the game loop, scrolling, and collisions from scratch. For an assembly project, build the ROM with a separately installed toolchain such as RGBDS. Then give the resulting .gb or .gbc file to the plugin to inspect and playtest.

Deploy to device

You’ll need a Chromatic, a compatible rewritable homebrew cartridge, and a USB data cable. Follow ModRetro’s quickstart to update the firmware and activate Developer Mode using the computer you’ll connect to the handheld.

Insert the cartridge, connect the Chromatic to your computer, and open the game preview in your local Codex chat.

Choose Install on Chromatic, select your connected device, and click Install. Read the confirmation carefully. Writing the new ROM erases the game on that cartridge and can erase its saves. The installer doesn’t back up the cartridge.

Choose Confirm Install when you’re ready. Leave the cable connected until the plugin reports success, then start the game on the Chromatic.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

“The Power of Science is Staggering!”

With the ModRetro plugin for Codex, you can prompt your way to original Game Boy Color games and use all the tools in the thriving GBC homebrew development ecosystem. This is going to be so, so much fun. You can order your own ModRetro Chromatic and explore ModRetro’s other projects. Happy Game Boy hacking!

Title: The Fridge-Hacking Spree Is an Internet-of-Things Wake-Up Call
Context: Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the...
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the technology at all—instead providing a stark reminder that cybersecurity fundamentals are still key to digital defense.

Three sites in France that handle blood and plasma bags were briefly impacted this week by widespread attacks on vulnerable internet-connected refrigerators. On Wednesday, the Établissement Français du Sang (EFS) confirmed that cold rooms storing blood were “raised to very high temperatures” on November 2. The blood samples, thankfully, weren’t altered or damaged, the EFS said, because the organization’s alarm facilities and staff quickly detected the changes and implemented fail-safe measures.

The incident, however, comes amid a wave of cyberattacks in recent days affecting supermarket chains in at least 11 European countries that also drastically increased the temperatures of their refrigerators. Pictures from across the continent show huge volumes of food being trashed following the spikes. Similar fridge attacks in October affected hundreds of French stores that were forced to throw away food. And in August, roughly six commissaries and grocery stores on United States military bases suffered similar incidents resulting in spoiled food. The Pentagon is investigating the incidents and is collaborating with French law enforcement, Reuters reported last week.

“It's been true for more than a decade now that our dependence on connected technology is growing faster than our collective will to protect it, which has exposed us to accidents, adversaries, and now potentially agents,” says longtime critical infrastructure researcher Josh Corman, who is currently the executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the nonprofit Institute for Security and Technology. “These fragile cold-chain systems are too critical to fail, but we keep experiencing hard lessons.”

It is still unclear who is behind the incidents and whether the attacks are all connected or being carried out by multiple actors. The first recent wave of attacks against French supermarkets last month appears to have been caused by attackers exploiting unpatched refrigeration controllers exposed to the internet—including software versions that allegedly used weak passwords formulated based on the date.

Many of the hacks stem from attackers exploiting vulnerabilities in temperature controllers made by the Danish firm Danfoss, and researchers say the attacks would not have been particularly difficult to pull off. Danfoss did not return WIRED’s request for comment.

Title: NHS breach helpline left staff carrying a 'significant emotional burden'
Context: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review...
Full Text: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found. The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers. A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables. Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress. Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process. "Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted. "This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those." Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed. "The staff working in the call centers had a short training session and then the calls started coming in within minutes of the team being set up," the review noted. "Some staff had not finished reading the pre-prepared script which had arrived only 30 minutes before the center went live." Most call handlers only learned that their own data had been exposed while already working on the helpline, sometimes minutes before supporting others affected. Call handlers also said they had little choice about taking on the work and were expected to maintain their usual duties alongside it. The review stated that some staff members gave up weekends and worked long past their scheduled hours to meet the demands of both roles. "It's typical NHS, it runs on goodwill," one staffer told the team that compiled the report. The call center was only supposed to run for two weeks in December 2025, but due to the volume of calls, it was eventually stood down after 11 weeks, in February 2026. According to officials speaking at a trust board meeting on Thursday, the review and its findings have since been circulated among staff, and published online. How the spreadsheet slipped through Responding to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request thought to be from a journalist researching a story about stress in the NHS, the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust uploaded a spreadsheet to its public FOI Disclosure log in February 2023. This contained personal data and inadvertently exposed sickness absence information and sensitive health data related to 7,715 staff, 288 non-trust workers, as well as a small number of unidentified records. Crucially, this spreadsheet was uploaded in a format that allowed users to access the pivot table from which some data was derived. The data in these pivot tables would normally have been too sensitive to be included in FOIA responses. The first failure was that the request was handled by the trust's e-Rostering team instead of the People Information Unit, which had the expertise in responding to FOIA requests with complex datasets. The e-Rostering team compiled the response using the team's own data, but incorrectly believed they had stripped the spreadsheet of the sensitive data that would later be exposed. Standard procedures instructed request handlers to follow several steps to ensure sensitive data was stripped before documents are published, some of which were skipped. For starters, one FOI officer assigned to the response either failed to run the spreadsheet through Excel's Document Inspector, which formed part of the usual procedures, or failed to act upon its recommendations. This feature can flag pivot tables and potentially hidden cached data, but cannot determine whether that data is sensitive or automatically remove the cache. Staff also failed to follow instructions to convert the spreadsheet to PDF. Investigators found that doing so prevented users clicking through to the underlying records, although they could not guarantee that no hidden data remained technically accessible. At the time, internal guidance did not require conversion to CSV, which would have removed the workbook's pivot-table functionality and embedded cache. The trust's sign-off process also focused on answering the request's questions and meeting their public relations duties, and falsely assumed that the data had been adequately sanitized before the final review. The spreadsheet was made available for 33 months, although the trust is not sure how many times it was viewed during that time. Its logs only covered the 12 months before a member of the public alerted it to the pivot table issue. These indicated that it had been accessed 340 times, although the review noted there was no way of knowing how many of these, if any, led to pivot tables being accessed, or even if it was viewed by a human, with web crawlers adding to the total view count. The trust has since implemented a number of changes to prevent a recurrence of the breach, including the mandatory password-protecting of any Excel workbook as part of FOIA responses. A senior information governance officer must now approve spreadsheet responses before executive sign-off. Revised guidance circulated in November 2025 also called for conversion to CSV, although investigators found that this requirement had not been incorporated into the formal operating procedure and recommended updating it. The review says the Information Commissioner's Office closed its case after the trust implemented its recommendations. A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall Hospitals said: "We are deeply sorry for the accidental sharing of sickness absence data which we reported in November 2025, and for the distress and concern it caused those colleagues whose data was involved. "An independent investigation has now been completed, and the report has been published in full on our website in the interests of transparency and accountability. "The investigation has helped us understand what happened and identify areas where improvements were needed. We have already implemented a number of measures to strengthen our processes, particularly around the management of Freedom of Information requests and responses. "The protection of personal information is of the utmost importance to us, and we remain committed to learning from this incident and preventing a similar event from happening again. "We continue to provide support to colleagues who have been affected." ®

Title: Stealing more than the spotlight. [Research Saturday]

This week, we are joined by Matt Poto, Associate Triage Analyst at Huntress, discussing their work on "Grand Theft Auto VI Hype Leads to Malware." Threat actors are exploiting the hype surrounding the upcoming release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA6) by distributing fake leaked game downloads designed to infect unsuspecting gamers.

Huntress identified malicious ISOs promoted through search engine poisoning, gaming forums, torrent sites, and social media that contain multiple types of malware, including remote access trojans (RATs), an infostealer, and ransomware. The malware can steal credentials and personal information, give attackers control of compromised systems, and encrypt or destroy files, with evidence suggesting the campaign may be targeting Russian-speaking gamers.

Title: Keeping cyber threats on ice.
Context: Attackers may exploit authentication bypass vulnerabilities, code injection flaws, and weak security configurations to remotely manipulate refrigeration settings. Attackers exploited a self-registration feature lacking multifactor authentication to access archived records between June 27 and July 2.
Full Text:
Federal agencies warn of cyberattacks on industrial refrigeration systems. Healthcare cybersecurity could get a post-midterm boost. Chainalysis exposes customer credentials, and DigiCert discloses a breach. OpenAI's latest model learns to respect boundaries. D-Link warns of unpatched switch vulnerabilities. The EU accuses TikTok of leading users down harmful rabbit holes, while tech giants challenge California's child safety law. Federal prosecutors charge three suspects in a $129 million AI-powered impersonation scheme. Our guest is Greg Notch, CTO of Expel, sharing thoughts on how pacing AI won't stop the bad actors. Meta's AI feeding frenzy gets put on a diet.

Today is Friday November 6th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

The Feds warn of ongoing cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration.

Five U.S. government agencies are warning of ongoing cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems worldwide. CISA, the FBI, and the departments of Health and Human Services, Agriculture, and Transportation say attackers are targeting temperature controllers used in grocery stores, cold storage facilities, and refrigerated transportation.

Attackers may exploit authentication bypass vulnerabilities, code injection flaws, and weak security configurations to remotely manipulate refrigeration settings. They could force equipment into continuous heating or defrost cycles, potentially spoiling food and medicine, damaging equipment, creating fire hazards, and putting consumers at risk. Attackers could also prevent operators from seeing accurate temperature readings.

The agencies urge organizations to remove refrigeration controllers from the public internet, segment operational technology networks, strengthen authentication, patch vulnerable devices, and monitor for suspicious activity. They also recommend establishing safe temperature limits and alerts.

The warning highlights how cyberattacks against relatively simple industrial controllers can have serious physical consequences.

Post-midterms, healthcare cybersecurity could see renewed attention.

With Democrats poised to control both chambers of Congress in January, healthcare cybersecurity, AI safety, and health data privacy could receive renewed attention. Experts expect bipartisan interest in strengthening security standards and helping rural hospitals defend against cyberattacks, but disagreements over funding and regulatory costs could complicate legislation.

The Trump administration's deregulatory agenda presents another obstacle. A sweeping overhaul of the HIPAA Security Rule, proposed under President Biden, remains uncertain, with final action delayed until at least July 2027.

Lawmakers may also scrutinize AI use in healthcare and sensitive health information collected by apps and chatbots operating outside HIPAA protections.

Industry experts warn that healthcare organizations shouldn't wait for Washington to act. Cyberattacks continue threatening patient safety, clinical operations, and sensitive data, regardless of who's running Congress.

Chainalysis says all customers suffered breach exposure.

Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis says attackers exposed usernames, password hashes, and live authentication tokens for all customers, expanding an earlier breach disclosure involving customer identity information. The company attributes the intrusion to attackers using AI-driven techniques and an on-path attack. Chainalysis has taken several products and its login portal offline while strengthening security. Customers will be required to reset passwords and rotate API keys. The company says it has found no evidence that attackers accessed investigative data or manipulated its blockchain attribution records.

DigiCert discloses a data breach.

DigiCert has disclosed a data breach exposing business customers’ contact information and, in some cases, identity documents. The incident began when an internal archiving system was inadvertently exposed to the internet. Attackers exploited a self-registration feature lacking multifactor authentication to access archived records between June 27 and July 2. DigiCert discovered the data exposure in October and has since strengthened security controls. The company says its certificate issuance systems were unaffected. It has not disclosed how many customers were impacted.

OpenAI says their latest model is better at respecting boundaries.

OpenAI has unveiled GPT-6 Cyber, a new security model rated Critical for cybersecurity capabilities under the company's Preparedness Framework. The model significantly outperformed its predecessor in exploitation benchmarks while demonstrating improved adherence to authorized testing boundaries. In Linux kernel research, it reproduced more than 1,700 vulnerabilities and developed working privilege escalation exploits for 948. It also identified 81 high-severity Firefox vulnerabilities, with Mozilla already rolling out patches. OpenAI says it has reported 304 critical issues to maintainers. New safeguards monitor authorized activity and restrict assistance with attacks on critical infrastructure. Dragos helped evaluate protections for industrial systems. Access is initially limited to approved customers participating in OpenAI's Daybreak Red program, with broader availability planned for authorized security researchers.

D-Link warns of multiple vulnerabilities in its managed switches.

D-Link is warning of multiple unpatched vulnerabilities affecting its DGS-3130 series managed switches. The flaws involve authentication, access controls, and information handling in the D-Link Discovery Protocol. Attackers with network access could potentially steal sensitive information, modify configurations, change credentials, or disrupt services. D-Link hasn't assigned public CVE identifiers and is investigating whether other products are affected. Until firmware updates are available, administrators should disable the discovery protocol, restrict management access, remove unnecessary SNMP community strings, and monitor for suspicious configuration changes or unexpected resets.

The EU accuses TikTok of taking users down harmful rabbit holes, while US companies sue California over a law designed to protect children 15 and younger from addictive social media features.

The European Commission is accusing TikTok of violating the Digital Services Act by allowing its recommendation algorithm to draw users into potentially harmful content rabbit holes. Regulators say the platform repeatedly serves videos about sadness, self-harm, and body image, potentially damaging the mental health of young and vulnerable users. Investigators analyzed roughly 20,000 videos and concluded that TikTok's existing safeguards are ineffective. They want recommendations based more on users' explicit preferences rather than engagement signals like viewing time. The case marks an unprecedented challenge to the engagement-driven business model of a major social media platform. TikTok disputes the findings, calling them fundamentally inaccurate. The conclusions remain preliminary, and the company can challenge the evidence. If violations are confirmed, TikTok could face fines reaching 6% of its annual global revenue. European officials say they're also examining similar recommendation practices on other platforms.

Meta, TikTok, and Google are suing California to block a new law designed to protect children 15 and younger from addictive social media features. Assembly Bill 1709, scheduled to take effect January 1, prohibits platform designs the state considers psychologically exploitative. The companies filed separate federal lawsuits arguing the law violates First Amendment protections and conflicts with Section 230, which limits platforms' liability for user-generated content. They also contend that parents, rather than the government, should determine appropriate online safeguards for children. California Attorney General Rob Bonta says the state will defend the legislation. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the measure in September, citing concerns about technology's impact on children. Google warns the law could undermine existing tools designed to deliver age-appropriate content.

Federal prosecutors charged three people with using AI to impersonate corporate executives.

Federal prosecutors have charged three people with using AI-generated impersonations of corporate executives and attorneys to allegedly steal approximately $129 million. Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit are accused of targeting thousands of companies worldwide over more than 18 months. According to the indictment, the defendants contacted accounting departments posing as CEOs requesting confidential financial transactions. They then used AI to impersonate executives during phone or video calls before directing employees to supposed attorneys, also impersonated by the conspirators. Victims were instructed to wire money to international bank accounts, with proceeds converted into cryptocurrency to conceal their origins. The defendants face charges including wire fraud, aggravated identity theft, and money laundering. The alleged victims include hospitals, financial institutions, and other businesses.

Coming up after the break, I speak with Greg Notch, CTO of Expel, about how pacing AI won't stop the bad actors.

And, that was Expel's CTO Greg Notch.

Meta's AI feeding frenzy gets put on a diet.

Meta has hit the brakes on a controversial plan to expand its rights to use content from business customers’ websites. The proposed commercial terms would have allowed Meta to collect material from linked domains and web pages, potentially including news articles, to train its AI products. Journalists and publishers objected to having their work swept into Meta’s training pipeline without explicit permission. Meta initially delayed the changes from October 30 to November 20, then paused them indefinitely. A Norwegian court issued a temporary injunction against the terms, while British regulators announced plans to investigate. Meta had already softened some language, removing explicit references to AI training. For now, existing terms remain in place. Apparently, even in the age of artificial intelligence, permission is still a thing.

Title: UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes
Context: The UK has announced major investments in strengthening its cyber defenses, designed to stave off the rise of faster, more complex attacks enhanced by AI tools
Full Text:
The UK has announced major investments in strengthening its cyber defenses, designed to stave off the rise of faster, more complex attacks enhanced by AI tools. In late October, the government unveiled a funding package of approximately $800 million to strengthen cyber defenses and AI security investments.

The move comes as Kanishka Narayan, the UK's minister of artificial intelligence, said in a speech last month that "it seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber-defenses will be breached." He cited the recent trend of misaligned models escaping containment, citing the OpenAI incident in June during which an agent hacked an Australian government health agency.

But the UK government is also pushing toward another, related goal: digital sovereignty. In his speech, Narayan emphasized the need to "build in Britain to keep the public safe in Britain" and become less dependent on foreign providers, which has become a common goal for some countries following the US government's export control order for Anthropic earlier this year.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

"We want the world's leading companies investing here, but we will not accept dependence as the price of that investment," Narayan said.

But industry-watchers argue that government investment to strengthen cyber-defenses while also achieving greater sovereignty by encouraging homegrown tech might be difficult to do all at once.

UK "Tech-xit" Investments: Are They Enough?

Two turning points appear to have shifted government policy in the UK and Europe this year, both involving the same US company: Anthropic. The first came with the AI company's unveiling of Project Glasswing in April for its Mythos frontier model, which sparked concerns about a coming "vulnpocalypse" for enterprise security teams.

"It created an almighty whirlpool of conversations," says Tim Williams, CEO of London-based Quod Orbis, which specializes in continuous controls monitoring. "And then there were lots of concerns about what that meant, and everybody seemed to panic. I think that panic has settled down now."

But another event — the Trump administration's ban on foreign nationals using Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models has had a far more lasting effect. The ban didn't just impact overseas companies and government agencies; the export controls effectively forced Anthropic to pull all access for the two models for several weeks.

The implications of abruptly losing access to valuable — and perhaps critical — AI technology through a sudden change in US policy accelerated an already growing conversation about reducing dependency on American tech companies. A crucial part of the UK government's funding package is designed to fuel British AI startups and invest in home-grown companies.

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

It's a solid idea, but infosec professionals see two issues with that approach. First, the funding package is split up between a number of initiatives, with approximately £154 million of the £600 million total devoted to strengthening current cyber-defenses, for example.

"If you look at the amount that they're putting into it, is that enough? Is that significant?" Williams asks.

Secondly, the UK is already well behind the curve with fueling homegrown AI and cloud companies. Amir Khan, managing director at Wire, tells Dark Reading that there's been chronic under-investment in emerging technologies in the country, which has led to missed opportunities in the past.

"In the UK, we had DeepMind before it was sold to Google [in 2014]," Khan says. "Had they known the impact that DeepMind would have now, would they still have sold it, or doubled down on it? Who knows? But it's another example of a large organization that grew in the UK, leaving to go to the US."

In fact, due to that kind of ongoing tech emigration, Khan says you could argue that the last good thing to come out of UK's technology industry was Cambridge Analytica — a company that become embroiled in a scandal involving Facebook.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

Achieving Digital Sovereignty in the AI Era

Time and again, experts have argued that organizations can't counter AI-driven threats effectively without AI-enabled defenses. But that complicates matters for the UK, which is looking to achieve tech sovereignty in the aftermath of the Anthropic ban.

For one, in some part because of the issues outlined above, many of the major AI companies — OpenAI, Meta, SpaceXAI (now SpaceX Super Intelligence), and Palantir Technologies — are also based in the US. And while there are plenty of AI startups these days, those companies may not have the scale needed for national defense systems.

Additionally, there's also the cost component. Williams says many of Quod Orbis' customers are looking to reduce their dependency on a single vendor or provider, whether it's for cloud, software, AI, or other technologies. "There's no question that, in speaking to our clients, that concentrated risk is a concern for them," he says.

But moving from, for example, one cloud provider to four or five can be challenging, especially for mid-market organizations, he says. They may not have the budgets of large enterprises, and they probably rely more heavily on the commercial discounts that the cloud giants like AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud Platform provide. "If they're spreading that investment out across multiple cloud providers, that can become more expensive for them," Williams says.

Khan agrees and points to the recent example of France migrating off Windows for government workstations and moving to Linux. But leaving the Microsoft ecosystem will require France to add several more technologies from different vendors. "That, for me, defeats the purpose because you've essentially taken away one provider and pulled in six," he says. "That doesn't really give you the flexibility you want."

Khan argues the UK sometimes sets the wrong target for tech sovereignty. "We talk as though we have to build every chip, every cloud, and every application ourselves," he says. "As you can imagine, that's an enormous undertaking, and it doesn't really get to the heart of the issue. For me, the questions are, can we make our own decisions about the technology that we depend on? Can we operate it on our terms?"

The UK can retain such operational authority, he says, by choosing providers and vendors that build that kind of customer controls directly into their products and services; for example, Khan notes that Wire offers customer a private cloud option for the messaging platform that organizations can control and operate based within whatever country they're located.

Whichever providers or vendors the UK government chooses, officials should be asking several key questions before investing: who holds the encryption keys, who can interrupt the service, and how realistic is it to move off that technology?

In the meantime, the UK government will continue to focus on strengthening the country's cyber defenses through these investments and efforts like the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill currently. But Williams is unsure if they will be enough.

"It's a step in the right direction, absolutely," he says. "But is it the investment I would expect to see in terms of being really concerned about the threat to the UK?"
