Weaponize your identity debt: Identity Security, decoys, and tripwires in the age of AI attacks
Context: Without this differential between appearance and security, and supported by traditional detection and response alone, adding designed ‘honey tokens’ in the age of machine-speed...
Full Text:
Every enterprise has identity debt: over-privileged accounts, insecure credential storage, and poor control of account lifecycle are just a few weaknesses we see all the time. But what if that debt could be turned into a strategic advantage against attackers?

CISA recently described decoys, tripwires, breadcrumbs, and honeytokens as practical mechanisms for detecting post-compromise activity. It got me thinking about how we can apply this defensive concept at the identity layer, where an attempted authentication can become both a detection signal and an inline containment decision. In other words, is there a world where we can weaponize Identity Security controls as a set of simple but effective tripwires across enterprise environments?

I think there is—and, even better, I think it has potential to turn any environment into the kind of classic laser hallway you see in heist movies, with red beams criss-crossing the route to the goal, ready to alert and ready to stop the latest threats.

So, in this blog, we’re going to look at how organizations can turn the same weaknesses attackers target into opportunities to generate rapid, high-fidelity signals with minimal operational risk.

But first: What are cyber decoys?

Cyber decoys are legitimate-looking systems, accounts, and data designed to distract and detect adversaries or facilitate collection of threat intelligence.

When operationalized with monitoring and alerting, they can become tripwires to provide high-fidelity signals to defenders. CISA also recommends mapping decoy coverage to MITRE ATT&CK and MITRE Engage, continuously testing the controls, and refining them based on observed adversary behaviour.

Why does this matter now?

The Hugging Face attack alone generated 17,000 unique events to analyse and correlate in a matter of a few days. As we prepare for a reality where attacks like these are commonplace, generating signal from noise to drive effective detection, response and containment has never been more important.

The focus is primarily on enhancing correlation. Hugging Face recommended that organizations focus on this in their post-incident call, having used an open-source model successfully—evidently a good investment. However, even the world’s most effective correlation engine will remain subject to data pipeline and ingestion constraints, some of which are owned by platform providers and cannot be optimized directly.

Generating high-fidelity signals as events unfold complements runtime controls that contain the threat, providing deeper visibility into attacker activity while enabling more informed defensive actions in real time.

Safe deception in the age of machine-speed threats

The aim of a deception strategy is to expose attackers and increase the cost and difficulty of attacks by creating a misleading picture of the environment and its resources (i.e., identities).

In agentic terms, the goal is to increase the compute/token cost of attack, use up context window, and buy time. In the future, it’ll be to funnel agentic attackers towards pre-designed traps to cause the agent to loop without escape.

Deception relies on something—for example, an identity with high privileges and easily-acquired credentials—appearing significantly less monitored, controlled, and secure than it actually is.

Without this differential between appearance and security, and supported by traditional detection and response alone, adding designed ‘honey tokens’ in the age of machine-speed threats may not generate a response fast enough to prevent exploitation of the token itself. Decoys and tripwires must therefore be safe. In other words, they must not have possible negative security implications in and of themselves.

Importantly, a safe tripwire turns the traditional detect > contain methodology, and reliance on response-time, on its head: the containment action that took place is the detection that arms your SOC with a signal, with full context of what happened.

Finally, given the rise of machine-speed threats, tripwires must not provide additional information as to the defensive posture of the organization when triggered. Transparency of the tripwire—which must not be able to be enumerated or discovered directly will become key to identifying and defeating machine-speed threats.

Identity is where the attack becomes the control point

AI attacks do not move through an environment in neat, human-sized steps. They enumerate identities, test permissions, reuse valid credentials and tokens, and pivot across trust boundaries until they find a path that works.

As we’ve already seen, the Hugging Face investigation reconstructed more than 17,000 attacker actions, grouped into approximately 6,280 clusters. The important lesson is not only the volume of activity, but the repeated identity pivots hidden inside it: credential theft, workload impersonation, token reuse, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.

That makes identity a powerful place to deploy tripwires. The tripwire should not only sit on a file, share, or endpoint. It should sit on the attempted identity path itself:

An identity requests access to an unexpected resource, in an unexpected protocol, or in a way that deviates from its baseline.

The request is evaluated using identity, source, destination, protocol, behaviour, and context.

The access is denied or fenced inline.

The same event generates a high-fidelity signal for the SOC.

Related identities and adjacent attack paths can be investigated or contained.

The attacker sees a normal access denial. The SOC sees the identity, attempted destination, protocol, source, sequence of activity, and potential attack path.

Silverfort sits inside the authentication path, where it can enforce identity-based deny and segmentation before an attacker completes lateral movement or privilege escalation.

For a machine-speed attack, detection alone often arrives too late. An identity tripwire functions as a control-flow interrupt: it breaks the sequence between authentication and the next step in the attack chain.

Instead of allowing the attacker to authenticate, discover, pivot, and escalate while defenders correlate events after the fact, the control can deny the risky authentication attempt at the point where the path is exercised. This changes the operating model from detect → correlate → respond to deny → detect → contain, resulting in a synchronous control that limits blast radius while preserving the evidence needed for investigation.

How can we leverage identity debt for this?

Identity is ripe for deception. Traditional identity debt such as over-privileged accounts, shadow admins, insecure credential storage, use of legacy protocols, and loose account lifecycle management is common—maybe even ubiquitous. These do not need to be designed and created because they already exist!

I want to be clear here: hygiene is still really important. Just because it’s possible to weaponize these existing issues, doesn’t mean good hygiene practices can be neglected.

The real question is how do we create safe tripwires?

There are three key premises to creating effective, safe tripwires:

A differential exists between the outward appearance of the account (utility to attackers), and the security state (monitored, controlled).

Usage of the tripwire does not have security implications (i.e., it does not make our security position worse).

Tripping the tripwire must not provide additional defensive context to the attacker to learn from; it must be to the attacker.

Inline identity controls allow for us to meet these three conditions. For example, deny policies create the tripwire alert to the SOC team, while denying the attacker information about why the containment activity occurred. Likewise, service accounts can be ‘fenced’ down to their standard, accepted, recorded usage behaviour and deny anomalies so, should anomalous usage be detected, we can both directly deny the usage of the account, and notify the SOC with a high-fidelity, rapid alert with full context for further action and wider correlation. All of this can happen without the agent seeing anything except ‘access denied’.

Some other cases where we can weaponize identity as tripwires (you can read more in the appendix below):

If connections to Tier 0/1 must be via bastions or PAW and are not

If dormant accounts become active

If admin accounts are used in a highly unusual way

If a legacy protocol is being used to access a sensitive server

If a low-privilege identity is attempting to reach a Tier 0 system

When one of these edges is exercised, the response should combine three actions: deny or restrict the attempted access, generate a high-confidence alert, and expose the surrounding identity relationships for investigation. This is specifically a control against AI attacks and their speed, persistence, and ability to test many paths in parallel.

What this means for security in the age of machine-speed threats

As we move into the next phase of threats—autonomously driven by AI models with the capacity to enumerate and hold your full environment and its vulnerabilities in their context window—two challenges emerge:

How do we generate signal amongst the massive volume of noise?

How do we do this in a way that does not require a loop of detect > correlate > respond, dependent on replication and processing times and humans in the loop?

CISA defines tripwires as decoys where interaction generates an alert. Silverfort extends that idea into the authentication path, where identity-based deny and segmentation can block access before lateral movement or privilege escalation completes. While a conventional tripwire detects interaction, an identity tripwire can detect, deny, and contain the attempted path in the same control loop.

Rethinking how we weaponize identity against attackers—by leveraging the identity debt that already exists—allows us to generate high-quality signal to cut through the noise, while having containment built-in. The containment activity generates the signal, rather than the signal requiring containment activity.

Doing this allows for more rapid threat detection, safely, while denying any information to the model that may help it progress its attack—and gives us a pathway to active defense in the future by funnelling agents to useless traps in an endless loop.

If you want to see how Silverfort can stop AI attacks inline and at runtime, book a demo here.

Identity tripwire appendix

Tripwire

Suspicious interaction

Recommended response

Decoy service account

Authentication from any source or destination outside its tightly defined baseline

Generate an alert and apply a virtual fence

Dormant privileged account

Login attempt against a disabled, unused, or never-used account

Deny the request and investigate the originating identity and host

Decoy SPN/Kerberos path

TGS request for a decoy service identity from an unexpected system

Alert on possible service-account discovery or credential theft and virtually fence it

Tier-0 access edge

Non-admin identity attempts authentication to domain controllers or identity infrastructure

Block inline and surface the full attempted path

Legacy protocol path

NTLM or other weak protocol used against a sensitive resource from an unusual source

Deny or segment the protocol-level access and generate an alert

Executive/admin breadcrumb

A decoy link, file, or share is accessed by an identity that should never touch it

Treat as a likely compromise signal and initiate identity containment

Full Text:
If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. But building one that works seamlessly across multiple models and surfaces is incredibly hard. You need to solve for performance, quality, and cost. And then you have to maintain it, which is even harder.

Luckily, the GitHub engineering team built a best-in-class, truly multi-model harness, which we’ve adopted company-wide. The Microsoft Copilot harness powers Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, the GitHub Copilot app, the CLI, VS Code, and more. And today, we’re making that harness available through Microsoft Foundry. That gives developers and enterprise customers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. You get the right model for the job without switching the harness or the rest of your tech stack. That frees up your time, energy, and resources to focus on your bottom line.

What’s a harness, and why is it hard?

If the model supplies the intelligence, the harness is everything around the model. It’s the orchestration layer that gives an agent the right instructions, context, execution environment, and controls to accomplish meaningful work. And a harness worth its salt has support for open standards like MCP and agent skills, as well as agent plugins.

This is a fast-moving space. A frontier model today might fall behind tomorrow. And building your own harness or model router to keep up can be painful and slow. Now, you can build on the same harness Microsoft and GitHub ship in our own products, and you don’t have to maintain it.

We invest in science and engineering work to continually improve and evolve the harness and ensure high-quality, efficient, and low-cost performance across a range of models and workloads. The benefits compound for us and our customers who use the harness to build and run their own agents. Improve the harness, and every surface it touches benefits.

Born in GitHub, battle-tested at enterprise scale

The Copilot harness was built by the same GitHub engineers behind new technologies like our multi-model orchestration. And those technologies are only possible because we built our own harness. Designed to be fast, token-efficient, and predictable, it was our original, high-quality harness. And it had the highest satisfaction among our most demanding audience: developers. That’s why we’re standardizing all of our Copilot experiences on the strongest foundation possible.

The harness is built to perform across model families, with 20+ frontier models plus bring your own key, so you can use the right model for the right job. Instead of doing the work to keep up with and eval new models, lean on us to intelligently route work to the right model or models based on the task.

Our harness is flexible and configurable to any type of app, agent, or service. We recently ported the harness runtime to Rust, which has resulted in industry-leading performance and reductions in both session overhead and time-to-first token. With the Copilot harness, Microsoft runs the agent loop and sandbox, with governance and optimization built in from day one. You bring the instructions, skills, tools, and model choice.

Title: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A virtual desktop service provider in Japan has told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by hackers.

GMO Internet’s Onamae.com service is delivered via a network of tens of thousands of servers operated by the firm and is popular with foreign-exchange traders.

However, the firm was forced to suspend the service on October 21 after discovering the day before that “malicious programs” had been installed in “some customers’ server environments.”

A security alert claimed that some information may have been accessed and that as many as 26,739 servers may have been impacted. Some reports suggest the hackers may have accessed trading accounts and made unauthorized transactions.

An extortion email sent on October 21 demanded a ransom of around eight billion yen ($50.7m).

Read more on ransomware attacks in Japan: Japanese Railway Operators Hit with Weekend Cyber Attacks

Having refused to pay the ransom, GMO Internet was notified by its attackers that they would deploy ransomware on October 27 as 12pm. As a result, it advised its customers to perform a full virus scan on their devices, back up all data, and then disconnect their PC from the internet and turn off the power.

In the meantime, GMO Internet has been asking for customers to ship their PCs so that its security team can investigate.

“As of [October 27, 11:59], no malware (including ransomware) has been detected in the devices that have been analyzed,” it explained.

“However, the analysis is still ongoing, and we have not yet confirmed the security of all customer devices. More devices from customers are expected to arrive in the future. We will proceed with the analysis as soon as they arrive.”

Japan Inc Under Fire

“This demonstrates how a vulnerability in a remote access service can have consequences far beyond the compromised system,” said Suzu Labs chief security evangelist, Phillip Wylie.ㅤ

"Attackers don’t necessarily need to deploy ransomware to cause significant damage. If they can steal sensitive information, compromise accounts, and threaten to publicly release data, they already have multiple ways to pressure an organization.”

Wylie added: "The biggest takeaway is that preventing the initial compromise is important, but limiting what attackers can do once they gain access is equally critical.”

The breach is the latest in a string of security incidents impacting Japanese firms this year. Organizations as diverse as Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (eight million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million) have suffered major data breaches.

Title: Hive ransomware affiliate jailed, years after FBI infiltrated the gang’s systems
Context: Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector
Full Text:
A Ukrainian man has been sentenced to 70 months in a US prison for his role in a series of ransomware attacks.

36-year-old Artem Stryzhak became an affiliate of the Nefilim ransomware group around June 2021, receiving an 80% cut of the ransoms he managed to extort in attacks against hospitals, government organisations, law firms, and businesses around the world.

The rest of the ransom would go to Nefilim's administrators - including fellow Ukrainian Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who was charged last year in relation to attacks against hundreds of corporate victims using the LockerGoga and MegaCortex ransomware, as well as Nefilim.

At the time of writing, Tymoshchuk is not in US custody and a US $11 million bounty has been offered by the US State Department for information leading to his arrest.

Nefilim was not the only ransomware gang that Stryzhak worked closely with. He was also an early affiliate of the Hive ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation which targeted businesses and, in particular, organisations working in healthcare.

The FBI later warned that Hive had extorted US $100 million from businesses and organisations globally in a period of just 18 months.

According to the US Department of Justice, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators were behind Hive ransomware attacks against a number of victims, including law firms, a dentist's office, and a healthcare provider, during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Such was the scale of the attacks that in 2022 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) described Hive as an "exceptionally aggressive" threat to the health sector.

In January 2023, it was revealed that a multinational law enforcement operation had secretly penetrated the Hive ransomware operation in late July 2022, capturing decryption keys and quietly passing them to victims so they did not have to pay a ransom.

The DOJ said that the operation saved corporate victims of Hive over US $130 million in ransom payments.

At the time I speculated that the take-down of Hive may lead to the identification and possible apprehension of some of those involved in Hive ransomware attacks. In June 2024, Stryzhak was arrested in Barcelona, and subsequently extradited to the United States where he pleaded guilty.

The infiltration into Hive's infrastructure took place in 2022. Stryzhak was arrested in 2024, and sentenced in 2026. If there's a lesson for ransomware affiliates who think they got away with it, it's that law enforcement is prepared to be patient, and the evidence does not go away.

That's something that Volodymyr Tymoshchuk may also want to consider.

In its 2026 Software Supply Chain Security report, JFrog identified over 900 malicious AI agent skills carrying high-impact payloads alongside 495 malicious AI models on Hugging Face and 56 malicious extensions on OpenVSX. Attackers are no longer just targeting code; they are targeting the autonomous tools that write, review, and deploy it.

Ford (Americas): Ford Motor Company has more than 15,000 developers spread across 80-plus global plants, which previously ran on separate repository tools and scanners with no shared visibility between them. As a result, the team now manages more than 43 million artifacts on the JFrog Platform with 99.99% uptime. The Trusted Intelligence Award recognizes teams that bring enterprise-grade governance to AI and model lifecycles, helping trust extend far beyond just supporting application code.

Here are the winners:

NVIDIA (Americas): Models repositories are under enterprise identity control, with a shared curation and scanning policy,which means a downloaded model faces the same checks as a package before it reaches production.

NVIDIA brought its AI model distribution surface under a governed perimeter by applying curation, scanning, and policy enforcement directly to its model mirrors. Thousands of AI model seats are now managed inside a controlled, auditable boundary, transforming what was once an unmanaged distribution surface into a demonstration of DevGovOps operating at true enterprise scale. To get there, NVIDIA leveraged JFrog Curation and JFrog’s scanning and policy tools, piloting them on the infrastructure through which its AI models flow.

After consolidating around the JFrog Platform and introducing software package scanning and policy-based controls earlier in the software development lifecycle, builds were progressively onboarded, providing teams with greater visibility into open-source dependencies and a more consistent approach to software component governance. Husqvarna Group validated JFrog Curation and JFrog Advanced Security in a hands-on pilot ahead of full deployment, and says the centralized visibility helps streamline security and governance workflows while supporting software traceability and reporting needs associated with evolving regulatory requirements, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act and NIS2.

As a result, late-stage release blocks from non-compliant dependencies are down 60-75% and the airline has full visibility of its compliance posture.

The Guardian Award recognizes software supply chain security operating at real enterprise scale – blocking threats before they reach production across large, highly distributed environments.

Here are the winners:

Automated weekly audits check configuration drift, access control, artifact integrity and artifact authenticity. Title: AI Is Turning CISOs Into Business-Risk Translators, Says Nvidia’s Head of Cyber
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
In the AI era, cybersecurity leaders must explain how AI-related risks connects to business goals and help executives understand who is responsible for accepting those risks, according to Nvidia’s head of cybersecurity policy, Mark Weatherford.

Speaking at ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Weatherford argued that the broad adoption of AI in the workplace, including in cybersecurity workflows, has transformed the CISO role from a security gatekeeper to a business-risk translator.

As organizations weigh AI adoption, CISOs must help executives understand the tradeoffs and clarify who owns the risk, he said.

Weatherford recalled a board meeting where a CISO struggled to explain the relationship between security and the business. Ultimately, the board challenged the CISO on their understanding of the company’s business model. This event, he said, had a negative impact on the perception the board had of the CISO’s credibility and ability to protect the business.

Weatherford said the exchange taught him that CISOs need to understand how their organizations generate revenue, not only how to protect them.

He added that business perspective is especially important as organizations weigh the potential benefits and risks of AI.

For instance, boards may worry that moving too slowly will cost them competitive advantage, Weatherford said, while moving too quickly can mean deploying tools without appropriate controls or an understanding of the risks.

While he argued that CISO rarely owns the business risk from deploying things like AI, he emphasized that modern CISOs must interpret that risk and make sure leaders understand who owns it.

Balancing AI Innovation With Cybersecurity Risks

Weatherford described two main challenges CISOs face with AI.

First and the “pace of technological change” makes their work more challenging.

Second, CISOs need to focus both on “security for AI and AI for security,” protecting the AI systems their organizations deploy while also considering how AI can support security operations.

Combined, these challenges mean traditional cybersecurity approaches may no longer be sufficient, he argued.

“If you’re not doing pentesting 24/7, 365, you’re probably behind the curve,” he said.

Weatherford also cautioned against investments driven by “fear of missing out.”

Leaders, he said, should do business due diligence before spending heavily on AI. CISOs can contribute by preparing concrete proposals for reducing risk. He recommended putting together a short plan that describes the proposed work and the resources it would require.

Vendor evaluation is another area where CISOs need to apply judgment. Weatherford said he looks for AI-native products that address security problems, rather than older products with AI added on.

He urged CISOs to consider supply-chain dependencies, too. Multiple vendors may depend on the same suppliers, creating single points of failure that can affect more than one product or service. Some dependencies may sit several tiers down the supply chain, beyond the suppliers an organization knows it relies on directly.

Weatherford’s advice for keeping pace with these changes was to stay curious and keep learning and even relearn things as technologies evolve.

For instance, he encouraged CISOs to “learn one new thing every week,” suggesting focusing on one AI topic at a time, such as model context protocol (MCP), prompt injections or sandboxing.

Finally, Weatherford recommended CISOs to join and create formal and informal peer communities. He mentioned that he created a CISO Exchange Network in which he invited CISOs from Nvidia’s major partners, customers and suppliers, where they share experience, concerns and tips.

Title: Energy Giant Engie Notifies Customers of Supply Chain Breach
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
One of the world’s largest natural gas suppliers has notified an undisclosed number of customers that their personal data may have been compromised in a recent breach.

French multinational Engie employs over 90,000 people across 30 countries, supplying gas, nuclear power, and renewables. Its revenue in 2025 was almost €72bn ($80bn).

According to screenshots of the customer notification posted to X, the compromised data could include: full name, postal and email address, telephone number, unique IDs for energy supply (PCE/PDL), customer ID, and contract number.

The firm confirmed that no banking data was involved in the breach.

Read more on cyber-attacks impacting French firms: French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Engie urged customers to be on the lookout for potential fraud and phishing stemming from the incident.

“A malicious person could use the information mentioned above to impersonate you or use your personal details to contact another organization in your name, obtain additional information, or attempt to make a payment,” it warned. “Fraudulent emails may appear to come from trusted sources, such as organisations you know, in order to deceive you.”

According to a statement from the firm sent to Infosecurity, its own IT systems weren’t compromised. Engie blamed a third-party marketing platform used by its partners which was then compromised by threat actors.

“Engie recently identified unusual data access activity within a tool used by partners as part of their customer prospecting activities and the marketing of energy offers in France,” it explained.

“As soon as this activity was detected, the relevant access was disabled. At the same time, Engie launched an in-depth technical investigation to understand the circumstances of the incident, accurately assess its scope by identifying customers potentially affected, and ensure that the situation was fully secured. Enhanced monitoring measures were also put in place.”

No Group Has Claimed Responsibility

At the time of writing, no extortion group had admitted responsibility for the breach, which Engie said is now contained.

However, in October last year, extortion group Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters listed the firm on its leak site, after compromising over 100 Salesforce instances and claiming to have extracted more than one billion records.

In that incident, Engie’s US retail energy business Engie Resources was the victim, with the group claiming to have obtained 3GB of data.

According to claims data from insurer Resilience shared with Infosecurity, no UK or European energy and utilities clients have reported ransomware since July 2025.

European claims with a recorded cost involved only fraud or exposed customer data. That contrasts with the US where ransomware comprises around 70% of incurred losses across claims on record in the sector, Resilience said.

Title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
Context: (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry,...
Full Text:
We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our AI for Science program, which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.

We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)

Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.

Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with HHMI Janelia Research Campus to develop the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the Allen Institute, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.

AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.

Science funders and societies

Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:

The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.

The Simons Foundation. This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.

Schmidt Sciences. Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.

Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy. This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.

The US National Science Foundation. This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.

CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.

Institutions

Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:

Space Telescope Science Institute. STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.

Wellcome Sanger Institute. One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.

The Francis Crick Institute. Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.

Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences. One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.

EMBL. The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.

Gladstone Institutes. An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.

Research projects and initiatives

As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:

FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience). It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.

LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system). Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.

AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research). Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.

gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease). The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.

Tau Ceti (mathematics). This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.

Centre for Population Genomics. A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.

What’s next

Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.

As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

Title: Introducing artifacts for legal work
Context: Since we launched Claude for Legal in May, the most common requests from legal teams have been for simpler setup and easier ways to work with colleagues
Full Text:
Today, we’re introducing ready-to-use artifacts that legal professionals can adapt to how their teams work and share with colleagues across the business. Since we launched Claude for Legal in May, the most common requests from legal teams have been for simpler setup and easier ways to work with colleagues.

Artifacts are interactive tools, such as trackers and dashboards, that teams can use and share in Claude. Our new legal gallery includes artifacts for specific tasks, such as reviewing a stack of contracts, tracking regulatory changes, and taking in legal requests from the business. Each artifact opens with an example, so legal professionals can see how the work comes together before adding their own data and connectors. Each answer or output has a link to its source.

We are also funding public interest groups building artifacts for access-to-justice work and legal education programs teaching tomorrow’s lawyers to build with Claude, and we are starting a Legal Ambassadors Program so legal professionals can learn from each other.

What’s in the gallery

With these artifacts, a legal professional brings their own documents and sources, Claude completes the first pass, and a lawyer applies their judgment to the results. They cover the work legal teams raised with us most often:

Cite check compares a legal document with its sources and flags quotes that don’t match, wrong page numbers, and sources that don’t support the claim.

Jurisdiction survey matrix compares a legal topic, such as data breach notice rules, across states or countries in one table, with links to the underlying law.

Matter board turns engagement letters, emails, or spreadsheets into one board of open matters, showing the owner, next step, and next deadline.

Playbook deviation board compares contracts with your company’s standard terms, flags each clause that differs, and sends it to the person who approves exceptions.

Regulatory horizon scan maps upcoming regulations on a timeline, based on your company’s business and where it operates, and ranks them by impact with links to the sources.

Tabular review builds a table from a set of contracts, showing the terms you ask about, such as severance or non-competes, with links to the exact language.

Tailored to how teams work and shared with guardrails

Every legal team works differently and artifacts work best when they’re connected to the systems legal teams already use. Legal professionals can ask Claude to tailor artifacts to their team and use connectors to bring in their playbooks or research sources, so nobody has to upload documents manually.

Since we launched Claude for Legal, we’ve added more than 60 legal connectors, including Bloomberg Law, Filevine, Ivo, Legora, and Patlytics. See our legal directory (opens in new tab) for the complete list.

Artifacts enable collaboration inside and outside the organization. A legal team can work on an artifact with colleagues across the business or with clients and partners, with sharing settings that ensure privacy and support ethical walls between teams.

Opening the gallery to legal tech and law firms

We partnered with legal tech companies and law firms to build artifacts for legal professionals. Each artifact is in the gallery for legal professionals to discover, test, and adapt to their work:

AI Governance Benchmark built by Goodwin (opens in new tab) benchmarks a company's approach to AI governance to surface potential gaps.

Harvey Intake built by Harvey (opens in new tab) gives business users one place in Claude to send legal questions and requests, answering routine ones from Legal’s own guidance in Harvey and routing the rest to a lawyer, whose reply comes back in Claude.

Obligations Checker built by Foley & Lardner (opens in new tab) reviews agreements for the obligations of both parties and helps validate expectations pre-closing and track expectations post-closing.

Subpoena Response Tool built by PwC (opens in new tab) turns your team's precedents, standard objections and templates into automated, audit-ready first drafts so lawyers can focus on the complex issues while responding faster.

We are excited to see legal tech companies, law firms, legal aid organizations create and share their own artifacts, and have more artifacts coming from Legora and Orrick.

Title: Introducing Route 53 Resolved IP Validation for AWS Network Firewall
Context: A supported deployment model – The feature works with distributed deployments, including multiple firewall endpoints, where clients reach a firewall endpoint in their own...
Full Text:
Your workloads reach most destinations by domain name, but a firewall can only act on what it sees in the traffic. For HTTP and HTTPS, AWS Network Firewall domain rules match the name that the client puts in the request, and the client chooses that name. The connections for protocols such as SSH and SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) don’t carry the domain name. The client uses the name only for the DNS lookup and then connects straight to the IP address that DNS returned. As a result, Network Firewall rules for these protocols have used IP addresses, which change over time. For web and non-web traffic alike, Network Firewall had no view of the answers that your DNS resolver returned, because that shared visibility between DNS and the firewall didn’t exist.

On October 21, 2026, we launched Route 53 Resolved IP Validation for AWS Network Firewall, at no additional charge. Amazon Route 53 Resolver now shares the IP addresses that it returns for each domain name with Network Firewall, and Network Firewall checks each new outbound connection against them. With this launch, you can now filter non-web traffic by domain name, and you can prevent Server Name Indication (SNI) manipulation on TLS traffic without needing to enable TLS inspection.

In this post, we explain how the feature works, show how to turn it on in alert mode, and walk through two common use cases. They’re examples; the same check applies to any outbound traffic that you control by domain name.

How it works

Amazon Route 53 Resolver answers DNS queries from resources in your virtual private cloud (VPC) configured to use it, and it’s available by default in every VPC. With this feature, Route 53 Resolver keeps the IP addresses that it returns for each domain name in a resolved IP cache. When a new outbound connection starts, Network Firewall checks the destination address against that cache.

The workload asks Route 53 Resolver at 10.0.0.2 for files.partner.example.com.

DNS Firewall checks the query first. Domain rules can block or alert on it; an empty rule group lets it through.

Route 53 Resolver answers 203.0.113.10 and records the answer in the resolved IP cache.

The SFTP connection to 203.0.113.10 on port 22 reaches the Network Firewall endpoint.

The policy checks the first packet. The address is in the cache, so the connection continues.

The stateful rule passes it, because Route 53 Resolver returned the address for files.partner.example.com.

The connection leaves through the NAT gateway and internet gateway.

The flow log and alert log record the new fields.

The feature has three parts:

An Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group – It defines the scope. The answers that Route 53 Resolver returns in every VPC associated with this rule group go into the resolved IP cache. The rule group can be empty. Add rules to it and the same rule group also filters the DNS queries themselves, for example, by blocking lookups of known threat domains. Together, DNS Firewall checks the lookup and Network Firewall checks the connection that follows.

The Network Firewall policy setting – On the first packet of each new connection, before your stateful rules run, Network Firewall checks whether Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for a domain name. If it did, the connection continues to your stateful rules. If it didn’t, Network Firewall applies the action you chose: Alert, Drop, or Reject.

Resolved-domain rules – In your stateful rule groups, these rules match a connection by the domain name that its destination address was resolved for, so they work with every protocol. Use the name that your clients look up.

The following diagram shows this architecture.

Figure 1. How Network Firewall checks the SFTP connection from use case 1 against the answers that Route 53 Resolver returned

The policy setting checks every connection, not only web traffic. A connection to an IP address that no client looked up through Route 53 Resolver, such as a hardcoded address, fails the check. If any of your workloads connect straight to IP addresses, add those addresses to Bypass destination validation IP ranges before you enforce. A stateful pass rule doesn’t exempt them because the policy check runs before your rules. The check is per address: when any client in an associated VPC looks up a name, its addresses pass the check for every client in scope in the same Availability Zone. For details, see Resolved IP validation in AWS Network Firewall in the AWS Network Firewall Developer Guide.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

DNS through Amazon Route 53 Resolver – Network Firewall can check only answers that Route 53 Resolver returned. Queries that reach Route 53 Resolver through Resolver endpoints or Resolver forwarding rules count.

A Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group associated with the VPCs whose DNS answers Network Firewall should check connections against.

The policy setting turned on before you add resolved-domain rules – Rules that use domain filtering (the aws_route_53_resolved_domain keyword) need Route 53 Resolved IP Validation turned on in the same firewall policy. Turn the setting on first, in alert mode, then add the rules.

A supported deployment model – The feature works with distributed deployments, including multiple firewall endpoints, where clients reach a firewall endpoint in their own Availability Zone, and with centralized deployments where the firewall is attached natively to AWS Transit Gateway. If routing sends a client to a firewall endpoint in another Availability Zone, its connections fail the check. To move a centralized deployment to a natively attached firewall, see Why and how to migrate to a Transit Gateway attached AWS Network Firewall.

How to turn it on in alert mode

Start in alert mode because clients cache DNS answers. Network Firewall recognizes only the answers that Route 53 Resolver returns after the DNS Firewall rule group is associated with the VPC and selected in the policy. A client that still uses an answer it cached earlier fails the check until it looks up the name again, usually when its cached record expires. Alert mode lets you see this without blocking anything. Allow about 24 hours in alert mode for clients to refresh their caches.

Create a DNS Firewall rule group (it can be empty) and associate it with the VPCs whose DNS answers Network Firewall should check connections against. For the steps, see Creating a rule group and rules.

Or, to use a DNS Firewall rule group that you already have, make sure it’s associated with those VPCs and only those. An answer returned in any associated VPC is valid for every client that the firewall checks. Which clients are checked is set by source IP ranges in step 6.

In the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console, under Network Firewall, choose Firewall policies, then choose the policy that your firewall uses. On the Traffic inspection tab, in the Route 53 Resolved IP validation section, choose Edit and select Enable Route 53 Resolved IP validation.

For Action, choose Alert. For DNS Firewall rule group, choose the rule group from step 1 or 2.

For DNS expiry exception policy, choose what happens to a connection that’s already open when its entry expires from the resolved IP cache. Continue keeps it running, Drop stops it silently, and Reject stops it with a TCP reset. We recommend Continue so that long-running sessions, such as file transfers, aren’t cut off midway. However, choose the option that fits your security requirements.

For source IP ranges, list the clients to check. If you don’t set it, Network Firewall checks clients in the firewall’s VPC and in any additional VPCs attached to the firewall. If your clients are in other VPCs, such as spoke VPCs that send traffic to a firewall attached to a transit gateway, enter their CIDR ranges; otherwise, Network Firewall doesn’t check their connections. Add destinations that you allow by IP address to Bypass destination validation IP ranges. Choose Save.

The following screenshot illustrates these steps.

Figure 2. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation turned on in alert mode

In alert mode, Network Firewall doesn’t block a connection that fails the check, and it doesn’t write an alert of its own. It records the result in your flow logs, in the route53_resolved_ip field of each connection. A value of true means Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for a domain name. A value of false means it didn’t, so enforcement would block the connection. The same field also appears in alert log records that a rule or the policy’s default action writes for the connection. Pass rules don’t write one unless they have the alert; keyword. The DnsUnresolvedFlows metric in Amazon CloudWatch counts the connections that fail the check, and DnsAzUnavailableFlows counts connections from an Availability Zone that doesn’t support the feature. The following alert log record (trimmed, with example values) was written by a default action that alerts, for a connection to an address that Route 53 Resolver returned:

{ "firewall_name": "egress-firewall", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "src_ip": "10.0.1.10", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 123, "proto": "UDP", "app_proto": "ntp", "route53_resolved_ip": true, "verdict": { "action": "alert" }, "alert": { "action": "allowed", "signature_id": 3, "signature": "aws:alert_established action" } } }

In alert mode, this record is for a TLS connection that presented an allowed domain name but went to an address that Route 53 Resolver didn’t return for it, blocked by the policy’s default action in use case 2:

{ "firewall_name": "egress-firewall", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "src_ip": "10.0.1.10", "dest_ip": "198.51.100.7", "dest_port": 443, "proto": "TCP", "app_proto": "tls", "tls": { "sni": "api.partner.example.com" }, "route53_resolved_ip": false, "verdict": { "action": "drop" }, "alert": { "action": "blocked", "signature": "aws:alert_established_app_layer_to_server action" } } }

Before you switch Action to Drop or Reject, check that connections that fail the check are ones you expect and that destinations you allow by IP address are in the bypass ranges. Reject sends a TCP reset, so a blocked TCP client fails right away instead of waiting for a timeout. After you enforce, blocked connections appear in your flow logs with route53_resolved_ip as false, not in your alert logs. For the metrics and log fields to watch, see Monitoring and troubleshooting resolved IP validation.

Use case 1: Filter non-web traffic by domain name

Before this launch, Network Firewall rules for protocols that carry no domain name, such as SFTP, used IP addresses. Now, you can allow them by domain name. In this example, a workload sends files over SFTP to a partner at files.partner.example.com on TCP port 22, and the partner can change the addresses behind that name at any time. The same approach works for SSH, MySQL, and other non-web protocols. You create it as a standard stateful rule. Follow these steps:

Under Network Firewall, choose Network Firewall rule groups, then choose Create rule group. Choose Stateful rule group and Standard stateful rule, and choose the rule evaluation order that your policy uses.

Choose Add rule. For Protocol, choose TCP. For Destination port, enter 22. Under Domain filtering, enter files.partner.example.com. For Action, choose Pass.

Create the rule group, then add it to your firewall policy.

Figure 3. A pass rule for SFTP on TCP port 22, scoped to the partner’s domain name

If you manage rules as code, the equivalent Suricata rule is shown in the following code. It adds the alert; keyword so that the firewall logs allowed connections. The console rule doesn’t add it.

pass tcp any any -> any 22 (alert; msg:"Allow TCP/22 to files.partner.example.com"; aws_route_53_resolved_domain:"files.partner.example.com"; sid:1;)

When the partner moves its server to a new address, the next DNS answer adds it to the resolved IP cache. There’s no IP list to maintain. The cache keeps earlier answers for longer than their DNS time to live (TTL), so the old address can still pass for a while.

Use case 2: Prevent SNI spoofing without TLS inspection

With SNI spoofing, a client presents an allowed domain name in its TLS request while it connects to a different server. Preventing that has required TLS inspection, which decrypts the traffic. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation prevents it without TLS inspection. In this example, a workload calls a partner API at api.partner.example.com over HTTPS. TLS traffic on port 443 must reach only the addresses that Route 53 Resolver returned for that name. You create a pass rule in a standard stateful rule group, as in use case 1, and the firewall policy’s default action drops everything that no rule passes. Follow these steps:

Under Network Firewall, choose Network Firewall rule groups, and then choose Create rule group. Choose Stateful rule group and Standard stateful rule, then choose Strict order.

Choose Add rule. For Protocol, choose TLS. For Destination port, enter 443. Under Domain filtering, enter api.partner.example.com. For Action, choose Pass.

Create the rule group, then add it to your firewall policy.

In the firewall policy, use strict rule order. For the stateful default actions, choose Application drop established (server-directed only) and Application alert established (server-directed only). The alert action logs what the drop action blocks. For why we recommend these default actions, see Firewall policy configuration in the AWS Security Services Best Practices guide.

Figure 4. A pass rule for TLS on port 443, scoped to the partner’s domain name

If you manage rules as code, the equivalent Suricata rule is:

pass tls any any -> any 443 (aws_route_53_resolved_domain:"api.partner.example.com"; sid:2;)

The pass rule matches the destination address, not the name in the TLS request. TLS traffic on port 443 passes only when Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for api.partner.example.com. If the partner’s addresses also serve other domain names, such as behind a content delivery network (CDN), those names pass too. To also require the partner’s name in the TLS request, add an exact SNI match to the same rule: tls.sni; content:"api.partner.example.com"; startswith; endswith; nocase;.

Without startswith and endswith, the content match accepts any SNI that contains the name.

A connection that presents the partner’s name but goes to another address doesn’t match the pass rule. If Route 53 Resolver never returned that address, the policy setting’s enforcement action blocks the connection before your rules run. In alert mode, the policy setting lets the connection through to your rules instead, and the stateful default action drops it because the pass rule doesn’t match. Its alert log record shows route53_resolved_ip as false, as in the second example previously. If Route 53 Resolver returned the address for a different domain name, the connection passes the policy check. The stateful default action then drops it because the pass rule doesn’t match, and that record shows route53_resolved_ip as true.

Best practices

We recommend that you follow these best practices:

Keep DNS on Route 53 Resolver – Block outbound UDP and TCP port 53 DNS to other resolvers, including DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT), on Network Firewall, so that clients don’t bypass the check. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation alone doesn’t do this. If any client looks up a public resolver’s name, such as dns.google, that resolver’s addresses pass the check.

Keep DNS Firewall rules in those VPCs – Route 53 Resolved IP Validation checks the connections that follow a DNS lookup, not the DNS queries themselves. DNS Firewall blocks lookups of known threat domains with AWS managed domain lists, and its advanced rule groups detect data leaving through DNS queries, such as DNS tunneling.

Start small – Add domain filtering to a few rules at a time, then add more when the results look clean. For domain allow list patterns, see Allow rules and domain allowlisting.

Turn on flow and alert logging and detailed monitoring – Connections that fail the resolved IP check show in your flow logs (route53_resolved_ip: false) and in the DnsUnresolvedFlows metric, not in your alert logs. Pass rules without the alert; keyword don’t write an alert log record.

Pricing and availability

Route 53 Resolved IP Validation is available today in all commercial AWS Regions (Regions other than the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions) where AWS Network Firewall and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall are available, at no additional charge. For the list of Regions, see AWS Capabilities by Region. A DNS Firewall rule group with no rules doesn’t incur DNS Firewall charges. Standard DNS Firewall pricing applies after you add rules. See AWS Network Firewall pricing and Amazon Route 53 pricing.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how Route 53 Resolved IP Validation works and how to turn it on in alert mode. Network Firewall now checks each connection’s destination against the IP addresses that Amazon Route 53 Resolver returned for the DNS query. Filtering SFTP, SSH, database, and other non-web traffic by domain name and preventing SNI spoofing without TLS inspection are two common examples of what that makes possible. To get started, turn the feature on in alert mode and review the results before you enforce. For the full walkthrough, see Getting started with resolved IP validation.

To learn more, visit the AWS Network Firewall product page and the feature documentation.

Title: The strategy behind the shield.
Context: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has unveiled CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, a strategy aimed at strengthening national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure resilience against cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats. CISA has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively known...
Full Text:
CISA unveils its 2030 cyber strategy. PHP2Shell exploits are in the wild. HHS preserves healthcare security requirements. Microsoft offers buyouts amid its AI spending spree. A cyberattack disrupts New Mexico hospitals. Google’s Finnish data center plans hit an environmental roadblock. Blue Initiative tracks maritime vulnerabilities. A Chinese national faces charges in a $37 million cryptocurrency scam. Our guest is Cal Al-Dhubaib, host of the new Authorized Intelligence podcast. Anthropic’s prospectus includes an existential disclaimer.

Today is Tuesday October 27th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

CISA plans to defend, harden and prevail.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has unveiled CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, a strategy aimed at strengthening national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure resilience against cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats.

The plan rests on three pillars. Defend focuses on securing networks, operational technology, software supply chains, and emerging technologies, including quantum computing and advanced AI. Harden emphasizes turning threat intelligence into action, improving risk prioritization, and accelerating incident response. Prevail seeks to strengthen national resilience through regional partnerships, emergency communications, and coordinated planning.

The strategy also prioritizes resilient 5G and 6G networks and satellite communications.

CISA will review its existing capabilities within 60 days, deliver an implementation plan within 180 days, and report on its progress within a year.

PHP2Shell is officially under active exploitation.

CISA has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively known as PHP2Shell, to its catalog of actively exploited flaws. The bugs could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable systems.

Researchers observed widespread exploitation attempts before patches were released October 21, though early attempts reportedly failed. Subsequent honeypot activity confirmed successful exploitation in the wild.

Federal civilian agencies have until Thursday to patch their systems.

HHS scales back plans to eliminate privacy and security certification requirements.

Federal health regulators have scaled back plans to eliminate privacy and security certification requirements for electronic health records, following widespread objections from healthcare providers and industry groups.

The Department of Health and Human Services’ final rule eliminates 14 health IT certification criteria, down from the 34 originally proposed. All 13 core privacy and security requirements will remain intact, including standards for authentication and access controls.

Commenters warned that eliminating those safeguards could shift security responsibilities onto healthcare providers, particularly smaller and rural organizations with limited resources.

However, the rule does eliminate transparency and risk-management requirements for AI-powered clinical decision support tools. Those provisions required developers to disclose information about their systems’ capabilities, limitations, and potential risks.

HHS says the changes will save health IT developers more than $1.5 billion in regulatory costs.

Most provisions take effect December 28, with others following in January.

Microsoft offers buyouts amidst AI-driven growth.

Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to approximately 60,000 employees, roughly 27 percent of its workforce, as it balances soaring AI infrastructure spending with efforts to control costs.

The offers cover eligible workers in the United States, Canada, India, and Britain, including some employees at the vice president level.

Microsoft expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion in the September quarter, driven largely by data center investments supporting AI services.

The company previously offered voluntary retirement packages in April and announced 4,800 layoffs in July.

Some engineering, sales, and marketing teams are excluded from the latest program. Eligible employees have until early December to decide, with departures scheduled for December 31.

Microsoft says the initiative will provide flexibility as the company reshapes its workforce around AI-driven growth.

New Mexico hospitals divert patients following a cyberattack.

A cybersecurity incident disrupted operations across the University of New Mexico Health System on Monday, forcing ambulance diversions, canceled appointments, and temporary restrictions on hospital access.

The disruption affected New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center, leaving the state without its highest level of emergency trauma care. Other healthcare providers stepped in to accommodate additional patients.

Employees reported hearing messages broadcast through hospital computers claiming that student, employee, and patient information had been stolen. Those claims have not been verified.

The health system declined to discuss the incident’s nature or scope, citing an active law enforcement investigation. The FBI confirmed it was assisting.

Hospitals and clinics began gradually resuming operations Monday afternoon, although the full extent of the disruption remains unclear.

Cleared trees halt development of a Google AI data center in Finland.

Google’s massive AI infrastructure expansion in Finland has run into an environmental backlash after the company cleared hundreds of thousands of trees without completing required environmental assessments.

At one site in northern Finland, an estimated 250,000 trees were removed across 815 acres. Conservationists estimate another 150,000 were felled at a second location.

Finnish regulators have ordered work stopped at both sites. Google has apologized, saying it acted according to its understanding of local regulations.

The controversy threatens to complicate Google’s €13 billion investment in Finnish data centers, part of a broader AI infrastructure boom attracted by the country’s cool climate and abundant energy.

Supporters point to jobs and tax revenue. Critics question the environmental costs, electricity demands, and limited economic benefits.

More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding tighter regulation and compensation for affected communities.

Google says it will comply with regulators and plans to replant trees.

Blue Initiative tracks vulnerabilities affecting ships, ports, and maritime infrastructure.

A coalition of cybersecurity and maritime organizations has launched Blue Initiative, a free public database tracking vulnerabilities affecting ships, ports, and maritime infrastructure.

The project helps operators identify and prioritize security risks across IT and operational technology systems.

The database currently contains nearly 30,000 vulnerabilities, including more than 2,000 rated critical and over 580 known to be exploited.

Users can search, filter, and receive alerts about vulnerabilities, while researchers and industry partners review entries and contribute new findings.

A Chinese national faces federal charges in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment scam.

A Chinese national has been extradited from the Netherlands to face federal charges in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment scam that defrauded at least 174 Americans of nearly $37 million.

Prosecutors say 44-year-old Zheng Zhao participated in an international fraud network operating partly from scam centers in Cambodia.

The scheme allegedly involved contacting victims through social media, dating sites, and text messages, building relationships, then persuading them to invest through fraudulent cryptocurrency platforms.

Investigators say the stolen money moved through American bank accounts to the Bahamas, where it was converted into Tether cryptocurrency and transferred to wallets controlled in Cambodia.

Eight alleged co-conspirators have already pleaded guilty.

Zhao faces a money laundering conspiracy charge carrying a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

Anthropic’s prospectus includes an existential disclaimer.

Anthropic is preparing to go public, and its pitch to investors comes with an unusual warning: the company’s products could potentially threaten human civilization.

In its 335-page IPO filing, Anthropic devotes 93 pages to potential risks, ranging from employee retention and computing costs to AI systems developing beyond human control.

The company warns that increasingly autonomous models could conduct cyberattacks, spread misinformation, help develop dangerous weapons, or take harmful actions without human intervention.

There’s also the possibility that AI development could outpace Anthropic’s ability to evaluate and safeguard its own technology.

And then there are more conventional business concerns, including expensive data centers, regulatory scrutiny, and dependence on major customers.

Anthropic argues that its commitment to AI safety makes it uniquely positioned to manage these dangers.

So, the investment proposition is essentially this: help us build extraordinarily powerful AI, and we’ll do our best to keep it from ending civilization.

Not your typical prospectus.

And that’s the CyberWire.
