Title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
Context: Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those...
Full Text:
Amaç Herdağdelen, Hailey Joren, Alex Tamkin

When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call.

We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper, we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded.

Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead.

Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed.

Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment.

We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. Real agents will sometimes lean one way or another—with no lean assigned, Claude Opus 4.8 made the same five choices in 112 out of 123 runs—but in this case we strengthened their preferences on purpose to measure their effect. When agents aren’t given clear preferences and instructions to voice them, the effect might be smaller.

This isn’t a simple cautionary tale against working with AI. Analysts who used the agent finished the task faster and made far fewer serious errors than those who chose to work without it, although the latter group was small and less experienced, so we are wary of reading too much into it. But as AI takes over more of the hands-on work, decisions like these are increasingly where human judgment and values will affect the result. If experts defer to agents without realizing it, the agents’ preferences—which could be arbitrary or misaligned—could shape important decisions about policy proposals or research directions without anyone having chosen those preferences. This is particularly important for research into keeping AI safe. Researchers have begun using agents to run and analyze experiments and a human reviewer is only an independent check if their judgment is their own.

Study design

We recruited 61 analysts for a randomized controlled trial. All came from a pre-screened pool of professionals who had passed a causal-inference knowledge check, used the programming languages Python or R regularly, and had hands-on experience with observational causal analysis, which means studying cause and effect using real-world data rather than a controlled experiment.

The task was set at a fictional organization, the Greenfields Farming Cooperative, which runs an (equally fictitious) voluntary, paid advisory program to help its member farms improve their crop yields. About 40% of members have enrolled. The co-op’s board must decide whether to subsidize and expand the program, or discontinue it. The board will expand the program only if it improves farms’ productivity by a set margin, roughly 3–4%, but it doesn’t say exactly how productivity should be measured.

We deliberately left four analytical decisions open, each with two reasonable options:

Outcome: measure productivity as crop yield per hectare, or as yield per unit of operating cost?

Comparison method: look at how enrolled farms’ yields changed after joining compared with how other farms’ yields changed over the same period (a “difference-in-differences” design), or compare yields directly while adjusting statistically for differences between the farms?

Which farms the assessment covers: measure the effect only in the enrolled farms, or across the cooperative’s entire membership?

Weighting: count every farm equally, or give larger producers more weight?

These four choices led into a final recommendation: whether to roll out the program to everyone, or to discontinue it. Analysts and agents could also propose a one-year extension.

Each of the analytical decisions could move the estimated productivity gain by several percentage points, which is important when the board’s threshold is 3–4%.

For each of the five decisions presented to each analyst, the agent’s lean was set by a coin flip. We gave the agent its leans in hidden instructions (a system prompt) that told it to hold each lean as its own view, to raise it when the decision came up, and to make the strongest case for it that the data allowed. The same instructions told it to change its mind if the evidence turned decisively against it, and never to misrepresent results, hide data, or make an argument the numbers didn’t support.

Out of 61 participants, 11 chose not to use the agent and are left out of the analysis unless noted. Among the remaining 50, 65% held a master’s or doctorate or had six or more years of experience, and 90% rated themselves proficient or expert in observational causal inference (of the 48 who answered the survey). The median time on the task was 65 minutes, and half of the analysts took between 50 and 79 minutes. They worked in a web-based version of the VS Code editor with Claude Code built in, running Claude Opus 4.8 at High effort.

When they finished, analysts submitted their four analytical choices and their final recommendation alongside an estimate of the program’s effect on productivity, with a confidence interval. They then completed a post-task survey. A separate AI model read each submission and its code to record which option the analyst had chosen on each decision. Where its reading disagreed with the analyst’s own survey answer, we made the final call.

Results

Analysts mostly went with their agents’ lean. On each of the four analytical decisions, analysts’ choices matched their agents’ lean the large majority of the time: 92% for the outcome measure, 82% for the comparison method, 81% for which farms the estimate covered, and 90% for weighting. Across all four combined, the result was 86%. Figure 2 shows how much the agents’ lean shifted analysts’ choices on each decision, including the final recommendation.

Agents’ lean had a weaker effect on the final recommendation, but its earlier input still shaped the result. When the agent leaned toward rolling out the program, 54% of analysts recommended it, compared with 36% when it leaned the other way. (A one-year extension counts as not rolling out.) We think the effect was weaker because, once the analysts had their estimate, the recommendation largely followed from whether it cleared the board’s 3–4% threshold, which left less room for judgment. But by then, an agent’s lean on the analytical decisions had already shaped the estimate itself. Using only those four leans, a statistical model correctly predicted 82% of the analysts’ recommendations, compared with 61% for always guessing the most common recommendation. (This excludes analysts who proposed an extension.) So we could largely predict what an analyst would recommend from the coin flips alone, before they had even started the task.

Analysts who had already picked an option often switched when their agent disagreed. In 38 cases, an analyst had expressed a preference on one of the analytical decisions before the agent expressed its lean. When the lean went against their choice, they switched 60% of the time, compared with 6% when it agreed with their choice. That’s a gap of 54 percentage points, but because this rests on only 38 cases, the estimate is imprecise, and the 95% confidence interval runs from 24 to 82 percentage points. We also can’t be sure that the difference is caused by the AI’s influence: the analysts who expressed a preference may have been systematically different in some way from those who didn’t.

Experience and expertise did not predict who deferred. In an exploratory analysis, we checked whether any of 10 characteristics predicted how often analysts’ decisions followed their agents’ lean: years of experience, self-rated expertise in causal inference, education, score on a causal-inference quiz, trust in AI, how often they used AI, “need for cognition” (a measure of how much people enjoy effortful thinking), open-mindedness, gender, and age. Only age showed a statistically significant link, with older analysts following the lean more often. But we don’t read very much into that: if you test many different things, you’re more likely to get one positive result just by chance, and when we adjusted for that the result disappeared. Because most analysts followed their agent on most decisions, there was little variation to explain anyway, so even real differences would have been hard to detect.

Analysts who followed their agent’s lean still called the recommendation their own. On the post-task survey, 52% of analysts rated the final recommendation as more their own than their agent’s. The rest said it was more the agent’s recommendation. But both groups were roughly equally influenced by their agents: the former’s choices shifted about 65 percentage points toward their agents’ lean, on average, compared to 79 percentage points for the latter, a difference within the margin of error. Analysts’ confidence in their own recommendation showed a similar pattern. They were asked to rate their confidence from 0 (“it’s a coin flip”) to 100 (“I’d stake my professional reputation on it”). Those who followed the lean on all four analytical decisions averaged 71, compared to 73 for the rest.

Analysts explained their choices in their agent’s words. After the task, the survey asked about each decision: “Briefly, why that choice rather than the alternative? If it wasn’t an active choice, just say so.” Analysts couldn’t look back at their conversations with the agent while answering. Even so, 77% repeated their agent’s argument in at least one answer, sometimes word for word, and only 15% credited the agent anywhere.

When explicitly asked what they thought the study was about, six of the 48 correctly guessed that it was about the AI’s influence on their choices, but none suspected that the AI’s own preferences had been manipulated.

Analysts who worked without AI made more serious errors and took longer. Of the 11 participants who chose not to use the agent, six (55%) made serious methodological errors that invalidated their results, compared with three of the 50 (6%) who did use it. Two AI models flagged the errors, and one of the study’s authors checked each one without knowing which group the analyst was in. The analysts who worked without an agent also took longer, with a median time of 90 minutes, compared to 65 for the others.

The two groups were not directly comparable, so we can’t be sure whether the different outcomes were caused by the decision to use or not use AI. Those who worked without AI were less experienced on average: fewer held a master’s degree or a doctorate (four out of 11, compared to 24 out of 46 who used the agent), more had two years or less in analysis roles (six out of 11, compared to 15 out of 48), and fewer rated themselves proficient or expert in causal inference (eight of 11, compared to 43 out of 48).

Our study’s limitations

We deliberately strengthened the agents’ lean. Our instructions made the agent hold and voice a preference reliably, so that we could measure its effect. The rates we report show what happens when an agent leans one way and says so, but how much that applies to real-world work will depend on how strong the expert’s own views are, how clearly the decisions involved are defined, and how the model behaves, including whether it has a preference and whether it volunteers it.

We studied one task, in one field, with one model. The task took about an hour, it was specifically about farming, and the agent ran on Claude Opus 4.8. The analysts were experts in causal inference but new to farming. In real work, they would know the field better, and probably have stronger views of their own. They could also interview relevant people, talk to the board, and in other ways narrow down the reasonable options, which might reduce the agent’s influence.

Our estimates are averages across analysts. Because the coin flips differed between analysts, comparing analysts whose agents leaned in opposite ways tells us the lean’s average effect. We didn’t record each participant’s own view before the agent voiced its lean, so we can’t say how much any single participant was influenced.

We recorded which option analysts chose, but not how strongly they preferred it. One possible explanation for deferring is that the expert didn’t have strong opinions of their own. We measured only whether analysts’ choices shifted, not how confident they were in their choice.

What this means

One reason analysts deferred so readily may be that experts don’t always arrive with their views fully formed. They often work out, or even discover, what they think while weighing the options. The agents in our study were told not to mislead, and they were often open about how the results would change under each option. But they rarely made a strong case for why an expert might prefer the other option, which might have helped analysts make a better-informed choice. With only one side argued well, the analysts could adopt the agent’s assumptions without working out their own.

For individual experts, this could mean losing agency over their own work, a form of what researchers call disempowerment. The work still goes out under the expert’s name, but the decisions that most depend on their judgment are in reality settled by the agent’s prior beliefs.

The stakes extend beyond individuals, though, because so much of science and policy rests on judgment calls like these. When separate research teams reach the same result, we trust it more, because we assume each team reached it independently. If those teams all defer to models with the same preferences, their agreement may no longer be independent. An apparent consensus might reflect one model’s preferences, and if those preferences are arbitrary or misaligned, the same bias would shape many results at once.

The same problem applies to AI safety research. Researchers have begun to use AI agents to run and analyze experiments, in part because there is more work than human staff can keep up with. Keeping a human in the loop assumes that the human’s judgment provides an independent check. But in our study, analysts signed off on work in which judgment calls had largely been settled by the agent’s randomly assigned preferences. Our full paper also shows that agents without an assigned lean have weaker preferences of their own, and sometimes push back against users.

Deferral of this kind is hard to detect. Checking AI-assisted work for errors, or against a reference answer, assumes there is a correct answer. But where there isn’t one, as in judgment calls, the work can look sound whichever option is chosen. Asking experts afterward may not help either, because they may not notice the agent’s influence.

This isn’t an argument for using AI less. Used well, AI could expand people’s agency rather than eroding it. We suggest three areas for future study:

Measuring deferral. We could measure deferral in our study because we randomized the agent’s lean, which is rarely possible in real work, and our results suggest that people may not be able to report it accurately themselves. We need ways to measure it in everyday settings, and recent work that estimates how someone would have carried out a task without AI is a good start. We also need a better picture of models’ default preferences and how they express them, so that people can engage with models in a more informed way.

Designing agents differently. Agents could make the best case for each option, or ask experts for their own view before offering one. But this could quickly become overwhelming for users. A single analysis can involve many open decisions, and much of the value of AI is that people don’t have to think through each one. Agents would need to raise only the decisions that matter most, but picking those is itself a judgment call. How a model speaks probably matters too, since confidence and fluency can sway people. A model that sounds very sure of itself might tilt people more than is warranted, but a mealy-mouthed model will just irritate the people who try to use it.

Changing institutions. Institutions often treat an expert’s sign-off as evidence of independent judgment. As AI does more of the work, that assumption becomes shakier. Organizations will need to decide deliberately which decisions need a person’s own informed judgment, and give people the time and resources to form one. Judgment also depends on skill, and people who stop making these decisions may lose the ability to make them. As models become more capable, institutions will need an explicit strategy for establishing the role of humans and the development of their skills. Even with extremely capable AI systems, institutions may want to protect human skills and oversight for reasons of safety or resilience, or because they value them for their own sake.

There may be no single right division of labor between people and AI. Some decisions may be fine to hand over, and others worth keeping. With the right tools, that split can be something we choose, instead of something we drift into.

Title: Using Codex for education at Dagster Labs
Context: Because our users come from varied technical backgrounds, we’ve found it essential to meet each persona at the right technical depth
Full Text:
At Dagster Labs, we produce a lot of technical educational content for data engineers, machine learning engineers, and analysts to better understand how to use Dagster, an open source workflow orchestration framework. Because our users come from varied technical backgrounds, we’ve found it essential to meet each persona at the right technical depth.

In this post, I’ll share how we use OpenAI’s Codex to accelerate documentation, translate content across mediums, and even measure how complete our docs are.

The power of CONTRIBUTING.md files

To make it easier for our community members and internal engineers to contribute documentation, we overhauled our CONTRIBUTING.md file. To our surprise, we had inadvertently significantly improved the utility of Codex. It turns out there is serious value in clearly outlining the hierarchy, structure, and best practices for writing documentation in your code base. Both for humans and robots.

# Contributing documentation ## Content ### Links #### Use full paths instead of relative links Docusaurus doesn't always render relative links correctly, which can result in users seeing intermittent 404s when accessing those links. Use full paths instead of relative links, like this: ``` For more information, see "[Defining assets](/guides/build/assets/defining-assets)". ``` instead of this: ``` For more information, see "[Defining assets](defining-assets)". ``` #### Use non-trailing slash links to Dagster docs e.g. use `/guides/build/assets/defining-assets` instead of `/guides/build/assets/defining-assets/`. **Context:** Links to Dagster docs with trailing slashes automatically redirect to non-trailing slash links. While that's helpful for docs links we don't control, too many redirects on our own pages can confuse search engines and cause SEO issues. ### API documentation ...

Codex is only as good as the scaffolding you give it. A well-structured CONTRIBUTING.md becomes both documentation for humans and a map for AI.

Codex for understanding

Beyond writing docs, Codex can act as an always-available code explainer. For developer advocates and technical writers, this has been invaluable. In open source projects, or projects with many engineers, it can often be difficult to stay up-to-date on all of the features being developed, and how they work. This is especially true for smaller teams of developer advocates and technical writers. We’ve found that some of the best assistance Codex provides is through explaining pull requests, or pointing it to a part of the codebase and asking for an explanation.

A tip we’ve found here is to leverage the gh command from within Codex to explain pull requests. Ask it to review the PR description and diff, summarize why the feature was implemented, and explain how it should be exposed to end users.

The power of the mono repo

This might be a controversial opinion, but I’m a big fan of mono repos. When context is key, having everything accessible in a single repository makes it so much easier to get access to what you need, and in the case of Codex, this means complete context: code, docs, and examples all in one place.

While some people have expressed concern about tools like Codex failing to scale with repositories, I’ve found this not to be the case. By making use of file references within Codex (@) you can give Codex the initial sub directory or file to start with before further exploration. And there are some serious benefits to having your framework code alongside your documentation in a single repository. This setup lets us prompt Codex to read framework code and draft initial documentation scaffolds that we can then refine.

Here’s an example where we prompted Codex to review an existing pull request, and add a section to the documentation on how exactly these environment variables are useful when configuring your deployment.

>_ You are using OpenAI Codex in ~/src/dagster To get started, describe a task or try one of these commands: /init - create an AGENTS.md file with instructions for Codex /status - show current session configuration and token usage /approvals - choose what Codex can do without approval /model - choose what model and reasoning effort to use ▌ Review the changes made in pull request 32557 using `gh pr diff <number>`, review the environment ▌ variables that were introduced and already exist for configuring the gRPC server, then update ▌ docs/docs/deployment/oss/oss-instance-configuration.md page to outline the configuration options. > I’ll fetch the diff for PR 32557 and scan for added/updated gRPC-related environment variables, then cross-check with existing env var usage in the repo. • Ran gh pr diff 32557 | sed -n '1,200p' • Ran gh pr diff 32557 | sed -n '200,400p' • Explored └ Search DAGSTER_GRPC_[A-Z_]+ in dagster Read api.py, code_server.py, oss-instance-configuration.md Search DAGSTER_CODE_SERVER_[A-Z_]+ Read constants.py Search DAGSTER_(REPOSITORY|SCHEDULE|SENSOR)_GRPC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS| DAGSTER_GRPC_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD in dagster Read proxy_server_manager.py > Next, I’ll expand the gRPC servers section of the instance configuration docs to include API gRPC server variables and communication timeouts/limits, keeping style consisten ...

You can find the pull request that was produced by this session at dagster-io/dagster # 32558.

Translating between content mediums

Different personas prefer different learning formats, but the underlying ideas are often the same. Because of that, we produce a variety of content mediums: blog posts, tutorials, online courses, YouTube videos, and more. The core content of these materials can often be the same, just presented differently depending on the target persona.

Codex works exceptionally well at translating between these mediums. For example, taking a tutorial and producing a transcript for a YouTube video. Or taking a low-level tutorial, and abstracting it slightly for a blog post. In the below screenshot you can find an example prompt used to take one of our example projects and produce a video transcript. This approach saves hours of rewriting while keeping our messaging consistent across channels.

>_ You are using OpenAI Codex in ~/src/dagster ▌Review the example project: examples/docs_projects/project_dagster_modal_pipes ▌and produce a video transcript to teach users the core Dagster and Modal concept ▌covered. Break the transcript into sections, and include code snippets to be ▌showcased in the video. The prose of the script should be fun but professional. ▌Save this to MODAL_VIDEO_TRANSCRIPT.md. > I’m going to scan the example project to understand its structure and code before drafting the video transcript. • Ran └ bash -lc 'ls -la' bash -lc 'ls -la examples/docs_projects/ project_dagster_modal_pipes' bash -lc "rg --files examples/docs_projects/ project_dagster_modal_pipes | sed -n '1,120p'" • Explored └ List project_dagster_modal_pipes Search rg --files examples/docs_projects/project_dagster_modal_pipes Read README.md, definitions.py, __init__.py, resources.py, constants.py, feeds.py, pipeline_factory.py, summarize.py, config.py, transcribe.py, hello_dagster.py, verify_cloud_mount.py • Added MODAL_VIDEO_TRANSCRIPT.md (+335 -0)

See the full video transcript here!

Evaluating documentation coverage

One of the more experimental ways we’re using Codex is as a proxy for human understanding.

By using documentation as the source-of-truth, and base context for Codex, we can have it generate code. For example, people often use Dagster for running and observing their dbt data models alongside other data processing code.

By prompting Codex to reference the documentation and produce the code for this project, we can then run a test suite on the resulting code to check that it operates as expected. If it works as expected we can assume that our documentation has adequate coverage of the required content. If Codex can generate working code purely from our documentation, it’s a strong signal that humans can as well which becomes an indirect measure of documentation completeness.

Summary

All in all, the Dagster team has found Codex to be immensely helpful for creating, reviewing, and translating education content. It has enabled us to scale beyond our original capacity, helped us ensure that we have adequate documentation coverage as the framework evolves, and more importantly, it has made it so that we can more easily support our community.

Codex has underscored how important context and structure are. For us, that means refining our documentation architecture so both humans and AI can navigate it easily. This feedback loop, powered by AI, has improved both how we create content and how users generate framework code. As AI tools evolve, the line between documentation, code, and automation will blur. Teams that treat documentation as structured data will have a major advantage.

Title: The breach wasn't in the model.
Context: An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update. Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on...
Full Text:
A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic. The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs. AI developers get a crash course in key management. A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges. Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers. Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes. Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals. Patching what matters…matters. Monday business briefing. Tim Starks from CyberScoop is discussing targeted ads as a security risk. Championship rings come with a catch.

Today is Monday October 26th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic.

Cybersecurity startup Cathedral says its researchers used AI agents to gain access to sensitive internal systems at Anthropic in less than twelve hours. According to The Washington Post, the researchers exploited vulnerabilities in third-party business software, accessing systems containing meeting transcripts, salary information, and internal Slack messages.

Anthropic confirmed the intrusion but said access was limited to certain sales, human resources, and IT systems. Customer conversations, proprietary code, and AI model weights were not exposed. The company says its monitoring detected some suspicious activity, and it disabled the affected systems and worked with vendors to address the vulnerabilities.

Cathedral, founded by former DOGE employees, conducted the research through Anthropic’s security testing program. Anthropic disputes the startup’s characterization of the national security implications and says researchers violated some program rules.

The findings highlight a familiar security problem with potentially higher stakes: even cutting-edge AI companies depend on ordinary enterprise software, with all its ordinary vulnerabilities.

The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs.

The Pentagon has quietly established a new agency dedicated to disrupting foreign military technology programs through covert operations.

According to POLITICO, the Technology Support Office, established in April, consolidates two classified intelligence programs and aims to expand capabilities including cyberattacks, supply-chain sabotage, and deception operations.

The agency reportedly employs engineers, intelligence officers, and special operations personnel to develop tools that could delay adversaries’ technological advances, particularly in artificial intelligence and advanced weapons systems.

Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg spearheaded the initiative, which has attracted opposition from Cyber Command and Special Operations Command over competing responsibilities and resources.

Supporters argue the effort is necessary to preserve America’s military advantage. Critics worry its secrecy could enable questionable operations and undermine congressional oversight.

The Pentagon disputes POLITICO’s reporting, calling its underlying claims inaccurate.

AI developers get a crash course in key management.

A supply-chain attack affecting tens of thousands of AI developers began with a security mistake made months earlier.

LiteLLM says it accidentally published a configuration file containing a master key in May. Although the file was removed, the key was never revoked. An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update.

Security firm Wiz says the malicious package was downloaded roughly 49,000 times. Within hours, attackers were testing stolen AWS credentials for access to AI models, suggesting a possible LLMjacking operation.

LiteLLM warns anyone who installed version 1.107.0 to assume their credentials were stolen and rotate them.

No organization has publicly confirmed a resulting breach. It’s LiteLLM’s second supply-chain compromise this year.

A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges.

A Florida businessman faces federal fraud charges for allegedly charging ransomware victims millions of dollars to recover their data while secretly paying the hackers responsible.

Prosecutors say Zohar Pinhasi, who operated the data recovery firm MonsterCloud, claimed he could decrypt files without paying ransoms. Instead, investigators allege he collected more than $19 million from clients while paying hackers over $8 million. In one case, an $8,200 ransom payment reportedly became a $150,000 customer bill.

The indictment follows a 2019 ProPublica investigation exposing the alleged scheme. MonsterCloud’s clients included law enforcement agencies that believed they were avoiding payments to criminals.

Pinhasi has pleaded not guilty and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

For victims already paying one extortionist, prosecutors allege MonsterCloud effectively added another.

Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers.

Dutch police have arrested two men accused of using AI-generated phone calls to steal more than $425,000 from 170 bank customers.

The scheme began with automated calls warning of suspicious account activity. Victims who pressed a button were connected to a fake bank employee, who instructed them to download an app and scan their debit cards.

The app captured contactless payment data, which accomplices used to withdraw cash from ATMs.

The suspects, ages 23 and 25, were arrested October 6. Police also seized servers, phones, and laptops.

Both remain in custody as the investigation continues.

Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes.

Four months after European law enforcement disrupted the StealC malware operation, its seller is back with a new product.

Researchers at Varonis say Stadia RAT builds on StealC’s credential-stealing capabilities, adding remote desktop control, command execution, file management, and the ability to deploy additional malware.

The Windows malware targets browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and messaging applications. It also avoids systems configured for several Eastern European and Central Asian languages, establishes persistence through scheduled tasks, and can disable portions of Microsoft Defender’s protection.

Subscriptions range from $300 to $900 a month, with former StealC customers offered a free trial.

Researchers confirmed that Stadia reuses code from StealC, illustrating a familiar limitation of law enforcement takedowns: dismantling criminal infrastructure doesn’t necessarily put its operators out of business.

Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals.

Researchers at Korea University have demonstrated a technique for extracting sensitive information from air-gapped computers using USB power-management signals.

Called SPECTER, the method allows malware with administrator privileges to encode data through changes in USB device states, without conventional network connections or USB data transfers.

Researchers demonstrated three ways to receive the signals: monitoring smartphone charging indicators, observing changes in USB peripherals, and detecting electromagnetic emissions from USB cables.

Transmission speeds were extremely slow, topping out at one bit per second, making the technique more suitable for stealing passwords or cryptographic keys than large files.

The attack also requires hardware or firmware modifications, and some configurations produced no usable signals.

Researchers suggest monitoring unusual USB power-management activity, although the effectiveness of that approach remains untested.

Patching what matters…matters.

Security teams are patching more vulnerabilities than ever, but new research suggests all that effort isn’t necessarily making organizations safer.

According to Qualys, vulnerability closures increased sixfold between 2022 and 2025, reaching 473 million. Yet the percentage of critical vulnerabilities remaining unpatched after seven days actually increased.

The problem? Prioritization.

Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on severity scores rather than evidence of real-world attacks.

Meanwhile, attackers are moving faster. Across the most critical exploited vulnerabilities, manual remediation failed to keep pace 88 percent of the time.

Qualys recommends shifting toward intelligence-driven, automated remediation that prioritizes actual exploitation and business impact.

The takeaway: Security isn’t necessarily about patching more. It’s about patching what matters.

Monday business briefing.

Investment and acquisition activity remains brisk across cybersecurity, with AI security attracting particular attention.

San Francisco-based Reach Security raised $50 million in Series B funding to expand its exposure management platform. AI agent security startup Opsin secured $21 million, while Asymptote Labs raised $5.5 million for its AI runtime security technology. AI penetration testing firm ManticoreAI also announced an undisclosed seed round.

On the acquisition front, Proofpoint agreed to buy data and AI security company Varonis for $6.3 billion, potentially creating a combined business serving more than 16,000 enterprises.

Anthropic acquired confidential AI data specialist OPAQUE, while Canadian AI company Cohere agreed to purchase Czech vulnerability management provider AISLE.

Elsewhere, legal technology firm Lineal acquired Swiss digital forensics company Forentec, and Britain’s Bytes Technology Group purchased Microsoft security specialist CyberOne.

The common thread across these deals is growing investment in AI security, data protection, and automated vulnerability management.

Championship rings come with a catch.

The New York Knicks celebrated their first NBA championship in more than half a century by offering employees free championship rings. Unfortunately, the offer was fake, and the real prize was mandatory cybersecurity training.

According to The New York Times, Madison Square Garden sent employees a simulated phishing email inviting them to choose between two ring designs. Anyone who clicked the link earned a trip to cybersecurity class instead.

The exercise followed a real security incident in which attackers reportedly used phished employee credentials to hack and extort the organization.

MSG acknowledged that using championship rings as bait was an unfortunate mistake. The company says it’s distributing more than 275 actual rings and pieces of jewelry worth over $3.7 million.

For employees who fell for the phishing test, the championship celebration apparently came with a refresher course in disappointment.

Title: Gheist Attackers Stumble in Attempt to Abuse GitHub Tokens
Context: A recent campaign targeting GitHub repositories has been disrupted after attackers were found planting secret-stealing workflows across more than 13,500 branches across...
Full Text:
A recent campaign targeting GitHub repositories has been disrupted after attackers were found planting secret-stealing workflows across more than 13,500 branches across repositories using stolen access tokens.

In research published October 25, Wiz said it had tracked the campaign, dubbed Gheist, since September 15 and recovered the branches from more than 850 compromised accounts. The operation targeted every repository the stolen tokens could reach, from personal projects to private enterprise repositories.

Wiz identified infostealer logs and earlier supply chain compromises, such as the March compromise of the Trivy security scanner, as sources of the stolen tokens. Some of the accounts were also being used for malware distribution and cryptomining.

Workflow Trick Meets GitHub Approval Hold

The attackers used the tokens to create branches and commit a GitHub Actions workflow that printed repository secrets into its own log. They then downloaded the log through GitHub's application programming interface (API) and deleted the run seconds later, so the campaign needed no external command-and-control (C2) server.

The campaign's main obstacle has been a GitHub control introduced July 28 that places potentially malicious workflow runs in public repositories on hold until a collaborator approves them. Wiz said every public Gheist run it examined, across all variants, remained in an action_required state, preventing the malicious workflows from executing.

The protection does not extend to private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server. In those environments, Wiz observed workflows completing on attacker-created branches before the runs were removed.

Read more on stolen supply chain secrets: TeamPCP Explores Ways to Exploit Stolen Supply Chain Secrets

Private Repositories Remain Exposed

In enterprise organizations, Wiz observed the attackers cycling through user and automation account tokens and cloning private repositories. Hours later, cloud credentials from the same organizations were used to enumerate Amazon Web Services' Secrets Manager.

Two variants of the tool ran in parallel. One added support for deployment environments, exposing environment-scoped secrets that are often production credentials. It later gained a job that searched self-hosted runners for credentials and other sensitive files, though Wiz described the job as "buggy."

As of October 24, roughly two-thirds of implicated accounts were no longer available on GitHub, which Wiz said likely reflected response activity after it reported the campaign to GitHub. However, the researchers said Gheist remained ongoing and continued to evolve.

The campaign demonstrates how stolen GitHub tokens can turn legitimate automation features into a credential theft mechanism, while newer platform controls can disrupt some abuse without eliminating the underlying risk from compromised credentials.

Title: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A working exploit for a Linux kernel flaw has been made public before the bug received a CVE identifier or a merged upstream fix.

Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent that report and five others to maintainers and public mailing lists on October 20 and 21, according to analysis published by the Sysdig Threat Research Team on October 24.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported when Sysdig published its analysis, but several flaws still had no fix in any released kernel.

Public Disclosure Creates Patch Gap

ZDI-CAN-33367, the flaw with the public exploit, is a local privilege escalation (LPE) bug in the Linux networking stack that ZDI gave a CVSS score of 7.8. It can allow an unprivileged user to alter the in-memory contents of files they can only read.

It sits in a code path the kernel's fix for the earlier Dirty Frag page-cache flaws missed. Linux support provider TuxCare reproduced a root shell with the public proof of concept (PoC) on AlmaLinux 8 through 10, CloudLinux 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Sysdig said.

Two of the other five, ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, are the highest rated, at 9.0, and affect ksmbd, the kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) server. The first is a remote, pre-authentication flaw that can leak kernel memory and crash systems, while the second requires SMB Direct, a Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) interface and a writable share.

Read more: Rushed Patches Follow Broken Embargo on New Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

Exposure Varies Across Linux Systems

Of the remaining three, ZDI-CAN-34068 is an LPE rated 8.8 in the kernel's VMware graphics driver. Sysdig said there was no patch and only the report's title was public.

The last two are ZDI-CAN-34076, an information leak in the kernel's Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target, and ZDI-CAN-32005, a userspace stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager.

Sysdig said defenders should prioritize by the components they run rather than CVSS scores. It advised unloading ksmbd where it is not needed, restricting port 445 to trusted networks where it must stay and watching for a vmwgfx patch on VMware guests.

For ZDI-CAN-33367, Sysdig said restricting unprivileged user namespaces should block the public PoC, though TuxCare had not validated this, and noted that rootless containers depend on them. AlmaLinux had patched kernels in testing, but not production, by October 23.

The disclosure leaves a fragmented patching picture, but the public root exploit makes ZDI-CAN-33367 the most immediate concern of the six.

Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Microsoft has released out-of-bound (OOB) security updates for its .NET developer platform, which includes a fix for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability.

The tech giant published the updates for .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 Release Candidate 3 on October 25. Platform users have been urged to apply the updates as soon as possible to reduce the risk of compromise.

They contain patches for two newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as well as two flaws that were not fully addressed in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday rollout.

Single updates are available for each of the affected .NET versions and .NET 11 RC2 users should update to RC3 to receive these fixes.

.NET is a free, open-source framework that developers can use to build apps and cloud services. It is managed by Microsoft and is supported on Windows, Linux and macOS operating systems.

Updates Address Critical Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

One of the new vulnerabilities addressed is CVE-2026-111497, which affects .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 across all operating systems.

The vulnerability is contained in the Brotli decompression algorithm, which is used by .NET. It can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory, leading to information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege.

Microsoft said that applications may be affected if they process Brotli-compressed data through ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient automatic response decompression or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs.

The flaw has a critical CVSS Score of 9.2. Users of Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 also need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries to the latest available version.

Brotli was designed by two engineers at Google in 2015 to allow developers to speed up algorithm compression for developers.

Microsoft’s OOB update also addresses CVE-2026-114148, which can allow an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally by exploiting unsafe ownership metadata in affected .NET tarballs.

CVE-2026-114148 affects .NET versions 7-11, but only for Linux systems. For .NET 10 and .NET 11, CVE-2026-114148 affects source-build tarballs only. For .NET 8 and .NET 9, it also affects ASP.NET Core distributions obtained through ASP.NET Core tarballs, including users who do not build .NET from source, the advisory noted.

It has not been assigned a CVSS score at the time of writing but has been reserved by a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA).

In addition, Microsoft has re-issued fixes for two vulnerabilities disclosed in its October 13 Patch Tuesday rollout. These are for CVE-2026-70197, a memory corruption flaw affecting .NET versions 8-11, and CVE-2026-102870, a code injection vulnerability affecting .NET 10 and 11.

Remediation Guidance for Developers

Microsoft issued advice for .NET users on how to update their applications and build environments in light of the updates. These include:

Install the updated runtime for the .NET version for your framework-dependent application, then restart the application

Rebuild and republish self-contained applications with the updated runtime

Rebuild and redeploy containers using updated .NET container images

Obtain the updated source-build artifacts for your .NET version and rebuild your packages to incorporate the tarball ownership fix

For ASP.NET Core tarball users on .NET 8 and 9, update your installation using the refreshed ASP.NET Core Runtime tarball for your .NET version

An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

Full Text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

Title: Code security for new coders
Context: There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when
Full Text:
Coding agents enable anyone to turn their ideas into reality. However, building with security in mind is imperative to keep your application secure. There’s a lot of reference information about application security out there, but it often is jargon-heavy and targets developers or security professionals, not vibe coders. There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when. This post breaks down essential security terms and tools so that you can build safely from the start.

If you aren’t sold on the importance of application security or think it only matters to large companies, consider the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October 2026. These two vulnerabilities affect PHP, a programming language used by more than 70% of websites. They could allow an attacker to take control of a website’s server. The vulnerabilities are so serious that some organizations temporarily took services offline while installing security updates.

What is code security?

In simple terms, code security is the practice of writing secure code. Because application security starts with code security, taking a proactive approach early prevents major vulnerabilities later.

There are two main things we need to be concerned with when thinking about code security: the code you (or your agent) is writing (i.e., first-party code), and the code that is written by someone else but being used by your application (i.e., third-party code). With first party code, you are directly responsible for fixing the problem. Third-party code is treated differently because you are not the one who can fix the code, but you are responsible for using a version that does not have vulnerabilities. We often refer to third-party code as being part of the software supply chain, but more on that later.

What is first-party code?

First-party code is the code that you are producing and are thus responsible for. While being responsible for maintaining secure code might seem intimidating, you can most likely fix security issues by prompting the agent to fix them. There are automated security scans you can run to discover vulnerabilities, or you can simply ask the agent to do a security check. Checking for OWASP top ten vulnerabilities is always a good place to start.

What are secrets?

One of the simplest, yet most impactful ways to improve security is to avoid hardcoding secrets. This means that you should never write in the code any password, token, key, or any secret or credential that can be used to gain access to your resources. Instead, you can use environment variables that act as a placeholder that point to a specific hidden configuration file or a secret manager.

What is the software supply chain?

The software supply chain refers to everything that is used to develop and run an application, including dependencies, tools, and infrastructure. There are also open source code components used in the software supply chain, such as GitHub actions and Docker images, which can help you deploy and run your code. Of all these elements, third-party dependencies are usually the main focus in discussions about code security.

Now you might be thinking, why do I need to use third-party code? Technically you don’t, but it makes writing code much easier, whether it’s done by you or an agent. By relying on these open-source dependencies, you are using code that was already written by someone else and that is shared with the community to solve a problem. What’s important to understand in the context of AI-generated code is that coding agents use dependencies by default, often relying heavily on outdated versions.

Dependencies rely on other dependencies, so the risk starts to grow as you start to use them. There are two things in particular you need to be concerned about with third-party dependencies: vulnerabilities and malicious packages. Vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies are accidental code issues that usually require upgrading to the latest version once the issue is fixed. Malicious packages represent a more intentional threat and are becoming more common. With these packages, someone has purposefully added a malicious script in the version and released it for personal gain.

Overall, the concern with using third-party code is that dependencies can quickly accumulate vulnerabilities if the maintainer doesn’t have the time to address these security flaws.

Security questions to ask your coding agent

The cool thing about vibe coding is that you can ask the agent any questions you may have. The difficulty can be knowing exactly what to ask. Below is a list of good places to start, but it is not exhaustive.

Setup questions

These are the types of questions that should be asked before any code is written. The goal is to have some security requirements planned out so an agent has a path to follow.

What sensitive data will this app handle (passwords, payment info, personal data, API keys), and how should each type be protected?

What authentication and authorization approach fits this app, and what are the tradeoffs?

Follow-up questions

After the code is written, you should make sure the agent made the best decisions for security. Ask questions that make the agent explain why certain security decisions were made. This will force the agent to go back through the code, which might lead it to suggest a change.

Can you do a security review on the application? Are there any concerns?

Do any OWASP top 10 vulnerabilities exist in this code?

What security tradeoffs did you make to keep this simple, and what would you fix before real users touch this?

If you were a penetration tester, what's the first thing you'd try to break in this app?

What third-party packages did you use? Are any of them outdated? Do any have known vulnerabilities?

Does any of this code contain hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens? If so, where, and how do I move them to environment variables or to a secrets manager?

Are default credentials or debug modes left enabled anywhere?

Is there a .env or config file here, and is it excluded from version control (.gitignore)?

Are there any insecure coding patterns or logic flaws present?

Is there anything concerning about the current authentication and access controls configuration?

Are cloud storage buckets, databases, or admin panels publicly accessible when they shouldn't be?

If this is deployed, what's exposed to the internet that doesn't need to be?

What are the different types of code security tools?

Security tools come in all shapes and sizes. While many tools are paid, there are also open source tools that function similarly. The list below includes the most common types of tools.

Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

Tools of this type scan all the open-source dependencies that are being used in the application and alert you if there are any vulnerabilities. Most providers will also tell you what version you can upgrade to in order to eliminate that vulnerability.

Static Application Security Testing (SAST)

This type of tool is focused on looking at your first-party code for vulnerabilities. Most commonly, these tools scan the written code without running that code. They are good for early detection while you are actively coding but can provide more false positives than other tools do.

Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)

Tools in this category look at how data is flowing into a running application to find code vulnerabilities. Since they require a running application, they are generally used later in the software delivery life cycle compared to SAST tools. However, they also tend to be more accurate.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)

Tools that perform this type of security scan run pre-configured automated tests against a running application. They are not interchangeable with SAST or IAST tools.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Scanning

Tools that use this type of scanning are focused on looking at any IaC files for risky settings and misconfigurations.

Secret Scanning

Secret scanners search your codebase for hardcoded credentials, API keys, and passwords.

How Datadog can help

Security scans are a great way to understand what is happening in your code. Datadog Code Security has many types of tools you can use to gain visibility into your application, including SCA, SAST, IAST, IaC, and Secret scanning tools.

Datadog also has two open source tools that can be used for supply chain security: GuardDog to flag malicious packages and Supply Chain Firewall to block malicious packages from being installed.

Conclusion

The good news is that you do not need to become a security expert before bringing an idea to life. Start with a few basics: keep secrets out of your code, scan both first-party and third-party code, update your dependencies, and ask your coding agent to check for common vulnerabilities.

The goal is not to build a perfectly secure application on your first try. It is to understand what your application uses, recognize the risks, and make security part of how you build from the start. Addressing issues along the way is much easier than responding after your application or its users have been put at risk.

Title: Speech models in Ollama
Context: The first speech model is Phonon, a family of small, state-of-the-art text-to-speech models from Gradium
Full Text:
Ollama can now turn text into speech. The first speech model is Phonon, a family of small, state-of-the-art text-to-speech models from Gradium. Speech models are now available for macOS, with Windows and Linux support coming soon.

ollama run phonon "Hello from Ollama."

Unedited output from Ollama 0.40.11 on a MacBook Pro with M5 Max.

Performance on Apple Silicon

On Apple Silicon, Ollama is accelerated by MLX, Apple’s machine learning framework, for state-of-the-art throughput. On a MacBook Pro with M5 Max, Ollama was 35% faster than the next fastest engine, Gradium’s own runtime.

Throughput

Times faster than real time

Measured on a MacBook Pro with M5 Max, generating 45 seconds of speech. Median of 10 runs. Gradium's own runtime, ptts, uses 8-bit weights on the CPU, fp16 on the Neural Engine and f32 on the GPU; Ollama runs the model in bf16.

Ollama’s implementation is just as accurate, matching the word error rate of the reference implementation in Hugging Face Transformers:

Accuracy

Word error rate

Lower is better. 200 sentences from the Seed-TTS English test set, transcribed with Whisper large-v3.

Voices

Choose a voice with --voice, or voice in the API:

ollama run phonon --voice Hadley "Hello from Ollama."

The voices come from Gradium’s voice catalog. ollama show phonon lists them all.

Languages

Model

Language

phonon

English

phonon:40m-fr

French

phonon:40m-de

German

phonon:40m-es

Spanish

phonon:40m-pt

Portuguese

phonon:40m-multilingual

All five

phonon is released under Apache 2.0. The 40M models are released under CC BY-NC 4.0, which limits them to noncommercial use.

Read replies aloud

Pipe a chat model’s reply into Phonon. Text is spoken as it arrives, so the reply starts playing after its first sentence:

ollama run gemma4 --hidethinking "Tell me a fun fact about owls in two sentences." | ollama run phonon

Run ollama run phonon with no text to type lines at a prompt, or redirect the output to save a WAV file:

ollama run phonon "Save this to a file." > speech.wav

API

Phonon works with the OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech endpoint, so existing code that uses the OpenAI SDK only needs a new base URL.

curl http://localhost:11434/v1/audio/speech \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "phonon", "voice": "Zoey", "input": "Hello from Ollama." }' --output speech.wav

from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama") with client.audio.speech.with_streaming_response.create( model="phonon", voice="Zoey", input="Hello from Ollama.", response_format="wav", ) as response: response.stream_to_file("speech.wav")

import fs from "node:fs" import OpenAI from "openai" const openai = new OpenAI({ baseURL: "http://localhost:11434/v1", apiKey: "ollama" }) const response = await openai.audio.speech.create({ model: "phonon", voice: "Zoey", input: "Hello from Ollama.", response_format: "wav", }) fs.writeFileSync("speech.wav", Buffer.from(await response.arrayBuffer()))

The response streams while the audio is generated, so it can play right away:

curl -sN http://localhost:11434/v1/audio/speech \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "phonon", "input": "Playback starts right away."}' \ | ffplay -nodisp -autoexit -loglevel error -

Audio is 24 kHz mono, returned as WAV by default or as raw 16-bit samples with "response_format": "pcm".

Title: The apps are only the beginning.
Context: Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.
Full Text:
Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. Railway confirms a cyberattack. HPE patches critical ArubaOS flaws. Quest Diagnostics investigates a disruptive intrusion. Capcom reports a data breach. China-linked hackers put AI-powered attacks on autopilot. And researchers uncover a Microsoft 365 campaign that hijacks authentication tokens to bypass MFA. Our guest is Anudeep Parhar, COO at Entrust, sharing his thoughts on AI kill switches. eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

Today is Friday, October 23rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Attackers ramp up attempts to exploit critical PHP vulnerabilities.

Attackers are ramping up attempts to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell, but researchers have yet to confirm a successful compromise in the wild.

The flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution and prompted emergency patches on October 21. Sophos identified attempts to deploy Potassium, a Mirai botnet variant, although the attack it examined was unsuccessful.

Researchers say exploitation is proving more difficult than initially feared, largely because successful attacks require specific server configurations or ways around memory protections.

VulnCheck has developed an exploit that bypasses one such protection, while an exposed attacker server revealed custom exploitation tools and unsuccessful attempts against dozens of targets.

Meanwhile, patching remains a challenge. Qualys estimates roughly 110 million PHP instances run unsupported versions that won’t receive fixes.

Security researchers have identified 426 mobile apps connecting to servers running PHP versions potentially affected by the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.

NowSecure analyzed more than 15,000 Android and iOS apps, finding that 170 connected to servers running outdated PHP versions that no longer receive official security updates.

The vulnerabilities affect backend servers, not the mobile apps themselves, and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication.

Importantly, researchers caution that identifying a potentially vulnerable PHP version doesn’t establish whether a server remains unpatched or exploitable.

The findings also highlight the risks of third-party dependencies. One advertising provider’s server was contacted by 151 different apps.

NowSecure recommends developers work with their infrastructure providers to verify patching, upgrade unsupported PHP installations, and investigate potential exploitation.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI and PHP.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs says artificial intelligence is fueling an unprecedented surge in software vulnerability discoveries, creating what some are calling “Black October” for cybersecurity.

Appearing on CNBC, Krebs said AI-powered tools are uncovering security flaws at a pace that threatens to overwhelm organizations’ ability to patch them.

He pointed to the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities as an example. While attackers have attempted exploitation, Krebs said no successful compromises have been confirmed.

His biggest concern isn’t necessarily large enterprises, which generally have the resources to respond quickly. It’s smaller businesses, rural hospitals, utilities, and managed service providers that lack dedicated security teams.

Krebs warned that vulnerabilities in third-party services could expose entire networks, while legacy systems can complicate patching.

He expects the situation to get worse before it improves, as AI continues uncovering vulnerabilities faster than organizations can address them.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack that may have exposed customer passwords, API keys, and other secrets stored in encrypted environment variables. The company believes the breach affected a subset of customers but is urging all users to revoke and rotate their credentials as a precaution. Railway temporarily suspended new builds and deployments while investigating. The number of affected customers, the attack’s root cause, and the systems compromised remain unknown.

Railway suspects the incident is part of a broader campaign targeting AI inference providers. Earlier this week, AI coding tool OpenCode reported a similar attack that exposed credentials belonging to more than one percent of its customers. Railway says it plans to publish a detailed post-mortem.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise patches critical vulnerabilities in ArubaOS.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise has released security updates addressing 72 vulnerabilities in ArubaOS, including eight maximum-severity flaws that could allow attackers to bypass authentication or remotely execute malicious code.

The vulnerabilities affect multiple versions of ArubaOS 8 and 10, which power enterprise wireless networking equipment, including access points, controllers, and gateways. All eight maximum-severity flaws can be exploited remotely without authentication, using relatively simple attacks that require no user interaction.

HPE is strongly urging customers to install the patches, citing the number and potential impact of the vulnerabilities. The company also recommends restricting access to management interfaces through network segmentation and firewall controls.

So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a disruptive cyberattack.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a cyberattack that may have exposed patient information and disrupted access to medical test results.

The company discovered unauthorized access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform, which healthcare providers use to order tests and retrieve results. Quest took the system offline Thursday and temporarily paused several other systems as a precaution.

The company believes some patient data was accessed but hasn’t determined what information was compromised. Quest says its other operations weren’t affected and is working with law enforcement.

Healthcare providers can use paper requisitions while the system is unavailable. Quest expects to restore service Friday.

The company says the attack is unrelated to recently disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. No threat actor has claimed responsibility.

Capcom discloses a data breach.

Japanese gaming giant Capcom has disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 11.8 million records associated with its CAPCOM ID service.

The compromised information includes email addresses, account identifiers, and login activity. Attackers also changed passwords on 196 accounts, which Capcom has since reset.

The company says it has no evidence that customers’ original passwords were compromised, and credit card information remains unaffected.

Capcom has contained the unauthorized access and notified Japanese authorities. Customers are being warned to watch for phishing attempts impersonating the company.

Megaman, please call your office.

A China-linked threat actor is using Artex to automate cyberattacks.

Microsoft says a China-linked threat actor is using an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Artex to automate cyberattacks against hundreds of organizations.

The group, tracked as Storm-0940, used the tool in an October campaign targeting ConnectWise customers, accelerating reconnaissance, password spraying, and abuse of OAuth applications.

Microsoft observed more than 151,000 failed login attempts, along with successful authentication using compromised ConnectWise application identities.

The attackers attempted to access more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, sometimes progressing beyond authentication to modify credentials, manipulate directory settings, and establish persistent access.

In one burst of activity, the group targeted more than 300 accounts across eight organizations at over 2,900 attempts per minute.

Microsoft says the campaign illustrates how AI-assisted automation can dramatically accelerate established attack techniques, giving defenders less time to respond.

Researchers uncover a campaign that compromises Microsoft 365 accounts by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Security researchers at Huntress have uncovered a ten-week campaign that compromised Microsoft 365 accounts at 79 organizations by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Attackers used adversary-in-the-middle phishing and other techniques to capture legitimate login sessions, allowing them to bypass multifactor authentication without needing victims’ passwords.

Huntress observed at least 497 successful sign-ins alongside more than 200,000 failed attempts. Once inside, attackers registered 48 rogue devices, replaced victims’ authentication methods, and created hidden inbox rules to conceal suspicious communications.

In one case, a compromised account was used to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact.

The attacks relied partly on infrastructure belonging to a German hosting provider.

Huntress recommends properly configured Conditional Access policies and warns that password resets alone won’t eliminate persistent access. Organizations must also revoke sessions and remove unauthorized devices and authentication methods.

eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

From our “you can’t fire me, I quit!” desk, Indian digital trust company eMudhra is getting out of the global SSL/TLS certificate business following a security incident that attracted considerable scrutiny.

The company says it revoked the affected certificate authorities within 14 hours, with no infrastructure compromise, data breach, or affected customer certificates issued.

But eMudhra’s chairman says the resulting social media attention was disproportionate, particularly for a business representing just one percent of company revenue.

Add rising compliance costs and competition from free certificates, and the board decided it was time to pursue other opportunities.

eMudhra promises a smooth transition, including free replacement certificates for affected customers.

Its other digital trust services remain unaffected.

And so, after careful consideration, eMudhra has decided that SSL certificates just aren’t its thing anymore.
