Full Text: Title: Edimax BR-6478AC firmware v2.20 - authenticated command injection Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware CVE: pending Description: Edimax BR-6478AC firmware image BR6478AC_v2.20.bin, the closed-source dual-band AC1750 SOHO wireless router from Edimax Technology Co., Ltd. (Taiwan), whose SquashFS root filesystem of roughly 2.3 MB targets MIPS 32-bit big-endian MIPS-I with a uClibc C library and carries an internal build timestamp from 2015, contains an OS command injection (CWE-78) in the WAN-configuration form handler of bin/webs, the embedded GoAhead-style HTTP server serving the management interface on TCP port 80. That binary is ELF 32-bit MSB MIPS, 762904 bytes, SHA256 ec39c0f9332361e37ab92f1999ac5f00f5742dd6db75f7cb26c0652cfedb32a1, reads etc/boa/boa.conf, writes /var/run/webs.pid and is kept alive by the boot path cleanlog.sh:131 invoked from init.sh:1115. The registration websFormDefine("setWAN", ...) at 0x478484, handler at 0x441cec, name string at 0x4a6250, publishes POST /goform/setWAN. Inside the handler the WAN mode is taken from the request and dispatched: websGetVar(wp, "wanMode", "") at 0x441d3c, atoi at 0x441d44, apmib_set(0x102, &wanMode) at 0x441d54, then addiu v1, zero, 2 at 0x441d60 and beq v0, v1, 0x441e74 at 0x441d6c. On the PPP branch, wanMode 2, the username field is read by websGetVar for pppUserName, name string at 0x4953f4, copied with strcpy at 0x441e94 into a fixed stack buffer, measured with strlen at 0x441ea8 and then scanned by an inline byte loop between 0x441ebc and 0x441ee4 whose only comparison is addiu a0, zero, 0x3b, a semicolon; finding one, the loop writes a NUL and stops. That single-character scan is the entire sanitisation on the path. The value is then formatted by sprintf at 0x441ee8 with the format string at 0x49a510, echo %s > /tmp/UserName, and passed to system(buf2) at 0x441f1c through the PLT slot at 0x4c6d60, which hands the line to /bin/sh -c. A pipe, an ampersand, a backtick, a dollar sign with parentheses and an embedded newline are never inspected, so a username containing no semicolon reaches the shell untouched: the payload |id > /tmp/marker # builds the command line "echo |id > /tmp/marker # > /tmp/UserName", in which the shell treats the hash as a comment swallowing the sink's own redirect and runs id as the right-hand side of a pipeline. An escape loop replacing a hash with a backslash-escaped hash does exist between 0x441f4c and 0x441fb0, but the instruction order places it after system() at 0x441f1c with no branch back to it, and it writes the configuration buffer at sp+0x18 that apmib_set(0x6d, ...) stores at 0x44200c rather than the buffer handed to the shell, so the hash character is escaped for storage and for nowhere near execution. Between websGetVar and system there is no regex call, no inet_aton, no isdigit, no isalnum, no strchr, no strcspn, no vendor validation helper and no custom validator; the inet_aton calls that do exist in the function, at 0x441dd0 and 0x441e14, belong to the static-IP branch, wanMode 1, reached via the branch at 0x441d8c, which the wanMode 2 comparison never enters, so a quick read of the decompilation misleads a reviewer into thinking this function validates addresses. The same construction appears three times in this handler and one root cause yields three reachable parameters: pppUserName on wanMode 2 with sink region 0x441e74 to 0x441f1c and configuration object 0x6d written after the sink, pptpUserName on wanMode 3 from 0x4420d0 onward with configuration object 0xf3, and L2TPUserName on wanMode 6 from 0x44246c onward with configuration object 0x128, each selected by a value the request supplies and each using the same immediate-0x3b scan, the same echo format string and the same system() call shape, so a patch confined to the PPP path leaves the PPTP and L2TP paths injectable. Reaching the handler requires a valid administrative session: the gate auth_authorize at 0x404d00 reads configuration object 0x1bc, the setup-wizard flag, through apmib_get, and once past setup the security store at 0x4c7004, a single / entry of type Basic registered from the directive Auth / /etc/boa/boa.passwd, covers every /goform/ path with HTTP Basic authentication. The product has no second lower-privileged role, so Privileges Required is High: one realm entry, one password file, one account, an Allow directive handler at 0x407688 that is a stub answering "This version of Boa doesn't support access controls", a type-None string at 0x49070c never passed to auth_add, and a shipped configuration carrying one Auth directive and no Allow directive. The route is not one of the four carrying a post-boot uptime gate, /mp.asp, /goform/mp, /advanced_management.asp and /goform/formAdvManagement, which redirect to /index.asp once /proc/uptime exceeds 600 seconds, so it is reachable at any time the device is up. The calling process is root because etc/boa/boa.conf declares User root, the server performs no setuid, chroot, namespace or capability drop and writes /var/run/webs.pid, which requires root on this filesystem, so the landing identity is uid=0(root) with no escalation step in the chain. This handler is one instance of a broad construction: a count of the shipped registration table found 91 /goform/form* handlers of which roughly 85 reach a system() or popen() call. Two adjacent observations are reported without a score: the strcpy at 0x441e94 copies attacker-controlled bytes with no length argument into a fixed stack buffer, for which no overflow was developed and no exploitability claim is made, and because the semicolon scan writes a NUL at the first semicolon a legitimate username containing one is silently truncated before storage, a correctness defect independent of the injection. The firmware image ships a populated /etc/boa/boa.passwd for the single realm and the model's published factory login is admin:1234; that is reported separately as CWE-798, carries no score, is never described as the vector for this injection, and no cryptographic match against the shipped MD5-crypt digest is claimed because the digest string captured during analysis was recorded incompletely. One detail is left unresolved rather than smoothed over: the single account entry in the image is recorded under the name root while the model's published management login is admin, and because no device was ever authenticated against, which user name the realm accepts was not established. Absence of privilege separation is likewise reported separately as CWE-250. A static comparison against a second firmware image, BR-6208AC_V2_1.03, whose webs is a different build, ELF 32-bit MSB MIPS-I, 816568 bytes, SHA256 3ad10a41d11c8cd59185eab6c9ce67b18cd2118942eb2201f48540d7846a0328, found a setWAN implementation matching instruction for instruction, handler at 0x448710, websGetVar for pppUserName at 0x4488b8, strcpy at 0x4488bc, the same inline immediate-0x3b scan at 0x4488dc to 0x4488fc, the same sprintf at 0x448920 with format string 0x4a6954, system() at 0x448940, the same three parameters on the same three wanMode values and the same single-realm Basic authentication behind the same configuration flag, which points to a shared source component in the vendor's router software base; that model was not tested, nothing was executed from that image, no score covers it and it is not an exploited finding on it. A second independent command injection on the same image, in the formWlanMP manufacturing-test handler reaching sprintf at 0x462fd0 and system() at 0x46308c through POST /goform/formWlanMP with no sanitisation across thirty radio-calibration fields, is published as a companion advisory; it is a different handler, format string, sink address and sanitiser, so one patch point does not close both. No prior public record was found whose root cause is command injection in this setWAN handler. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, from ISS = 1 - 0.44^3 = 0.914816, Impact at S:U = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119, Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708 and Base = Roundup(5.873119 + 1.234708) = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. The provenance of that figure is disclosed because it is a correction: the research notes carried 8.8 next to a PR:H vector, and 8.8 is the arithmetic of PR:L, so the score was recomputed from the vector and published at 7.2, lowering the researchers' own number by 1.6 points. Four further readings are printed with their arithmetic in the public analysis. Privileges Required Low is rejected at 8.8 High, Exploitability 2.835255 and Base Roundup(8.708373), because the product has no basic-user role. Scope Changed is rejected at 9.1 High, Impact at S:C 6.128026, Exploitability 2.286496 and Base Roundup(1.08 x 8.414522), because webs is root before the attack and root after it. Attack Complexity High is rejected at 6.6 High, Exploitability 0.705547 and Base Roundup(6.578666), because success depends on no condition outside the attacker's control, the only branch to satisfy, wanMode, being attacker-supplied. An adjacent-vector reading is published as a labelled alternative at 6.8 High, Exploitability 0.900610 and Base Roundup(6.773729), and is the honest description of a stock device whose WAN-side input policy drops new connections, the shipped firewall script dropping WAN-originated SYN at firewall.sh:180, installing a default DROP input policy at firewall.sh:187 and accepting input on other interfaces at firewall.sh:189; AV:N is retained because the service is bound to the device's own network stack and addressable over IP by every host on the segment the router serves, including guest wireless clients and anything bridged or compromised behind it, and because remote management on the WAN side or forwarding port 80 are ordinary documented features. Default internet exposure is not claimed. Two readings at 9.8 Critical, CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H from Exploitability 3.887043 and Base Roundup(9.760161), are published only as explicitly labelled conditionals and never as the headline: the first applies where a deployment still accepts the factory credential and is reasoned rather than demonstrated, since no device was authenticated against; the second applies to a device still in its pre-configuration setup state, where auth_authorize returns success without a challenge for paths outside /mp.asp, /index.asp and / at 0x4052d0 while /generate_204 answers 204, and that branch is structural inference only, read from the binary and never exercised, with three shipped artefacts identifying the state as the setup wizard rather than normal operation, namely formwizResetDefault at 0x44cdbc displaying Resettowizard, formWizSetup printing NO - LOGIN-WEB when the flag is 1, and pages such as web/inter_wan.asp:214 and web/admin_timezone.asp:95 reading the same flag. That conditional's Scope Changed variant computes to 10.0 and is deliberately not published, and if the setup window has to be contested rather than found open the reading is 8.1 High from Exploitability 2.221167 and Base 8.094286. No version range is claimed: only firmware BR6478AC_v2.20.bin was examined, and only the wanMode 2 path was replicated, so no claim is made for other BR6478AC builds, for the separately marketed BR-6478AC V2 hardware revision whose firmware line is a different little-endian MIPS-II build of webs, for the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances beyond the structural reading of the same handler, or for any other model. Impact: arbitrary operating-system command execution as root on the router from a single authenticated POST indistinguishable from a legitimate WAN settings submission, since the payload travels in the PPP username field of the form the product's own wan.asp page posts. Root on this device exposes every stored secret, including precisely the PPP, PPTP and L2TP credentials this handler writes into configuration objects 0x6d, 0xf3 and 0x128, so an attacker who reaches the device can read the ISP or VPN account details the owner entered, together with the administrator password file, wireless pre-shared keys and per-station key material, VPN parameters and any certificate or key on the filesystem. It grants control of the configuration and routing plane: firewall and NAT rules, the DNS resolver handed out to clients, DHCP leases and a malicious default gateway, port forwards, wireless SSIDs and the WAN uplink itself, including rewriting the WAN mode, which is exactly the configuration path this handler owns. It grants firmware-level persistence, since root can write the flash-backed configuration area and install a boot-time startup mechanism, so a compromise survives reboots and can survive a partial configuration reset, with recovery requiring a full reflash of a known-good image. It grants availability at will over wireless, routing, DHCP, DNS and the management service. There is no rate limit on the handler and no lockout in the Basic realm, so the route is repeatable and leaves no alert behind. Detection is poor by construction but this sink leaves one usable anomaly: a submitted WAN configuration produces ordinary behaviour and the sink's visible effect, a username written into /tmp/UserName and then into the configuration store, is what a legitimate submission does, so the indicator is the absence of the expected /tmp/UserName destination on a submission that should have created it. An injection also corrupts stored configuration in a way the owner may not notice, the semicolon scan truncating at the first semicolon and a pipe-and-hash payload storing a username the WAN link cannot authenticate with, a self-inflicted availability event that doubles as a fingerprint. One operational caution: the injection is not side-effect free. A successful submission overwrites the stored WAN username and can break the uplink, which is what the handler does on any successful submission, so any demonstration must record and restore the device's original WAN configuration. Verification boundary: no physical device was powered on and no end-to-end HTTP request was ever accepted by the product. The HTTP leg, being request parsing, the authentication gate, form registration, mode dispatch and PPP branch selection, is evidenced at instruction level from the shipped binary, its configuration and its boot scripts. The execution leg is evidenced dynamically by replication of the sink's semantics rather than by detonation, because a MIPS big-endian uClibc userspace with a board-specific bootloader could not be booted end to end in the research environment: the extracted binaries faulted with SIGBUS under the available user-mode translator and full-system emulation of the board was not brought up. The question under test is not the device but whether a shell evaluates a pipeline and honours a trailing comment in a string built by the vendor's own sprintf and handed to /bin/sh -c, which is a question about POSIX shell semantics that are architecture independent, combined with the exact format string read out of the binary. The string sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 was reconstructed byte for byte for a request whose pppUserName field is |id > /tmp/marker_sw # and handed to /bin/sh -c in an isolated POSIX sandbox whose invoking shell ran as root, producing a 39-byte marker file owned by root:root containing uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) with shell exit status 0, while the sink's own /tmp/UserName destination was not created, that absence being the proof that the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment rather than being escaped, since a protected sink would have left the file behind. A benign control submitting an ordinary username created its destination containing that username and produced no marker. The same replication was repeated on a workstation under an ordinary unprivileged user account and reproduced the semantics at that identity, ruling out the alternative explanation that running as root caused the marker to appear. The harness removes any pre-existing marker and destination before each run and deletes its scratch files afterwards. Consequently the on-device landing identity of uid=0(root) is inferred from the shipped User root directive plus the root-identity replication and is not an observation from hardware; AV:N is argued from the product's transport and authentication model rather than measured across a network; the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances are a structural reading of the same handler rather than a demonstrated result; the sibling-model comparison is static only with nothing executed from that image and no score covering it; no setup-state request was sent; no dictionary or credential attack was attempted; and no overflow was developed against the unbounded stack copy. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-setwan-command-injection-root-rce Companion advisory, same product and image, different handler: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-formwlanmp-command-injection-root-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/edimax/br-6478ac-v2.20/setwan-command-injection-root-rce/exploit/edimax_br6478ac_setwan_command_injection_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target, and it is built so that it cannot be used accidentally against a live network. Its default mode is replication: it reconstructs the exact string the device's sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 and hands it to /bin/sh -c locally, asserting both that the injected pipeline ran and that the sink's own redirect target was not created, which is what proves the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment, then running a benign username as a negative control and asserting the opposite. That replication mode, not a device run, produced the evidence above. Arguments cover target host, Basic realm username and password, the WAN mode to select, which of the three username fields carries the payload, an option to iterate all three modes, a single non-destructive command defaulting to id, the marker path, the submit-url field value defaulting to /wan.asp, a user agent and a per-request timeout. A send mode additionally POSTs the request to the target and is refused for any non-loopback target unless an explicit allow-remote flag is given, and a print-request mode emits the exact HTTP request that would be transmitted while making no connection at all. Safety rails are loopback-only by default, one non-destructive marker command, no callback listener, no reverse shell, no persistence, and removal of every local file the run created. The tool's own documentation carries the warning that sending against a real device does change stored WAN configuration, because that is what the handler does on any successful submission, so the device's WAN settings must be restored afterwards. The model's published factory password appears in the tool only as a placeholder default so the request shape is self-documenting; the injection does not depend on it and the credential is reported as a separate weakness. Use only against systems you own or are authorised to test. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Full Text: Title: Exasol Database 7.1.30 - command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux Advisory: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/exasol-database-default-credential-python-udf-os-popen-rce CVE: pending Description: Exasol Database 7.1.30 from Exasol AG (Germany), an in-memory MPP analytical database examined in its docker-db single-container deployment form, accepts the credential pair sys / exasol on the binary SQL protocol served by the exacts process on port 8563 over TLS, and that pair is the vendor's own published text rather than a leak: the upstream docker-db README instructs the reader, under the heading "Connecting to the Database", to authenticate with username sys and password exasol, and two image-internal CI test scripts authenticate a freshly initialised database with the same pair on the same port, basic_test.sh:112 carrying $X -c n11:8563 -u sys -P exasol -jdbcparam validateservercertificate=0 and basic_sc_test.sh:98 using -u sys -P exasol as well, both cited as artifacts observed inside the 7.1.30 image at /usr/opt/EXASuite-7/EXAClusterOS-7.1.30/docker/test/ because the current upstream repository now carries documentation only. Nothing rotates the constant, and that was traced rather than assumed: the running controller process command line carries no -defaultSysPasswordHash argument; the [DB:DB1] stanza of EXAConf carries no DefaultSysPasswdHash key; db_jobs.py:104 sets self.sys_passwd_text = secrets.token_hex(20), which generates an additional random password rather than replacing the built-in one; database.py:57 passes -defaultSysPasswordHash only when EXAConf configures it explicitly; the container's init-sc path does not configure it; and no forced first-login change-password gate, must-change flag or service refusal exists anywhere in the container's start path, while the README carries guidance about persistent volumes, hugepages, resource limits and license mounting with no instruction to change the SYS password. Both the built-in default and the generated per-deployment random are accepted, so the presence of random generation in the provisioning code is not a defence. The contrast the product itself supplies is what makes this a defect rather than a design choice: Exasol generated per-deployment randoms for two of its three service credentials, the ConfD AuthenticationToken and the BucketFS WritePasswd, and did not do so for the most privileged one, and an attacker must read EXAConf to recover either random while sys / exasol is a constant every installation shares and the documentation prints. SYS is the database administrator, so the constant buys the whole warehouse over the SQL channel on its own, and it also buys the right to create script objects, which converts that administrative access into operating-system command execution (CWE-1392 primary, CWE-94 co-equal, with CWE-798, CWE-78, CWE-1188 and CWE-250 recorded alongside and CWE-284 and CWE-862 reported separately for the absent source-address restriction on 8563 and the absent authorisation distinction for script creation, neither of which raises a metric). The sink is a PYTHON3 scalar UDF body created with CREATE OR REPLACE ... AS whose run(ctx) calls os.popen("<attacker command>").read() and returns the result behind a marker string, after which the caller issues SELECT poc_udf() and the ordinary result set carries the command's stdout back. That construction is a sink rather than a curiosity for three reasons: the os module is importable with no declaration, allow-list or capability request; the command string is an ordinary Python literal built from what the caller supplied, so shell metacharacters, pipelines and quoting all work, and the measured round used cat /etc/passwd | head -3 whose pipeline was honoured by the shell os.popen starts; and the return value crosses the trust boundary back to the caller, which removes the need for any DNS, HTTP or ICMP exfiltration channel and means egress filtering on the host does not defeat it. Sanitisation over what the body does is absent, there being no module allow-list or deny-list, no policy forbidding os or subprocess, no capability gate, no per-statement approval, no audit prompt and no privilege required beyond SYS itself. What does exist is well-formedness checking rather than a security control: the engine validates the language alias, submitting PYTHON instead of PYTHON3 yields its own diagnostic "no definition found for language: PYTHON", and it enforces SQL syntax and the forward-slash script terminator, both of which the payload satisfied without any evasion. That alias diagnostic is itself useful evidence, because it shows script languages are resolved through a named alias table inside the engine, that the table carries the standard aliases PYTHON3, LUA, JAVA and R, and that EXAConf contains no [ScriptLanguages] stanza customising it, so reachability of the sink is not conditional on an operator having installed or enabled a language pack. Three independent detonations returned real system data through the result set, and the identity reported by id was uid=500(exadefusr) gid=500(exausers) groups=500(exausers),0(root): a dedicated script-execution account that carries root only as a supplementary group. That identity is the whole of what was measured. It is not uid=0, root is not claimed, no escalation was attempted, and this submission is not a root compromise. Three of the container's four authentication surfaces were characterised and ruled out as doors, ConfD on 443 requiring a Bearer token that is the per-deployment AuthenticationToken from EXAConf, BucketFS on 2580 returning 403 to a write attempt because the bucket WritePasswd is likewise a per-deployment random and 400 to a path traversal attempt, and OpenSSH on 22 performing ordinary host authentication with nothing product-specific observed, which is what makes this a credential-hygiene defect rather than an authentication-bypass defect. A negative control establishes that the acceptance is specific to the shipped value rather than to a broken check: five incorrect passwords, admin, password, EXASOL, exasol123 and 123456, were tried against the same transport and the same client invocation and all five returned [28000] authentication failed. The chain involves no memory corruption, no deserialisation gadget, no file upload, no protocol bypass, no local foothold and no second vulnerability; leg one is a documented product constant and leg two is a documented product feature, and what makes the pair a vulnerability is that the product neither rotates the constant nor restricts what a holder of it may execute. The vendor's own repository states that this docker distribution is an open source project that is not officially supported by Exasol, that the base image is an end-of-life CentOS 7 release, that official support for docker-db 7 is no longer available and that users should move to a newer release line, that the repository now only contains documentation with the binaries on Docker Hub, that issues are disabled, and that the project is mainly intended for automatic testing of Exasol deployments. None of that reduces the mechanism, because the credential is a property of the shipping database and the script engine is a supported core feature of the product rather than a container add-on, but it means that on the vendor's own statements no fix is planned for this deployment form, which is a reason the research was published rather than held for a patch and which raises operator exposure rather than lowering it. Only version 7.1.30 in this deployment form was executed: other 7.1.x releases, the supported non-container installation and the vendor's newer release line share the mechanism and are plausibly affected, but none was tested, that is stated as an explicitly labelled inference, and no version range is claimed. Type rationale, stated precisely because EDB's type taxonomy is coarser than CVSS: the exploit is delivered over the network to a networked database service, which is why the type is remote rather than local, and the proof of concept connects to port 8563 as a client would. The published Attack Vector is nonetheless Adjacent rather than Network, for the evidential reason given in the CVSS section below, and no reader should infer an AV:N rating from the type field. CVSS: 8.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, and it is not 9.8. Derivation, shown so a reader can reproduce it with the CVSS 3.1 base algorithm and its round-up-to-the-tenth rule: ISS = 1 - ((1-0.56) x (1-0.56) x (1-0.56)) = 1 - 0.44^3 = 0.914816; Impact at Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x AV(A: 0.62) x AC(L: 0.77) x PR(N: 0.85) x UI(N: 0.85) = 2.835255; Base = 8.708373 rounded up to the nearest tenth, which is 8.8. Attack Vector is Adjacent because the listener binds all interfaces inside the container and no source-address restriction of the product's own was observed in its configuration or listener behaviour, but no shipped artifact establishes that a single-container deployment binds 8563 on 0.0.0.0 by default: the vendor's documented stand-alone run command publishes -p 127.0.0.1:9563:8563 and the page explains that port 8563 within the container is exposed on local port 9563 to be used for database connections, with the persistent-volume variant on the same page using the same loopback-bound publication, while the documented multi-node run uses --network=host under which the vendor states that there is no need to expose ports in that mode because they are all accessible on the host, and the image's FAQ adds that checking from outside the Docker network requires port forwarding, confirming host-side reachability is an explicit operator action; under default bridge networking with no publication, which several of the README's own example commands use including the license-mount and resource-limit examples, the port is reachable from the host and from every other container attached to the same bridge, a logically adjacent topology. An earlier research note asserted that the production docker deployment exposes 8563 on all interfaces by default and scored the chain as remotely reachable on that basis; that assertion rested on the state of the researchers' own harness and on a general expectation about database deployments rather than on any product artifact, it does not survive contact with the vendor's documentation, it is therefore withdrawn in that form and replaced by the narrower artifact-backed statements above, and the withdrawal lowered the published score from 9.8 to 8.8 rather than raising it, so a reader who disagrees about the deployment posture ends up with the larger figure and not the smaller one. Attack Complexity is Low because the constant is published, the self-signed certificate carries no subjectAltName so the client needs a SHA256 fingerprint in the connection string as host/FINGERPRINT:port but that fingerprint is readable from an unauthenticated TLS handshake, the PYTHON3 alias is registered by default with no [ScriptLanguages] configuration required, and there is no race, no window and no operator action to wait for, all three rounds having succeeded on their first attempt. Privileges Required is None, argued rather than inherited: CVSS 3.1 reads PR:N as the attacker being unauthorized prior to attack and not requiring any access to settings or files of the vulnerable system, and both halves hold, since no account was ever provisioned to the attacker and no trust decision by the defender admitted them, and the value is obtained from vendor documentation rather than from the target's own EXAConf or logs. User Interaction is None. Impact is High on all three axes, grounded in the SQL-layer authority of SYS so that it does not depend on the cross-namespace reach that was not established. Scope is Unchanged because the SQL service, its script engine and the database it administers are one product on one host and executing a script is what the engine is built to do, so reaching the operating system from inside it does not cross an authority boundary the product itself maintains. Conditional reading A, where 8563 is reachable from another host, is 9.8 Critical (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.85 x 0.85 = 3.887043, Base = 9.760161 rounded up, and it applies to the documented multi-host --network=host form, to any operator publication of the port without a loopback restriction, to a deployment reachable across a management network or NAT, and to the supported non-container installation whose entire purpose is to answer client connections on 8563; it is labelled conditional everywhere it appears because the deployment form actually executed published loopback-only and the cross-host leg was argued from vendor artifacts rather than detonated. Conditional reading B, loopback-only publication exactly as the stand-alone quickstart documents, is 8.4 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.55 x 0.77 x 0.85 x 0.85 = 2.515145, Base = 8.388264 rounded up, applying where the attacker therefore needs local access to the host, a realistic position for anything else already running there including a sibling container. Three further readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic: Privileges Required Low, 8.0 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), Exploitability 2.068068, Base 7.941187 rounded up, which treats the constant as a credential the attacker supplies and is rejected for charging the attacker a privilege the defender never granted, and is also the honest reachable reading where the factory credential has been rotated but a provisioned non-administrative account still holds script-creation rights; Privileges Required High, 6.8 Medium (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), Exploitability 0.900610, Base 6.773729 rounded up, reading the metric as the authority level the successful attack needs since SYS is the database's most privileged account, rejected more strongly than PR:L because it would rate a constant requiring no grant as though it were a personal administrator account, and computing to 7.2 Medium under a Network vector; and Scope Changed, 9.7 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), impact term 7.52 x (0.914816 - 0.029) - 3.25 x (0.914816 x 0.9731 - 0.02)^13 = 6.128026, Base = 1.08 x (6.128026 + 2.835255) = 9.680344 rounded up, with the same reading under a Network vector capped by the formula at 10.0 Critical, rejected as the headline because the namespace boundary measured as a boundary in one direction and not the other, a file written inside it not appearing outside, and because no cross-boundary effect was demonstrated. A fourth state deserves its own sentence because an operator can enter it deliberately: with the factory credential rotated and no other account holding script-creation privilege, there is no path from the network to the sink and this finding does not arise, the script engine then being a documented feature used by authorised administrators, which is why rotation moves the finding from 8.8 to not applicable and heads the operator recommendations. No score is published for the sibling sinks os.system, subprocess and the LUA, JAVA and R aliases because none was detonated, none for the BucketFS anonymous read of the default bucket because it is separate and smaller with its own root cause, none for other 7.1.x releases or the non-container installation because neither was executed, and no figure is quoted for escalation to uid=0 because it was not attempted. Impact: full administrative takeover of the database by anyone who can reach port 8563, and then operating-system command execution as uid=500(exadefusr) with root present only as a supplementary group. The SQL layer does not depend on the sink at all and is the larger half: SYS reads and writes every schema, table, view, user and privilege in an analytical platform, which typically holds whatever the organisation consolidated into it, and can stop the database, so the complete warehouse is exposed with no further exploit step and no unusual protocol activity. Integrity control extends to the account catalogue, so further accounts can be created with chosen privileges, giving an attacker a durable and legitimate-looking second entry point that survives rotation of the factory credential. Availability follows the same authority: the database can be stopped, schemas dropped and resources consumed by the same session, and the deployment runs privileged as the vendor's README requires for permissions management, UDF support and environment configuration, which widens what such consumption inside the container can reach beyond it; that widening was not tested and is not scored. The sink adds command execution with stdout returned through the ordinary SELECT result set, so the attack is non-blind and needs no exfiltration channel, and file reads inside the script namespace. Persistence is cheap and quiet: the payload uses CREATE OR REPLACE, so re-running the attack rewrites one script object rather than creating a new one per command, and the object is ordinary product state that survives the session and is visible only to someone who enumerates script definitions. Detection is weak by construction because every step is legitimate documented product usage, a TLS handshake, a SYS login, script creation and a SELECT, so a SYS session from an unexpected address is indistinguishable from a real administrator and an operator who never rotated the constant has no means of telling them apart; the highest-value signal is script-object creation with the creating user and source address, which the default deployment does not surface, and the second-best is a trial sequence of [28000] authentication failed responses against the sys user on 8563, no rate limit and no lockout having been observed on SQL authentication. The root supplementary group under the vendor-documented privileged container mode is a recognised escalation position on Linux, since gid 0 governs access to files and devices whose group is root, and it is reported as an untested position: the conditional sentence is the whole of what the evidence supports, namely that if an attacker there could write a setuid binary or reach a device node exposed by privileged mode an effective root identity would follow, and neither was tested. A separate smaller finding is reported alongside and deliberately not folded into any metric: the BucketFS default bucket is Public=True, which permits unauthenticated read listing, while a write attempt returned 403 because the bucket WritePasswd is a per-deployment random and a path traversal attempt returned 400. Verification boundary: live verification against one container built from the vendor's docker-db image at 7.1.30, pulled onto an isolated cloud sandbox, started with the privileged flag the vendor's README requires, with a host directory mounted at /exa and the SQL port published to the host loopback only. Researcher-side commands ran under an ordinary unprivileged account and nothing in the chain depended on elevated privileges on the researchers' host. The three detonations drove the vendor's own console client inside the container against the container's loopback on 8563, so this is a real product executing real commands rather than an emulation or a protocol replica, and no step of the chain was driven from a separate network host. The cross-host legs, that a client on another machine can complete the same TLS handshake, retrieve the fingerprint, authenticate and submit the same statements over 8563, follow from the protocol being a network protocol and from the in-container listener binding all interfaces, and they are argued from the vendor's documented deployment forms and the observed bind rather than demonstrated between two machines; that is why the headline Attack Vector is Adjacent and why the 9.8 Network reading is labelled conditional. Measured, with the returned values reproduced in the advisory: authentication with the shipped constant; rejection of five wrong passwords with [28000] authentication failed; creation of a PYTHON3 scalar UDF by SYS; execution of os.popen inside it; return of the command's stdout through the result set; the executing identity uid=500(exadefusr) gid=500(exausers) groups=500(exausers),0(root); visibility of the host kernel release 5.10.134-19.2.al8.x86_64 from inside the UDF; and readability of /etc/passwd from the UDF process, whose output began root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash. Three rounds, each an independent create-and-select cycle with a different command, each returning real system data, each succeeding on its first attempt; there was no fourth round and no round was repeated merely to demonstrate determinism, three successes with three different commands being evidence of repeatability on their own. Not verified and not claimed: cross-host remote detonation; escalation to uid=0; any write or execution crossing from the UDF namespace into the container's or the host's filesystem view, a separate write-marker test having shown that a file written by the UDF did not appear in the container's own view, so the two views are distinct mount namespaces and the account names in the id output come from the namespace's own view, which is also why even the /etc/passwd read is not asserted to have been the container's file or the host's; persistence; the effect of the chain on a non-container installation or on another 7.1.x release; and the sibling sinks os.system, subprocess and the LUA, JAVA and R aliases. Read from source or documentation rather than detonated: the absence of -defaultSysPasswordHash on the controller command line, the absence of DefaultSysPasswdHash in EXAConf, the behaviour of db_jobs.py:104 and database.py:57, the contents of the image's test scripts, the ConfD token generation scheme, and every documented deployment command quoted above. One inconsistency is disclosed rather than smoothed over: the notes record the host-side port publication as 8562 in one place and 8563 in another, and because every measured leg ran through the container loopback that discrepancy is not load-bearing for anything claimed here. Exactly three commands were executed as payloads, an identity capture, a file read and a kernel-version read; no product file was modified or deleted and no data was destroyed. Prior public coverage was checked before publication: a keyword search of the NVD for the vendor name returned exactly one record, concerning a client-side JDBC driver component rather than the database server, separate searches for the database product name and for the docker deployment name returned no records at all, no published advisory was found whose root cause is either leg of this chain, the single unrelated record is deliberately not cited in the advisory, and no neighbouring identifier should be inferred as related. Exploit notes: the four statements are CREATE SCHEMA, OPEN SCHEMA, CREATE OR REPLACE PYTHON3 SCALAR SCRIPT with the body and its forward-slash terminator, and SELECT. Because the certificate has no subjectAltName the connection string must carry the fingerprint in the form host/FINGERPRINT:port, obtainable from an unauthenticated handshake. The return type is declared as a wide VARCHAR so command output is not truncated by the declared width, and the marker prefix distinguishes the returned value from the echoed statement text. The command is embedded as a Python double-quoted string literal, so backslashes and double quotes are escaped and nothing else is. Two client behaviours had to be engineered around, both recorded because they were the difference between a hanging tool and a working one: the vendor client's single-statement mode rejects a multi-statement payload containing the slash terminator and reports an unfinished command, so the payload is fed on stdin, and the client does not exit at end of file on stdin, so the tool starts it with a pipe, waits a bounded interval, kills it and keeps the partial stdout, by which point the result set has already been printed; an early transcript parser matched the marker inside the echoed CREATE SCRIPT source, and the fix filters matches followed by a quote, a space or a plus sign, which is how echoed source differs from a real result. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/exasol-database-default-credential-python-udf-os-popen-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/exasol/database-7.1.30/default-credential-python-udf-os-popen-rce/exploit/exasol_database_default_credential_python_udf_os_popen_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target. It refuses a non-loopback target unless --allow-remote is passed; acquires the certificate fingerprint with an unauthenticated TLS handshake and prints only the first and last few hex characters so that a per-deployment value is not written into a research log, with --fingerprint to supply the value instead and --no-encryption for a deployment that disabled TLS; asserts the credential gate with a trivial query before doing anything else; and creates and selects the UDF once per requested command. --rounds 3 reproduces the verification method by cycling through three different commands, --control runs the negative control alone and creates nothing, --gate probes only the credential, and --cleanup drops only the schema the run created. Nothing destructive is performed: the tool establishes no listener, opens no reverse shell, writes no file, installs no persistence, touches no other container or host service, does not attempt to reach uid=0 and does not attempt to cross the UDF namespace boundary. The default command is id. Those omissions are deliberate, the finding being that command execution is reachable at all from a documented constant, and demonstrating more would add risk without adding evidence. Exasol AG was notified through the vulnerability-reporting mailbox published in its RFC 9116 security.txt, which is the only intake the vendor offers and which welcomes responsible disclosure of vulnerabilities in its products and services. Nothing was submitted to any pre-publication intake form, none being published, and no individual was addressed by name. The notification was sent unconditionally and in clear text, the security.txt publishing no inline key field: the research is already public, no permission was asked for, no embargo was requested and nothing is withheld pending a reply. The vendor states that this docker deployment form is not officially supported and that official support for it has ended, so no fix is planned for it. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Context: The write primitive is a HashSet forcing hashCode() on a TiedMapEntry wrapping a LazyMap whose factory is a ConstantTransformer holding attacker bytes and whose decorated map is...
Full Text: Title: Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform 10.7.5- JSP command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux CVE: pending Description: Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform (CTP) from Parasoft (United States), a closed-source commercial continuous-testing product bundling environment management, service virtualisation and test-data management, distributes an em web application running on Tomcat 10.1.57 with the Jasper JSP engine and Java 17 inside the vendor's own container image, and contains three composing first-party defects that yield unauthenticated remote code execution in two HTTP requests: an unfiltered ObjectInputStream over an uploaded backup archive (CWE-502, primary), a licensing filter that decides whether to run at all by testing the raw un-normalised request URI (CWE-436, primary and co-equal, with CWE-863 as its authorisation consequence), and a remember-me authentication service that hands an anonymous request an authenticated administrator principal when no external security provider has been configured (CWE-287, enabling gate). Defect one, the licensing filter: EMLicenseFilter is 175 lines and reads request.getRequestURI() raw at line 165, testing it at line 166 against exemption clauses including endsWith("about"), endsWith("welcome"), endsWith("forgot"), endsWith("notlicensed"), contains("/resources/") and contains("/images/"), none anchored by a separator or segment boundary, with a further branch at lines 167 to 171 that reassigns the entire exemption set rather than accumulating into it when the request accepts JSON. That test has exactly one consumer in the class, shouldNotFilter() at line 47 calling isLicenseRequired() at line 48, so a matching URI suppresses the whole doFilterInternal() body rather than weakening one decision, taking with it the /tdm/api/v guard at line 99 and the unlicensed-instance redirect to /em/license at line 118. Because a servlet container strips semicolon-delimited path parameters from each segment before servlet mapping, filter and router disagree about the identity of one request, and a target of /em/database/restore;welcome is exempted by the filter while still being routed to the restore handler. Defect two, the sink: com.parasoft.ctp.core.database.backup.AbstractDatabaseBackup, a class of 518 lines and 19,851 bytes, wraps the uploaded database.ser zip member at line 111 with new ObjectInputStream(in), reads an int at line 112 and calls readObject() at line 117 casting the result to TableMetadata, nine lines above the getConnection() call at line 126, so the cast constrains nothing (the gadget executes during the call and the ClassCastException is thrown afterwards) and no database needs to exist, be reachable or accept the supplied parameters for the payload already to have run. The caller is the web-layer controller EMDatabaseController, 1359 lines, whose restore handler at lines 707 and 708 takes a StandardMultipartHttpServletRequest and hard-compares zip member names against the literals "version.txt" at line 725 and "database.ser" at line 733, a shape check that says nothing about content. The absence of a filter is a corpus-wide artefact measurement rather than an inference: ObjectInputStream appears in 68 files with 149 occurrences in the core tree and in 3 files in the web layer, readObject appears in 81 files, and ObjectInputFilter appears in 0 files, jdk.serialFilter in 0 files and serialFilter in 0 files, three zeros across a class name, a system property and its short alias against a positive control of 81 files containing readObject. Two sibling readObject() calls on the same class of untrusted stream sit at lines 323 and 435 of the same class, in a row-draining and a row-binding routine, read from source and not detonated, named so a fix covers the class rather than the call site. Defect three, the fail-open gate: EMRememberMeServices is 483 lines and, at line 140 to 142, returns null when an Authorization header is present, then at line 146 fetches PSTSecServiceClient.getInstance() and at line 148, when that client is null, returns createAuthenticationToken("admin", "admin", EmUserInfo.Role.ADMIN, request), which registers new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN") inside a Spring Security User whose authenticated flag is true, so the resulting principal is a genuinely authenticated administrator rather than the container's anonymous principal and satisfies the authenticated() matcher that CTPSecurityWebConfig line 283 demands for /database. Neither hop is an unprotected route, /database being explicitly matched to authenticated() and the images allow-list being /images/welcome/* rather than a widened glob, so the accurate description is not that the endpoints are unauthenticated but that the product mints an administrative principal for an anonymous request. CsrfSecurityRequestMatcher is a 28-line class whose anchored exemption alternation at line 19 includes /database, so the state-changing POST needs no CSRF token. The write primitive is a HashSet forcing hashCode() on a TiedMapEntry wrapping a LazyMap whose factory is a ConstantTransformer holding attacker bytes and whose decorated map is an aspectjweaver SimpleCache$StoreableCachingMap with an absolute folder field, reaching writeToPath(folder + File.separator + key, bytes). That class was read at the bytecode level for four facts: folder is declared private final String, is not transient, and the class declares no readObject of its own, so it is populated by the inherited HashMap.readObject path through defaultReadObject and both writer routines read it with an explicit getfield that the compiler has not inlined; writeToPath is getfield folder, StringBuilder, separator, key, store, with no forced extension appended to the key, an assumption that had to be disproved at the bytecode level because it would have removed any execution surface, and the value passes a checkcast to a byte array so the content is any bytes at all; validation is absent in every form, with zero occurrences of File.getName(), Path.normalize(), getCanonicalPath(), startsWith(), a regular expression or a length truncation in that write path, keys carrying slashes or relative traversals both working, and an absolute destination reachable because concatenation with an empty folder yields a leading double separator that POSIX treats as a valid absolute path; and the gadget does not fire on deserialization alone, because HashMap.readObject reconstitutes entries through putVal, which is package-private, final and not overridden, so it bypasses the overridden put containing the write, which is why the TiedMapEntry to LazyMap to Map.put prefix is needed to force a virtual dispatch. The only content constraint anywhere is that the bytes must not equal the four-byte sentinel IDEM, and the published carrier sets storingTimer to Integer.MAX_VALUE to suppress the index file the caching map would otherwise write alongside the payload. The execution sink is the product's own container configuration: conf/web.xml declares the Jasper jsp servlet and its mapping at lines 274-275 and 448-450, and webapps/em/images/ is inside the deployed web application root the mapping covers, writable by uid 1000 as drwxrwxr-x parasoft root, and exempt from the licensing filter by the contains("/images/") clause at line 166, so fetching the written page needs no bypass of its own and the product compiles it into work/Catalina/localhost/em/org/apache/jsp/images/<stem>_jsp.java and .class. A second independent execution sink was also detonated and is recorded so a fix removing JSP compilation does not close half the problem: WEB-INF/classes/com/parasoft/rest/api/core/docs/templates/ is the FreeMarker template root, its prefix from an init-param in webapps/em/WEB-INF/web.xml at lines 206-207 with FreeMarker 2.3.34 through jersey-mvc-freemarker 3.1.12, and because freemarker.template.utility.Execute is on no restriction list the new() built-in is usable, a template performing 7*119 returning 200 with a 4-byte body containing 833 and a template invoking Execute with id returning 200 with a 61-byte body containing the full identity string. Measured chain: one anonymous multipart POST to the restore path carrying a semicolon-welcome suffix, with no cookie, no Authorization header and no CSRF token, returning HTTP 500 with the product's own 119-byte "An error occurred while applying changes to the database configuration" message, which is the success signature rather than a failure because readObject() precedes getConnection(); the product log then carried one occurrence per run of a stack trace naming AbstractDatabaseBackup.restore(AbstractDatabaseBackup.java:114) with "class java.util.HashSet cannot be cast to class ...TableMetadata" and a java.lang.ClassCastException, counted at 2, then 4, then 6 across runs, and distinguishable from a malformed payload which produces a ClassNotFoundException instead. One anonymous GET of the written page then returned 200 with a 538-byte body containing a per-run marker with a 12-hex nonce, JSP_EVAL=42 from server-side evaluation of the expression 6*7, proving evaluation rather than source echo, SIZE_SELF=1372 agreeing with the length of the payload the client built, which proves byte-exact content control, the identity string uid=1000(parasoft) gid=1000(parasoft) groups=1000(parasoft), an ls line showing the page owned by the product's own service account, a /proc/1/status line reporting Uid: 1000 1000 1000 1000, and two /etc/passwd lines read by the product process. Two end-to-end detonations of the two-hop chain are recorded as successful, and two intermediate iterations failed inside the client script rather than against the product. No vendor-supplied credential, no licence installation or forgery, no outbound connection, no DNS or RMI callback, no cross-version payload adaptation, no memory corruption and no privilege escalation is involved: the upstream libraries carrying the gadget are carriers and not the root cause, executing a jsp page is the product's own configuration, and the landing identity is the product's unprivileged service account, uid=1000(parasoft), confirmed three ways (id inside the executed page, the written file's ownership and mode, and the product process's own /proc/1/status read from inside the container rather than through a container runtime which would report root regardless), with root not reached and not claimed. CVSS: 9.8 Critical (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, recomputed from the vector with the CVSS 3.1 base formula rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - ((1 - 0.56) x (1 - 0.56) x (1 - 0.56)) = 0.914816; Impact for Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 (AV:N) x 0.77 (AC:L) x 0.85 (PR:N) x 0.85 (UI:N) = 3.887043; base = min(5.873119 + 3.887043, 10) = 9.760161; rounded up to the nearest tenth = 9.8. AV:N because the chain is two ordinary HTTP requests to TCP listeners the product serves itself over HTTP 8080 and HTTPS 8443, both accepting connections from outside the container, with no shipped reverse proxy, WAF or management-plane separation in front of em, and the loopback publication of the test port being the research testbed's containment rather than a product restriction. AC:L because there is no timing window to win (this is the steady factory state, not a first-run race), no host-specific reconnaissance, no memory-layout condition, no database reachability requirement (the readObject at line 117 runs before getConnection at line 126), no outbound callback and no cryptographic work; the only condition is a configuration state the vendor's own image is in when no external security provider has been configured. PR:N because no credential belonging to anybody is supplied or consumed, the authenticated subject being manufactured by the product itself for an anonymous request. UI:N because no administrator action, browser session, induced click or human upload step exists anywhere in the chain. C:H, I:H and A:H describe compromise of the product, its managed data and its availability, and do not depend on the landing identity being privileged, nor rise if a deployment runs the platform as root, which was not measured. Scope Unchanged, with Scope Changed considered and rejected on an argument stated here so the call cannot be read as a scoring maneuver: the rejected S:C variant of the same metrics, CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H, computes to 10.0 from ISS 0.914816, Impact for Scope Changed 6.128026, Exploitability 3.887043 and 1.08 times their sum capped at the maximum, so the reading rejected here is the higher one and rejecting it lowers the published number from 10.0 to 9.8. It is not two authorities because the filter, the deserialising controller, the security service, the web application root and the JSP mapping all belong to one deployed application in one JVM, the platform being a single product with several routers rather than several products; because executing a page inside its own web application root is the documented intended behaviour of the shipped container configuration, so the transition from write to execution crosses no boundary the product defines; and because the executed code carries the product process's own uid in that process's own filesystem view, entering no other account, machine or security domain. Three labelled conditional readings accompany the published score and none replaces it. Conditional A, external security provider configured and the attacker holding any valid account, is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.8 High (Exploitability 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.62 x 0.85 = 2.835255, Impact 5.873119, base 8.708373 rounded up), since the security matcher for the restore path is authenticated() rather than hasRole("ADMIN") so low privileges suffice while the licensing gate is still bypassed and the sink still unfiltered; this deployment state was not detonated, and it is the reading an operator of a configured deployment should work from because it depends on no unverified capability. Conditional B, external security provider configured with the subject supplied by an offline-forged session cookie, is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 9.8 Critical, arithmetically identical to the published score, and is a static and structural inference that was never verified: the platform signs its remember-me cookie PST_LT_FEATURES_INFORMATION, whose signed plaintext takes the form user:expiry::localAddr:"rememberMeAuthenticated", with a key that is a compile-time string literal and a signature scheme, bcrypt, that carries no secret, so anyone holding the shipped class can compute a cookie offline, and forgery was exercised only in the unconfigured state where it buys nothing, while the combination of a configured deployment driven end to end with a forged subject has no run behind it at all; building a fake security provider to test it was deliberately abandoned because installing one would have manufactured the condition being measured. Conditional B is published so an operator of a configured deployment knows which exposure to check and so the vendor knows which mechanism to replace, never as a demonstrated capability and never as the headline score, and the published PR:N rests on the measured fail-open behaviour of the untouched image rather than on any forgery. Conditional C, listeners reachable only from a management network, is CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.8 High (Exploitability 8.22 x 0.62 x 0.77 x 0.85 x 0.85 = 2.835255, Impact 5.873119, base 8.708373), conditional on a deployment change that was not tested and downward rather than upward, so an operator who hardens the network position can see that it is worth one point of severity and fixes nothing else.
