Full Text: Title: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E v2.2.44 - Unsigned Firmware Upgrade Package Executed as Root Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware Advisory: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce CVE: pending Description: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E, version v2.2.44, the industrial wireless radio from ProSoft Technology, Inc. (United States) whose research designation is RLX-IH 24E, installs and executes code submitted over its management interface without performing any signature, hash or CRC check on it. The appliance is a closed-source embedded device and an OEM build of the MicroHard Systems IPx21 platform on the MHX-910 board design: an Intel IXP425 XScale processor, ARM big-endian, Linux 2.4.24-uc0, with static management pages under /usr/web and 57 ARM big-endian CGI programs under /usr/lib/cgi-bin/ served by boa over HTTP and boa_ssl over HTTPS. The classification is CWE-494, download of code without integrity check, with CWE-345 and CWE-347 co-equal, because the only authenticity check in the path is a non-cryptographic string equality and no signature is verified anywhere. CWE-434, CWE-73, CWE-250 and CWE-269 contribute. It is explicitly not CWE-78 and a command-injection remediation would not fix it: the shared platform helper SubProgram_Start at offset 0xbd5c splits its argument string on spaces with strtok into at most eight tokens and then calls vfork and execvp directly, so no shell is ever invoked and shell metacharacters are inert here. The upload hop is in usr/lib/cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi, routine HandleSubmit at offset 0x8d1c, with its formatting string at rodata offset 0x2b1c. On the file1 part of a multipart/form-data POST to /cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi it calls cgiFormFileName and cgiFormTempFileName, builds the move argument with sprintf(buf, "%s /upgrade/upgrade/%s", tempfile, origfilename), runs SubProgram_Start("/bin/mv", buf), which must succeed, and then runs SubProgram_Start("/sbin/upgrade", origfilename). The client-supplied original filename is therefore used unmodified twice, once as the destination of the move and once as the installer's only argument, which makes the file extension and so the installer branch entirely the requester's choice. The handler applies no extension whitelist, no digest comparison and no path canonicalisation. The install hop is /sbin/upgrade, a short POSIX shell script shipped in the same package, running with the CGI's own privileges, which are root. It dispatches on ${FILE##*.} and its three consequential branches are: ".pkg", which tests gzip stream integrity with gunzip -t, unpacks with tar -xf into a staging tree, compares the appliance's PRODUCT_NAME read from /etc/MHX_CONFIG against a LOCK_NAME read from a lockfile inside the package itself, prints "Match image." on equality, executes ./pre, applies the inner archive with tar -xf extract/upgradepkg.tar -C /, executes ./post, prints "Upgrade Successful" and then reboots unconditionally; ".passwd", which copies the upload over both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original; and ".factory", which copies the upload over /etc/db1, the configuration store holding the management interface's own transport flags, accounts and radio behaviour. The equality test is the only gate before code execution and both of its operands are available to the requester: the expected value is the compile-time platform constant IPx21PROSOFT recoverable by reading the shipped firmware once, and the asserted value is carried inside the package being installed. A package whose identity is validated against data carried inside that same package cannot be a source of assurance about it. The defect is the absence of an authenticity step, not a weak one, and strengthening the compatibility check would change nothing while both operands come from the same side. Impact: root command execution on the appliance from a single multipart/form-data POST followed by the product's own documented install sequence, with requester-authored shell code running both before and after an unconstrained archive extraction into the root of the filesystem. Attacker code reading the pre-execution state, an arbitrary rootfs write through the inner archive whose entry names are constrained in no way, and attacker code running post-write are all present in one request. The .passwd branch reaches the same privilege ceiling without executing anything, replacing both the live account database and its backup copy so that the device's own recovery path restores the modified database rather than the shipped one; since the factory admin entry is uid 0 with the restricted shell /bin/txtUI, an added uid-0 entry with /bin/sh converts an administratively restricted login into a general root shell at the next interactive login. The .factory branch lets a requester rewrite the device's security configuration, widening or narrowing the exposure of the surface they arrived through and surviving a later reconfiguration by the operator. Persistence is native to the product rather than improvised, because the install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. Availability is controlled at will, both by that reboot and by installing content that stops the device serving traffic, which for a radio carrying traffic between a process network and its field instruments is also a position on the path that traffic takes. Detection is weak by construction: every step is documented product behaviour, the request is an ordinary firmware upload, the response is the vendor's own success page, and a legitimate upgrade prints exactly the same "Match image." and "Upgrade Successful", so the usable indicators are post-hoc and filesystem-level, namely an installed package whose LOCK_NAME and VERSION pair corresponds to no release the operator obtained, an unexpected file under /upgrade/upgrade/, and a uid-0 account whose shell is not the vendor's restricted interface. Verification boundary, stated exactly because it is narrower than the headline suggests, and because the classification above depends on it. The installer half of the chain was measured and the upload half was not. No HTTP request was ever issued at this product and no physical appliance was used at any point, so nothing here is an exploit run against a live device and it is not presented as one. What was executed is the firmware's own /sbin/upgrade, byte-for-byte unmodified, inside an isolated chroot sandbox built on a copy of the upgrade package's own root filesystem. A crafted .pkg printed "Match image." then "Upgrade Successful" and exited 0; the pre script left a marker proving it executed and wrote PRE-RAN-AS-UID=0 into a second marker, the post script left its own marker, and the inner archive applied an entry to the root of the filesystem. The uid marker is the load-bearing evidence: the payload wrote that value at runtime rather than having it read from a configuration file, so it is the executing identity and not an inference about it. The recorded landing identity is uid=0(root). A .passwd run replaced both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original with the uploaded text, proven by a pre-run digest of the pre-seeded database that no longer matched afterwards and by a marker line present in both copies. A negative control was run to establish that none of this came from the harness: a structurally identical package, same outer tar layout, same metadata files, same inner archive, same marker-writing scripts, with exactly one deliberate difference, LOCK_NAME=WRONGPRODUCT, was refused with "This unit doesn't support the image." and produced no markers anywhere. That control also isolates the product-string comparison as the single cause of refusal and makes the positive and negative runs mutually exclusive. Four substitutions existed in the harness and none in the code under test: an x86 busybox build supplied /bin/sh, tar, gunzip, mv and cp because the firmware's own copies are ARM big-endian and the host is not; a stub replaced the platform mhx utility; /etc/MHX_CONFIG was populated with the product identity the firmware itself ships; and /etc/passwd was pre-seeded with three factory-style entries for comparison. Two transcript lines, "logger: not found" and "mhx: not found", are absent helpers in the sandbox PATH and are not product behaviour. The run count is one positive .pkg run, one positive .passwd run and one negative control, in one sandbox on one host, each effect observed once, never repeated across sandbox builds and never performed on hardware. Not measured, and not claimed: the web server and its access control, because /bin/boa lives in the device base flash and is not contained in the system upgrade package, so the access control gating this CGI could be neither proved nor disproved from the artefacts available; the CGI binaries and the firmware's ARM helpers, for the architecture reason; the closing reboot, since the sandbox is a directory tree with no init, though the path up to it was observed; any privilege escalation, the chain starting from the administrative identity the product's own account database already grants uid 0; any reach into the radio baseband image RLX-IFH24E_v5089.mhx, identified but not exercised; and any impact on an attached control system, PLC or historian. Consequently the Type field above reflects the documented delivery vector, a network POST to a CGI on the management listener, and the Platform field reflects a firmware and hardware target; the part that was actually executed was the vendor's own installer acting on a supplied file, and a reader should weight the two halves of this chain differently. That is what the published advisory is written to allow. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, computed from first principles rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - (0.44 x 0.44 x 0.44) = 0.914816; Impact at Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708; Base = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. AV:N because the entry point is a network service and the firmware's own default configuration record inside the shipped package enables the web interface on both transports, UI_Access_HTTP=B and HTTPS=B, with non-default values for the Telnet and SSH entries; that shipped record is the evidence for a default, and the Network classification comes from the transport the artefact establishes rather than from a reach we observed. AC:L because the chain is deterministic, with no race, no timing window, no memory-layout dependency and no on-path position, and the single piece of environment knowledge it needs is a platform string published inside the shipped firmware. PR:H because installing firmware is an administrative function, the handler is a maintenance CGI linked directly from the interface's own menu pages, and the only account model the package documents for that interface is a uid-0 admin entry with a password-change page and a configurable RADIUS mode; no lower-privileged principal was demonstrated reaching the handler. UI:N because once a session holds that privilege the move, the install, both script executions and the reboot all follow from one request with no operator action and no confirmation step in the recovered handler path. Scope Unchanged because the vulnerable component and the impacted component are the same appliance operating system, the CGI already running as root, the installer already running as root and the rootfs extracted by that same root process, so no authority boundary is crossed. Three readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic: low privilege (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 8.8 and is available only by assuming that the shipped uid-500 upgrade account, whose home directory is the upload staging path and which shares the admin password hash, can reach the maintenance handler, which was not tested; Scope Changed (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 9.1 and is rejected because an unproven boundary crossing may not raise a published score; high attack complexity (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 6.6 and is rejected because the control run isolates a wrong product string as the sole cause of refusal. Two of those rejected readings score higher than the number published, and the advisory says so itself. Two further readings are labelled conditionals and neither is the headline. An unauthenticated HTTP layer (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) would compute to 9.8 and was NOT demonstrated; it is a structural inference that applies only if the management listener does not gate the handler, and the binary that would answer that question is not in the package analysed. The supporting observation about the package is narrower and is weaker than that reading: none of the 57 shipped CGIs imports crypt, none parses or sets a session cookie and no login CGI exists in the directory, so the handler layer adds no authentication of its own, which says nothing about what the web server does before it forks a CGI. A factory credential still in place on a deployed unit would remove the need to discover any secret, but it was not demonstrated either, no authentication was performed against any appliance and no first-login behaviour was tested; under CVSS the metric prices the privilege level of the account used rather than whether its secret was public, so that reading leaves the vector unchanged at 7.2 and is published as a deployment amplifier for operators to assess. The factory password hash is deliberately not reproduced in this submission or in the advisory. No version-range claim is made: only the system upgrade package RLX-IFH24E_v2244.pkg was analysed, no other build of this model, no other version of the OEM IPx21 platform and no other product of either company is claimed as affected, although the upgrade path is a shared platform component rather than a per-product script, so a wider population of devices built on the same OEM platform plausibly shares the root cause, and that is stated as a likelihood rather than scored. Adjacent structural observations recorded in the analysis and deliberately excluded from this finding are a startup configuration that symlink-exposes /etc/MHX_CONFIG, /var/log/messages and /etc/system.debug into the web document root as configuration, syslog and debug views; a legacy debug CGI named request.cgi whose first-argument dispatch includes sending AT commands to the radio module, which was never executed and to which no AT command was sent; and SNMP community strings public and private shipped on the platform, which belong to the configuration plane. Public records were searched by product designation, by the RLX-IH name, by the OEM platform name and by the vendor name with no result describing this appliance and this root cause; the one record associated with the vendor's RadioLinx engineering-software line concerns a pseudo-random number generator in that software family, a different product and a different defect class, and records naming the platform manufacturer's own product families concern different platforms and different chains. Proof of concept, published unconditionally. The shipped script is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target: the target address, port, scheme, credentials, command, lock name, product name, uploaded filename, marker token and output path are all command-line arguments and default to inert values, the default target being loopback and the default payload command being true. It builds a gzip-compressed tar containing the file and lockfile metadata the installer reads, the pre and post scripts at mode 0755 and extract/upgradepkg.tar, and can either write that package to disk for inspection or carry it in a multipart/form-data POST under the part name file1. Its modes and the flags that matter: Build the package locally only, performing no network access at all: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --build-only --out demonstration.pkg Refuse a filename that would break the hand-off. The tool rejects any name containing a space or a path separator before it builds anything, because SubProgram_Start splits its argument string on spaces before execvp, so an extra token would change what /bin/mv is asked to do: --filename "payload.pkg" accepted --filename "pay load.pkg" rejected by the tool itself Build the negative control, for an operator who owns the hardware to confirm that the success path really is gated by the product string and by nothing else: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --control --build-only --out control.pkg Build the account-database variant as a local file, which is never sent unless --send is also given: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --passwd-mode --passwd-entry "marker:*:0:0:INERT-DEMONSTRATION-ENTRY:/root:/bin/sh" Deliver the built package to a management listener the operator owns and is authorised in writing to test, over HTTP or HTTPS, with optional HTTP Basic credentials: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 80 --user <user> --password <pass> python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 443 --https --user <user> --password <pass> The default payload is deliberately non-destructive: pre touches one marker file and writes the executing uid into a second, post touches a third, and the inner archive writes a single marker entry under the root of the filesystem. Nothing is deleted, encrypted or modified beyond those markers. Title: PHP2Shell - Critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): detection, analysis, and remediation
Context: What happened On October 21, 2026, PHP released security updates for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619
Full Text:
Key points and observations

PHP disclosed two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. We independently reproduced them and confirmed that application-level authentication can't block an attack: PHP processes the malicious request before any application code runs.

AWS reported PHP2Shell exploitation attempts in the wild as early as October 17, 2026, four days before public disclosure and the release of patches.

Only patching fixes these vulnerabilities. Mitigations circulating in the community, such as setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in the PHP configuration file, don't fully protect you.

Successful command execution doesn’t necessarily crash the worker. Memory disclosure, including the PHPSESSID technique, can provide addresses needed for exploitation.

To investigate, look for large form submissions, memory-exhaustion errors during request initialization, and unexpected shell processes.

Controls at a reverse proxy or another boundary in front of PHP can block requests before they reach the vulnerable parser.

What happened

On October 21, 2026, PHP released security updates for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both have a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2. PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12 contain the fixes. Older PHP branches are also affected. Although PHP 8.1 and earlier are outside normal upstream support, the PHP security team provided source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Users of older branches should check their vendor’s security advisory for patched packages or upgrade to a supported version.

Before the public disclosure, our team built exploits for the vulnerabilities so we could analyze them and develop detections. Our reproduction triggers the out-of-memory corruption described in CVE-2026-109618 on PHP 8.5.11 with an unauthenticated HTTP POST request. The request never reaches the target application's code. Instead, PHP runs the attacker's command while it cleans up the failed request. Any PHP script exposes the vulnerable path, even one that only prints a response.

The two flaws affect different stages of the request life cycle:

CVE-2026-109618: After a memory allocation fails, PHP leaves invalid data behind for its cleanup routine to process.

CVE-2026-109619: A PHP worker can reuse stale state from a previous request.

Our detailed walkthrough primarily covers CVE-2026-109618, although we will discuss CVE-2026-109619 as well.

How to know if you're affected

Any PHP runtime that serves HTTP requests is in scope. PHP's release announcement warns that all web deployments are affected, including Apache modules, PHP FastCGI Process Manager (PHP-FPM), php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed.

When you build your inventory, include containers and applications that bundle their own PHP interpreter. Don't rely solely on the command-line PHP installation: it can use a different version or configuration than the runtime that serves your web application.

Fixed versions

The advisories for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 list the same fixed versions for each supported branch:

PHP branch

Affected releases

Remediation steps

For each deployment:

Record the PHP version, the package or image source, the owner, and the update process.

Apply the upstream or distributor update. If you use a vendor package, check the vendor's advisory, because vendors sometimes backport fixes without changing the upstream version number.

Rebuild and redeploy affected container images.

Restart or replace every worker that still runs the old runtime.

PHP 8.1 and older

PHP 8.1 and older are outside the PHP project's normal support window. To address this vulnerability, PHP published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, but expect slower fixes for these branches as vendors have more work to do in order to validate the fix. If you run those older branches, check whether your vendor covers it or move to a supported PHP branch.

If you can't patch immediately

Restrict public access to exposed applications. Where immediate remediation isn't possible, CERT-EU recommends isolating internet-facing applications. Controls at a reverse proxy or another boundary in front of PHP can block requests before they reach the vulnerable parser.

PHP's temporary mitigation guidance also describes measures for each vulnerability:

CVE-2026-109618: Enforce memory_limit=-1 at the administrator level, and pair it with request limits at the frontend and memory limits on the container. Limit the size of decoded request bodies, including requests without a usable Content-Length header. Don't substitute process limits such as RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, because they can trigger the allocation failures this vulnerability depends on. Even with these measures, allocation failures can still happen, and an attacker who exhausts system memory can destabilize the host.

CVE-2026-109619: Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and, on PHP 8.5, fatal_error_backtraces=0. Apply both settings in configuration that loads before PHP parses the request, then restart every worker. Remove any per-request settings that generate early diagnostics. Hiding the errors doesn't prevent access to stale state.

These measures reduce your exposure while you update, but none of them fully fixes the vulnerabilities. Patching is the only complete fix.

How the vulnerabilities work

Both vulnerabilities follow the same pattern: a fatal error interrupts PHP partway through an operation, and PHP later treats the incomplete state as valid.

CVE-2026-109618: Interrupted initialization after memory exhaustion

PHP converts form submissions into the $_POST array. Internally, PHP stores the array's keys and values in a hash table, in entries called buckets. Before application code reads a submitted field, PHP allocates memory for the field name, creates any nested arrays, and inserts the values into those hash tables.

The flaw appears when an insertion stops halfway through. In the version we tested, _zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i() increments the hash table's entry counters before it allocates a copy of the new key. Here is the relevant sequence in PHP's source:

idx = ht->nNumUsed++; ht->nNumOfElements++; p = ht->arData + idx; p->key = key = zend_string_init(str, len, GC_FLAGS(ht) & IS_ARRAY_PERSISTENT);

If the key allocation exceeds memory_limit, PHP raises a fatal error and abandons the insertion. At that point, the counters already include the new bucket, but PHP never initialized the bucket's key or value.

PHP still cleans up the failed request. When it destroys the array, it visits every counted bucket and interprets its contents as PHP values. The unfinished bucket holds bytes left over from an earlier allocation. An attacker who controls those leftover bytes controls what the cleanup code does next, up to running a shell command.

This hash table bug is one instance of the broader flaw that PHP's CVE-2026-109618 advisory describes: a memory error abandons an operation while the internal state is incomplete, and cleanup then treats that state as valid. Multiple public PoCs have demonstrated other code paths with the same flaw, so don't build defenses around the specifics of the hash table exploit.

CVE-2026-109619: Stale state crosses request boundaries

A PHP worker handles many requests over its lifetime. Some worker-wide fields point to memory that belongs to a single request. If PHP frees that memory without clearing the fields, a later request can follow a stale pointer into freed memory. This class of bug is called a use-after-free.

According to the PHP advisory, stale state appears in two ways: a fatal error interrupts PHP while it resets state, or a late shutdown diagnostic recreates state after cleanup. The advisory confirms two exploitable cases:

Fatal-error backtraces (PHP 8.5 only): Fatal-error reporting keeps backtrace state after shutdown. A configuration diagnostic in a later request reads that state before PHP initializes it. PHP confirmed that this case leads to command execution on mod_php.

Upload processing: After a fatal error, upload processing can leave session or decoder state behind. A later upload reads that state before normal initialization. PHP confirmed command execution on both mod_php and PHP-FPM. On PHP-FPM, the attack also needs the application to perform a suitable operation after startup succeeds.

The upload case matters because of session upload progress, which tracks uploads before the target script runs. PHP enables this feature by default, and it runs even if the application never calls session_start().

To exploit CVE-2026-109619, an attacker's requests must reach the same worker. A larger worker pool lowers the success rate of each attempt, but it doesn't remove the flaw.

Exploitation walkthrough for CVE-2026-109618

Our reproduction runs PHP 8.5.11, built from commit 678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8, on Debian 12 (ARM64). It uses Apache's prefork worker model with mod_php, and sets memory_limit=16M, post_max_size=64M, and automatic POST parsing. To make allocations and failures easier to observe, our lab runs a single worker, disables OPcache, and shows errors in responses. The exploit ends by calling glibc's system().

The exploit works in three stages: reach the interrupted insertion, fill the unfinished bucket with controlled data, and turn request cleanup into a system() call.

Stage 1: Reach the interrupted insertion

The request carries three form fields:

=<binary value>&a=1&<very long field name>[x]=1

Each field plays a role:

The empty-name field prepares memory for reuse.

The a=1 field makes PHP allocate hash table storage.

The oversized name field triggers the incomplete insertion.

The array syntax tells PHP to create a nested array. In the version we tested, that path reaches a string-key insertion helper that allocates the key after it updates the hash table's counters. A plain field name takes a different path that uses an already-created key that is not vulnerable.

PHP's filter extension registers the submitted variable in an internal array and then in $_POST. We size the field name so that PHP's first key allocation succeeds and the second exceeds memory_limit. The failed insertion leaves an incomplete bucket in $_POST, which PHP destroys during request shutdown.

The failure happens during request initialization. Nothing in the target script can impact or defend against the exploit (authentication, filtering…).

Stage 2: Fill the unfinished bucket with controlled data

The attacker needs the unfinished bucket to hold useful bytes, not random leftovers. Our reproduction arranges those bytes through heap grooming: a sequence of allocations and frees that steers PHP into reusing a chosen block of memory.

In this build, a small hash table uses a 320-byte allocation. The binary value in the empty-name field is 276 bytes, and once PHP adds a string header and terminator, its allocation lands in the same 320-byte size class.

PHP copies that value while it processes the field, then frees the copies because the field name is empty. The a=1 field that follows makes the hash tables reuse the freed memory, so most of the binary content survives past the first valid bucket. When the oversized field triggers the fatal error, PHP has counted the second bucket but not initialized it, so PHP reads its contents from the stale bytes the attacker planted. The payload shapes those bytes to resemble a PHP value that points to a fake array.

Stage 3: Turn array cleanup into a function call

PHP arrays hold a destructor callback, the function PHP calls to clean up each element when it deletes the array. The attacker sets the expected location of this callback to the address of system() and points the array's element at a command string.

During shutdown, PHP follows the stale value into the fake array and calls the supplied callback with the supplied element. In our lab, the call becomes system(<command>). The attacker controls the callback address and its pointer argument, allowing the cleanup routine to call system() with a command string.

Here is the full sequence:

Request initialization fails → Request shutdown destroys $_POST → PHP interprets the unfinished bucket as an array → PHP destroys the fake array → The destructor callback invokes system(command)

Our system-call trace records a shell running the command, and the process tree shows its children under an Apache worker. The command runs with the worker's privileges, which are www-data in our lab.

Our refined exploit returns HTTP 200 with the memory-exhaustion error in the response body, and finishes in 3.10 seconds. Process snapshots show the same Apache worker still running during and after the command. A successful HTTP status doesn't mean a request was harmless, and the exploit doesn't need to crash a worker. The process trace is stronger evidence of execution than the response delay alone.

Exploit requirements and limitations

An attacker faces two main constraints: they must size a request to fail allocation at the right moment, and they must defeat ASLR to find valid memory addresses. Neither constraint prevents exploitation, and reports of active attacks are already circulating.

Request and memory limits

The exploit needs one field name small enough to fit inside the accepted request body but large enough that copying its key exceeds memory_limit. When PHP parses a form-field name, it makes several copies along the way. The attacker uses that extra memory to force an allocation failure while PHP copies the name into a hash table.

PHP's default memory limits are vulnerable. Setting memory_limit=-1 blocks the known exploitation path, but don't treat it as a long-term fix: if the underlying allocation still fails, an attacker may still reach remote code execution.

Address discovery is a separate requirement

To turn the cleanup bug into command execution, the attacker needs valid memory addresses for the fake data structures and for the function they want to call, such as system(). Address space layout randomization (ASLR) randomizes those addresses, so guessing them can take repeated requests and crash workers.

A memory leak removes much of that guesswork. Wiz describes using the PHPSESSID cookie to leak process memory back to the attacker. If the leaked bytes include pointers that stay valid in the target worker, the attacker can use them to make the exploit more reliable.

Public reports of exploitation

As of October 21, we have multiple reports of active exploitation in the wild. We’re also aware of broad untargeted scanning going on.

How the patch addresses both flaws

The PHP security patch changes how memory exhaustion interrupts execution. A soft limit now defers the error until PHP reaches a safe point, which lets an in-progress operation finish initializing its data. If memory use crosses a higher hard limit, PHP terminates the worker at once with _exit(137) instead of running normal cleanup over a potentially invalid state.

The patch also resets request-owned global state before anything can reuse it. During shutdown, PHP clears error and exception state, and it initializes serialization and session state before early request processing can reach it.

The hash-table insertion still updates its counters before it allocates the key, even in PHP 8.5.12. The fix changes the surrounding error handling instead, so an allocation failure no longer leaves the halfway-initialized entry for ordinary cleanup to process.

The fix looks complete for the known exploit, but we consider the underlying pattern risky. Updating metadata before allocating the memory it describes leaves the door open to similar bugs. If an attacker finds another way to interrupt initialization so that the surrounding metadata still counts unallocated memory as valid (for example, an array that records a size of 2 when an allocation failure leaves only one item), the same class of flaw can return.

The patch suggests the PHP team knows about the pattern but judged the refactor to remove it too large to finish before the fix shipped. We expect more of these bugs to surface as researchers find exploitable instances of the pattern, and backporting each one may not stay sustainable. It’s also likely that instances of this pattern unique to older versions of PHP will be found and left unpatched.

How to detect exploitation

Look for signals at three layers: the incoming HTTP request, the PHP error log, and the processes that web workers spawn. No single signal is conclusive on its own, so correlate them. A successful exploit doesn't necessarily crash the worker or return an error.

Suspicious form submissions

While there are a number of ways to trigger the vulnerability, each of them relies on delivering attacker-controlled data through PHP's request parser, which runs before the target script. For detection, look for unusual field names, encodings, and transport behavior alongside request size. Start from what your application's legitimate submissions contain and flag departures from that baseline.

Based on an analysis of multiple public PoCs, the majority begin with a similar multipart form upload. An abbreviated request looks like this:

POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----XYZ ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" aabb00cc ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" pwn ------XYZ Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="a.txt" Content-Type: application/octet-stream ------XYZ ...hundreds more parts, or one multi-megabyte fill field... ------XYZ--

These field names are useful indicators when an application doesn't normally use them. They can also appear in legitimate submissions: PHP documents the upload-progress field in browser forms, and its transparent session handling can add session identifiers to forms. Investigate unexpected use of these fields, especially alongside the structural anomalies below.

The requests create memory pressure in different ways. Some public tools append fill fields of 100 MB or more. Others use deeply nested, machine-generated names, such as files[R00001][a][a][a], repeated across hundreds of parts. Public examples fit roughly 900 parts into less than 1 MB. PHP's allocations while parsing these fields can greatly exceed the size of the body on the wire, so body size alone is a weak signal. Also monitor parts per request, brackets per field name, and nesting depth.

Inspect upload filenames for PHP tags or serialized-object fragments, such as <?php or |O:. These chains can stage payloads in filenames because PHP stores the filename in the session record.

Another path to the vulnerable function can be reached through large application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST requests whose body carries a single field name of many megabytes (3-60 MB, depending on the memory_limit of the target), along with a binary value containing raw null bytes and control characters.

Two other traffic patterns can support these chains. Uploads that declare a large Content-Length and then trickle or never finish can keep a session record alive for the exploit. On deployments with multiple workers, a burst of connections that become slow or silent while other requests proceed normally can indicate an attempt to occupy every worker but one. This helps an attacker send both requests in a state-reuse chain to the same process.

Also inspect response headers. A Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID= header containing an unusually long, percent-encoded value or binary content outside the application's expected session-ID format can indicate the memory-disclosure stage returning heap contents. It can follow an otherwise unremarkable request. Compare the value against the application's normal format: valid PHP session IDs aren't limited to hexadecimal characters.

Configure your web application firewall (WAF) or reverse proxy around these behaviors, and verify what its inspection engine actually sees. A rule can't inspect bytes the engine truncates, fields its parser discards, parts it never enumerates, or bodies it handles differently because they arrived chunked.

Memory exhaustion errors

Our exploit attempt generated this fatal error in the PHP error log:

PHP Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 16777216 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 3500032 bytes) in Unknown on line 0

The Unknown on line 0 location means PHP failed during request initialization, before any script started running. Correlate these errors with oversized POST requests, upstream connection resets, and worker crashes. Memory exhaustion alone doesn't prove an attack, because legitimate workloads can also exhaust memory.

When the exploit guesses a memory address incorrectly, the Apache worker crashes with a segmentation fault. In our lab, the Apache error log recorded this message:

AH00052: child pid ... exit signal Segmentation fault (11)

Also treat a short burst of these errors as a possible setup event, prior to the actual exploit payload being sent. Because modern versions of these chains recover addresses without crashing workers and can leave a persistent include active after a single successful fire, a complete attack can produce as few as two to four memory exhaustion errors and then go quiet. A handful of these errors on one PHP worker in a short window (especially paired with any of the request indicators above) deserves investigation even if nothing crashes afterward.

Unexpected shell processes

A web worker that spawns a shell is the most direct evidence of successful exploitation. In our capture, an Apache worker spawned a shell, which then launched the attacker's commands:

apache2 (www-data) └── sh -c <reverse-shell command> └── bash [outbound connection to c2.example:443]

Investigate any shell that a web worker launches, especially when it coincides with the request or error log signals above. If your application runs external commands on purpose, build a baseline of expected activity so you can spot deviations.

Don't make your detection depend on our demonstration's command names, a specific HTTP status, or a worker crash. In our refined exploit, the request returns HTTP 200, and the same Apache worker keeps running after it executes the command.

Signals for CVE-2026-109619

For CVE-2026-109619, review early configuration warnings, shutdown diagnostics, fatal errors, and execution timeouts on routes that attackers can reach. These events can point to the state-retention paths that PHP's advisory describes.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Workload Protection has out-of-the-box coverage for PHP applications executing a shell. This detection will catch exploits of those vulnerabilities. You can check for suspicious activity using this query. Review uncommon or unusual command lines.

Datadog Cloud SIEM includes detections that can help identify PHP2Shell exploitation attempts and associated command execution:

Shell spawned by web server or PHP process detects shells, download utilities, and reconnaissance commands launched by web servers or PHP processes using process activity events with parent process information.

Shell spawned by web process uses Linux auditd logs to detect shells or download utilities executed in a web server context.

PHP2Shell PHP-FPM session memory exhaustion with session decode failure or FPM worker segfault on the same host and service uses PHP error logs and PHP-FPM master logs to correlate memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or PHP-FPM worker segmentation faults on the same host and service.

PHP2Shell memory exhaustion with worker crash or session decode failure on an Apache host uses Apache and PHP error logs to correlate memory exhaustion before any script runs with session subsystem errors, session decode failures, or worker crashes on the same host.

Datadog Cloud Vulnerability Management can help identify PHP vulnerability findings on supported hosts and container images. Its package scanning support covers official operating system packages; self-compiled runtimes such as our lab build need separate inventory checks. PHP application dependencies managed through Composer are also distinct from the interpreter itself.

Conclusion

Both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities that can lead to remote code execution in default PHP configurations. If you run PHP, update to a fixed release or your vendor’s patched package as soon as possible. Rebuild affected container images and restart or replace workers so they’re running the updated code. Configuration changes can block some attack paths, but patching is the only complete fix.

Title: LiteLLM supply chain compromise: What you need to know
Context: 0, latest, main-latest, main-stable What happened According to LiteLLM’s analysis of the incident, attackers used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three engineers' accounts...
Full Text:
On October 21, 2026, attackers published a malicious release of litellm, a popular Python proxy library for LLM providers with about 23 million weekly downloads. The malicious release, version 1.107.0, was available on PyPI and in LiteLLM's official Docker images for approximately two hours before being removed. It installed a credential stealer that runs whenever Python starts and also contained a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT) backdoor. The infostealer payload targets cloud, developer, AI-tool, browser and LiteLLM proxy credentials.

This marks the second supply chain compromise of LiteLLM in 2026, with the earlier incident (affecting versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8) being linked to TeamPCP activity by Datadog Security Research. No connection between the two compromises has been established at time of writing.

What happened

According to LiteLLM’s analysis of the incident, attackers used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three engineers' accounts to launch LiteLLM’s private release workflow. At time of writing, it was not yet clear how the affected credentials were initially compromised.

The three stolen credentials were used to launch, approve and subsequently delete evidence of an unauthorized run of the legitimate build pipeline against a malicious fork, Berri-AI/litellm, whose name differs from the legitimate BerriAI/litellm fork by one hyphen. The similarity of the malicious fork’s name to the real project seems intended to evade casual detection by a human reviewer. The resulting wheels and images were published through LiteLLM's normal release channels and with seemingly legitimate build provenance that faithfully recorded the malicious fork as the source.

Payload analysis

The release adds three files to the victim Python installation’s site-packages directory:

cook.pth

cook.py

sitecustomize.py

Python runs .pth files and sitecustomize.py automatically every time the interpreter starts. Any Python process in the environment runs the malware, even if LiteLLM is never imported.

Credential stealer (cook.py): Collects secrets and sends them, encrypted with AES-256 and RSA-4096, to the lookalike domain www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck.

Backdoor (sitecustomize.py): Every hour, checks a certain file hosted on a fixed GitHub repository (letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt, now removed) for a domain, then downloads and runs Python code from it. That file only ever held test values, so no second stage payload was observed in the wild.

Deleting the litellm package directory does not remove these files. Running the environment's own python or pip triggers the malware again. Instead, the dropped payload files must be manually removed.

Data exfiltration

Cloud: AWS, GCP and Azure credentials, including from instance metadata; Kubernetes, Docker, Vault and Terraform secrets

Developer: SSH, GPG and TLS keys, Git, npm and PyPI tokens, .env files, shell history

AI: LLM provider API keys, and sessions for Claude, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot and other AI coding tools

Browsers: saved passwords and cookies

LiteLLM proxy: If a database is configured, it queries the tables where the proxy stores upstream provider credentials.

What to do if you are affected

Manually remove the malicious cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py from the site-packages directory.

Remove all code and data associated with the malicious litellm==1.107.0 release.

Revert to litellm==1.106.2, the latest safe version of the package.

From a clean machine, immediately rotate all affected credentials.

Audit relevant logs for use of exposed credentials during the exposure window.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Code Security customers can rely on the Security Research Feed to easily identify if your environment is affected by this compromise. Use Code Security to easily identify affected hosts, containers or build environments.

Final thoughts

In this case, stolen developer tokens were used to point a trusted release pipeline at the wrong source. In order to ensure the validity of build provenance, it is essential to put in place adequate controls on which branches are eligible for building. Maintainers should lock release workflows to approved repositories and treat developer CLI tokens as the high-value secrets that they are.

Title: Cloudy with a chance of outages.
Context: Bank of America hires an army to patch AI-discovered flaws. The research demonstrates why behavioral detection can remain effective even when malware continually changes its appearance.
Full Text:
A Google Cloud outage disrupts UK banks. DHS bans DeepSeek. Shape-shifting ransomware targets Macs. Bank of America hires an army to patch AI-discovered flaws. Canada looks to bypass the U.S. with a transatlantic cable. A contractor breach exposes California student data. Cybersecurity hiring slumps, but AI skills are booming. Researchers expose the Silent Ransom Group’s playbook. A suspected Qilin ransomware operator takes a vacation straight into custody. Our guest is Roman Arutyunov, Co-Founder of Xage Security, discussing the next era of Zero Trust. A hotel phishing scheme gets a chilly reception.

Today is Tuesday October 20th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A Google Cloud outage disrupts UK banking.

A disruption at Google Cloud’s London data center Tuesday knocked several banks and other services offline, highlighting the growing dependence on a handful of cloud providers. Digital bank Revolut reported widespread outages affecting card payments, ATM withdrawals, and other services, though it said customer funds and data remained safe. ING Germany and Halifax Bank also reported online banking problems. Outage reports extended to other financial institutions, delivery services, and Britain’s National Health Service, though their connection to Google’s disruption wasn’t confirmed. Google said engineers were investigating the problem at its europe-west2 facility. The incident comes amid heightened regulatory scrutiny of cloud providers. Both British and European regulators have designated Google Cloud a critical third-party supplier to the financial sector, reflecting concerns about the systemic risks of shared infrastructure.

DHS bans DeepSeek AI products.

The Department of Homeland Security is ordering U.S. civilian federal agencies to remove DeepSeek AI products and third-party services built using the Chinese company’s models from government systems. Agencies are also prohibited from acquiring them. DHS warns that DeepSeek could expose sensitive government information to China, potentially provide intelligence on U.S. citizens and federal agencies, and introduce malware or security vulnerabilities. The department previously instructed agencies to monitor government website traffic for potential DeepSeek-related threats. Several federal agencies and states have already banned the technology. The move is part of the Trump administration’s broader crackdown on Chinese technology, including restrictions on drones, consumer routers, and telecommunications equipment. The FCC is also preparing to vote on banning Chinese laboratories from testing electronics destined for the U.S. market.

Metamorphic ransomware targets macOS.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle has uncovered Heartbreaker, an unusual macOS ransomware sample that attempts to rewrite and rebuild itself to evade detection. Written in Rust, Heartbreaker carries its own source code, allowing it to generate modified versions of itself with different file hashes while preserving its malicious behavior. The malware encrypts files in a victim’s Downloads folder, establishes persistence, and demands a Bitcoin ransom. Fortunately, its developers made a critical mistake: a hard-coded encryption key allows victims to recover their files without paying. Wardle also tested Heartbreaker against his open-source RansomWhere? tool, which successfully detected and suspended the malware by monitoring suspicious file encryption activity. The research demonstrates why behavioral detection can remain effective even when malware continually changes its appearance.

Bank of America throws people at an AI problem.

Bank of America has brought in 1,000 outside contractors to help patch software vulnerabilities that advanced AI models, including Anthropic’s Mythos, can uncover and exploit. CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC the contractors are working alongside 3,000 existing personnel to strengthen the bank’s internal systems and vendor software. The effort began earlier this year as increasingly capable AI models raised concerns about previously undiscovered security flaws. Moynihan said the bank spent more than $200 million in the third quarter on software remediation and anti-money laundering compliance issues, though he expects those costs to decline. Meanwhile, AI is delivering savings elsewhere. Bank of America has roughly 130 internal AI projects and expects annual savings from those initiatives to grow from $300 million this year to $700 million by 2027.

A proposed undersea cable could boost digital sovereignty.

A Norwegian infrastructure company wants to build a transatlantic undersea cable connecting Canada directly to Europe, bypassing the United States. Dubbed Project Leif Erikson, the proposed 2,800-mile cable would run from Norway to Newfoundland and Labrador, then continue overland to Montreal. Developer Bulk Infrastructure says the project would strengthen Canada’s digital sovereignty and reduce its dependence on American infrastructure, an increasingly attractive proposition amid strained relations between Washington and Ottawa. The cable would support AI, telecommunications, and cloud computing, but significant hurdles remain. Bulk needs a majority investment partner, regulatory approvals, and additional financing for the project, estimated to cost more than $620 million. First proposed five years ago, the cable is gaining renewed interest as geopolitical tensions reshape digital infrastructure priorities.

A contractor data breach exposes personal information of California public school students.

Personal information belonging to current and former California public school students has been stolen from Educational Testing Service, a contractor that administers state testing programs. According to California’s Department of Education, attackers used compromised credentials to access a file transfer system between May and September, copying student records. The exposed information includes names, addresses, birth dates, demographic details, and potentially sensitive disability and testing records. The breach affects students enrolled during the previous three school years and potentially some who left California schools as far back as 2006. No victim count has been disclosed, though California currently enrolls more than 5.7 million public school students. ETS says there’s no evidence the stolen information has been published. Affected students are being offered two years of identity protection.

The cyber job market stalls, except for AI.

The U.S. cybersecurity job market has hit a four-year low, according to a new report from CyberSN. Job postings fell 26 percent during the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, dropping to roughly 236,000. But demand for certain AI-related skills is booming. Openings for AI Security Engineers surged 268 percent, while Cyber Data Scientist postings jumped 204 percent. By September, one in five cybersecurity job listings mentioned AI. Meanwhile, demand for traditional roles declined sharply, with postings for insider threat analysts, penetration testers, threat hunters, and cybersecurity risk analysts all falling substantially. CISO openings dropped nearly 39 percent, although they’re roughly level with 2024. The report tracks hiring demand, but doesn’t establish what’s driving these changes.

Researchers unpack the Silent Ransom Group.

New research from Guide Point Security into the Silent Ransom Group reveals a cybercrime operation that relies less on malware than on social engineering and physical intrusion. The group allegedly recruits U.S.-based accomplices to impersonate IT personnel, infiltrate offices, and steal sensitive data using USB drives and legitimate remote-access software. Its targets include major law firms, whose executives receive direct calls demanding payment. Internal communications document increasingly aggressive plans involving coercion, kidnapping, and armed intimidation, though researchers found no evidence those schemes were carried out. The criminals’ own records claim nearly $207 million in ransom payments from 27 organizations in 2026, but those figures remain unverified. Researchers say the findings highlight the importance of verifying IT requests, restricting remote-access tools, and enforcing physical security procedures.

A suspected Qilin ransomware member is arrested while on holiday.

German police have arrested a 28-year-old Russian man suspected of being a key member of the Qilin ransomware gang. Identified as Vladimir K, the suspect was detained in Japan in May and subsequently extradited to Germany. Investigators initially linked him to a 2024 ransomware attack against a German logistics company, but are now examining his possible involvement in the devastating attack on London pathology provider Synnovis. That incident disrupted blood-testing services across several hospitals, forcing cancellations of operations and appointments. An NHS investigation subsequently determined that delayed blood test results contributed to a patient’s death. British police are reportedly considering whether unlawful killing charges might be appropriate. Qilin has operated since at least 2022, reportedly targeting thousands of organizations and extorting more than $140 million.

Today on Industry Voices, we’re exploring why the next era of Zero Trust is about actions, not just access with Roman Arutyunov. And a hotel phishing scheme gets a chilly reception. Stick with us after the break for more.

We’re joined by Roman Arutyunov, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer at Xage Security, to discuss how Zero Trust is evolving beyond access control. Here’s our conversation.

If you enjoyed our conversation with Roman Arutyunov, check out the full interview. You can find the link in the show notes.

A hotel phishing scheme gets a chilly reception.

Japanese police have arrested a Chinese couple accused of turning a Kobe hotel room into an unlikely phishing headquarters. Investigators say 39-year-old Ye Jiafeng and an accomplice entered the hotel posing as guests, hid a small computer behind the refrigerator, connected it to the hotel’s Wi-Fi, and departed. The device allegedly sent some 480,000 phishing emails impersonating credit card companies. The operation unraveled when a suspicious recipient traced the messages to the hotel, where staff discovered the hardware. Apparently, the minibar wasn’t the only thing running up a tab.

Ye and his wife, Shen Qi, also face allegations involving fraudulent credit card purchases. Police recovered 74 smartphones from their home and are investigating transactions potentially totaling 10 million yen. Investigators believe others may have remotely operated the phishing computer, demonstrating that sometimes exploiting a network requires little more than a room key and a conveniently placed refrigerator.

Title: Head of AI Security Roles Surge in Large Organizations
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A head of AI security role has been established in 65% of large organizations with an annual revenue of $10bn plus, according to new data.

The research, conducted by IANS and Artico Search, found that large businesses are taking steps to update their security organizational structure to enhance accountability and board level oversight for enterprise AI governance.

Around a fifth (18%) of all $10bn+ firms have made the head of AI security a dedicated position, while 47% combined it with another leadership role, making it “one of the fastest emerging functional roles,” according to the researchers.

Head of AI security was observed to be less common in medium and small companies, with the position established in 9% of organizations with a revenue of $1-$10bn, and 6% in firms with under $1bn in revenue.

Steve Martano, IANS Faculty and partner at Artico Search’s cyber practice, commented: “The growth of AI is creating a premium for leaders who can bridge technical security, risk and compliance while still understanding how the business wants to use the technology.”

AI Governance Rarely Falls Under the CISO Remit

The IANS report, published on October 20, found that despite the growth of dedicated head of AI security roles in large organizations, overall accountability for enterprise AI governance remains unsettled.

CISOs hold primary accountability in 26% of small businesses, in 11% of medium firms and just 7% of large organizations. The position that most often is held accountable for AI governance in large businesses are chief AI officers, at 22%.

Read now: AI Agent Adoption Creates Risk as Oversight Struggles to Keep Pace, Splunk Finds

Across all three tiers, 14-19% of organizations reported that no single executive is accountable.

In addition, most organizations have not yet fully implemented a board committee dedicated to AI ethics or responsible AI, with 43-48% across all three tiers stating that they have no such committee planned.

Martano said organizations must restructure security teams to ensure that their governance strategies keep pace with rapid AI adoption.

“Companies need to strategically think about what they need from the function and whether they can develop that expertise internally before going to an increasingly competitive external market,” he noted.

Experience the Biggest Dictator of Security Pros’ Pay

The report assessed experience level as the single biggest driver of compensation differences in the same role – more significant than factors such as company size and geographic location.

In $10bn+ businesses, security professionals with eight to 15 years’ experience earn about $35,000 more than those with fewer than eight years’ experience.

The gap grows to around $50,000 between early-career staff and professionals with more than 16 years’ experience.

In large businesses, the average salary for Deputy CISOs was $350,000 per annum.

BISOs earnt a similar amount on average, at $342,000.

Data around average compensation levels for CISOs was not included in the report.

Full Text:
The Pillar Security team reported the vulnerability privately via GitHub Security Advisory with full reproduction material at the end of August 2026.

A month later, Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, confirmed it had received the report, but said malicious MCP servers are “outside their threat model.”

Pillar Security researchers said Anomaly patched the vulnerability on September 28 in version 1.18.33 – without a CVE or security advisory. “As a result, conventional vulnerability scanners and dependency alerts will not identify affected installations, potentially leaving enterprises unaware that they need to upgrade,” Pillar Security researchers warned.

URL Validation Falls Short of Preventing OpenCode RCE Attacks

Pillar Security researchers claimed that the standard fix isn’t enough to fully remediate this vulnerability, which they assessed should be allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.8.

According to the researchers, URL scheme validation alone cannot prevent the attack because the malicious payload can be embedded in a seemingly legitimate HTTPS URL.

On Windows, the vulnerable open dependency passed the URL to PowerShell without properly escaping it, allowing the shell to interpret part of the URL as a command.

Although OpenCode added URL scheme checks in version 1.18.33, the researchers said the crucial fix was to update the dependency to a version that correctly quotes the URL, preventing PowerShell from interpreting the payload as executable code.

They recommend that developers avoid passing untrusted URLs through shell commands altogether, instead using argument-based process execution to reduce the risk of command injection.

OpenCode RCE Flaw Unrelated to Recent Console Security Breach

This vulnerability report comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Pillar Security’s Cohen stressed that this newly disclosed vulnerability was not related to the Console breach.

“The breach hit a legacy system behind a hosted key proxy, and exposed provider keys users had stored there. The vulnerability we reported runs the other way: a malicious remote MCP server executing code on a developer's own machine during the OAuth handshake. Different target and attacker position,” he explained.

Nevertheless, Cohen highlighted that both incidents come down to the same thing, “Who you let hand credentials and inputs to an AI coding tool, and what that tool does with them.”

Title: Introducing a new AI chapter in the NCSC research problem book
Context: Concepts such as vulnerability management, incident response and risk management will need to evolve to account for both AI-enabled systems and AI-enabled attackers
Full Text:
The latest frontier AI capabilities are re-writing what is possible for both cyber attackers and defenders, with recent publications from the NCSC highlighting the opportunities and risks presented by AI.

The Five Eyes cyber security agencies have warned that AI is accelerating the pace and scale of cyber threats, while the NCSC’s Cyber Shield initiative sets out an ambitious vision for harnessing AI to strengthen cyber defence.

Turning this vision into reality will require more than advances in AI capability alone; it will require answers to difficult questions around system design, assurance, security and trust.

To help focus innovation across this new AI-enabled world, we’ve re-written our NCSC research problem book to include an entirely new chapter 'AI in cyber security problems’.

For years, AI and machine learning have helped defenders analyse data, identify threats and automate routine tasks. The new generation of AI systems (particularly generative AI and agentic AI) can plan, reason, use tools, and take actions with increasing autonomy. This is game-changing, making some things much easier to automate but in the process, creating new problems to overcome.

Many of the assumptions that underpin today’s cyber security best practice were developed before this kind of AI existed. Concepts such as vulnerability management, incident response and risk management will need to evolve to account for both AI-enabled systems and AI-enabled attackers. This evolution may require a re-design of processes from the ground up to fully leverage the potential benefits to defenders.

Our new problem book chapter on ‘AI in cyber security’ identifies seven areas spanning three broad themes:

the use of AI to strengthen cyber defence

the security and assurance of AI systems themselves

the use of data-driven methods to improve cyber resilience at scale

A common thread runs throughout them all: human-AI collaboration. As AI systems become more capable, we need to understand where autonomy can provide genuine value, where human judgement remains essential, and how meaningful oversight can be maintained without losing the benefits of machine-speed operations.

AI has the potential to fundamentally reshape cyber security. Whether that future is secure, resilient and trustworthy will depend on the choices we make today and the research we undertake tomorrow. The new problem book should focus attention on some of the most important challenges ahead.

Addressing these challenges will require a collective effort across the cyber security and AI communities. We welcome feedback on the challenges identified in the problem book, suggestions for additional research questions, and examples of ongoing or planned research that could help address them. Insights from across academia, industry and government will help ensure that future cyber security approaches remain effective, resilient and trustworthy in an AI-enabled world.

If you would like to contribute to the discussion, please complete our feedback form.

Paul J, Technical Director for Cyber AI Research, NCSC

Brad A, Principal Data Science & AI Researcher, Industry 100 Secondee & Alan Turing Institute Visiting Collaborator

Title: Siemens Customers Targeted by ClickFix Attackers Exploiting DLL Side-Loading Flaw
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Siemens has warned customers that attackers are actively exploiting a dynamic link library (DLL) side-loading vulnerability in its Software Center to distribute malware.

The company has attributed the activity to the Romulus multi-platform ClickFix campaign.

Romulus is a server hosting panel that was identified by Forescout researchers on October 14. The panel allows cybercriminals to deploy ClickFix tactics into an entire ecosystem which can be repeatedly used to deliver multiple forms of malware to victims.

ClickFix is a popular attack technique among cybercriminals. It relies on social engineering to trick the victim into running attacker-supplied commands on their own machine.

The Siemens blog, published on October 19, detailed how attackers are targeting CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS 8.4) to load malicious DLL files into a directory that the Siemens Software Center searches for. They use a genuine copy of the application with a valid signature and place their own files next to it.

The attackers then attempt to distribute these files to customers by using a ClickFix lure.

Version 3.5.8.7 of Software Center loaded helper files from its own folder without checking them, the firm admitted.

If a user follows the ClickFix commands, malicious code will execute on the device with the privileges of the affected application.

“Never paste a command from a web page into Win+R, the Run box or PowerShell. A real ‘I am not a robot’ check never asks for this,” Siemens wrote.

How to Defend Against the Romulus Campaign

Siemens urged Software Center customers update to version 4.0.9.8, which contains a fix for the flaw. Existing installations update automatically the next time they start.

Customers should also look out for the following indications that their PC is affected by the campaign:

"Siemens Software Center" in the start-up apps or Task Scheduler of a PC that never had it installed

A folder called SM Software Provisioning Service inside AppData\Local\Programs is created by the malware

Files named activate.bak or statinfosta.DB next to SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe

A folder called FTSuite containing a file ftc.uml inside AppData\Local

Network connections to 96.62.218[.]59

If a PC has been found to be compromised, customers should isolate the device, stop the process first, then remove the start-up entry and task and reset passwords.

Siemens added that detection tools should focus on the folder and suspicious behavior, not on the Siemens file fingerprint as the file itself is genuine.

Customers should also ensure that they only download Siemens software from official Siemens sources and block the active IP address and domain listed in the advisory.

Police arrest Qilin ransomware suspect on holiday, as links made to Synnovis hack that contributed to patient’s death
Context: A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed
Full Text:
A 28-year-old Russian man has been arrested by German police, suspected of being a key member of the Qilin ransomware gang. As BBC News reports, detectives have linked the man to the 2024 attack against blood-testing firm Synnovis, that disrupted London hospitals, and resulted in the death of a patient.

The suspect, who has been named by German media only as "Vladimir K" was originally detained in May in Japan, after he travelled there on holiday. According to German officials, the man's vacation plans were intercepted and Japanese police were waiting for him on arrival. Earlier this month he was extradited to Germany.

Germany's interest in "Vladimir K" is related to a cyber attack in September 2024, which saw around US $160,000 worth of cryptocurrency extorted from a logistics firm. According to the BBC, German detectives have now included in their investigation possible links to the June 2024 attack which saw the Qilin ransomware group disrupting pathology services at various London hospitals, and resulted in the cancellation of operations and outpatient appointments.

The incident is said to have crippled Synnovis’s IT systems, and caused a critical shortage of O-type blood in hospitals. A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed.

As a consequence, British police are reportedly examining whether their own inquiry could lead to a charge of unlawful killing.

No ransom was paid by Synnovis, a decision the firm made jointly with the NHS trusts to which it provides services.

Ransomware gangs have been accused of causing deaths in the past. For instance, in 2020 a different gang disrupted systems at a Düsseldorf hospital and caused a seriously-ill woman to be diverted to another health facility 30 km away.

According to reports, as a result of the attack doctors were not able to start treating the patient for an hour and she died.

The Qilin ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group has been operating since at least 2022, and has reportedly hacked more than 4000 organisations, and extorted over US $140 million. High profile victims include Japanese beer-maker Asahi, potentially exposing the data of more than 1.5 million customers and around 275,000 current and former employees and their families.

Full Text:
Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require.

This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate.

Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work.
